parameters: torchinfo 49   our count 49




Code
os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
graph = draw_graph(model, input_size=(400, 1), expand_nested=True)
png = graph.visual_graph.render("figures/lab003_sequential_graph", format="png", cleanup=True)   # Graphviz writes the PNG file
display(Image(png))





The parameters of the two Linear layers, \[32 + 17 = 49 , \tag{22}\] reproduce the count \(3N + 1\); the activation Tanh has none. Our drawing shows what a dense layer is, a set of neurons connected to all neurons of the previous layer, but it becomes unreadable for networks with thousands of neurons per layer or with layers that are not dense. The table and the graph show only layers and shapes, and they work for every model, including the convolutional networks and networks with skip connections of later lectures.

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
7. Model classes
For anything non-trivial we define a class that inherits from nn.Module. Two methods are required. __init__ creates the layers and parameters, and must always call super().__init__() first. forward(x) describes the computation; the model is then called as model(x), not model.forward(x). Parameters wrapped in nn.Parameter (and all parameters of sub-layers) are registered automatically.
Both rules have a reason. super().__init__() runs the __init__ of nn.Module, which creates the internal lists in which parameters and sub-layers are registered; assigning an nn.Parameter before this call fails with AttributeError: cannot assign parameters before Module.__init__() call. Calling model(x) runs forward together with additional bookkeeping of PyTorch (so-called hooks), which a direct call of forward would skip.
Below, the Universal Approximation Theorem (UAT) ansatz is implemented explicitly — exactly the formula from the lecture. In def __init__(self, N, activation=torch.tanh) the argument activation has a default value: it is used when the caller does not give this argument. A function such as torch.tanh can be passed and stored like any other object.
The initial values are chosen as follows. W1 and b are drawn from the standard normal distribution. Neuron \(i\) switches (its \(\tanh\) changes sign) at \[x_i^\ast = -b_i/W^{(1)}_i ; \tag{23}\] with W1 and b of order one, most of these points (about 80 %) lie in \([-3, 3]\), the range of inputs of the plots, so most neurons are not saturated there. The output bias c (\(b^{(2)}\) above) only shifts \(f\) up or down; there is no reason to start with a shift, so it starts at 0.


Code
class UATNet(nn.Module):
    """f(x) = sum_i W2_i * sigma(W1_i * x + b_i) + c   (single hidden layer, N neurons)."""

    def __init__(self, N, activation=torch.tanh):
        super().__init__()
        self.W1 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))        # input weights
        self.b = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))         # biases
        self.W2 = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N) / N**0.5)  # output weights, scaled by 1/sqrt(N) (explained below)
        self.c = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(1))         # output bias
        self.activation = activation

    def forward(self, x):                             # x: shape (B,) -> output (B,)
        hidden = self.activation(self.W1 * x[:, None] + self.b)   # (B, N) by broadcasting
        return hidden @ self.W2 + self.c

torch.manual_seed(0)
net = UATNet(N=8)
print(net)            # prints only sub-modules (layers); our parameters are listed separately:
print("parameters:", [(n, tuple(p.shape)) for n, p in net.named_parameters()])
x = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)    # shape (200,): this class takes a 1D tensor, nn.Sequential above needed shape (200, 1)
print("output shape:", net(x).shape)


UATNet()
parameters: [('W1', (8,)), ('b', (8,)), ('W2', (8,)), ('c', (1,))]
output shape: torch.Size([200])


The output weights are divided by \(\sqrt N\), and the reason is statistical. The output is a sum of \(N\) terms, \[f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} W^{(2)}_i h_i(x) + c, \qquad h_i = \tanh(\dots)\in[-1,1] . \tag{24}\] If the \(W^{(2)}_i\) are independent random numbers with mean 0 and variance \(\sigma_W^2\), the terms are uncorrelated with mean zero and their variances add: \[\mathrm{Var}\, f(x) = N\,\sigma_W^2\,\overline{h^2}, \qquad \text{standard deviation of } f \;\propto\; \sqrt{N}\,\sigma_W , \tag{25}\] where \[\overline{h^2} = \frac1N\sum_i h_i(x)^2 \le 1 \tag{26}\] is the mean squared hidden activation (the variance is taken over random \(W^{(2)}\) at fixed \(x\), with vanishing \(c\)). With unit \(\sigma_W\) an untrained network with many neurons would produce outputs that grow like \(\sqrt N\), far from the order-one values of typical targets. With \(\sigma_W\) of \(1/\sqrt N\) the variance of the output is of order one for every \(N\). The same rule, weights scaled by \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) with \(n_{\rm in}\) the number of inputs of the layer, is the basis of the standard initialisations (LeCun, Xavier/Glorot), and nn.Linear uses it by default. The first layer has a single input, so W1 is not scaled. The standard deviation of \(f\) over the inputs and 50 random initialisations is measured with and without the factor; the 50 outputs of shape (200,) are joined by torch.cat into one vector of 10 000 values, of which std() computes the sample standard deviation (normalised by the number of values minus one, which makes no difference for 10 000 values).


Code
x_test = torch.linspace(-3, 3, 200)[:, None]                   # shape (200, 1)
print("   N   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1)   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1/N)")
for n_hidden in [1, 10, 100, 1000]:
    stds = {}
    for scaled in [False, True]:
        outputs = []
        for seed in range(50):                                 # 50 random networks
            torch.manual_seed(seed)
            W1, b1 = torch.randn(n_hidden), torch.randn(n_hidden)
            W2 = torch.randn(n_hidden) / (n_hidden**0.5 if scaled else 1.0)
            outputs.append(torch.tanh(x_test * W1 + b1) @ W2)  # (200,) for this network
        stds[scaled] = torch.cat(outputs).std().item()
    print(f"{n_hidden:5d}   {stds[False]:20.2f}   {stds[True]:22.2f}")


   N   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1)   std of f, W2 ~ N(0, 1/N)
    1                   0.67                     0.67
   10                   2.77                     0.87


  100                   7.52                     0.75


 1000                  21.90                     0.69


Without the factor the standard deviation grows by roughly a factor of 3 for every tenfold increase of \(N\) (expected: \(\sqrt{10}\), about 3.2; with 50 random networks the estimate fluctuates); with the factor it stays of order one, independent of \(N\).
A model can be moved to the GPU with model.to(device), and switched to double precision with model.double().

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
8. Summary
Tensors are NumPy arrays with two additions, GPU support and automatic differentiation. Their default dtype is float32; float64 is used for precise physics. torch.from_numpy shares memory with a NumPy array while torch.tensor copies it, and .numpy(), .item() and .cpu() lead back. Among the shape operations, reshape and view change the shape while keeping the row-by-row order, transpose and permute reorder axes (producing non-contiguous views), unsqueeze and squeeze add or remove axes of length 1, cat joins along an existing axis and stack along a new one; batched products are computed with @ or einsum. The device is chosen with device = "cuda" if available else "cpu", and all tensors in one operation must be on the same device. nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) computes \(\mathbf W\mathbf z+\mathbf b\) on batches (B, n_in), nn.Sequential stacks layers, and our own models subclass nn.Module with __init__ and forward. When a network is only evaluated, the computation goes inside with torch.no_grad():.

title: Lab 003: PyTorch tensors, devices and layers
text:
9. Exercises

Exercise 1 — Ising chain energy in PyTorch
Implement the vectorised energy of a periodic Ising chain, \[E = -\sum_{i=1}^{L} s_i s_{i+1}, \qquad s_{L+1} = s_1 , \tag{27}\] in PyTorch (torch.roll, torch.sum(..., dim=1)). Generate the random spins with torch.randint(0, 2, (M, L)) * 2 - 1. Run it on 100 000 configurations with chains of 64 spins and check the mean and standard deviation of the energy (about 0 and about \(\sqrt{L}\)).

Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
M, L, J = 100_000, 64, 1.0

# torch.randint(0, 2, ...) gives 0 or 1; *2 - 1 maps them to -1 or +1.
# .float() converts integers to floats so that sums and std() work as expected.
spins = (torch.randint(0, 2, (M, L)) * 2 - 1).float()

# np.roll -> torch.roll, axis -> dims/dim (for readers who know NumPy)
E = -J * torch.sum(spins * torch.roll(spins, shifts=-1, dims=1), dim=1)

# .item() converts a one-element tensor to a Python number for printing
print(f"mean = {E.mean().item():.3f},  std = {E.std().item():.3f},  sqrt(L) = {L**0.5:.3f}")
# Why sqrt(L): with periodic boundaries the L products s_i s_{i+1} of independent random spins are pairwise independent
# (uncorrelated) numbers +-1 with mean 0 and variance 1, so their variances add: the sum has mean 0 and variance L,
# hence standard deviation sqrt(L).


mean = 0.050,  std = 7.986,  sqrt(L) = 8.000





Exercise 2 — Tensor shapes in a multilayer network
Build model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10)) — the classic network for MNIST (Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology database: 70 000 grey-scale images of handwritten digits 0–9, each of \(28\times28\) pixels) from the next lecture. 1. Feed a random batch of 32 “images” of shape (32, 28, 28). It fails; read the error message and fix the problem with reshape. 2. Print the shape of the output. What do the 10 numbers per image represent? 3. Count the parameters, on paper from \[P = \sum_l n_l(n_{l-1}+1) \tag{28}\] for layer sizes \(n_0, n_1, \dots\), and with sum(p.numel() ...). 4. The softmax \[p_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_j e^{z_j}} \tag{29}\] turns the 10 outputs \(z_k\) into probabilities. Apply torch.softmax(out, dim=1) and check that each row sums to 1.

Solution


Code
model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10))
images = torch.rand(32, 28, 28)               # 32 random 28x28 "images", values uniform in [0, 1) like pixel intensities

# 1) The first layer expects input of shape (batch, 784). A (32, 28, 28) tensor is interpreted as
#    32*28 = 896 rows of length 28, which does not match 784 -> error.
try:
    model(images)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("Error:", e)

# Fix: flatten every image into a vector of 28*28 = 784 numbers; with -1, PyTorch computes that size.
flat = images.reshape(32, -1)
print("flattened shape:", flat.shape)
out = model(flat)

# 2) One row per image, 10 numbers per row: one score (logit) per digit class 0..9
print("output shape:", out.shape)

# 3) Parameters: layer n_in -> n_out has n_out * n_in weights and n_out biases
by_hand = 128 * (784 + 1) + 64 * (128 + 1) + 10 * (64 + 1)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), " explicit formula:", by_hand)

# 4) Softmax over the class dimension (dim=1) turns the scores into probabilities: p_k = exp(z_k) / sum_j exp(z_j)
#    is positive and the p_k sum to 1. The unnormalised scores z_k that enter the softmax are called logits.
with torch.no_grad():                   # no gradient tracking needed here (otherwise the output shows grad_fn)
    probs = torch.softmax(out, dim=1)
print("row sums:", probs.sum(dim=1)[:5])


Error: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (896x28 and 784x128)
flattened shape: torch.Size([32, 784])
output shape: torch.Size([32, 10])
parameters: 109386  explicit formula: 109386
row sums: tensor([1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000, 1.0000])





Exercise 3 — Random networks of different depth
Using nn.Sequential, build networks with layer sizes \([1, W, \dots, W, 1]\), \(\tanh\) activations, width 64 and depth (number of hidden layers) \(1, 3, 10\). For each depth draw 5 random initialisations and plot \(f(x)\) on \([-5,5]\). Do this twice: (a) with PyTorch’s default initialisation, (b) with all weights redrawn from \(\mathcal N(0, (3/\sqrt{n_\text{in}})^2)\), where \(n_\text{in}\) is the number of inputs of the layer. How does the shape of a random function change with depth in the two cases? (The factor 3 is one choice among many; for \(\tanh\) networks the boundary between the two kinds of behaviour shown by (a) and (b) lies at a factor of about 1, and any factor well above 1 shows the effect of (b).) Hint: build the list of layers in a loop and pass it as nn.Sequential(*layers); torch.nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, std=...) redraws the weights of a layer.

Solution


Code
def make_mlp(depth, width=64, activation=nn.Tanh, weight_std_factor=None):
    """1 -> width -> ... -> width -> 1 network with `depth` hidden layers.
    weight_std_factor=None: PyTorch default initialisation; otherwise weights ~ N(0, (factor/sqrt(n_in))^2)."""
    layers = [nn.Linear(1, width), activation()]                  # activation is a class (nn.Tanh); activation() creates a layer object
    for _ in range(depth - 1):                                    # remaining hidden layers
        layers += [nn.Linear(width, width), activation()]
    layers.append(nn.Linear(width, 1))                            # linear output layer
    if weight_std_factor is not None:
        for layer in layers:
            if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):                      # True if layer is an nn.Linear object; only these have weights
                n_in = layer.weight.shape[1]
                # the trailing underscore of normal_ marks an in-place operation: the existing weight tensor is overwritten
                nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, mean=0.0, std=weight_std_factor / n_in**0.5)
    return nn.Sequential(*layers)                                 # *layers passes the list elements as separate arguments

x = torch.linspace(-5, 5, 500)[:, None]                           # shape (500, 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 7))
for row, (factor, row_name, plain_name) in enumerate([(None, "default init", "default init"),
                                                     (3.0, r"std $3/\sqrt{n_{in}}$", "std 3/sqrt(n_in)")]):
    for ax, depth in zip(axes[row], [1, 3, 10]):
        ranges = []
        for seed in range(5):
            torch.manual_seed(seed)                               # a different random network for each seed
            with torch.no_grad():                                 # evaluation only, no gradients
                y = make_mlp(depth, weight_std_factor=factor)(x).squeeze()
            ax.plot(x.squeeze(), y)
            ranges.append((y.max() - y.min()).item())
        ax.set_title(f"{row_name}, depth = {depth}")
        ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$f(x)$")
        print(f"{plain_name:17s} depth {depth:2d}: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks:", np.round(ranges, 4))
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
# (a) Default initialisation draws weights uniformly from [-1/sqrt(n_in), 1/sqrt(n_in)] (variance 1/(3 n_in)).
#     Every tanh layer then shrinks the signal, and depth does NOT increase complexity: the outputs of the
#     10-layer networks vary by less than 1e-2 over the whole interval, i.e. they are almost constant.
# (b) With larger weights each layer stretches the signal and folds it through tanh; deep random networks
#     then become rapidly oscillating functions; the larger the factor, the more local maxima and minima
#     the deep networks have on [-5, 5].
# Depth can produce complicated functions, but only if the weights have a suitable scale; this is one
# reason why the initialisation of deep networks matters.


default init      depth  1: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [0.9912 2.7868 0.471  1.1998 0.9899]
default init      depth  3: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [0.0978 0.1152 0.2639 0.3197 0.1088]
default init      depth 10: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [0.0015 0.0027 0.0035 0.0065 0.0054]


std 3/sqrt(n_in)  depth  1: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [ 1.1431  1.5322  3.401   5.2946 12.0745]
std 3/sqrt(n_in)  depth  3: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [ 4.3558  4.1454  3.6766 10.2046  6.8429]
std 3/sqrt(n_in)  depth 10: range of f over [-5, 5] for the 5 networks: [11.8048 10.9719  9.7572  8.4522 10.6725]








Exercise 4 (advanced) — A custom layer
Write an nn.Module called GaussianRBF implementing \[f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} a_i\, \exp\!\big(-(x-\mu_i)^2 / (2 s_i^2)\big) \tag{30}\] with trainable \(a_i, \mu_i, s_i\) (nn.Parameter). Initialise \(\mu_i\) on a uniform grid on \([-3,3]\), all \(s_i\) at 0.5 and \(a_i\) drawn from \(\mathcal N(0,1)\). Plot the output and the individual Gaussians for 6 Gaussians. (Radial-basis-function networks are also universal approximators.)

Solution


Code
class GaussianRBF(nn.Module):
    """f(x) = sum_i a_i exp(-(x - mu_i)^2 / (2 s_i^2)) with trainable a, mu, s."""

    def __init__(self, N):
        super().__init__()
        # nn.Parameter registers the tensor as a trainable parameter of the module
        self.a = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(N))                 # amplitudes
        self.mu = nn.Parameter(torch.linspace(-3, 3, N))      # centres on a uniform grid
        self.s = nn.Parameter(0.5 * torch.ones(N))            # widths; for N = 6 the centres are 1.2 apart, so neighbouring
                                                              # Gaussians of width 0.5 overlap and their sum is a smooth curve

    def basis(self, x):
        """The N Gaussians evaluated at all points: shape (B, N)."""
        return torch.exp(-(x[:, None] - self.mu)**2 / (2 * self.s**2))

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.basis(x) @ self.a                         # weighted sum -> shape (B,)

torch.manual_seed(0)
rbf = GaussianRBF(6)
print("parameters:", [(name, tuple(p.shape)) for name, p in rbf.named_parameters()])

x = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 400)
with torch.no_grad():
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
    ax.plot(x, rbf.basis(x) * rbf.a, lw=1, alpha=0.7)        # (400, 6): ax.plot draws one curve per column = one weighted Gaussian
    ax.plot(x, rbf(x), "k", lw=2.5, label="sum $f(x)$")
    ax.legend(); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$f(x)$ and its Gaussian terms"); plt.show()


parameters: [('a', (6,)), ('mu', (6,)), ('s', (6,))]








Exercise 5 — einsum strings

Without running code, write down the shape of the result and the formula for: "ij,jk,kl->il" with shapes \((2,3),(3,4),(4,5)\); "bij->bj" with \((6,3,4)\); "ij,kl->ijkl" with \((2,3),(4,5)\); "bii->b" with \((6,3,3)\). Then check with code.
Write einsum strings for: (a) the sum of squares \[S = \sum_i u_i^2 ; \tag{31}\]

the matrix \(A^{T}A\); (c) for a batch of matrices \(A_b\) of shape \((B, n, n)\), the traces \(\mathrm{tr}\,A_b\);
the quadratic form \[q_b = \sum_{ij} x_{bi} Q_{ij} x_{bj} \tag{32}\] for a batch of vectors \(x_b\). Verify each against a computation without einsum.

Write a function quadratic_form(x, Q) that computes \[q = \sum_{ij} x_i Q_{ij} x_j \tag{33}\] for every vector along the last axis of x, whatever the number of batch axes in front (use ...). Test it with x of shapes (3,), (6, 3) and (2, 6, 3).


Solution


Code
torch.manual_seed(5)
# 1) shapes and formulas
a, b, c = torch.randn(2, 3), torch.randn(3, 4), torch.randn(4, 5)
r1 = torch.einsum("ij,jk,kl->il", a, b, c)      # r_il = sum_jk a_ij b_jk c_kl = (a @ b @ c)_il, shape (2, 5)
print("ij,jk,kl->il :", tuple(r1.shape), " equals a @ b @ c:", torch.allclose(r1, a @ b @ c, atol=1e-6))
t = torch.randn(6, 3, 4)
r2 = torch.einsum("bij->bj", t)                 # r_bj = sum_i t_bij, shape (6, 4)
print("bij->bj      :", tuple(r2.shape), " equals t.sum(dim=1):", torch.allclose(r2, t.sum(dim=1)))
r3 = torch.einsum("ij,kl->ijkl", a, c)          # r_ijkl = a_ij c_kl (nothing summed), shape (2, 3, 4, 5)
print("ij,kl->ijkl  :", tuple(r3.shape), " element check:", torch.allclose(r3[1, 2, 3, 4], a[1, 2] * c[3, 4]))
sq = torch.randn(6, 3, 3)
r4 = torch.einsum("bii->b", sq)                 # r_b = sum_i sq_bii (trace of every matrix), shape (6,)
print("bii->b       :", tuple(r4.shape), " equals traces:", torch.allclose(r4, sq.diagonal(dim1=1, dim2=2).sum(dim=1)))

# 2) writing strings
u = torch.randn(5)
A43 = torch.randn(4, 3)
As = torch.randn(6, 3, 3)
xb, Q = torch.randn(6, 3), torch.randn(3, 3)
print("(a) i,i->        :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("i,i->", u, u), (u**2).sum()))
print("(b) ki,kj->ij    :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("ki,kj->ij", A43, A43), A43.T @ A43, atol=1e-6))
print("(c) bii->b       :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("bii->b", As), torch.stack([torch.trace(m) for m in As])))
print("(d) bi,ij,bj->b  :", torch.allclose(torch.einsum("bi,ij,bj->b", xb, Q, xb),
                                           ((xb @ Q) * xb).sum(dim=1), atol=1e-6))

# 3) one string for any number of batch axes: '...' stands for all axes before the last one
def quadratic_form(x, Q):
    return torch.einsum("...i,ij,...j->...", x, Q, x)

for shape in [(3,), (6, 3), (2, 6, 3)]:
    xs = torch.randn(shape)
    reference = ((xs @ Q) * xs).sum(dim=-1)
    print(f"quadratic_form for x of shape {str(shape):10s}: result shape {str(tuple(quadratic_form(xs, Q).shape)):8s}"
          f" agrees: {torch.allclose(quadratic_form(xs, Q), reference, atol=1e-5)}")


ij,jk,kl->il : (2, 5)  equals a @ b @ c: True
bij->bj      : (6, 4)  equals t.sum(dim=1): True
ij,kl->ijkl  : (2, 3, 4, 5)  element check: True
bii->b       : (6,)  equals traces: True
(a) i,i->        : True
(b) ki,kj->ij    : True
(c) bii->b       : True
(d) bi,ij,bj->b  : True
quadratic_form for x of shape (3,)      : result shape ()       agrees: True
quadratic_form for x of shape (6, 3)    : result shape (6,)     agrees: True
quadratic_form for x of shape (2, 6, 3) : result shape (2, 6)   agrees: True





Exercise 6 — Predicting shapes
For t = torch.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4), first predict on paper, then check with code: 1. the shapes of t.reshape(4, -1), t.transpose(0, 2), t.permute(1, 2, 0), t.flatten(1), t.unsqueeze(1), t[:, None, :, None]; 2. the value of t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1]; 3. which of the results in 1. are contiguous; 4. whether t.transpose(0, 2).view(-1) works.

Solution


Code
t = torch.arange(24).reshape(2, 3, 4)

# 1) and 3): shapes and contiguity
results = {
    "t.reshape(4, -1)": t.reshape(4, -1),            # 24 / 4 = 6  -> (4, 6)
    "t.transpose(0, 2)": t.transpose(0, 2),          # axes 0 and 2 swapped -> (4, 3, 2)
    "t.permute(1, 2, 0)": t.permute(1, 2, 0),        # old axes (1, 2, 0) -> (3, 4, 2)
    "t.flatten(1)": t.flatten(1),                    # axes 1 and 2 merged -> (2, 12)
    "t.unsqueeze(1)": t.unsqueeze(1),                # new axis at position 1 -> (2, 1, 3, 4)
    "t[:, None, :, None]": t[:, None, :, None],      # new axes at positions 1 and 3 -> (2, 1, 3, 1, 4)
}
for name, r in results.items():
    print(f"{name:22s} shape {str(tuple(r.shape)):16s} contiguous: {r.is_contiguous()}")
# reshape, flatten and inserting axes of length 1 keep the row-by-row order of the elements (contiguous);
# transpose and permute only change the strides, so the elements are no longer stored row by row

# 2) element [2, 3, 1] of t.permute(1, 2, 0) is element [1, 2, 3] of t (old axis 0 is now last)
print("t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1] =", t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1].item(), "= t[1, 2, 3] =", t[1, 2, 3].item(),
      "= 1*12 + 2*4 + 3")

# 4) view on a non-contiguous tensor
try:
    t.transpose(0, 2).view(-1)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("view fails:", e)


t.reshape(4, -1)       shape (4, 6)           contiguous: True
t.transpose(0, 2)      shape (4, 3, 2)        contiguous: False
t.permute(1, 2, 0)     shape (3, 4, 2)        contiguous: False
t.flatten(1)           shape (2, 12)          contiguous: True
t.unsqueeze(1)         shape (2, 1, 3, 4)     contiguous: True
t[:, None, :, None]    shape (2, 1, 3, 1, 4)  contiguous: True
t.permute(1, 2, 0)[2, 3, 1] = 23 = t[1, 2, 3] = 23 = 1*12 + 2*4 + 3
view fails: view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride (at least one dimension spans across two contiguous subspaces). Use .reshape(...) instead.





Exercise 7 — A batch of rotations

For 6 angles \[\varphi_b = b\pi/6 \tag{34}\] build a tensor R of shape (B, 2, 2) of rotation matrices \(\begin{pmatrix}\cos\varphi & -\sin\varphi\\ \sin\varphi & \cos\varphi\end{pmatrix}\) using torch.stack (no loop).
Rotate the unit vector \((1, 0)\) by every angle in three ways: with @ and unsqueeze/squeeze, with torch.einsum, and with torch.bmm (which multiplies batches of matrices). Check that the results agree and plot the rotated vectors.
Verify \[R^{T}R = 1 \tag{35}\] for all matrices at once.


Solution


Code
n_rot = 6
phi = torch.arange(n_rot) * torch.pi / 6                  # shape (n_rot,)
c, s = torch.cos(phi), torch.sin(phi)
# 1) stack the four entries: first the two rows (each of shape (B, 2)), then the rows into matrices
row1 = torch.stack([c, -s], dim=1)                        # (n_rot, 2)
row2 = torch.stack([s, c], dim=1)                         # (n_rot, 2)
R = torch.stack([row1, row2], dim=1)                      # (n_rot, 2, 2): R[b] = [[c, -s], [s, c]]
print("R shape:", tuple(R.shape))

# 2) rotate the unit vector e_x by every angle
e_x = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0]).expand(n_rot, 2)          # the same vector for every rotation (expand adds the batch axis)
rot1 = (R @ e_x.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2)                  # (n_rot, 2, 2) @ (n_rot, 2, 1) -> (n_rot, 2, 1) -> (n_rot, 2)
rot2 = torch.einsum("bij,bj->bi", R, e_x)
rot3 = torch.bmm(R, e_x.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2)
print("all three agree:", torch.allclose(rot1, rot2) and torch.allclose(rot1, rot3))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 4))
angle_labels = ["$0$", r"$\pi/6$", r"$2\pi/6$", r"$3\pi/6$", r"$4\pi/6$", r"$5\pi/6$"]
for b in range(n_rot):
    ax.arrow(0, 0, rot1[b, 0].item(), rot1[b, 1].item(), head_width=0.04, length_includes_head=True, color=f"C{b}")
    ax.text(1.12 * rot1[b, 0].item(), 1.12 * rot1[b, 1].item(), angle_labels[b], ha="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlim(-1.3, 1.3); ax.set_ylim(-0.3, 1.3); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
plt.show()

# 3) R^T R for all rotations at once: transpose the last two axes
RtR = R.transpose(1, 2) @ R                               # (n_rot, 2, 2)
print("max |R^T R - 1|:", (RtR - torch.eye(2)).abs().max().item())


R shape: (6, 2, 2)
all three agree: True





max |R^T R - 1|: 0.0





Exercise 8 — Applying a layer to every time step
A batch of 8 time series (\(B\)), each with 50 time steps (\(T\)) and 3 measured quantities per step (\(F\)), is stored as a tensor of shape (B, T, F). 1. Apply nn.Linear(3, 5) to every time step by reshaping to (B*T, F), applying the layer, and reshaping back to (B, T, 5). 2. Apply the layer directly to the (B, T, F) tensor and compare: nn.Linear acts on the last axis and treats all other axes as batch axes. 3. What goes wrong if the tensor is stored as (B, F, T) instead? Fix it with transpose.

Solution


Code
n_series, T, F = 8, 50, 3
torch.manual_seed(0)
series = torch.randn(n_series, T, F)
lin = nn.Linear(F, 5)

# 1) merge batch and time axes, apply the layer, split them again
out1 = lin(series.reshape(n_series * T, F)).reshape(n_series, T, 5)
# 2) directly: Linear acts on the last axis
out2 = lin(series)
print("shapes:", tuple(out1.shape), tuple(out2.shape), "  agree:", torch.allclose(out1, out2))

# 3) features before time: the last axis has length T = 50, not F = 3
series_ft = series.transpose(1, 2)                        # (B, F, T)
try:
    lin(series_ft)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", e)
    # Linear merges all leading axes into one batch axis, (8 * 3) x 50 = 24 x 50, and multiplies it with W^T, which is 3 x 5
    # (the stored weight has shape (5, 3)): the inner dimensions 50 and 3 do not match
out3 = lin(series_ft.transpose(1, 2))                     # back to (B, T, F) before the layer
print("after transposing back:", tuple(out3.shape), "  agrees:", torch.allclose(out3, out1))


shapes: (8, 50, 5) (8, 50, 5)   agree: True
RuntimeError: mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (24x50 and 3x5)
after transposing back: (8, 50, 5)   agrees: True

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
1. Three ways to compute derivatives

1.1 Finite differences
From the definition of the derivative, for a small step \(h\), the forward difference \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \approx \frac{f(\vec x + h\vec e_i) - f(\vec x)}{h} \tag{2}\] has an error of order \(h\), and the central difference \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i} \approx \frac{f(\vec x + h\vec e_i) - f(\vec x - h\vec e_i)}{2h} \tag{3}\] an error of order \(h^2\). Here \(\vec e_i\) is the unit vector along axis \(i\) (only \(x_i\) is changed), and “an error of order \(h\)” means that the error is proportional to \(h\) for small \(h\). The method has two problems. The first is its cost: a gradient in \(m\) dimensions needs \(\mathcal O(m)\) evaluations of \(f\), which is impossible for \(10^9\) parameters. The second is its accuracy. The computer stores \(f(x+h)\) and \(f(x)\) with a relative rounding error of about the machine epsilon \(\epsilon_\text{machine}\). For small \(h\) the two values are nearly equal; their difference keeps an absolute error of about \(\epsilon_\text{machine}|f|\), and dividing by \(h\) enlarges it. This round-off error therefore grows in inverse proportion to \(h\). There is an optimal \(h\), and it is not known in advance.
The accuracy problem is visible already for the sine function at the point 1 (exact derivative \(\cos 1\)), with both formulas evaluated for 100 values of \(h\) between \(10^{-16}\) and 1 and the absolute error plotted on log–log axes. The two dotted and dashed reference lines show only the slopes, \[e_{\rm round}(h)=\frac{10^{-16}}{h},\qquad e_{\rm trunc}(h)=0.5\,h . \tag{4}\] The round-off line uses a constant of the order of the machine precision, about \(2.2\times10^{-16}\), and the truncation line a constant close to the prefactor of the forward-difference error, \[\frac{|f''(1)|}{2} = \frac{\sin 1}{2} \approx 0.42 . \tag{5}\]


Code
f, df_exact, x0 = np.sin, np.cos(1.0), 1.0
hs = np.logspace(-16, 0, 100)
err_fwd = np.abs((f(x0 + hs) - f(x0)) / hs - df_exact)
err_cen = np.abs((f(x0 + hs) - f(x0 - hs)) / (2 * hs) - df_exact)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.loglog(hs, err_fwd, label="forward difference")
ax.loglog(hs, err_cen, label="central difference")
ax.loglog(hs, 1e-16 / hs, "k:", lw=1, label=r"round-off $\sim\epsilon/h$")
ax.loglog(hs, 0.5 * hs, "k--", lw=1, label=r"truncation $\sim h$")
ax.set_xlabel("step $h$"); ax.set_ylabel("absolute error of $f'(1)$")
ax.set_ylim(1e-13, 1); ax.legend()
plt.show()





The plot is read from the right. For large \(h\) the error decreases along the truncation line (linearly in \(h\) for the forward and quadratically for the central difference). Below the optimum it grows again along the round-off line, and the curves become jagged because rounding errors behave like random numbers. The best achievable accuracy is about \(10^{-9}\) (forward, at a step near \(10^{-8}\)) or \(10^{-11}\)–\(10^{-12}\) (central, at a step near \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-5}\)), far from machine precision, of order \(10^{-16}\). The position of the optimum follows from adding the two errors. The Taylor expansion \[f(x+h) = f + hf' + \tfrac12h^2f'' + \tfrac16h^3f''' + \dots \tag{6}\] gives the truncation error of the forward formula, proportional to \(f''\); in the central formula the \(f''\) terms of \(f(x+h)\) and \(f(x-h)\) cancel, and the first remaining term is proportional to \(f'''\). For the forward difference the total error is about \[e_{\rm fwd}(h)\approx\frac{\epsilon}{h} + \frac{|f''|\,h}{2}, \tag{7}\] smallest at \[h\sim\sqrt{\epsilon}\approx10^{-8}. \tag{8}\] For the central difference it is about \[e_{\rm cen}(h)\approx\frac{\epsilon}{h} + \frac{|f'''|\,h^2}{6}, \tag{9}\] smallest at \[h\sim\epsilon^{1/3}\approx10^{-5}. \tag{10}\] Both estimates agree with the positions of the minima in the plot to within an order of magnitude.


1.2 Symbolic differentiation
Computer algebra (Mathematica, sympy) applies the rules of calculus to expressions. The result is exact and interpretable, but expressions can grow enormously (“expression swell”) and the approach does not work for functions defined by programs (loops, if statements, matrix diagonalisation…).


Code
import sympy as sp
x = sp.symbols("x")
expr = x
for _ in range(4):                     # a 'deep network' of 4 nested layers sin(x*sin(...))
    expr = sp.sin(x * expr)
d = sp.diff(expr, x)                   # symbolic derivative
print("function  :", expr)
# sp.count_ops counts the elementary operations (+, *, sin, cos, ...) in an expression
print("derivative has", sp.count_ops(d), "operations (function has", sp.count_ops(expr), ")")
print("first part of derivative:", str(d)[:200], "...")


function  : sin(x*sin(x*sin(x*sin(x**2))))
derivative has 43 operations (function has 8 )
first part of derivative: (x*(x*(2*x**2*cos(x**2) + sin(x**2))*cos(x*sin(x**2)) + sin(x*sin(x**2)))*cos(x*sin(x*sin(x**2))) + sin(x*sin(x*sin(x**2))))*cos(x*sin(x*sin(x*sin(x**2)))) ...


The function with 4 nested layers has 8 operations, its derivative 43. With 6 layers the numbers are 12 and 89: the derivative grows much faster than the function. This growth is the expression swell.


1.3 Automatic differentiation
AD sits in between: every program — however complicated — is a composition of elementary operations (\(+,\times,\sin,\exp,\log,\dots\)) whose derivatives are known. AD records these operations and combines their local derivatives with the chain rule, giving derivatives that are exact to machine precision at a cost of a small multiple of evaluating \(f\) itself.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
2. The computational graph
Consider the following function (adapted from the example in Baydin et al., Automatic differentiation in machine learning: a survey, JMLR 2018): \[y = f(x_1, x_2) = \ln x_1 + \cos x_2 - x_1 x_2 . \tag{11}\] A computational graph is a diagram of a calculation: each node is one intermediate value, and an arrow from \(v_a\) to \(v_b\) means that \(v_a\) is used to compute \(v_b\). We break the function into elementary steps. Following Baydin et al., the inputs get the indices \(-1\) and \(0\), so that the intermediate variables are numbered \(v_1,\dots,v_5\):



computational-graph.png


The forward evaluation at the point \((2, 1)\) reads the graph from left to right: \[
\begin{aligned}
v_{-1} &= x_1 = 2,\\
v_0 &= x_2 = 1,\\
v_1 &= \ln v_{-1} = \ln 2 = 0.693,\\
v_2 &= v_{-1}\times v_0 = 2,\\
v_3 &= \cos v_0 = \cos 1 = 0.540,\\
v_4 &= v_1 - v_2 = -1.307,\\
y = v_5 &= v_3 + v_4 = -0.767 .
\end{aligned} \tag{12}
\] Analytically, \[\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1} = \frac{1}{x_1} - x_2 = -0.5,\qquad \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2} = -\sin x_2 - x_1 = -2.841; \tag{13}\] AD must reproduce these numbers.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
4. Reverse-mode AD and backpropagation
Reverse mode first runs the program forward and records the graph. Then it goes backwards from the output, computing the adjoints \[\bar v_i = \frac{\partial y}{\partial v_i}. \tag{21}\] The chain rule says that the adjoint of a node is a sum over all nodes \(v_j\) that use it: \[\bar v_i = \sum_{j\,:\,v_i\to v_j}\bar v_j\,\frac{\partial v_j}{\partial v_i}. \tag{22}\] Starting from the output, at the point \((2,1)\): \[
\begin{aligned}
\bar v_5 &= \frac{\partial y}{\partial y} = 1,\\
\bar v_4 &= \bar v_5\,\frac{\partial v_5}{\partial v_4} = \bar v_5 = 1,\\
\bar v_3 &= \bar v_5\,\frac{\partial v_5}{\partial v_3} = \bar v_5 = 1,\\
\bar v_2 &= \bar v_4\,\frac{\partial v_4}{\partial v_2} = -\bar v_4 = -1,\\
\bar v_1 &= \bar v_4\,\frac{\partial v_4}{\partial v_1} = \bar v_4 = 1,\\
\bar v_0 &= \bar v_3\,(-\sin v_0) + \bar v_2\, v_{-1} = -0.841 - 2 = -2.841,\\
\bar v_{-1} &= \bar v_1 / v_{-1} + \bar v_2\, v_0 = 0.5 - 1 = -0.5 .
\end{aligned} \tag{23}
\] The last two lines agree with equation (13).
One backward pass gives the derivatives with respect to all inputs. Cost: a small constant times one evaluation of \(f\), independent of the number of parameters. This is why reverse mode, called backpropagation in the neural-network language, is the method used to train neural networks.
A minimal implementation of what PyTorch does internally (in the spirit of A. Karpathy’s micrograd) fits in a few lines. Each Var stores its value, the Vars it was computed from (parents) and the local derivatives with respect to them. The method backward must visit the nodes in an order in which every node comes after all nodes it depends on (a topological order). The inner function build produces it by a depth-first traversal: it first calls itself on all parents and only then appends the node, and a node used twice, such as \(x_1\), is placed only once. The reversed list visits the output first and the inputs last.


Code
class Var:
    """A scalar that remembers how it was computed, so that gradients can flow back."""

    def __init__(self, value, parents=(), local_grads=(), name=""):
        self.value = value
        self.grad = 0.0                  # will hold dy/d(this) after backward()
        self.parents = parents           # the Vars this one was computed from
        self.local_grads = local_grads   # d(this)/d(parent) for each parent
        self.name = name

    def __add__(self, other): return Var(self.value + other.value, (self, other), (1.0, 1.0))
    def __sub__(self, other): return Var(self.value - other.value, (self, other), (1.0, -1.0))
    def __mul__(self, other): return Var(self.value * other.value, (self, other), (other.value, self.value))

    def backward(self):
        # 1) order the graph so that every node comes after all nodes it depends on (topological sort)
        order, visited = [], set()
        def build(v):
            if id(v) not in visited:
                visited.add(id(v))
                for p in v.parents:
                    build(p)
                order.append(v)
        build(self)
        # 2) seed and propagate adjoints from the output back to the inputs
        self.grad = 1.0
        for v in reversed(order):
            for parent, local in zip(v.parents, v.local_grads):
                parent.grad += v.grad * local     # chain rule; '+=' sums over all paths

def v_log(v): return Var(math.log(v.value), (v,), (1.0 / v.value,))
def v_cos(v): return Var(math.cos(v.value), (v,), (-math.sin(v.value),))


With Var objects the forward pass builds the graph, and one backward pass gives both derivatives.


Code
x1, x2 = Var(2.0, name="x1"), Var(1.0, name="x2")
y = v_log(x1) + v_cos(x2) - x1 * x2       # forward pass builds the graph
y.backward()                              # ONE backward pass
print(f"y = {y.value:.4f}")
print(f"dy/dx1 = {x1.grad:.4f},  dy/dx2 = {x2.grad:.4f}")


y = -0.7666
dy/dx1 = -0.5000,  dy/dx2 = -2.8415

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
5. torch.autograd
PyTorch implements exactly this reverse-mode machinery for tensors and hundreds of operations (including matmul, eigh, fft, …). Setting requires_grad=True marks a tensor as a variable we want derivatives with respect to. Every operation on such a tensor records a node of the graph (grad_fn), and y.backward() runs the backward pass. The gradients land in .grad of the leaf tensors. A leaf is a tensor created directly by us (here x1 and x2), not as the result of an operation; the leaves are the inputs of the graph.


Code
x1 = torch.tensor(2.0, requires_grad=True)
x2 = torch.tensor(1.0, requires_grad=True)

y = torch.log(x1) + torch.cos(x2) - x1 * x2
print("y       :", y)                     # grad_fn=<SubBackward0>: the last operation recorded in the graph
y.backward()
print("dy/dx1  :", x1.grad.item())      # .item() converts a one-element tensor to a Python number
print("dy/dx2  :", x2.grad.item())


y       : tensor(-0.7666, grad_fn=<SubBackward0>)
dy/dx1  : -0.5
dy/dx2  : -2.8414709848078967


The recorded graph can be traversed backwards from y.grad_fn. It contains the same elementary operations as the graph in Section 2; the grouping differs because Python evaluates log(x1) + cos(x2) first and subtracts x1*x2 last.


Code
def show_graph(fn, depth=0):
    # Print the name of each graph node, indented by its distance from the output.
    # fn.next_functions lists the nodes that fn received its inputs from (pairs (node, index));
    # type(fn).__name__ is the class name of the node, e.g. 'MulBackward0' for a multiplication.
    if fn is None:                                   # inputs that need no gradient appear as None
        return
    print("  " * depth + type(fn).__name__)
    for parent, _ in fn.next_functions:
        show_graph(parent, depth + 1)

y = torch.log(x1) + torch.cos(x2) - x1 * x2
show_graph(y.grad_fn)     # 'AccumulateGrad' = a leaf: the place where .grad is stored


SubBackward0
  AddBackward0
    LogBackward0
      AccumulateGrad
    CosBackward0
      AccumulateGrad
  MulBackward0
    AccumulateGrad
    AccumulateGrad



5.1 Derivatives of a whole curve at once
backward() starts from a single number (a scalar), so for a tensor \(x\) of many points we sum the outputs first. Since each term of the sum depends only on its own point, \[\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}\sum_j f(x_j) = f'(x_i): \tag{24}\] the gradient is the derivative at every point. Here the function is \[f(x) = e^{-x^2/2}\sin 3x , \tag{25}\] and its derivative is compared with the analytic result.


Code
x = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 400, requires_grad=True)
y = torch.exp(-x**2 / 2) * torch.sin(3 * x)
y.sum().backward()

xd = x.detach()                                   # detach: a plain tensor without graph, for plotting
analytic = torch.exp(-xd**2 / 2) * (3 * torch.cos(3 * xd) - xd * torch.sin(3 * xd))
print("max |autograd - analytic| =", (x.grad - analytic).abs().max().item())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(xd, y.detach(), label="$f(x)$")
ax.plot(xd, x.grad, label="$f'(x)$  (autograd)")
ax.plot(xd[::15], analytic[::15], "k.", label="$f'(x)$  (analytic)")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(); plt.show()


max |autograd - analytic| = 4.440892098500626e-16





The largest difference, about \(4\times10^{-16}\), is at the level of float64 rounding: the autograd derivative is exact up to machine precision.


5.2 Higher derivatives
The function torch.autograd.grad(y, x) returns the gradient instead of storing it in .grad. With create_graph=True the gradient computation itself is recorded, so it can be differentiated again. A physics example is a potential \(V(x)\), from which follow the force \[F = -V'(x) \tag{26}\] and the curvature \(V''(x)\); the curvature at the minimum gives the vibration frequency \[\omega = \sqrt{V''(r_0)/\mu}, \tag{27}\] where \(\mu\) is the reduced mass. Take the Morse potential \[V(r) = D\,\big(1 - e^{-a(r - r_0)}\big)^2, \tag{28}\] a model of the bond between two atoms (\(D\) is the depth of the well, \(r_0\) the bond length, \(a\) sets the width), for which \[V''(r_0) = 2Da^2 \tag{29}\] (the values of \(D\), \(a\), \(r_0\) below are arbitrary).
torch.autograd.grad returns a tuple with one gradient per input tensor, even when there is only one input.


Code
D, a, r0 = 4.0, 1.5, 1.0
r = torch.tensor(r0, requires_grad=True)
V = D * (1 - torch.exp(-a * (r - r0)))**2

(dV,) = torch.autograd.grad(V, r, create_graph=True)   # first derivative, still differentiable
(d2V,) = torch.autograd.grad(dV, r)                    # second derivative
print(f"V'(r0)  = {dV.item():.3e}   (equilibrium -> 0)")
print(f"V''(r0) = {d2V.item():.6f}   exact 2 D a^2 = {2*D*a**2}")


V'(r0)  = 0.000e+00   (equilibrium -> 0)
V''(r0) = 18.000000   exact 2 D a^2 = 18.0




5.3 Four common pitfalls
Four mistakes with autograd are common. The first is that gradients accumulate: every call of backward() adds the new gradient to .grad instead of overwriting it. The derivative of \(w^2\) at the point 3 is 6, but three backward passes without a reset give 6, 12 and 18. Every training loop must therefore reset the gradients before each backward pass, with w.grad = None or optimizer.zero_grad() (Section 7).


Code
# Pitfall 1: gradients ACCUMULATE. Calling backward twice adds up the gradients.
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
for i in range(3):
    loss = w**2
    loss.backward()
    print(f"iteration {i}: w.grad = {w.grad.item()}   (true gradient: 6)")
# -> every training loop must reset them: w.grad = None  or  optimizer.zero_grad()  (Section 7)


iteration 0: w.grad = 6.0   (true gradient: 6)
iteration 1: w.grad = 12.0   (true gradient: 6)
iteration 2: w.grad = 18.0   (true gradient: 6)


The second is that the graph is freed after backward() to save memory, so a second gradient needs a new forward pass, which every training step makes anyway.


Code
# Pitfall 2: the graph is freed after backward(); calling backward on it again raises an error
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
loss = w**2
loss.backward()
try:
    loss.backward()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", str(e)[:90], "...")


RuntimeError: Trying to backward through the graph a second time (or directly access saved tensors after ...


The third: a tensor that requires gradients cannot be converted to NumPy before .detach().


Code
# Pitfall 3: .numpy() cannot be called on a tensor that requires grad -> use .detach() first
w = torch.tensor([1.0, 2.0], requires_grad=True)
try:
    (w**2).numpy()
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", str(e)[:80], "...")
print("fixed:", (w**2).detach().numpy())


RuntimeError: Can't call numpy() on Tensor that requires grad. Use tensor.detach().numpy() ins ...
fixed: [1. 4.]


The fourth concerns parameter updates written directly in the code, without an optimiser. The update itself is an operation on w; if it were recorded, the graph would keep growing from one step to the next. Inside with torch.no_grad(): nothing is recorded. The update must also be in place (w -= ...): it changes the numbers stored in the existing tensor w, which stays the same leaf tensor with requires_grad=True. Writing w = w - 0.1 * w.grad would instead create a new tensor and bind the name w to it. Inside no_grad the new tensor does not require gradients at all; outside no_grad it is not a leaf and its .grad stays None after the next backward pass. In both cases the training stops working.


Code
# Pitfall 4: parameter updates must NOT be recorded in the graph -> wrap them in torch.no_grad()
w = torch.tensor(3.0, requires_grad=True)
loss = w**2
loss.backward()
with torch.no_grad():
    w -= 0.1 * w.grad          # an in-place update of a leaf, outside the graph
w.grad = None                  # reset for the next step (pitfall 1)
print("updated w:", w)


updated w: tensor(2.4000, requires_grad=True)

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
6. Differentiating through a diagonalisation
Consider the double-well potential (harmonic trap and Gaussian barrier of height \(\kappa\)): \[\hat H(\kappa) = -\frac{1}{2}\frac{d^2}{dx^2} + \frac{1}{2}x^2 + \kappa\, e^{-x^2/2}. \tag{30}\] We ask how the energies \(E_n(\kappa)\) respond to changes of the barrier, that is, we want the derivatives \(dE_n/d\kappa\).
The program is: build the matrix \(\bar H(\kappa)\) (the bar denotes the matrix of \(\hat H\) on the grid) → diagonalise → pick eigenvalue \(n\). No formula for \(E_n(\kappa)\) is available, but every step (including torch.linalg.eigh) is differentiable, so autograd gives \(dE_n/d\kappa\) exactly (up to the grid discretisation).
Two wells appear because \[V'(x) = x\,\big(1 - \kappa e^{-x^2/2}\big), \tag{31}\] \[V''(0) = 1-\kappa . \tag{32}\] For a barrier height above 1 the origin becomes a maximum, and two minima appear at \[x_{\min} = \pm\sqrt{2\ln\kappa}, \tag{33}\] for example at \(\pm1.67\) for the barrier height 4.
The box \([-6, 6]\) is much wider than the low-lying states. With 300 grid points the spacing \(\Delta x\) is about 0.04, small compared with the scale (of order 1) on which these states vary. The lowest four energies at the barrier height 4 change by less than \(10^{-3}\) (relative change below \(2\times10^{-4}\)) when the number of grid points \(N_x\) is increased from 300 to 1000, so any \(N_x\) of a few hundred gives the same picture; larger \(N_x\) only makes the diagonalisation slower.
torch.linalg.eigvalsh(H) returns only the eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix (in ascending order) and does less work than torch.linalg.eigh(H), which also returns the eigenvectors.


Code
# Grid: psi''(x_i) ~ (psi_{i+1} - 2 psi_i + psi_{i-1}) / dx^2, and psi = 0 beyond the ends of the grid
# (hard walls at x = -6 and x = 6, far from where the wavefunctions live).
L_box, Nx = 12.0, 300
x = torch.linspace(-L_box / 2, L_box / 2, Nx)
dx = x[1] - x[0]

# kinetic part (does not depend on kappa): built once
ones = torch.ones(Nx - 1)
H_kin = -0.5 / dx**2 * (torch.diag(ones, 1) - 2 * torch.eye(Nx) + torch.diag(ones, -1))

def potential(x, kappa):
    return 0.5 * x**2 + kappa * torch.exp(-x**2 / 2)

def hamiltonian(kappa):
    """Matrix of H(kappa) on the grid; differentiable w.r.t. kappa."""
    return H_kin + torch.diag(potential(x, kappa))

def energies(kappa, n_levels=4):
    return torch.linalg.eigvalsh(hamiltonian(kappa))[:n_levels]


The figure shows the potential and the densities of the four lowest states (shifted by their energies) for four barrier heights. eigh returns the eigenvectors as the columns of psi: psi[:, n] is the \(n\)-th eigenstate, not the row psi[n]. The eigenvectors are normalised as vectors, \[\sum_i|\psi_n(x_i)|^2 = 1 ; \tag{34}\] dividing by \(\Delta x\) turns this into a probability density with \[\sum_i \frac{|\psi_n(x_i)|^2}{\Delta x}\,\Delta x = 1, \tag{35}\] the discrete form of the normalisation of the integral of \(|\psi|^2\).


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(15, 3.5), sharey=True)
for ax, kappa in zip(axes, [0.0, 2.0, 4.0, 10.0]):
    E, psi = torch.linalg.eigh(hamiltonian(torch.tensor(kappa)))
    ax.plot(x, potential(x, torch.tensor(kappa)), "k", lw=2)
    for n in range(4):
        ax.plot(x, E[n] + 1.5 * psi[:, n]**2 / dx, lw=1.5)       # |psi_n|^2 (scaled by 1.5) shifted by E_n
        ax.axhline(E[n], color="gray", lw=0.4)
    ax.set_title(rf"$\kappa = {kappa}$"); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_xlim(-5, 5); ax.set_ylim(0, 9)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$V(x)$, $\;E_n + |\psi_n(x)|^2$")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





In the figure, without a barrier the levels are those of the harmonic oscillator, \[E_n = n + \tfrac12 . \tag{36}\] As \(\kappa\) grows, the barrier pushes the states out of the centre and the levels move up. For the barrier height 10 they form pairs of almost equal energy, with \[E_1 - E_0 \approx 5\times10^{-4},\qquad E_3 - E_2 \approx 9\times10^{-3}, \tag{37}\] and the two curves of each pair lie on top of each other.
A single derivative, \(dE_0/d\kappa\) at the barrier height 4 (in the double-well regime), is checked first.


Code
kappa = torch.tensor(4.0, requires_grad=True)
E0 = energies(kappa)[0]
E0.backward()
print(f"E_0(kappa=4) = {E0.item():.6f},   dE_0/dkappa = {kappa.grad.item():.6f}")


E_0(kappa=4) = 3.089526,   dE_0/dkappa = 0.388432


Two independent computations confirm this number. The first is the Hellmann–Feynman theorem: for a normalised eigenstate, \[\frac{dE_n}{d\kappa} = \Big\langle\psi_n\Big|\frac{\partial\hat H}{\partial\kappa}\Big|\psi_n\Big\rangle = \langle\psi_n|\,e^{-x^2/2}\,|\psi_n\rangle . \tag{38}\] Here \(\langle\psi_n|\hat A|\psi_n\rangle\) is the expectation value of \(\hat A\) in the state \(\psi_n\). On the grid (eigenvectors from eigh are normalised as vectors) it is \[\frac{dE_n}{d\kappa} = \sum_i |\psi_n(x_i)|^2 e^{-x_i^2/2},\qquad \frac{d\bar H}{d\kappa} = \mathrm{diag}\big(e^{-x_i^2/2}\big). \tag{39}\] On the grid the theorem follows in one line. With \[E_n = \vec\psi_n^T\bar H\vec\psi_n,\qquad \vec\psi_n^T\vec\psi_n = 1, \tag{40}\] the product rule gives \[\frac{dE_n}{d\kappa} = \vec\psi_n^T\frac{d\bar H}{d\kappa}\vec\psi_n + 2\,\vec\psi_n^T\bar H\,\frac{d\vec\psi_n}{d\kappa}. \tag{41}\] Since \(\bar H\) is symmetric, \[\vec\psi_n^T\bar H = E_n\vec\psi_n^T, \tag{42}\] and the last term of equation (41) is \[2E_n\vec\psi_n^T \frac{d\vec\psi_n}{d\kappa} = E_n\,\frac{d(\vec\psi_n^T\vec\psi_n)}{d\kappa} = 0 . \tag{43}\] The change of the eigenvector does not contribute.
The second is a central finite difference. Section 1 found the optimal step near \(10^{-6}\)–\(10^{-5}\) for the sine. Here any step between about \(10^{-3}\) and \(10^{-5}\) gives agreement with autograd to better than \(10^{-8}\); we take the step \(10^{-4}\). Autograd and Hellmann–Feynman agree to all ten printed digits (0.3884316631), and the finite difference differs only in the last one.


Code
k0 = 4.0
_, psi = torch.linalg.eigh(hamiltonian(torch.tensor(k0)))
hf = torch.sum(psi[:, 0]**2 * torch.exp(-x**2 / 2)).item()
h = 1e-4
fd = ((energies(torch.tensor(k0 + h))[0] - energies(torch.tensor(k0 - h))[0]) / (2 * h)).item()
print(f"autograd          : {kappa.grad.item():.10f}")
print(f"Hellmann-Feynman  : {hf:.10f}")
print(f"finite difference : {fd:.10f}")


autograd          : 0.3884316631
Hellmann-Feynman  : 0.3884316631
finite difference : 0.3884316634


The full picture is \(E_n(\kappa)\) and \(dE_n/d\kappa\) for the four lowest levels for barrier heights from 0 to 12 (121 values, step 0.1). torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(f, x) returns the matrix of derivatives \(\partial f_i/\partial x_j\) (one backward pass per output \(f_i\)); here \(f\) maps one number \(\kappa\) to four energies.


Code
kappas = torch.linspace(0, 12, 121)
E_all, dE_all = [], []
for k in kappas:
    E_all.append(energies(k).detach())
    dE_all.append(torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(energies, k))   # shape (4,): dE_n/dkappa
E_all, dE_all = torch.stack(E_all), torch.stack(dE_all)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.5))
for n in range(4):
    axes[0].plot(kappas, E_all[:, n], label=f"$n={n}$")
    axes[1].plot(kappas, dE_all[:, n], label=f"$n={n}$")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$E_n(\kappa)$"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$dE_n/d\kappa$  (autograd)")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel(r"barrier height $\kappa$"); ax.legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The derivative in equation (38), the expectation value of the barrier shape \(e^{-x^2/2}\), has a simple meaning: it is the probability-weighted overlap of the state with the barrier. For large \(\kappa\) all four states are pushed out of the centre and \(dE_n/d\kappa\) decreases (for the level 2 only above a barrier height of about 4; below that it first increases); the pairs of levels \((0,1)\) and \((2,3)\) merge into quasi-degenerate tunnelling doublets (pairs of nearly equal energy; the two states of a pair are spread symmetrically and antisymmetrically over the two wells, and their small splitting is caused by tunnelling through the barrier) — and their derivatives become equal, because both states of a doublet see the barrier the same way.

One subtle point deserves attention. Derivatives of eigenvalues are well defined. Derivatives of eigenvectors, \[\frac{d\vec\psi_n}{d\kappa} = \sum_{m\neq n}\frac{\vec\psi_m^T\,(d\bar H/d\kappa)\,\vec\psi_n}{E_n - E_m}\,\vec\psi_m , \tag{44}\] contain energy differences in the denominator and blow up at (near-)degeneracies. PyTorch’s backward formula for eigh builds these factors for all pairs of eigenvalues, so exact degeneracies anywhere in the spectrum give inf, and inf multiplied by zero gives nan, even for pairs that do not contribute mathematically. The PyTorch documentation of eigh warns about this.

In short, any computation built from differentiable operations can be differentiated. The same mechanism that trains neural networks is used to optimise Hamiltonians, quantum circuits (the variational quantum eigensolver VQE and the quantum approximate optimisation algorithm QAOA, later in the course) and control pulses.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
7. Gradient-based optimisation

7.1 Gradient descent
Minimise the Rosenbrock function \[f(x, y) = (1-x)^2 + 100\,(y - x^2)^2 , \tag{45}\] whose minimum, at \((1,1)\), lies at the bottom of a long, curved, flat valley — a simple model of a hard loss landscape.
The starting point \((-1.5, 2)\) lies on the far side of the curved valley, so the path has to follow its whole length; the 3000 steps show the slow motion along the valley, not convergence. The positions are stored with p.detach().clone(): detach() alone shares memory with p, which is changed in place, so all stored entries would end up equal to the final position.


Code
def rosenbrock(p):
    return (1 - p[0])**2 + 100 * (p[1] - p[0]**2)**2

def gradient_descent(lr, n_steps=3000, start=(-1.5, 2.0)):
    p = torch.tensor(start, requires_grad=True)
    path = [p.detach().clone()]
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        loss = rosenbrock(p)
        loss.backward()                  # 1) gradient by autograd
        with torch.no_grad():
            p -= lr * p.grad             # 2) step downhill
        p.grad = None                    # 3) reset accumulated gradient
        path.append(p.detach().clone())
    return torch.stack(path)

path = gradient_descent(lr=1e-3)
print("final point:", path[-1], " f =", rosenbrock(path[-1]).item())


final point: tensor([0.7796, 0.6068])  f = 0.048669156394873424


The values of \(f\) on the plot range from 0 to about \(2.5\times10^3\), so the colour scale shows the decimal logarithm of \(f\) shifted by \(10^{-3}\); the red star marks the minimum.


Code
xg, yg = torch.linspace(-2, 2, 300), torch.linspace(-1, 3, 300)
XG, YG = torch.meshgrid(xg, yg, indexing="xy")
FG = rosenbrock(torch.stack([XG, YG]))

def landscape(ax):
    ax.contourf(XG, YG, torch.log10(FG + 1e-3), levels=40, cmap="Greys_r", alpha=0.8)
    ax.plot(1, 1, "r*", ms=15)
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
landscape(ax)
ax.plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], ".-", color="C0", ms=2, lw=1, label="gradient descent, $\\eta=10^{-3}$")
ax.legend(loc="lower right"); plt.show()





Gradient descent (GD) quickly falls into the valley, then crawls slowly along it. A larger learning rate helps along the valley — but makes the steps across the steep walls unstable. The limit can be computed. Near a minimum, \(f\) is approximately quadratic with the Hessian matrix \(\partial^2 f/\partial x_i\partial x_j\) as curvature. There the gradient is approximately \[\nabla f \approx \nabla^2 f\,(\vec x - \vec x^\ast), \tag{46}\] where \(\nabla^2 f\) is the Hessian and \(\vec x^\ast\) the minimum, so one GD step maps \[\vec x - \vec x^\ast \;\to\; (\mathbf 1 - \eta\,\nabla^2 f)(\vec x - \vec x^\ast). \tag{47}\] Along an eigenvector of the Hessian with eigenvalue \(\lambda\), one step therefore multiplies the distance from the minimum by \[q = 1 - \eta\lambda . \tag{48}\] The iteration converges only if \[|1-\eta\lambda| < 1 \ \ \text{for all eigenvalues} \iff \eta < \frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}}. \tag{49}\] At the Rosenbrock minimum the eigenvalues are 0.40 and 1001.6, so \(\eta\) must stay below \[\frac{2}{1001.6} \approx 2.0\times10^{-3}. \tag{50}\] The flat direction, with the eigenvalue 0.40, then shrinks per step only by the factor \(q\) of equation (48), about 0.9992, which is why GD is slow.
The comparison uses the learning rates \(10^{-3}\), \(1.9\times10^{-3}\) (slightly below the limit, much closer to the minimum after 3000 steps) and \(2.5\times10^{-3}\) (above the limit: the iteration diverges, and the result is nan, “not a number”). The range of usable learning rates is narrow. Better optimisers address the mismatch between flat and steep directions.


Code
for lr in [1e-3, 1.9e-3, 2.5e-3]:
    final = gradient_descent(lr=lr)[-1]
    print(f"eta = {lr:.1e}:  final point = {final.numpy().round(4)},  f = {rosenbrock(final).item():.2e}")


eta = 1.0e-03:  final point = [0.7796 0.6068],  f = 4.87e-02


eta = 1.9e-03:  final point = [0.9756 0.9517],  f = 5.97e-04


eta = 2.5e-03:  final point = [nan nan],  f = nan




7.2 Optimisers in torch.optim
PyTorch’s optimisers implement the update rule. For most optimisers the training loop has the same 4 lines (L-BFGS, used in Section 8, is an exception):
optimizer.zero_grad()   # reset gradients
loss = f(params)        # forward pass
loss.backward()         # backward pass
optimizer.step()        # update parameters
We compare four of them (see Lecture Notes, The Zoo of Optimization Algorithms). Plain stochastic gradient descent (SGD) updates the parameters with the gradient \(g\), \[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta g . \tag{51}\] The name stochastic refers to estimating \(g\) from a random part of the training data. Here there are no data, \(g\) is exact, and SGD is plain gradient descent.
SGD with momentum keeps a velocity \(v\), a “heavy ball” that builds up speed along the valley: \[v \leftarrow \gamma v - \eta g,\qquad \theta\leftarrow\theta + v . \tag{52}\] The conventional value of \(\gamma\) is 0.9: the velocity is then an average over roughly the last \[\frac{1}{1-\gamma} = 10 \tag{53}\] gradients.
RMSprop (root mean square propagation) rescales steep and flat directions with a per-parameter step, \[\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta\,\frac{g}{\sqrt{E[g^2]}},\qquad E[g^2] \leftarrow \rho\, E[g^2] + (1-\rho)\,g^2 , \tag{54}\] where \(E[g^2]\) is a running average of the squared gradient, kept separately for each parameter (PyTorch default for \(\rho\): 0.99).
Adam (adaptive moment estimation) combines momentum and RMSprop. Both running averages start at zero, which makes them too small in the first steps; the bias correction divides them by \[1-\beta^t , \tag{55}\] where \(t\) is the step number and \(\beta\) the decay factor of the average, by default 0.9 for the gradient and 0.999 for its square. Adam is the default choice in deep learning.
The learning rates differ between the optimisers because \(\eta\) means different things. With momentum, on a steady slope the steps add up to \[\frac{\eta}{1-\gamma} = 10\,\eta , \tag{56}\] so \(\eta\) is reduced. RMSprop and Adam divide the gradient by its typical size, so their \(\eta\) is roughly the step length in parameter space and can be much larger. Each value was chosen to give a stable run; the comparison shows typical behaviour, not the best possible setting of each method.


Code
def run(opt_class, n_steps=3000, start=(-1.5, 2.0), **opt_kwargs):
    p = torch.tensor(start, requires_grad=True)
    opt = opt_class([p], **opt_kwargs)
    path, losses = [p.detach().clone()], []
    for _ in range(n_steps):
        opt.zero_grad()
        loss = rosenbrock(p)
        loss.backward()
        opt.step()
        path.append(p.detach().clone()); losses.append(loss.item())
    return torch.stack(path), losses

setups = {
    "SGD (lr=1e-3)":               (torch.optim.SGD, dict(lr=1e-3)),
    "SGD + momentum (lr=3e-4, 0.9)": (torch.optim.SGD, dict(lr=3e-4, momentum=0.9)),
    "RMSprop (lr=1e-2)":           (torch.optim.RMSprop, dict(lr=1e-2)),
    "Adam (lr=5e-2)":              (torch.optim.Adam, dict(lr=5e-2)),
}
results = {name: run(cls, **kw) for name, (cls, kw) in setups.items()}

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
landscape(axes[0])
for i, (name, (path, losses)) in enumerate(results.items()):
    axes[0].plot(path[:, 0], path[:, 1], "-", color=f"C{i}", lw=1.5, label=name)
    axes[1].semilogy(losses, color=f"C{i}", label=name)
axes[0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right"); axes[0].set_xlim(-2, 2); axes[0].set_ylim(-1, 3)
axes[1].set_xlabel("iteration"); axes[1].set_ylabel("$f$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
for name, (path, losses) in results.items():
    print(f"{name:32s} final f = {losses[-1]:.2e}   final point = {path[-1].numpy().round(4)}")





SGD (lr=1e-3)                    final f = 4.87e-02   final point = [0.7796 0.6068]
SGD + momentum (lr=3e-4, 0.9)    final f = 1.95e-04   final point = [0.9861 0.9723]
RMSprop (lr=1e-2)                final f = 2.24e-02   final point = [0.9678 0.9514]
Adam (lr=5e-2)                   final f = 5.82e-29   final point = [1. 1.]


In the result, Adam reaches the minimum \((1, 1)\) to machine precision within 3000 steps, momentum comes close (\(f\) about \(2\times10^{-4}\)), and plain SGD is still moving slowly along the valley. RMSprop gets stuck at \(f\) of about \(2\times10^{-2}\), about 0.06 from the minimum. Since it divides the gradient by its own typical size, its steps stay about as long as \(\eta\) even near the minimum (0.014 on average over the last 500 steps), so it keeps jumping across the narrow valley (the spikes in its loss curve). A smaller learning rate lowers this final error (\(f\) about \(3\times10^{-3}\) with \(3\times10^{-3}\)), but makes the start slower (\(f\) about 0.2 after 3000 steps with \(10^{-3}\)).
No optimiser is universally best, and each has hyperparameters (here: the learning rate) that strongly affect the result. The same tools are used to fit neural networks, where the loss landscape has millions or more dimensions instead of two.

title: Lab 004: Automatic differentiation
text:
8. The inverse Schrödinger problem

8.1 Inverse problems in physics
The usual (direct) problem of quantum mechanics is: given a potential \(V(x)\), find the eigenstates and energies. Many questions in physics are inverse: they ask which potential produces a prescribed state. In experiments with ultracold atoms, the trapping potential is shaped with laser beams, and one wants the potential that gives a desired density profile of the atomic cloud. In semiconductor quantum dots, gate voltages define the confining potential, and one wants electrons localised in a prescribed way. In density-functional theory, the Kohn–Sham inversion problem asks for the potential whose ground-state density equals a given density.
The simplest version concerns one particle in 1D: find \(V(x)\) such that the ground-state probability density \(|\psi_0(x)|^2\) is as close as possible to a target density \(\rho_\ast(x)\).


8.2 Loss function and L-BFGS
On the grid of Section 6 the potential is the vector of its \(N_x\) values \(V_i\) at the grid points; these are our trainable parameters (here 300 of them). For given \(V\) we build \[\bar H = \bar H_{\rm kin} + \mathrm{diag}(V), \tag{57}\] diagonalise it and take the ground state \(\psi_0\). The loss compares amplitudes: \[\mathcal L(V) = \sum_i \Big(|\psi_0(x_i)| - \sqrt{\rho_\ast(x_i)}\Big)^2\,\Delta x . \tag{58}\] The factor \(\Delta x\) makes the sum an approximation of the integral \[\mathcal L(V) \approx \int\big(|\psi_0| - \sqrt{\rho_\ast}\big)^2dx , \tag{59}\] so its value does not depend on the number of grid points. We compare \(|\psi_0|\) with \(\sqrt{\rho_\ast}\) rather than \(|\psi_0|^2\) with \(\rho_\ast\): the square root gives more weight to regions where the density is small, which otherwise hardly influence the loss. The gradient \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial V_i\) for all 300 components comes from one backward pass through eigh. We minimise with L-BFGS (limited-memory Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno), a quasi-Newton method. Newton’s method jumps to the minimum of the local quadratic approximation of the loss, \[\Delta\vec V = -(\nabla^2\mathcal L)^{-1}\nabla\mathcal L , \tag{60}\] with the Hessian \(\nabla^2\mathcal L\) (Section 7). Computing and inverting the \(300\times300\) Hessian at every step is expensive; a quasi-Newton method instead builds an approximation of \((\nabla^2\mathcal L)^{-1}\) from the gradients of previous steps. This makes it fast for smooth problems with exact (non-stochastic) gradients. Within one step it evaluates the loss several times (a line search: several step lengths are tried along the chosen direction), so opt.step receives a function, called closure, that recomputes the loss and its gradient. One L-BFGS step contains up to max_iter such iterations (a setting explained in 8.3).
The optimisation starts from a vanishing potential, not from a harmonic one. The backward pass of eigh contains the energy denominators of equation (44) for all pairs of eigenvalues, also those of highly excited states that do not enter the loss. In a symmetric potential with high walls at the edges of the grid, such as the harmonic potential on \([-6, 6]\), the highest states come in pairs localised at the left and right edge with numerically equal energies; a vanishing denominator then turns the gradient into nan (this is the warning of Section 6 in practice). The spectrum of the flat potential has no such degeneracies.
Two properties of the problem matter. First, \(V\) is determined only up to a constant: adding a constant \(c\) to \(V\) shifts all energies by \(c\) and leaves the states unchanged. We fix the constant by a shift: in 8.3 the potential is matched to the exact one in the high-density region, in 8.4 its minimum in that region is set to zero. Second, where the target density is practically zero, the potential has almost no influence on the loss, so it is not determined there.


8.3 Harmonic potential
For a node-less ground state the Schrödinger equation can be inverted exactly. Dividing \[-\tfrac12\psi_0'' + V\psi_0 = E_0\psi_0 \tag{61}\] by \(\psi_0\), which is allowed because a ground state without nodes vanishes nowhere, gives \[V(x) = E_0 + \frac{1}{2}\frac{\psi_0''(x)}{\psi_0(x)}. \tag{62}\] For the Gaussian \[\psi_\ast(x)\propto e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)} \tag{63}\] we have \[\frac{\psi_\ast''}{\psi_\ast} = \frac{x^2}{\sigma^4} - \frac{1}{\sigma^2},\qquad V(x) = \frac{x^2}{2\sigma^4} + \text{const}, \tag{64}\] a harmonic potential. We use this case to test the method. The target density is \[\rho_\ast = |\psi_\ast|^2 \propto e^{-x^2/\sigma^2}. \tag{65}\]
An eigensolver may return \(\psi\) or \(-\psi\) (both are eigenvectors), and the sign can change from one iteration to the next. The ground state has no nodes, so torch.abs(psi[:, 0]) removes this ambiguity. Dividing by \(\sqrt{\Delta x}\) converts the vector normalisation of eigh, equation (34), into the normalisation of equation (35). The width \(\sigma\), here 0.7, is arbitrary: any width works that is much larger than \(\Delta x\), about 0.04 (so that the grid resolves the density), and much smaller than the half-width 6 of the box (so that the density vanishes at the walls).
In torch.optim.LBFGS, lr=1 means a full quasi-Newton step; the line_search_fn="strong_wolfe" then shortens or lengthens each step so that the loss really decreases by a sufficient amount. Without the line search a fixed step is taken, and the run still converged, but to a noticeably larger loss. The parameter history_size=50 is the number of past gradients used to estimate the curvature; values from 10 to 100 give a final loss of the same order. The parameters tolerance_grad and tolerance_change are the thresholds below which L-BFGS stops. The defaults (\(10^{-7}\) and \(10^{-9}\)) are of the size of the loss reached here, and with them the optimisation stops early (after roughly 150–200 evaluations) at a loss a few times larger, so we set them so small that they never stop the run.
Each call opt.step(closure) makes up to max_iter=50 iterations, and the line search adds further loss evaluations: the default n_steps=5 outer steps make about 270 evaluations of the loss, each with one diagonalisation and one backward pass. For the Gaussian target the small n_steps costs little accuracy: with n_steps=20 (about 1200 evaluations, four times longer) the final loss decreased in our tests by less than a factor of two and the plots looked the same. Harder targets profit more from extra steps (Section 8.4). Finally, opt.step(closure) returns the loss at the beginning of the step, so to record the loss after the last step closure() is called once more at the end.


Code
def ground_state_amplitude(V):
    # |psi_0| on the grid, normalised so that sum |psi_0|^2 dx = 1
    E, psi = torch.linalg.eigh(H_kin + torch.diag(V))
    return torch.abs(psi[:, 0]) / torch.sqrt(dx)

def invert(rho_target, n_steps=5):
    # Find V on the grid whose ground-state density is closest to rho_target (a tensor on the grid x)
    rho_target = rho_target / (rho_target.sum() * dx)            # normalise the target
    amp_target = torch.sqrt(rho_target)
    V = torch.zeros_like(x).requires_grad_(True)                 # start from a flat potential (see 'Starting point' in 8.2)
    opt = torch.optim.LBFGS([V], lr=1, max_iter=50, history_size=50, line_search_fn="strong_wolfe",
                            tolerance_grad=1e-12, tolerance_change=1e-16)
    history = []

    def closure():
        opt.zero_grad()
        amp = ground_state_amplitude(V)
        loss = torch.sum((amp - amp_target)**2) * dx
        loss.backward()                                          # gradient w.r.t. all components of V
        return loss

    for _ in range(n_steps):
        history.append(opt.step(closure).item())                 # step() returns the loss at the START of the step
    history.append(closure().item())                             # loss after the last step
    amp = ground_state_amplitude(V.detach())
    return V.detach(), amp**2, rho_target, history

sigma = 0.7
t0 = time.perf_counter()
V_opt, rho_opt, rho_star, hist = invert(torch.exp(-x**2 / sigma**2))
print(f"optimisation took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s, final loss {hist[-1]:.2e}")
print(f"max |rho_0 - rho_target| = {torch.max(torch.abs(rho_opt - rho_star)).item():.1e}")

max |rho_0 - rho_target| = 1.9e-04


The optimised potential is compared with the exact harmonic potential up to a constant. To fix the constant, we take the region where the target density exceeds \(10^{-3}\) of its maximum, where the loss carries information about \(V\), and shift \(V\) so that its mean difference from the exact potential in that region is zero. The threshold is arbitrary: with \(10^{-2}\) or \(10^{-4}\) the shift changes by about 0.02 and the picture is the same. Matching the potentials at the origin would be an equally valid choice.


Code
V_exact = x**2 / (2 * sigma**4)
inside = rho_star > 1e-3 * rho_star.max()                    # region where the density is not negligible
shift = torch.mean((V_opt - V_exact)[inside])                # remove the arbitrary constant

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
axes[0].semilogy(hist); axes[0].set_xlabel("L-BFGS step"); axes[0].set_ylabel("loss")
