title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
7. Sensitivity to initial conditions
Two double pendulums are released from angles differing by \(10^{-9}\) rad, and the distance between them in phase space is followed, \[d(t) = \|s_A(t) - s_B(t)\| . \tag{30}\] In a chaotic system it grows on average exponentially, \[d(t)\sim d(0)\,e^{\lambda t}, \tag{31}\] until it reaches the size of the accessible phase space. \(\lambda\) is the (largest) Lyapunov exponent. On a logarithmic vertical axis exponential growth appears as a straight line with slope \(\lambda\): \[\ln d(t) = \ln d(0) + \lambda t . \tag{32}\]
The perturbation \(10^{-9}\) rad is very small, so that the exponential phase lasts long before the distance saturates; any value well above the rounding level \(10^{-16}\) would do. (The shifts of \(10^{-3}\) rad in Section 6.3 and \(10^{-4}\) rad in Section 9 were instead chosen so that the separation becomes visible within the simulated time.) The distance \(d\) adds angles (rad) and angular velocities (rad/s), quantities with different units. This is acceptable: changing the weights of the coordinates in the distance changes only the prefactor of \(d(t)\), not its exponential growth rate \(\lambda\).
The exponent \(\lambda\) is the slope of a least-squares straight-line fit of \(\ln d(t)\) versus \(t\). The fit uses the times between 1 s and 8 s, because at the start \(d\) does not yet grow steadily: the perturbation first has to turn into the most unstable direction, and here \(d\) rises and falls again, staying of order \(10^{-8}\), up to about 2 s. The first second is left out; the remaining dip before 2 s barely affects the slope of a fit over seven seconds (starting the window at 2 s instead of 1 s changes \(\lambda\) by about 2 %). The upper limit keeps the fit far from saturation, which sets in after about 20 s. Both pendulums are integrated as one batch (two columns) with the time step \(5\times10^{-3}\) s for 25 s; with the step \(10^{-3}\) s the separation time and \(\lambda\) change by less than 1 %.


Code
q0 = np.deg2rad([120.0, -10.0])
q_AB = np.column_stack([q0, q0 + np.array([1e-9, 0])])          # shape (2, 2): column 0 = A, column 1 = B
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_dp, q_AB, np.zeros((2, 2)), T=25.0, dt=5e-3)
QA, QB, WA, WB = Q[:, :, 0], Q[:, :, 1], W[:, :, 0], W[:, :, 1]
dist = np.sqrt(np.sum((QA - QB)**2 + (WA - WB)**2, axis=1))
t_sep = t_arr[np.argmax(np.abs(QA[:, 1] - QB[:, 1]) > 0.1)]       # first time theta2 differs by more than 0.1 rad
print(f"theta2 of A and B first differ by more than 0.1 rad at t = {t_sep:.1f} s")

# slope of log(d) in the growth phase: a straight-line fit for 1 s < t < 8 s
sel = (t_arr > 1) & (t_arr < 8)
lam, c = np.polyfit(t_arr[sel], np.log(dist[sel]), 1)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
axes[0].plot(t_arr, QA[:, 1], label="pendulum A"); axes[0].plot(t_arr, QB[:, 1], "--", label="pendulum B")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$t$ [s]"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\theta_2$ [rad]"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].semilogy(t_arr, dist, label="$d(t)$")
axes[1].semilogy(t_arr[sel], np.exp(c + lam * t_arr[sel]), "k--", label=rf"fit $\propto e^{{\lambda t}}$, $\lambda \approx {lam:.2f}$ s$^{{-1}}$")
axes[1].set_xlabel("$t$ [s]"); axes[1].set_ylabel("phase-space distance"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


theta2 of A and B first differ by more than 0.1 rad at t = 19.2 s





After an initial transient (in the first one to two seconds \(d\) fluctuates without growing) the distance grows exponentially on average, but it becomes visible in the angles only when it reaches order \(10^{-1}\) (time printed above); after that the two pendulums, which started \(10^{-9}\) rad apart, move completely differently. The estimate of \(\lambda\) from a single pair of trajectories is rough: it depends on the fitting window (windows between 1 s and 15 s give \(0.9\)–\(1.1\) s\(^{-1}\), the window 0–3 s gives \(0.7\) s\(^{-1}\)); a reliable method is the subject of Exercise 3. A practical consequence follows: no numerical method can follow an individual chaotic trajectory for long times — rounding errors of \(10^{-16}\) are amplified in the same way. Statistical properties (such as the Poincaré sections below) are nevertheless reproducible.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
8. Phase space and Poincaré sections
The double pendulum has a 4-dimensional phase space \((\theta_1, \theta_2, \dot\theta_1, \dot\theta_2)\), and energy conservation restricts each trajectory to a 3-dimensional surface of constant energy. That is still hard to draw. Projections onto two coordinates are a first look. Two trajectories are released from rest, one with both angles \(10^\circ\) (small angles) and one with the angles \(120^\circ\) and \(-10^\circ\) (large angles); both are integrated with the time step \(5\times10^{-3}\) s for 30 s (for the trajectory of Section 6.1 this step gives a relative energy error of \(8\times10^{-5}\) over 10 s).


Code
q0_pair = np.deg2rad([[10.0, 120.0], [10.0, -10.0]])        # columns: (10, 10) deg and (120, -10) deg
_, Qp, Wp = simulate(accel_dp, q0_pair, np.zeros((2, 2)), T=30.0, dt=5e-3)
titles = [r"small angles: $\theta_1=\theta_2=10^\circ$", r"large angles: $\theta_1=120^\circ, \theta_2=-10^\circ$"]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.5))
for j, (ax, title) in enumerate(zip(axes, titles)):
    ax.plot(Qp[:, 0, j], Wp[:, 0, j], lw=0.3)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_1$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta_1$"); ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





Left (small angles): the curve stays inside a band and is woven in a regular pattern; two oscillations with different frequencies are superposed, and the trajectory never exactly repeats. Right (large angles): the curve wanders irregularly over a larger region. In both cases the lines cross each other, because the plot shows only two of the four coordinates. A projection of a chaotic trajectory fills an area and hides the structure. The tool for looking inside is the Poincaré section.

8.1 Phase space and flow
The state of the double pendulum is the point \[z = (\theta_1, \theta_2, \dot\theta_1, \dot\theta_2) \in \mathbb R^4 . \tag{33}\] The equations of motion determine, for every initial state \(z_0\), a unique trajectory, \[\dot z = F(z),\qquad z(t) = \varphi_t(z_0); \tag{34}\] the map \(\varphi_t\) is called the flow. Trajectories of an autonomous system (one whose equations, such as (34), do not contain the time explicitly) never cross each other in phase space: through every point passes exactly one trajectory.


8.2 The energy surface
The energy (4) is conserved, so a trajectory never leaves the 3-dimensional surface \[\{z : E(z) = E\} . \tag{35}\] Each trajectory is a curve on this 3D surface, which still cannot be drawn on paper. A projection onto two coordinates, as in the figure above, squashes the curve and makes it cross itself everywhere.


8.3 The surface of section
Choose a surface that trajectories keep passing through, here \[\Sigma = \{\, z :\ \theta_1 = 0,\ \ \dot\theta_1 > 0,\ \ E(z) = E \,\}. \tag{36}\] In words: the first rod passes through the vertical, moving to the right. The condition on \(\dot\theta_1\) is needed because during one swing the rod passes the vertical twice, once in each direction; counting only one direction makes every recorded point correspond to “the same phase” of the motion, and it guarantees that the trajectory really crosses \(\Sigma\) instead of touching it. \(\Sigma\) is 2-dimensional: fixing the first angle at zero removes one coordinate, and on this set the energy equation, quadratic in \(\dot\theta_1\), fixes the positive \(\dot\theta_1\) once \(\theta_2\) and \(\dot\theta_2\) are given (the formula is derived below). The pair \((\theta_2, \dot\theta_2)\) is therefore a complete set of coordinates on \(\Sigma\) (up to a two-fold ambiguity where both roots of the quadratic are positive; we then take the larger one, see below).


8.4 The Poincaré map
Start at a point \(z\) on \(\Sigma\), follow the flow, and stop when the trajectory comes back to \(\Sigma\) for the first time; call this time \(\tau(z)\), the return time. The point of return defines the Poincaré map \[P : \Sigma \to \Sigma, \qquad P(z) = \varphi_{\tau(z)}(z). \tag{37}\] A trajectory is thus turned into a sequence of points in a plane, \[z_{n+1} = P(z_n), \tag{38}\] a continuous flow in 4 dimensions is replaced by a discrete map in 2 dimensions, without losing information, because every \(z_n\) determines the whole trajectory through it.


8.5 Patterns on the section
Three kinds of motion leave three kinds of patterns. A periodic orbit that crosses \(\Sigma\) \(k\) times per period returns to the same \(k\) points: a fixed point of \(P^k\) (the map applied \(k\) times). Quasi-periodic motion combines two frequencies whose ratio is irrational; the trajectory then winds forever around a 2-dimensional torus in phase space without closing. (Each of the two oscillations is described by a phase angle that runs around a circle; the pair of angles lives on the surface of a doughnut, the torus.) The torus intersects \(\Sigma\) in a closed curve, and the points \(z_n\) fill this invariant curve densely. Chaotic motion lies on no torus; its points \(z_n\) scatter over a 2-dimensional region of \(\Sigma\).
For small oscillations the double pendulum is close to two coupled harmonic oscillators (Exercise 2), and all motion is quasi-periodic. With growing energy the nonlinearity grows; the Kolmogorov–Arnold–Moser (KAM) theorem states that most tori survive a weak perturbation but are progressively destroyed as it becomes stronger, leaving chains of islands (remnants of resonant tori) embedded in a chaotic sea. The four panels below show this sequence.


8.6 Coordinates on the section
For Hamiltonian systems (conservative systems without friction, such as all systems described by a Lagrangian of the form (2)) the Poincaré map preserves area, but in the canonical coordinates \((\theta_2, p_2)\), with the canonical momentum \[p_2 = \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot\theta_2} = \dot\theta_2 + \dot\theta_1\cos\theta_2 \quad\text{on }\Sigma \tag{39}\] (for unit masses and lengths; for a single particle this derivative is the ordinary momentum, equation (6)). We plot \((\theta_2, \dot\theta_2)\), which is more intuitive; it shows the same curves, islands and chaotic regions, but areas are slightly distorted.


8.7 Numerical detection of crossings
The integrator produces states \(z_n\) at the times \[t_n = n\,\Delta t . \tag{40}\] A crossing of \(\Sigma\) between steps \(n\) and \(n+1\) is detected by a sign change of the sine of the first angle while the rod points down, \[s = \sin\theta_1,\qquad s_n < 0 \le s_{n+1},\qquad \cos\theta_1 > 0 \tag{41}\] (the rod moves to the right; the condition on the cosine excludes the passage through the upright position, where the sine also changes sign). The sine is tested instead of \(\theta_1\) itself because the integrator does not reduce the angle to one period: after the first rod has gone over the top, \(\theta_1\) continues to \(2\pi, 4\pi, \dots\), and \(\sin\theta_1\) detects every passage through the downward vertical, modulo \(2\pi\). Within the step the motion is approximated by a straight line: the crossing happens at the fraction \[\beta = \frac{s_n}{s_n - s_{n+1}} \in (0, 1] \tag{42}\] of the step, and the state on \(\Sigma\) is estimated as \[z^\ast \approx z_n + \beta\,(z_{n+1} - z_n). \tag{43}\] The error of this linear interpolation is of order \(\Delta t^2\) (here the step is \(10^{-2}\) s). We measured it by locating the crossings exactly (by repeating the last step with an adjusted step size until the sine of the first angle vanishes): the typical error in \(\dot\theta_2\) is below \(10^{-3}\) rad/s and the largest about \(2\times10^{-2}\) rad/s, invisible on axes that span \(\pm 10\) rad/s. The angle \(\theta_2\) is brought back to \((-\pi, \pi]\) with np.arctan2(np.sin(th2), np.cos(th2)).


8.8 Initial conditions at fixed energy
Every trajectory starts on the section: set the first angle to zero, draw \(\theta_2\) and \(\dot\theta_2\) at random, and compute the positive \(\dot\theta_1\) from \(E\). For unit masses and lengths the energy on the section is \[E = \dot\theta_1^2 + \dot\theta_1\dot\theta_2\cos\theta_2 + \tfrac12\dot\theta_2^2 - 2g - g\cos\theta_2 , \tag{44}\] a quadratic equation for \(\dot\theta_1\), which SymPy confirms and solves.
\(\theta_2\) and \(\dot\theta_2\) are drawn at random, and a draw is rejected when no positive real \(\dot\theta_1\) gives the required energy (the energy is too low for these values); this is called rejection sampling. The kinetic part of equation (44) is smallest at \[\dot\theta_1 = -\tfrac12\dot\theta_2\cos\theta_2 , \tag{45}\] which gives \[E \ge \tfrac14\dot\theta_2^2(2 - \cos^2\theta_2) - 2g - g\cos\theta_2 \ge \tfrac14\dot\theta_2^2 - 3g , \tag{46}\] so on the section \[|\dot\theta_2| \le 2\sqrt{E + 3g}: \tag{47}\] 4.2 rad/s at the energy \(-25\) and 10.8 rad/s at zero energy. The sampling range \(\pm 10\) rad/s therefore covers almost the whole allowed region (at zero energy the narrow strips with \(|\dot\theta_2|\) between 10 and 10.8 rad/s are not sampled), and at low energy most draws are rejected (about 91 % at the energy \(-25\)). When both roots are positive, both give valid states with the same energy, and the larger one is taken by convention.


Code
q1s, q2s = dp["q"]; w1s, w2s = dp["w"]
E_sec = dp["E"].subs({**dict(zip(dp["m"], [1, 1])), **dict(zip(dp["l"], [1, 1]))}).subs(q1s, 0)
show(r"E\big|_{\theta_1 = 0} = ", sp.expand(sp.simplify(E_sec)))

E_sym = sp.symbols("E")
roots = sp.solve(sp.Eq(E_sec, E_sym), w1s)
show(r"\dot\theta_1 = ", roots[0], r"\quad\text{or}\quad", roots[1])
w1_of = sp.lambdify((q2s, w2s, E_sym, dp["g"]), roots, "numpy")     # both roots as NumPy functions


\(\displaystyle E\big|_{\theta_1 = 0} = - g \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} - 2 g + w_{1}^{2} + w_{1} w_{2} \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} + \frac{w_{2}^{2}}{2}\)


\(\displaystyle \dot\theta_1 = - \frac{w_{2} \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)}}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{4 E + 4 g \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} + 8 g - w_{2}^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(q_{2} \right)} - w_{2}^{2}}}{2} \quad\text{or}\quad - \frac{w_{2} \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)}}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{4 E + 4 g \cos{\left(q_{2} \right)} + 8 g - w_{2}^{2} \sin^{2}{\left(q_{2} \right)} - w_{2}^{2}}}{2}\)


poincare_sections integrates the trajectories of all requested energies as one batch (4 energies \(\times\) 30 trajectories = 120 columns), which costs little more than a single trajectory. For speed the step is \(10^{-2}\) s and the duration 100 s (10 000 steps, a few seconds); each trajectory then crosses the section about 50 times. The largest energy error at the end is printed in each panel title; T=300.0, dt=5e-3 (about a minute) gives denser and sharper pictures.


Code
def initial_conditions_on_section(E, n, rng, g=9.81):
    """n states with theta1 = 0, theta1_dot > 0 and energy E (m = l = 1)."""
    states = []
    while len(states) < n:
        th2, w2 = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi), rng.uniform(-10, 10)
        with np.errstate(invalid="ignore"):                 # sqrt of a negative number -> nan (energy not reachable)
            w1_candidates = np.array(w1_of(th2, w2, E, g), dtype=float)
        w1_ok = w1_candidates[np.isfinite(w1_candidates) & (w1_candidates > 0)]
        if w1_ok.size > 0:
            states.append([0.0, th2, w1_ok.max(), w2])       # if both roots are positive, take the larger one
    return np.array(states).T                               # shape (4, n): rows q1, q2, w1, w2

def poincare_sections(energies, n_traj=30, T=100.0, dt=1e-2, seed=0):
    """n_traj trajectories for each energy, all integrated as one batch; collect crossings of theta1 = 0 with theta1_dot > 0.
    Returns the points (column index, theta2, theta2_dot) and the largest energy error for each energy."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    s = np.hstack([initial_conditions_on_section(E, n_traj, rng) for E in energies])   # shape (4, n_energies * n_traj)
    E_target = np.repeat(energies, n_traj)                  # energy of every column
    q, w = s[:2], s[2:]
    points = []
    for _ in range(int(round(T / dt))):
        q_new, w_new = rk4_step(accel_dp, q, w, dt)
        # crossing: sin(theta1) changes sign from - to + while the rod points down (cos theta1 > 0)
        before, after = np.sin(q[0]), np.sin(q_new[0])
        crossed = (before < 0) & (after >= 0) & (np.cos(q_new[0]) > 0)
        if crossed.any():
            frac = before[crossed] / (before[crossed] - after[crossed])        # linear interpolation in time
            th2 = q[1, crossed] + frac * (q_new[1, crossed] - q[1, crossed])
            w2 = w[1, crossed] + frac * (w_new[1, crossed] - w[1, crossed])
            th2 = np.arctan2(np.sin(th2), np.cos(th2))                       # wrap the angle to (-pi, pi]
            points += list(zip(np.nonzero(crossed)[0], th2, w2))
        q, w = q_new, w_new
    dE = np.abs(energy_dp(q, w) - E_target).reshape(len(energies), n_traj).max(axis=1)
    return np.array(points), dE

print("minimum energy (both rods hanging down):", -3 * 9.81)


minimum energy (both rods hanging down): -29.43




8.9 Section and projection of a single trajectory
The difference between a projection and a section is clearest for one regular trajectory (energy \(-25\)) and one chaotic trajectory (zero energy), integrated together as a batch of two for 80 s with the step \(10^{-2}\) s. The left panels show the trajectory projected onto the plane \((\theta_2, \dot\theta_2)\) with the crossings of the section marked as dots; the right panels show the crossings alone.


Code
def single_trajectories_and_crossings(energies, T=80.0, dt=1e-2, seed=1):
    # one trajectory per energy, started on the section; returns the full paths and the section points of each
    s0 = np.hstack([initial_conditions_on_section(E, 1, np.random.default_rng(seed)) for E in energies])
    q, w = s0[:2].copy(), s0[2:].copy()                         # shapes (2, number of energies)
    path, crossings = [np.vstack([q, w])], [[] for _ in energies]
    for _ in range(int(round(T / dt))):
        q_new, w_new = rk4_step(accel_dp, q, w, dt)
        before, after = np.sin(q[0]), np.sin(q_new[0])
        for j in np.nonzero((before < 0) & (after >= 0) & (np.cos(q_new[0]) > 0))[0]:   # same condition as above
            frac = before[j] / (before[j] - after[j])
            crossings[j].append([q[1, j] + frac * (q_new[1, j] - q[1, j]), w[1, j] + frac * (w_new[1, j] - w[1, j])])
        q, w = q_new, w_new
        path.append(np.vstack([q, w]))
    return np.array(path), [np.array(c) for c in crossings]         # path: (steps, 4, number of energies)

paths, crossings = single_trajectories_and_crossings([-25.0, 0.0])
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 9))
for row, E in enumerate([-25.0, 0.0]):
    path, cross = paths[:, :, row], crossings[row]
    th2 = np.arctan2(np.sin(path[:, 1]), np.cos(path[:, 1]))        # theta2 wrapped to (-pi, pi]
    th2[1:][np.abs(np.diff(th2)) > np.pi] = np.nan                   # break the line where the angle jumps by 2 pi
    axes[row, 0].plot(th2, path[:, 3], color="0.75", lw=0.4)
    axes[row, 0].plot(np.arctan2(np.sin(cross[:, 0]), np.cos(cross[:, 0])), cross[:, 1], "o", color="C3", ms=3)
    axes[row, 0].set_title(f"E = {E:g}: projection of the whole trajectory (grey) and section points (red)", fontsize=9)
    axes[row, 1].plot(np.arctan2(np.sin(cross[:, 0]), np.cos(cross[:, 0])), cross[:, 1], "o", color="C3", ms=3)
    axes[row, 1].set_title(f"E = {E:g}: Poincaré section only ({len(cross)} points)", fontsize=9)
    for ax in axes[row]:
        ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_2$ [rad]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta_2$ [rad/s]")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





In the projection (left) the trajectory crosses itself everywhere, although in the 4D phase space it never does: the projection discards two coordinates. The section (right) keeps only the moments at which the state passes through the same surface, and there the structure is clear: for the regular trajectory the points line up on a closed curve (the cut through the torus on which the motion takes place), for the chaotic trajectory they scatter over an area. Each point of the section determines the next one (the Poincaré map), so the section is a 2D picture of the dynamics, not of a single moment.


8.10 Sections at four energies
Sections are computed at four energies, from slightly above the minimum \[E_{\min} = -3g \approx -29.4 \tag{48}\] to zero. For orientation: released from rest with both angles equal to \(\alpha\), the pendulum has the energy \[E = -3g\cos\alpha , \tag{49}\] so the energies \(-25\), \(-15\), \(-10\) and \(0\) correspond to \(\alpha\) of about \(32^\circ\), \(59^\circ\), \(70^\circ\) and \(90^\circ\) (both rods horizontal at zero energy). Each panel shows 30 trajectories, 100 s each, one colour per trajectory.


Code
energies = [-25.0, -15.0, -10.0, 0.0]
n_traj = 30
t0 = time.perf_counter()
pts, dE = poincare_sections(energies, n_traj=n_traj)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(20, 5))
for k, (ax, E) in enumerate(zip(axes, energies)):
    mine = (pts[:, 0] >= k * n_traj) & (pts[:, 0] < (k + 1) * n_traj)        # columns that belong to energy k
    ax.scatter(pts[mine, 1], pts[mine, 2], c=pts[mine, 0] % 20, cmap="tab20", vmin=0, vmax=19, s=1.0)
    ax.set_title(f"E = {E:g}   (energy error {dE[k]:.0e})", fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta_2$ [rad]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta_2$ [rad/s]")
fig.suptitle(r"Poincaré sections of the double pendulum: $\theta_1 = 0$, $\dot\theta_1 > 0$", y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
print(f"computed in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s")





computed in 5 s


At the energy \(-25\) (small oscillations) every trajectory draws a closed curve or a chain of small islands: the motion is regular. Near the minimum the double pendulum is close to two coupled harmonic oscillators (Exercise 2). At \(-15\) closed curves and chains of small islands coexist with regions of scattered points, a mixed phase space. At \(-10\) most of the section is a chaotic sea in which a few islands of regular motion survive, and at zero energy almost all initial conditions are chaotic.
The points fill a region whose outer edge is the edge of the energetically allowed part of \(\Sigma\). It is not symmetric under a change of sign of \(\dot\theta_2\), because \(\dot\theta_1\) must be positive: from the quadratic equation (44), for \(\theta_2\) of zero and the energy \(-25\) the allowed range of \(\dot\theta_2\) is from \(-4.2\) to \(3.0\) rad/s, in agreement with the vertical extent of the points in the first panel.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
9. A 5-link chain
For five links SymPy is skipped: the accelerations come from the Lagrangian alone, by autodiff. 20 chains are integrated at once, all released horizontally (all angles \(90^\circ\)), with the first angle of chain \(k\) shifted by \[\Delta\theta_1^{(k)} = k\times10^{-4}\ \text{rad},\qquad k = 0,\dots,19 . \tag{50}\]
accel_from_lagrangian of Section 5 is written for one state: one Hessian and one linear solve. vmap turns it into a function that processes a whole batch along the first axis, without rewriting it. This is exact but slow: every call of the torch.func transformations carries a fixed overhead of of order 10 ms (about 8 ms in the run of Section 5), and RK4 needs four calls per step, i.e. thousands of calls for one simulation. Long simulations therefore use a second, batched version, accel_batch, with torch.autograd.grad, which computes the same quantities with fewer and cheaper passes. The chains are independent, so the gradient of the sum of their Lagrangians with respect to q (shape (B, N)) contains \(\partial L_b/\partial q\) for every chain \(b\) at once; the same holds for qd. The function lagrangian_chain sums over the last axis, so it already returns the \(B\) Lagrangians of a batch. The option create_graph=True keeps the computational graph of these first derivatives, so that they can be differentiated once more. Differentiating \[S_i = \sum_b \frac{\partial L_b}{\partial\dot q_{b,i}} \tag{51}\] with respect to qd and q gives row \(i\) of \(M\) and row \(i\) of \(C\) for all chains, and \(N\) such passes give the whole matrices; retain_graph=True keeps the graph alive between the passes. Both versions agree, and their costs are compared.


Code
N_chain, n_copies = 5, 20
m_c, l_c, g_c = torch.ones(N_chain), torch.full((N_chain,), 0.4), 9.81
L_chain = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_chain(q, qd, m_c, l_c, g_c)

def accel_batch(L, q, qd):
    """Accelerations of B independent systems; q and qd have shape (B, N), L(q, qd) returns the B Lagrangians."""
    q = q.detach().requires_grad_(True)
    qd = qd.detach().requires_grad_(True)
    dL_dq, dL_dqd = torch.autograd.grad(L(q, qd).sum(), (q, qd), create_graph=True)
    M_rows, C_qd = [], []
    for i in range(q.shape[1]):
        # row i of M and of C, for all chains at once: derivatives of dL/dqd_i with respect to qd and q
        d_q, d_qd = torch.autograd.grad(dL_dqd[:, i].sum(), (q, qd), retain_graph=True)
        M_rows.append(d_qd)
        C_qd.append((d_q * qd).sum(dim=1))                  # (C qd)_i for every chain
    M, C_qd = torch.stack(M_rows, dim=1), torch.stack(C_qd, dim=1)       # shapes (B, N, N) and (B, N)
    return torch.linalg.solve(M, dL_dq - C_qd).detach()

# the torch.func version of Section 5, applied to a batch with vmap
accel_vmap = vmap(lambda q, qd: accel_from_lagrangian(L_chain, q, qd))

torch.manual_seed(0)
q_test, qd_test = 3 * torch.rand(n_copies, N_chain), torch.randn(n_copies, N_chain)     # random test states
print(f"max |accel_vmap - accel_batch| = {(accel_vmap(q_test, qd_test) - accel_batch(L_chain, q_test, qd_test)).abs().max():.1e}")
for name, f in [("vmap(accel_from_lagrangian)", lambda: accel_vmap(q_test, qd_test)),
                ("accel_batch", lambda: accel_batch(L_chain, q_test, qd_test))]:
    f()                                                     # warm-up call
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    for _ in range(10):
        f()
    print(f"{name:28s}: {1e3 * (time.perf_counter() - t0) / 10:.1f} ms per call for {n_copies} chains")


max |accel_vmap - accel_batch| = 3.6e-14
vmap(accel_from_lagrangian) : 9.7 ms per call for 20 chains
accel_batch                 : 1.4 ms per call for 20 chains


The simulation uses accel_batch. With rods of length 0.4 the chain has total length 2, the same as the double pendulum with unit rods, so the pictures have the same scale. The time step \(8\times10^{-3}\) s resolves the time scale of equation (29), here about 0.2 s, with 25 steps. The energy error at the end is printed; the chains start horizontally, where the energy is zero, so it is an absolute error, to be compared with the potential energy, which changes by up to about 60 during the motion. Halving the step reduces the error about 20 times (with twice the run time). The duration of 6 s is long enough for the chains to separate.


Code
def accel_chain(q, w):
    """NumPy wrapper with the (N, B) layout used by rk4_step (accel_batch uses (B, N), hence the transposes .T)."""
    return accel_batch(L_chain, torch.tensor(q.T), torch.tensor(w.T)).numpy().T

q = np.full((N_chain, n_copies), np.pi / 2)
q[0] += 1e-4 * np.arange(n_copies)                       # small differences in the first angle

dt, T_end = 8e-3, 6.0

snapshot_steps = [int(round(t / dt)) for t in (0, 2, 4, 6)]     # store the configuration at t = 0, 2, 4, 6 s
snapshots, frames_chain0 = {}, []
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for step in range(n_steps + 1):

    if step % 10 == 0:                                       # every 0.08 s: angles of chain 0, for the animation
        frames_chain0.append(q[:, 0].copy())
    if step < n_steps:
        q, w = rk4_step(accel_chain, q, w, dt)
E_end = energy_chain(torch.tensor(q.T), torch.tensor(w.T), m_c, l_c, g_c).numpy()
print(f"integration took {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s;  max energy error: {np.max(np.abs(E_end - E_start)):.1e}")

Compare with the double pendulum of Section 7, where a difference of \(10^{-9}\) needed about 19 s to become visible: here differences of \(10^{-4}\)–\(10^{-3}\) become visible after about 5 s. title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
10. Summary
SymPy works with symbols and provides simplify, diff, solve, Matrix, dsolve and lambdify. It gives exact formulas, but the expressions and the derivation time grow quickly with the size of the system. Lagrangian mechanics starts from the Lagrangian (2) in generalised coordinates and the Euler–Lagrange equations (3); for the \(N\)-link pendulum these take the form of equation (15).
With automatic differentiation the accelerations follow from equation (22), with \(M\) the Hessian of \(L\) with respect to the velocities, and only \(L\) has to be written; the result agrees with SymPy to \(10^{-13}\). The equations are integrated with RK4, whose error scales as \(\Delta t^4\), and energy conservation serves as a test of the integration. The dynamics shows exponential separation of nearby trajectories (the Lyapunov exponent), and Poincaré sections show the transition from regular to chaotic motion with growing energy.

title: Lab 005: The N-link pendulum with SymPy and automatic differentiation
text:
11. Exercises

Exercise 1 — The elastic pendulum
Replace the rigid rod of the single pendulum by a spring of stiffness \(k\) and rest length \(l_0\). The generalised coordinates are the length \(r\) and the angle \(\varphi\): \[L = \tfrac12 m\big(\dot r^2 + r^2\dot\varphi^2\big) + m g\, r\cos\varphi - \tfrac12 k\,(r - l_0)^2 . \tag{53}\] 1. Derive the two Euler–Lagrange equations with SymPy and solve them for \(\ddot r\) and \(\ddot\varphi\). 2. Write the same Lagrangian as a PyTorch function of q = (r, phi), qd = (r_dot, phi_dot) and check that accel_from_lagrangian gives the same accelerations at a few random states. 3. Simulate the system with \[m=1,\quad k=40,\quad l_0=1,\quad g=9.81,\qquad r(0)=1.2,\quad \varphi(0)=0.6, \tag{54}\] starting at rest, for 20 s (time step \(2\times10^{-3}\) s) with the SymPy accelerations. Plot the path of the mass in the \((x, y)\) plane and check energy conservation.
With these values the spring and the pendulum, whose length at equilibrium is \(l_{\rm eq}\), oscillate with \[\omega_{\rm spring} = \sqrt{k/m} \approx 6.3\ \text{rad/s},\qquad l_{\rm eq} = l_0 + \frac{mg}{k} \approx 1.25,\qquad \omega_{\rm pend} = \sqrt{g/l_{\rm eq}} \approx 2.8\ \text{rad/s}; \tag{55}\] the two motions have comparable frequencies and are coupled, so the mass does not move on a simple arc but traces loops.

Solution


Code
# 1) SymPy derivation
t = sp.symbols("t", real=True)
m, g, k, l0 = sp.symbols("m g k l_0", positive=True)
r = sp.Function("r")(t); phi = sp.Function("varphi")(t)
L_el = (sp.Rational(1, 2) * m * (sp.diff(r, t)**2 + r**2 * sp.diff(phi, t)**2)
        + m * g * r * sp.cos(phi) - sp.Rational(1, 2) * k * (r - l0)**2)
EL = [sp.diff(sp.diff(L_el, sp.diff(c, t)), t) - sp.diff(L_el, c) for c in (r, phi)]
sol = sp.solve(EL, [sp.diff(r, t, 2), sp.diff(phi, t, 2)], dict=True)[0]
r_dd, phi_dd = sp.simplify(sol[sp.diff(r, t, 2)]), sp.simplify(sol[sp.diff(phi, t, 2)])
show(r"\ddot r = ", r_dd)
show(r"\ddot\varphi = ", phi_dd)

# replace functions by plain symbols, then lambdify with the parameters fixed
R, P, Rd, Pd = sp.symbols("R P R_d P_d")
to_plain = lambda e: e.subs({sp.diff(r, t): Rd, sp.diff(phi, t): Pd}).subs({r: R, phi: P})
par = {m: 1.0, g: 9.81, k: 40.0, l0: 1.0}
acc_r = sp.lambdify((R, P, Rd, Pd), to_plain(r_dd).subs(par), "numpy")
acc_p = sp.lambdify((R, P, Rd, Pd), to_plain(phi_dd).subs(par), "numpy")
def accel_elastic(q, w):
    return np.array([acc_r(q[0], q[1], w[0], w[1]), acc_p(q[0], q[1], w[0], w[1])])

# 2) the same Lagrangian for autodiff (r = q[0], phi = q[1])
def L_elastic_torch(q, qd, m=1.0, g=9.81, k=40.0, l0=1.0):
    return 0.5 * m * (qd[0]**2 + q[0]**2 * qd[1]**2) + m * g * q[0] * torch.cos(q[1]) - 0.5 * k * (q[0] - l0)**2

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
for _ in range(3):
    q = np.array([rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5), rng.uniform(-1, 1)]); w = rng.uniform(-2, 2, 2)
    a_ad = accel_from_lagrangian(L_elastic_torch, torch.tensor(q), torch.tensor(w)).numpy()
    print("SymPy:", accel_elastic(q, w), "  autodiff:", a_ad)

# 3) simulation and energy check
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_elastic, [1.2, 0.6], [0.0, 0.0], T=20.0, dt=2e-3)
E = 0.5 * (W[:, 0]**2 + Q[:, 0]**2 * W[:, 1]**2) - 9.81 * Q[:, 0] * np.cos(Q[:, 1]) + 0.5 * 40 * (Q[:, 0] - 1)**2
print(f"relative energy drift: {np.max(np.abs(E - E[0])) / abs(E[0]):.1e}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5, 5))
ax.plot(Q[:, 0] * np.sin(Q[:, 1]), -Q[:, 0] * np.cos(Q[:, 1]), lw=0.6)
ax.plot(0, 0, "ks"); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$")
ax.set_title("elastic pendulum: path of the mass"); plt.show()


\(\displaystyle \ddot r = \frac{k l_{0} - k r{\left(t \right)} + m \left(g \cos{\left(\varphi{\left(t \right)} \right)} + r{\left(t \right)} \left(\frac{d}{d t} \varphi{\left(t \right)}\right)^{2}\right)}{m}\)


\(\displaystyle \ddot\varphi = - \frac{g \sin{\left(\varphi{\left(t \right)} \right)} + 2 \frac{d}{d t} r{\left(t \right)} \frac{d}{d t} \varphi{\left(t \right)}}{r{\left(t \right)}}\)


SymPy: [ 8.87665341 -2.55120653]   autodiff: [ 8.87665341 -2.55120653]
SymPy: [17.32871922  3.01864123]   autodiff: [17.32871922  3.01864123]
SymPy: [3.78776318 7.27982747]   autodiff: [3.78776318 7.27982747]


relative energy drift: 2.2e-11








Exercise 2 — Normal modes of the N-link pendulum
For small oscillations around the rest position the Lagrangian is quadratic, \[L \approx \tfrac12\dot q^{\top} M_0\,\dot q - \tfrac12 q^{\top} K q , \tag{56}\] with \[M_0 = \frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial\dot q\,\partial\dot q}\Big|_{0},\qquad K = -\frac{\partial^2 L}{\partial q\,\partial q}\Big|_{0}. \tag{57}\] The Euler–Lagrange equations of this quadratic Lagrangian are linear, \[M_0\ddot q = -K q . \tag{58}\] Inserting the ansatz \[q(t) = v\cos\omega t , \tag{59}\] in which all angles oscillate with one frequency and fixed amplitude ratios \(v\), gives \[-\omega^2 M_0 v\cos\omega t = -K v\cos\omega t , \tag{60}\] so the normal modes solve the generalised eigenvalue problem \[K v = \omega^2 M_0 v . \tag{61}\] 1. For two links of equal mass \(m\) and length \(l\), compute \(M_0\) and \(K\) with SymPy (from dp["M"] and the energy) and show that \[\omega^2 = \frac{g}{l}\big(2\mp\sqrt2\big). \tag{62}\] 2. Compute \(M_0\) and \(K\) by autodiff (hessian of lagrangian_chain) for two links and check the numbers; then for five links (unit masses, lengths 0.4) compute all frequencies with scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0) and draw the five mode shapes. scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0) solves the generalised eigenvalue problem (61) for a symmetric \(K\) and a positive-definite \(M_0\); it returns the values \(\omega^2\) in increasing order and the vectors \(v\) as the columns of a matrix. In SymPy, sp.hessian(V, q) builds the matrix of second derivatives \(\partial^2 V/\partial q_i\,\partial q_j\). 3. Start the double pendulum (unit masses and lengths) at rest in the slow mode with amplitude 0.01 rad. Check by simulation that the ratio of the two angles stays constant and that the period is \[T_1 = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_1}. \tag{63}\]

Solution


Code
import scipy.linalg

# 1) SymPy, N = 2 with equal masses and lengths
msym, lsym = sp.symbols("m l", positive=True)
eq_par = {dp["m"][0]: msym, dp["m"][1]: msym, dp["l"][0]: lsym, dp["l"][1]: lsym}
zero = {qq: 0 for qq in dp["q"]}
M0_sym = dp["M"].subs(eq_par).subs(zero)
V_sym = dp["E"].subs({ww: 0 for ww in dp["w"]}).subs(eq_par)            # energy at rest = potential energy
K_sym = sp.hessian(V_sym, dp["q"]).subs(zero)                           # K = d^2 V / dq dq at q = 0
show(r"M_0 = ", M0_sym, r",\quad K = ", K_sym)
omega2 = sp.Symbol("omega^2")
roots = sp.solve(sp.det(K_sym - omega2 * M0_sym), omega2)              # det(K - w^2 M0) = 0
show(r"\omega^2 = ", [sp.simplify(rt) for rt in roots])

# 2) autodiff: M0 = d^2L/dqd dqd, K = -d^2L/dq dq, both at q = qd = 0
def M0_K(N, m_vals, l_vals, g=9.81):
    L = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_chain(q, qd, torch.tensor(m_vals), torch.tensor(l_vals), g)
    z = torch.zeros(N)
    return hessian(L, argnums=1)(z, z).numpy(), -hessian(L, argnums=0)(z, z).numpy()

M0, K = M0_K(2, [1.0, 1.0], [1.0, 1.0])
omega_sq2, modes2 = scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0)                              # generalised eigenproblem: omega^2 and modes
print("autodiff N=2: omega^2 =", omega_sq2, "  exact:", 9.81 * (2 - np.sqrt(2)), 9.81 * (2 + np.sqrt(2)))

M0, K = M0_K(5, [1.0] * 5, [0.4] * 5)
omega_sq5, modes5 = scipy.linalg.eigh(K, M0)
print("N=5 frequencies omega [rad/s]:", np.sqrt(omega_sq5).round(3))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(16, 4), sharey=True)
for j, ax in enumerate(axes):
    v = modes5[:, j] / np.max(np.abs(modes5[:, j])) * 0.3                # small angles, scaled for display
    X = np.r_[0, np.cumsum(0.4 * np.sin(v))]; Y = np.r_[0, -np.cumsum(0.4 * np.cos(v))]
    ax.plot(X, Y, "-o"); ax.plot(0, 0, "ks"); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.set_xlim(-0.6, 0.6)
    ax.set_title(rf"mode {j+1}, $\omega$ = {np.sqrt(omega_sq5[j]):.2f} rad/s")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

# 3) simulation in the slow mode of the double pendulum (m = l = 1)
v1 = modes2[:, 0] / modes2[0, 0]                                          # normalise so that theta1 component = 1
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_dp, 0.01 * v1, [0.0, 0.0], T=10.0, dt=4e-3)    # small oscillations: a larger step is accurate
ratio = Q[:, 1] / Q[:, 0]
ok = np.abs(Q[:, 0]) > 2e-3                                               # avoid dividing by values near zero
print(f"theta2/theta1: expected {v1[1]:.4f}, observed between {ratio[ok].min():.4f} and {ratio[ok].max():.4f}")
up = np.nonzero((Q[:-1, 0] < 0) & (Q[1:, 0] >= 0))[0]                     # upward zero crossings of theta1
print(f"period: measured {np.mean(np.diff(t_arr[up])):.4f} s, 2pi/omega_1 = {2 * np.pi / np.sqrt(omega_sq2[0]):.4f} s")

Exercise 3 — The largest Lyapunov exponent
The fit in Section 7 is rough. A standard method (Benettin et al., 1980): follow a reference trajectory \(A\) and a neighbour \(B\) at the distance \(d_0\), here \(10^{-8}\); after every interval \(\tau\) measure their distance \(d\), add \(\ln(d/d_0)\) to a running sum, and move \(B\) back to distance \(d_0\) along the line joining it with \(A\). For the total time \(T\) the exponent is then \[\lambda \approx \frac{1}{T}\sum \ln\frac{d}{d_0}. \tag{64}\] The resetting keeps the separation small, so that it always grows at the exponential rate and never saturates. \(d_0\) must be small enough that the separation stays in this linear regime during one interval, yet far above the rounding level \(10^{-16}\); \(\tau\) must be short enough that \(d\) grows only by a modest factor within it (the factor \(e^{\lambda\tau}\) is about 1.1 for \(\lambda\) of about 1 s\(^{-1}\) and \(\tau\) of 0.1 s). For this system, \(d_0\) between \(10^{-9}\) and \(10^{-7}\) and \(\tau\) between 0.05 and 1 s give the same \(\lambda\) to three digits (checked for release from rest with both angles \(90^\circ\) and with both \(130^\circ\)). 1. Implement the method for the double pendulum (unit masses and lengths) with \(\tau\) of 0.1 s, a total time of 50 s and the time step \(10^{-2}\) s. (These values keep the run at a few seconds; 200 s and the step \(5\times10^{-3}\) s give better converged estimates.) 2. Start from rest with both angles equal to \(\alpha\), for \(\alpha\) from \(10^\circ\) to \(150^\circ\) in steps of \(20^\circ\), and plot \(\lambda(\alpha)\). Integrate all angles as one batch. 3. Where does chaos set in? Compare with the Poincaré sections (compute the energy for each \(\alpha\)).

Solution


Code
alphas = np.deg2rad(np.arange(10, 151, 20))
n = alphas.size
d0, tau, T_total, dt = 1e-8, 0.1, 50.0, 1e-2
steps_per_tau = int(round(tau / dt))

# reference trajectories A and perturbed trajectories B, all in one batch of 2n states
qA = np.vstack([alphas, alphas]); wA = np.zeros((2, n))
qB = qA + np.array([[d0], [0.0]]);  wB = wA.copy()
q = np.hstack([qA, qB]); w = np.hstack([wA, wB])          # shape (2, 2n): columns 0..n-1 = A, n..2n-1 = B

log_sum = np.zeros(n)
for _ in range(int(T_total / tau)):
    for _ in range(steps_per_tau):
        q, w = rk4_step(accel_dp, q, w, dt)
    # distance between A and B in the 4D phase space
    dq, dw = q[:, n:] - q[:, :n], w[:, n:] - w[:, :n]
    d = np.sqrt(np.sum(dq**2 + dw**2, axis=0))
    log_sum += np.log(d / d0)
    # renormalise: put B back at distance d0 from A, in the same direction
    q[:, n:] = q[:, :n] + dq * d0 / d
    w[:, n:] = w[:, :n] + dw * d0 / d
lyap = log_sum / T_total

E_alpha = energy_dp(np.vstack([alphas, alphas]), np.zeros((2, n)))
for a, E, lam in zip(np.rad2deg(alphas), E_alpha, lyap):
    print(f"alpha = {a:5.0f} deg   E = {E:7.2f}   lambda = {lam:.3f} 1/s")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
ax.plot(np.rad2deg(alphas), lyap, "o-")
ax.set_xlabel(r"initial angle $\alpha$ [deg]"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\lambda$ [1/s]")
plt.show()
# Up to alpha = 70 deg (E <= -10) the estimates are small (below 0.1 1/s); at alpha = 90 deg (E = 0) and above
# lambda is of order 1 1/s: the motion is chaotic. Along this family of initial conditions chaos therefore sets in
# between 70 and 90 deg. Small non-zero values do not prove chaos: for regular motion the finite-time estimate
# decreases roughly like ln(T)/T. Repeating the calculation with larger T distinguishes the two cases.
# The Poincaré section at E = -10 contains both regular islands and a chaotic sea, so at that energy the answer
# depends on the initial condition, not only on the energy.

Exercise 4 (advanced) — A pendulum made of rigid rods
Replace the point masses by uniform rigid rods of mass \(m_k\) and length \(l_k\) (no point masses). The kinetic energy of rod \(k\) is the energy of its centre of mass plus the rotational energy about it: \[T_k = \tfrac12 m_k |\mathbf v_{\mathrm{cm},k}|^2 + \tfrac12\,\frac{m_k l_k^2}{12}\,\dot\theta_k^2, \tag{65}\] \[\mathbf r_{\mathrm{cm},k} = \mathbf r_{\mathrm{joint},k-1} + \tfrac12 l_k(\sin\theta_k, -\cos\theta_k), \tag{66}\] and \[V = g\sum_k m_k y_{\mathrm{cm},k} . \tag{67}\] 1. Write lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m, l, g) in PyTorch (hint: the velocity of joint \(k-1\) is the cumulative sum up to \(k\) minus the term of rod \(k\)). 2. For one rod the exact equation is \[\ddot\theta = -\frac{3g}{2l}\sin\theta . \tag{68}\] Check accel_from_lagrangian against it at random states. For the derivation: the moment of inertia of a uniform rod about its centre is \(ml^2/12\); about the pivot it is, by the parallel-axis theorem, \[I = \frac{ml^2}{12} + m\Big(\frac l2\Big)^2 = \frac{ml^2}{3}. \tag{69}\] The gravitational torque is \(-mg\,(l/2)\sin\theta\), and \[\frac{ml^2}{3}\ddot\theta = -\frac{mgl}{2}\sin\theta . \tag{70}\] 3. Simulate a double rod pendulum (unit masses and lengths) from rest with both angles \(90^\circ\) for 3 s (time step \(10^{-2}\) s) with autodiff accelerations (accel_batch of Section 9, with a batch of one), and check energy conservation. Nothing except the Lagrangian has to be changed. Writing all sums over the last axis (dim=-1) makes the functions work for single states and for batches.

Solution


Code
def rod_kinematics(q, qd, l):
    """Centre-of-mass positions and velocities of a chain of uniform rods."""
    # joint velocities: cumulative sums over the last axis, as for the point-mass chain
    jvx = torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q) * qd, dim=-1)
    jvy = torch.cumsum(l * torch.sin(q) * qd, dim=-1)
    jy = -torch.cumsum(l * torch.cos(q), dim=-1)
    # velocity/position of the joint ABOVE rod k = cumulative sum minus the term of rod k itself
    prev_vx = jvx - l * torch.cos(q) * qd
    prev_vy = jvy - l * torch.sin(q) * qd
    prev_y = jy + l * torch.cos(q)
    # centre of mass: half-way along rod k
    vcx = prev_vx + 0.5 * l * torch.cos(q) * qd
    vcy = prev_vy + 0.5 * l * torch.sin(q) * qd
    ycm = prev_y - 0.5 * l * torch.cos(q)
    return vcx, vcy, ycm

def lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m, l, g):
    vcx, vcy, ycm = rod_kinematics(q, qd, l)
    T = 0.5 * torch.sum(m * (vcx**2 + vcy**2), dim=-1) + 0.5 * torch.sum(m * l**2 / 12 * qd**2, dim=-1)
    V = g * torch.sum(m * ycm, dim=-1)
    return T - V

def energy_rods(q, qd, m, l, g):
    vcx, vcy, ycm = rod_kinematics(q, qd, l)
    return (0.5 * torch.sum(m * (vcx**2 + vcy**2), dim=-1) + 0.5 * torch.sum(m * l**2 / 12 * qd**2, dim=-1)
            + g * torch.sum(m * ycm, dim=-1))

# 2) single rod: compare with the exact theta'' = -(3g/2l) sin(theta)
m1t, l1t = torch.tensor([1.0]), torch.tensor([0.7])
L1 = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m1t, l1t, 9.81)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)
err = 0.0
for _ in range(20):
    th, om = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi), rng.uniform(-5, 5)
    a = accel_from_lagrangian(L1, torch.tensor([th]), torch.tensor([om])).item()
    err = max(err, abs(a - (-1.5 * 9.81 / 0.7 * np.sin(th))))
print(f"single rod: max |autodiff - exact| = {err:.1e}")

# 3) double rod pendulum with autodiff accelerations only
m2t, l2t = torch.ones(2), torch.ones(2)
L2 = lambda q, qd: lagrangian_rods(q, qd, m2t, l2t, 9.81)
def accel_rods(q, w):
    # one state of shape (N,) -> a batch of one, shape (1, N), for accel_batch, and back
    return accel_batch(L2, torch.tensor(q)[None], torch.tensor(w)[None])[0].numpy()

t0 = time.perf_counter()
t_arr, Q, W = simulate(accel_rods, [np.pi / 2, np.pi / 2], [0.0, 0.0], T=3.0, dt=1e-2)
E = energy_rods(torch.tensor(Q), torch.tensor(W), m2t, l2t, 9.81).numpy()       # all time steps at once (batch)
print(f"simulated in {time.perf_counter() - t0:.0f} s;  max |E(t) - E(0)| = {np.max(np.abs(E - E[0])):.1e}  (E(0) = {E[0]:.3f})")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(t_arr, Q[:, 0], label=r"$\theta_1$"); ax.plot(t_arr, Q[:, 1], label=r"$\theta_2$")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$ [s]"); ax.set_ylabel("angle [rad]"); ax.legend(); ax.set_title("double pendulum of rigid rods (autodiff only)")
plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
1. Target function and dataset
We use the example from the Lecture Notes, \[g(x) = x^2\sin(\pi x) - \frac{1}{2+\cos x}, \qquad x\in[-2, 2], \tag{4}\] and a training set \[\mathcal D = \{(x_k, g(x_k))\}_{k=1}^{K} \tag{5}\] of \(K\) points \(x_k\), 100 of them, drawn at random (uniformly) from the interval. We deliberately do not use an equally spaced grid: in real experiments and simulations the sampling points are rarely regular, and a fit should be judged on how well it reproduces \(g\) between the sampling points. Therefore all fits are plotted on a separate dense grid x_plot.
The number of points follows from the size of the networks below, which have a few tens of parameters (30 for 10 neurons), and the number of data points should be several times larger than the number of parameters, otherwise the data do not determine the fit. Any \(K\) of order 100 serves the purpose. The seed 2026 of the random generator fixes the points, so that every run of the notebook gives the same numbers; its value is arbitrary (the same holds for all other seeds in this notebook).


Code
def g(x):
    """Target function from the Lecture Notes (Chapter 2)."""
    return x**2 * np.sin(np.pi * x) - 1.0 / (2.0 + np.cos(x))

K = 100
rng_data = np.random.default_rng(2026)
x_train = np.sort(rng_data.uniform(-2, 2, K))     # random, non-equidistant sampling points (sorted for convenience)
y_train = g(x_train)
x_plot = np.linspace(-2, 2, 1000)                 # dense grid, used only for plotting and for judging fits

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(x_plot, g(x_plot), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
ax.plot(x_train, y_train, "o", color="C3", ms=4, label=f"{K} random sampling points")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend()
plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
2. Building blocks

2.1 One neuron
A single hidden neuron contributes \(W^{(2)}\tanh(W^{(1)}x + b)\). The weight \(W^{(1)}\) sets the steepness, the ratio \(-b/W^{(1)}\) sets the position of the step, and \(W^{(2)}\) sets its height.
In the plotting code the labels are f-strings that contain LaTeX. Inside an f-string single braces {w} insert the value of a variable, so a literal brace, needed for the LaTeX superscript W^{(1)}, is written twice: f"$W^{{(1)}} = {w}$" produces the text $W^{(1)} = 0.5$.


Code
x = np.linspace(-3, 3, 400)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
for w in [0.5, 1, 3, 10]:
    axes[0].plot(x, np.tanh(w * x), label=f"$W^{{(1)}} = {w}$")
for b in [-2, 0, 2]:
    axes[1].plot(x, np.tanh(3 * x + b), label=f"$b = {b}$  (step at $x = {-b/3:.2f}$)")
axes[0].set_title(r"$\tanh(W^{(1)} x)$: steepness"); axes[1].set_title(r"$\tanh(3x + b)$: position")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()







2.2 Two neurons make a bump
The difference of two shifted steps is a localised bump: \[\tfrac12\big[\tanh(s(x - a)) - \tanh(s(x - c))\big] \approx \begin{cases} 1, & a < x < c, \\ 0, & \text{elsewhere.}\end{cases} \tag{6}\] A sum of such bumps with suitable heights can follow any continuous curve — this is the intuition behind the UAT. Each \(\tanh\) goes from \(-1\) to \(+1\), i.e. changes by 2 across its step; the difference of two steps therefore has height 2, and the factor \(\tfrac12\) normalises the bump to height 1. The values of \(s\), \(a\) and \(c\) below (8, \(-0.5\) and 1) are arbitrary illustration values.


Code
s, a, c = 8.0, -0.5, 1.0
step1, step2 = np.tanh(s * (x - a)), np.tanh(s * (x - c))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.8))
ax.plot(x, step1, "--", label=r"$\tanh(s(x-a))$")
ax.plot(x, -step2, "--", label=r"$-\tanh(s(x-c))$")
ax.plot(x, 0.5 * (step1 - step2), "k", lw=2.5, label="half of the sum: a bump on $[a, c]$")
ax.set_xlabel("$x$"); ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.show()

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
text:
3. A constructive approximation (no optimisation)
Divide \([-2,2]\) into \(N\) intervals with ordered nodes \(x_0, x_1, \dots, x_N\). A staircase that jumps by \(g(x_j) - g(x_{j-1})\) at the midpoint \(m_j\) of each interval is \[f_N(x) = g(x_0) + \sum_{j=1}^{N}\big[g(x_j) - g(x_{j-1})\big]\;\frac{1 + \tanh\big(s\,(x - m_j)\big)}{2}. \tag{7}\] The function \(\tfrac12\big(1+\tanh(s(x-m_j))\big)\) is a smooth step that goes from 0 far to the left of \(m_j\) to 1 far to the right of it, so each term adds the jump \(g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})\) once \(x\) has passed \(m_j\). This is a one-hidden-layer network with \(N\) neurons (plus a constant). We choose all parameters ourselves: \[W^{(1)}_j = s, \qquad b_j = -s\, m_j, \qquad W^{(2)}_j = \tfrac12\,[g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})] . \tag{8}\] The factor \(\tfrac12\) in \(W^{(2)}_j\) comes from \[\tfrac12(1+\tanh z) = \tfrac12 + \tfrac12\tanh z : \tag{9}\] each term is half a jump times \(\tanh\), plus half a jump as a constant. All these constants add up to the constant of the network, \[g(x_0) + \tfrac12\sum_j[g(x_j)-g(x_{j-1})] = \tfrac12[g(x_0)+g(x_N)] . \tag{10}\] As \(N\) grows without bound (with \(s\) growing so that steps stay sharp) the error goes to zero — a constructive version of the theorem.
Two details of the code concern the steepness and broadcasting. The intervals have width \(h\) and we take the steepness \(s\) as \[h = 4/N, \qquad s = 4N, \qquad s\,h = 16 : \tag{11}\] each step rises from 0 to 1 within a small fraction of its interval, and the network is a genuine staircase. The factor 4 is arbitrary. Smaller factors make neighbouring steps overlap; the sum then becomes a smoother interpolation and is in fact somewhat more accurate (with factor 1 the error for 64 neurons and more is about 2.5 times smaller), but the sharp version shows the construction better.
Indexing with None adds an axis of length 1: x[:, None] is a column of shape \((K, 1)\) and mids[None, :] a row of shape \((1, N)\). Their difference is broadcast to a \((K, N)\) table whose entry \((k, j)\) is \(x_k - m_j\), i.e. neuron \(j\) evaluated at point \(k\). The product hidden @ jumps then sums over the neurons.


Code
def staircase(x, N, steepness_factor=4.0):
    """Explicitly constructed one-hidden-layer tanh network approximating g with N neurons."""
    nodes = np.linspace(-2, 2, N + 1)
    mids = 0.5 * (nodes[1:] + nodes[:-1])
    jumps = g(nodes[1:]) - g(nodes[:-1])
    s = steepness_factor * N                       # steps get sharper as intervals shrink
    hidden = 0.5 * (1 + np.tanh(s * (x[:, None] - mids[None, :])))   # shape (len(x), N)
    return g(nodes[0]) + hidden @ jumps

x_fine = np.linspace(-2, 2, 2000)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4))
axes[0].plot(x_fine, g(x_fine), "k", lw=2, label="$g(x)$")
for N in [5, 10, 40]:
    axes[0].plot(x_fine, staircase(x_fine, N), label=f"$N = {N}$")
axes[0].set_xlabel("$x$"); axes[0].legend()

Ns = np.array([4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512])
sup_err = [np.max(np.abs(staircase(x_fine, N) - g(x_fine))) for N in Ns]
axes[1].loglog(Ns, sup_err, "o-", label=r"$\max_x |f_N(x) - g(x)|$")
axes[1].loglog(Ns, 20 / Ns, "k--", label=r"$\propto 1/N$")   # guide line; the prefactor 20 only places it near the points
axes[1].set_xlabel("number of neurons $N$"); axes[1].set_ylabel("sup error"); axes[1].legend()
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The construction works but is inefficient: the error decreases only like \(1/N\), and it needs \(g\) at equally spaced nodes of our choice. The \(1/N\) law follows from the shape of a staircase: within one interval it is (nearly) constant, while \(g\) changes by up to \(|g'|_{\max}\,h\), with \(h\) from equation (11). The error is therefore at most about half of such a change, \[\tfrac12|g'|_{\max}\cdot 4/N \approx 26/N , \qquad |g'|_{\max}\approx 12.9 \ \text{on}\ [-2,2] ; \tag{12}\] the measured error is about \(18/N\) for large \(N\). In practice the sampling points are given, and a minimiser has to choose all \(3N\) parameters, including the positions of the steps. Section 7 shows that an optimised network with about 8 neurons is more accurate than the staircase with 512 neurons.

title: Lab 006: Universal approximation and the choice of minimiser
section: 4. Loss function of the parameter vector
text:
4. Loss function of the parameter vector
Most minimisers (in particular scipy.optimize.minimize) work with a flat vector \(\vec\theta\) of \(3N\) parameters. We store \[\vec\theta = (W^{(1)}_1,\dots,W^{(1)}_N,\; b_1,\dots,b_N,\; W^{(2)}_1,\dots,W^{(2)}_N) \tag{13}\] and unpack it inside the model.
In the model, np.outer(x, W1) is the \(K\times N\) matrix with entries \(x_k W^{(1)}_i\). Adding the length-\(N\) vector b adds \(b_i\) to every entry of column \(i\) (broadcasting), so entry \((k, i)\) of the table is the argument of neuron \(i\) at point \(k\). Multiplying by W2 with @ sums the neurons with their output weights.
The random initial parameters are not arbitrary in their order of magnitude. We draw \[W^{(1)}_i,\ b_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 2^2), \qquad W^{(2)}_i \sim \mathcal N(0, 1/N) . \tag{14}\] On \([-2,2]\) a neuron \(\tanh(W^{(1)}x+b)\) is a step at the position \(-b/W^{(1)}\) of width about \(1/|W^{(1)}|\). Values of order 2 give steps that are narrower than the interval and positions \(-b/W^{(1)}\) that are of order 1, i.e. mostly inside the interval. Much smaller values give nearly linear neurons, much larger values give very sharp steps with vanishing slope almost everywhere. The output weights are drawn with variance \(1/N\). The output is a sum of \(N\) terms of random sign, so its variance is \(N\cdot\mathrm{Var}(W^{(2)})\) times a number of order 1. With the variance \(1/N\) of equation (14) the initial \(f(x)\) is of order 1, comparable to \(g\), for every \(N\) (the standard deviation of \(W^{(2)}\) scales as \(1/\sqrt N\)).
Ten neurons (30 parameters) are small enough for the gradient-free methods and the finite-difference gradients below to finish in seconds, and large enough for a good fit.


Code
def unpack(theta):
    """Split the flat parameter vector into (W1, b, W2), each of length N."""
    N = theta.size // 3                         # // is integer division: 30 // 3 = 10 (an integer, usable as an index)
    return theta[:N], theta[N:2 * N], theta[2 * N:]

def model(theta, x):
    """f(x; theta) = sum_i W2_i tanh(W1_i x + b_i), evaluated for all x at once."""
    W1, b, W2 = unpack(theta)
    hidden = np.tanh(np.outer(x, W1) + b)       # shape (K, N): neuron i evaluated at point k
    return hidden @ W2                          # shape (K,)

def loss(theta, x=x_train, y=y_train):
    """Mean squared error on the training set."""
    return np.mean((model(theta, x) - y)**2)

def init_theta(N, seed):
    """Random initial parameters: input weights and biases ~ N(0, 2^2), output weights ~ N(0, 1/N)."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    # np.concatenate joins the three length-N arrays into one flat vector of length 3N
    return np.concatenate([rng.normal(0, 2, N), rng.normal(0, 2, N), rng.normal(0, 1, N) / np.sqrt(N)])

N = 10
theta0 = init_theta(N, seed=0)        # ONE common starting point for all minimisers below
print("number of parameters:", theta0.size, "  initial loss:", loss(theta0))


number of parameters: 30   initial loss: 1.0398383815103345


The network whose 30 parameters are chosen by the minimisers has one input \(x\), one hidden layer of 10 neurons with \(\tanh\), and one output \(f(x)\) that sums the hidden neurons with the weights \(W^{(2)}_i\) (this network has no output bias). Each line from the input to hidden neuron \(i\) carries the weight \(W^{(1)}_i\), and the neuron adds its bias \(b_i\); each line from neuron \(i\) to the output carries \(W^{(2)}_i\).
draw_network is the drawing function used for network diagrams throughout the course. It draws a dense network as columns of circles, one column per layer and one circle per neuron, and joins every circle with every circle of the next column by a thin grey line, one line per weight. The height of a column grows with the logarithm of the layer size, so that a wide layer looks taller than a narrow one and a network that compresses its input visibly narrows. A layer with more neurons than max_nodes is drawn with its first and last few neurons and a vertical ellipsis in between; its true size is always written under the column. The colours follow one convention in all notebooks: grey for the data at the input and at the output, blue for hidden layers, orange for a latent (bottleneck) layer and green for an additional input such as a class label.
To draw your own network, pass the list of layer sizes from the input to the output, for example draw_network([784, 128, 64, 10]), and, if you wish, a list of names (labels) and of colours (colors) with one entry per column. An entry of layer_sizes can itself be a list, such as [16, 16], which stacks two blocks in one column; groups draws a bracket with a name above a range of columns, and no_input lists blocks that receive no edges from the previous column. The function returns the matplotlib axes, so the figure can be changed further or saved with ax.figure.savefig(...). It needs only NumPy and matplotlib and therefore also runs in Colab. The comments in the code explain each step (node positions, the truncation of large layers, the edges, the labels and the brackets), so that the function can be adapted to other diagrams.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle

# Colours used for the network drawings: grey for the data (input and output),
# blue for hidden layers, orange for the latent (bottleneck) layer and green
# for an extra conditioning input such as a one-hot class label.
GREY, BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN = "#8C8C8C", "#005CA7", "#EB6709", "#2E8B57"


def draw_network(layer_sizes, labels=None, colors=None, max_nodes=10,
                 groups=None, no_input=None, ax=None, node_radius=0.11,
                 x_gap=1.6, min_height=1.0, height_scale=1.1, fontsize=13):
    """Draw a fully connected network as columns of circles joined by edges.

    Parameters
    ----------
    layer_sizes : list
        One entry per column, from the input to the output. An entry is
        either an int (the number of neurons of one layer) or a list of ints
        (several blocks stacked in the same column, e.g. [16, 16] for the mean
        and the log-variance of a variational autoencoder, or [784, 10] for an
        image together with a one-hot condition).
    labels : list, optional
        Names shown under each column next to the true layer size. An entry
        may be None (size only), a string, or, for a stacked column, a list
        with one string per block.
    colors : list, optional
        Fill colour of the nodes of each column (or a list with one colour per
        block). By default the first and the last column are grey and all
        others blue.
    max_nodes : int
        Largest number of circles drawn for one block. A larger block is shown
        by its first and last few nodes with a vertical ellipsis in between;
        the true size is always shown in the label.
    groups : list of (text, first_column, last_column), optional
        Brackets drawn above a range of columns, e.g. ("encoder", 0, 2).
    no_input : list of (column, block), optional
        Blocks that receive no edges from the previous column, e.g. a condition
        c that enters the decoder from outside.
    ax : matplotlib Axes, optional
        Axes to draw into; a new figure is created when None.
    node_radius, x_gap : float
        Radius of a circle and horizontal distance between columns.
    min_height, height_scale : float
        The height of a block of size s is min_height + height_scale*log10(s),
        so that a narrow layer is visibly shorter than a wide one.
    fontsize : int
        Font size of all labels.

    Returns
    -------
    ax : the matplotlib Axes with the drawing.
    """
    n = len(layer_sizes)
    # Turn every entry into a list of blocks, so that a plain layer is a
    # column with a single block.
    blocks = [s if isinstance(s, (list, tuple)) else [s] for s in layer_sizes]
    if labels is None:
        labels = [None] * n
    if colors is None:
        colors = [GREY] + [BLUE] * (n - 2) + [GREY]
    no_input = set(no_input or [])

    def per_block(value, k):
        # Repeat a single value for all k blocks of a column, or keep a list.
        return list(value) if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)) else [value] * k

    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(1.9 * n + 1, 5.5))

    # ---- Node positions ---------------------------------------------------
    # Column i sits at x = i * x_gap. Inside a column the blocks are stacked
    # from top to bottom with a small gap, and the whole column is centred
    # on y = 0. Each block gets a height that grows with log10 of its size
    # (but is never too small for its circles to fit without overlapping);
    # the drawn nodes are spread evenly over that height.
    nodes = []            # nodes[i][b] = list of (x, y) of block b in column i
    tops, bottoms = [], []
    gap = 0.9             # vertical space between stacked blocks (holds a label)
    for i, blk in enumerate(blocks):
        cols = per_block(colors[i], len(blk))
        labs = per_block(labels[i], len(blk))
        heights = [max(min_height + height_scale * np.log10(s),
                       (min(s, max_nodes) - 1) * 2.3 * node_radius) for s in blk]
        total = sum(heights) + gap * (len(blk) - 1)
        x, y_top = i * x_gap, total / 2
        column = []
        for s, h, c, lab in zip(blk, heights, cols, labs):
            shown = min(s, max_nodes)
            if s <= max_nodes:
                # Small block: draw every neuron.
                ys = np.linspace(y_top, y_top - h, shown) if shown > 1 else np.array([y_top - h / 2])
            else:
                # ---- Truncation of large layers ----------------------------
                # Draw max_nodes circles: half in the upper 38 % of the block,
                # half in the lower 38 %, and a vertical ellipsis in the
                # middle to show that neurons are omitted.
                k = max_nodes // 2
                ys = np.concatenate([np.linspace(y_top, y_top - 0.38 * h, k),
                                     np.linspace(y_top - 0.62 * h, y_top - h, max_nodes - k)])
                ax.text(x, y_top - 0.5 * h, r"$\vdots$", ha="center", va="center",
                        fontsize=fontsize + 6, color=c, zorder=4)
            for y in ys:
                ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), node_radius, facecolor=c,
                                    edgecolor="black", lw=0.6, zorder=3))
            column.append([(x, y) for y in ys])

            # ---- Labels of stacked blocks ----------------------------------
            # In a column with several blocks each block is labelled just
            # below its last node, in its own colour, on a white box so that
            # the edges behind do not hide the text.
            if len(blk) > 1:
                text = f"{s}" if lab is None else f"{lab} {s}"
                ax.text(x, y_top - h - 0.2, text, ha="center", va="top",
                        fontsize=fontsize - 1, color=c, zorder=5,
                        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=0.5))
            y_top -= h + gap

        # ---- Label of a single-block column: name and true size below ----
        if len(blk) == 1:
            lab = labs[0]
            text = f"{blk[0]}" if lab is None else f"{lab}\n{blk[0]}"
            ax.text(x, -total / 2 - 0.3, text, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=fontsize)
        nodes.append(column)
        tops.append(total / 2)
        bottoms.append(-total / 2)

    # ---- Edges ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # A dense layer connects every neuron of one column with every neuron of
    # the next, so we draw a thin grey line for every pair of drawn nodes,
    # skipping the blocks listed in no_input. zorder=1 keeps lines behind
    # the circles.
    for i in range(n - 1):
        sources = [p for block in nodes[i] for p in block]
        for b, block in enumerate(nodes[i + 1]):
            if (i + 1, b) in no_input:
                continue
            for (x0, y0) in sources:
                for (x1, y1) in block:
                    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color="#B0B0B0", lw=0.35, zorder=1)

    # ---- Group brackets ------------------------------------------------------
    # A bracket above columns first..last with its text, e.g. "encoder".
    y_br = max(tops) + 0.45
    for text, i0, i1 in (groups or []):
        x0, x1 = i0 * x_gap - 0.3, i1 * x_gap + 0.3
        ax.plot([x0, x0, x1, x1], [y_br - 0.12, y_br, y_br, y_br - 0.12],
                color="black", lw=1.2)
        ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y_br + 0.1, text, ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=fontsize)

    # ---- Axes limits ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Leave room for the brackets above and the labels below.
    ax.set_xlim(-0.8, (n - 1) * x_gap + 0.8)
    ax.set_ylim(min(bottoms) - 1.3, y_br + (0.7 if groups else 0.2))
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    return ax




Code
W1, b, W2 = unpack(theta0)                    # the model is the flat vector theta; its parts give the layer sizes
sizes = [1, W1.size, 1]                       # one input, len(W1) hidden neurons, one output
assert W1.size + b.size + W2.size == theta0.size
ax = draw_network(sizes, labels=["input $x$", r"hidden, $\tanh$", "output $f(x)$"], max_nodes=sizes[1])
plt.show()





The libraries torchinfo and torchview need the network as a PyTorch module (nn.Module), whereas here it is a function of a flat parameter vector. The same architecture as an nn.Sequential, with bias=False in the output layer because \(f\) has no output bias, has the same \(3N\) parameters.
The library torchinfo prints a table of the layers. torchinfo.summary(model, input_size=...) passes a batch of zeros of the given shape through the model and records, for every layer, the shape of its output and the number of its parameters; the lines at the bottom give the totals and an estimate of the memory needed. The first number of input_size is the batch size: it appears as the first dimension of every output shape and does not change the parameter counts. The library torchview passes the same kind of batch through the model and draws the layers as a graph in which every box is one layer with the shapes of its input and output; with expand_nested=True a submodule that itself contains layers, such as an nn.Sequential block called inside a larger model, is drawn as a frame around its layers. The graph is rendered by the program Graphviz to a PNG (Portable Network Graphics) file in the folder figures.
The three views serve different purposes. The neuron-level drawing explains what a dense layer is but is practical only for small dense networks. The torchinfo table is the quickest check of shapes and parameter counts and the first thing to print when a model raises a shape error. The torchview graph shows how the layers are connected, which matters as soon as the data flow is not a single chain, for example with skip connections or several inputs.
