Finally the drawing by torchview. draw_graph passes a batch of the given shape through the model and records every layer it meets; .visual_graph is the resulting Graphviz graph, which render writes to a PNG file in the folder figures; display(...) (available in every Jupyter/Colab notebook without import) shows the image, which is needed here because it is created inside a try block. Every box is one layer with the shapes of its input and output; the first dimension (8) is the batch. Unlike our draw_network, which draws individual nodes (up to max_nodes per layer), this drawing shows layers and shapes, and it works for any model, also for models with skip connections. If Graphviz is missing, the except branch prints a message instead.


Code
try:
    import os
    from torchview import draw_graph
    from IPython.display import Image
    graph = draw_graph(model, input_size=(8, 1), expand_nested=True)
    os.makedirs("figures", exist_ok=True)
    png = graph.visual_graph.render("figures/lab008_model_graph", format="png", cleanup=True)   # Graphviz writes the PNG file
    display(Image(png))
except Exception as err:
    print("torchview drawing not available:", err)





The tools are faster to use, and they are the right choice for large models. The torchinfo table is the quickest check of shapes and parameter counts; the torchview graph shows how the layers are connected, which matters once the data flow is not a single chain (skip connections, several inputs). The direct computations of Sections 1.1–1.6 remain useful: they show what the numbers mean, and they can be extended to any quantity a tool does not provide (e.g. the saturation of the activations in Section 2.3).

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
2. The network before training

2.1 Damped-oscillation data
The data are noisy measurements of a damped oscillation \[y(t) = e^{-0.2t}\cos(2t), \qquad t\in[0, 10], \tag{7}\] with noise of standard deviation \(\sigma\), 0.1, and deliberately few training points, so that overfitting (Section 4) becomes visible: 30 points for training, 40 for validation, 40 for testing. The input is rescaled to \([-1, 1]\).
The numbers are chosen for this purpose. The noise \(0.1\) is about 10% of the amplitude of the signal, which starts at 1: large enough for overfitting to be visible, small enough for the oscillation to remain recognisable. With only 30 training points the network of Section 1 (8513 parameters) can memorise the training set. The validation and test sets are larger (40 points each) because their losses are used to choose and to evaluate the model, and a larger set gives a less noisy estimate. The positions \(t\) are drawn uniformly at random, so the three sets cover the interval in the same way; all 110 points are drawn at once, and the first 30, the next 40 and the last 40 form the three sets.
Besides the data, the cell creates t_plot (400 equally spaced values) and the corresponding network input X_plot. These are not data: they are a dense grid on which functions are evaluated for plotting, and on which the hidden layers are examined in Section 2.3. The rescaling \[t \;\to\; t/5 - 1 \tag{8}\] maps \([0, 10]\) onto \([-1, 1]\). \(\tanh\) changes only for arguments of order one; with the raw inputs (up to 10) and first-layer weights in \([-1, 1]\), 52% of the first-layer activations of the untrained network would be saturated (Section 2.3), with the rescaled inputs below 0.1%.


Code
def damped_oscillation(t):
    return np.exp(-0.2 * t) * np.cos(2 * t)

noise = 0.1
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
t_all = rng.uniform(0, 10, 110)
y_all = damped_oscillation(t_all) + noise * rng.normal(size=110)

def to_tensor(t, y):
    """Inputs rescaled to [-1, 1] and targets, both of shape (B, 1), float32."""
    X = torch.tensor(t / 5.0 - 1.0, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
    Y = torch.tensor(y, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
    return X, Y

X_train, Y_train = to_tensor(t_all[:30], y_all[:30])        # the points are in random order already
X_val, Y_val = to_tensor(t_all[30:70], y_all[30:70])
X_test, Y_test = to_tensor(t_all[70:], y_all[70:])
print("training:", tuple(X_train.shape), " validation:", tuple(X_val.shape), " test:", tuple(X_test.shape))

t_plot = np.linspace(0, 10, 400)
X_plot = torch.tensor(t_plot / 5.0 - 1.0, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.5))
ax.plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
ax.plot(t_all[:30], y_all[:30], "o", label="training (30)")
ax.plot(t_all[30:70], y_all[30:70], "s", ms=4, label="validation (40)")
ax.plot(t_all[70:], y_all[70:], "^", ms=4, label="test (40)")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2); plt.show()


training: (30, 1)  validation: (40, 1)  test: (40, 1)







2.2 Initial weights
PyTorch initialises the weights of nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) uniformly in \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}},\ 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\). The first layer (one input) therefore has weights in \([-1, 1]\), the hidden layers (64 inputs) in \([-0.125, 0.125]\). The histograms below show the weights of every Linear layer of the untrained model, with these bounds as dashed lines. The biases are drawn from the same interval.
The scale \(1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\) keeps the size of the weighted sum \[s = \sum_{i=1}^{n_{\rm in}} w_i x_i \tag{9}\] independent of the number of inputs: for independent \(w_i\) and \(x_i\) with zero mean \[{\rm Var}(s) = n_{\rm in}\,{\rm Var}(w)\,{\rm Var}(x), \tag{10}\] which does not grow with \(n_{\rm in}\) when \[{\rm Var}(w)\propto 1/n_{\rm in} . \tag{11}\]


Code
linear_layers = [layer for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(linear_layers), figsize=(16, 3.2))
for k, (ax, layer) in enumerate(zip(axes, linear_layers)):
    w = layer.weight.detach().numpy().ravel()
    bound = 1 / np.sqrt(layer.in_features)
    ax.hist(w, bins=30)                                         # bins: enough to show the shape, a matter of readability
    ax.axvline(-bound, color="k", ls="--"); ax.axvline(bound, color="k", ls="--")
    ax.set_title(f"Linear {k + 1}: {layer.in_features} -> {layer.out_features}\n{w.size} weights")
    ax.set_xlabel("weight value")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The weight histograms above are flat between the dashed bounds, as expected for a uniform distribution; the panels with only 64 weights are irregular because 64 samples are few.


2.3 Activations and saturated nodes
The 400 inputs of the dense grid X_plot are passed through the network, and the output of every activation layer is recorded. A node computes \(\tanh\) of its weighted input \(z\), \[h = \tanh z, \qquad \frac{dh}{dz} = 1 - \tanh^2 z = 1 - h^2 . \tag{12}\] A node is saturated when \[|h| > 0.95, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad \frac{dh}{dz} = 1-h^2 < 0.0975 \approx 0.1 : \tag{13}\] its derivative is small, so gradients passing through it are damped by a factor of ten or more. The threshold 0.95 is a convention; any value between about 0.9 and 0.99 gives the same qualitative picture. The saturated fraction of a layer, shown in the panel titles below, is the fraction of activation values \(h\) (over all nodes and all 400 inputs) that satisfy the condition (13).


Code
def hidden_activations(model, x):
    """Outputs of all activation layers of an nn.Sequential model for the input batch x."""
    outputs = []
    with torch.no_grad():
        for layer in model:
            x = layer(x)
            if not isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):     # keep the outputs of the activation layers only
                outputs.append(x.numpy().copy())   # .numpy() shares memory with the tensor; copy() makes the stored array independent
    return outputs

acts = hidden_activations(model, X_plot)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(acts), figsize=(15, 3.2))
for k, (ax, h) in enumerate(zip(axes, acts)):
    saturated = np.mean(np.abs(h) > 0.95)
    ax.hist(h.ravel(), bins=40, range=(-1, 1))     # the full range of tanh, the same in every panel so that they can be compared
    ax.set_title(f"hidden layer {k + 1}: std {h.std():.3f},\nsaturated {100 * saturated:.0f}%")
    ax.set_xlabel("activation $h$")
axes[0].set_ylabel("count")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





With the default initialisation practically no activation is saturated (below 0.1%), and the spread of the activations shrinks from layer to layer: the signal becomes weaker with depth.


2.4 Gradients in every layer
One forward and one backward pass on the training set give the gradient of the loss with respect to every weight matrix. Its norm tells how strongly each layer would be changed by the first step of gradient descent.
model.zero_grad() first sets the stored gradients to zero, because PyTorch adds new gradients to those already in .grad. nn.functional.mse_loss(a, b) is the function form of nn.MSELoss()(a, b) and gives the same value. For a matrix, .norm() is the Frobenius norm \[\|g\| = \sqrt{\sum_{ij} g_{ij}^2} , \tag{14}\] the length of the matrix viewed as one long vector.


Code
def gradient_norms(model, X, Y):
    """Norm of dL/dW for the weight matrix of every Linear layer (one backward pass)."""
    model.zero_grad()
    nn.functional.mse_loss(model(X), Y).backward()
    return [layer.weight.grad.norm().item() for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]

for k, g in enumerate(gradient_norms(model, X_train, Y_train)):
    print(f"Linear {k + 1}: |dL/dW| = {g:.2e}")


Linear 1: |dL/dW| = 1.41e-02
Linear 2: |dL/dW| = 4.85e-01
Linear 3: |dL/dW| = 5.12e-01
Linear 4: |dL/dW| = 7.12e-01


The gradient of the first layer is the smallest. Gradient norms of different layers are, however, not directly comparable: the first weight matrix has only \(64\) entries, the hidden ones 4096 (a \(64\times64\) matrix), and the norm sums over all entries. Comparisons are meaningful for the same layer between different models or different epochs, as in Sections 2.5 and 3.2.


2.5 The influence of the initialisation scale
The analysis of Sections 2.3–2.4 is repeated for a deeper network (6 hidden layers of width 64) whose weights are drawn from \(\mathcal N(0, (c/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}})^2)\), the normal (Gaussian) distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation \(c/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}\), for three values of \(c\). The table lists, for every hidden layer, the standard deviation of the activations and the fraction of saturated nodes, and the gradient norm of every weight matrix.
The three values stand for a too small, a standard and a too large scale. Their effect is multiplied once per layer, so a network deeper than that of Section 1 makes it easier to see. A normal distribution is used instead of PyTorch’s uniform one, because only the standard deviation matters for the argument. For comparison, the default uniform distribution on \([-1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}, 1/\sqrt{n_{\rm in}}]\) has standard deviation \(1/\sqrt{3n_{\rm in}}\), which corresponds to \[c = 1/\sqrt3 \approx 0.58 ; \tag{15}\] this is why the activations of Section 2.3 shrink with depth.
In the code, the functions of nn.init overwrite the values of an existing tensor in place (in PyTorch a trailing underscore, as in normal_, marks an in-place operation), and the biases are set to zero so that only the weight scale is varied. The activations are measured on the dense grid X_plot, which samples the input interval evenly; the gradients are those of the training loss and need the training data. Finally, pivot rearranges the long table (one row per pair (\(c\), layer)) into a wide one with one row per layer and one column per quantity and value of \(c\), so that the three values of \(c\) stand side by side; round(4) only affects the display.


Code
def init_scaled(layer_sizes, c, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
    for layer in m:
        if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear):
            nn.init.normal_(layer.weight, mean=0.0, std=c / np.sqrt(layer.in_features))
            nn.init.zeros_(layer.bias)
    return m

deep_sizes = [1] + [64] * 6 + [1]
rows = []
for c in [0.5, 1.0, 3.0]:
    m = init_scaled(deep_sizes, c)
    acts = hidden_activations(m, X_plot)
    grads = gradient_norms(m, X_train, Y_train)
    for k, h in enumerate(acts):
        rows.append({"c": c, "hidden layer": k + 1, "activation std": h.std(),
                     "saturated (%)": 100 * np.mean(np.abs(h) > 0.95), "|dL/dW| of this layer": grads[k]})
init_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
init_table.pivot(index="hidden layer", columns="c", values=["activation std", "saturated (%)", "|dL/dW| of this layer"]).round(4)

For the smallest scale, \(c\) of 0.5, the activations shrink by about a factor of two per layer, and all gradients are more than twenty times smaller than for the standard scale 1, decreasing slightly towards the first layers: the signal fades in both directions (vanishing gradients). For the standard scale the activations decrease with depth only slowly (for \(\tanh\) the derivative is below 1, so this scale does not exactly preserve the signal), and the gradients are of similar size in hidden layers 2–6 (layer 1 has only 64 weights, so its norm is smaller; see Section 2.4). For the largest scale, 3, a large fraction of the nodes (up to about half in the deeper layers) is saturated, and the gradients are tens of times larger than for the standard scale: the first optimisation steps would be very large (exploding gradients).
The weight scale therefore has to be chosen with the depth and the activation in mind; standard choices are derived from such arguments. Xavier (Glorot) initialisation uses \[{\rm Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{\rm in}+n_{\rm out}} , \tag{16}\] a scale \(c\) of 1 for square layers, and is meant for \(\tanh\)-like activations. He initialisation uses \[{\rm Var}(w) = \frac{2}{n_{\rm in}} , \tag{17}\] a scale \(c\) of \(\sqrt2\), which compensates for the rectified linear unit (ReLU), \[\mathrm{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z) , \tag{18}\] which sets negative inputs (about half of them) to zero.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
3. Monitoring training
The training function below is a standard training loop (full batch, Adam) with additional bookkeeping. After every epoch it records the training loss and the validation loss, the norm of the gradient of every weight matrix, and the relative change of every weight matrix since the start, \(\|W(e) - W(0)\| / \|W(0)\|\), where \(e\) is the epoch. It also keeps a copy of the parameters at the epoch with the smallest validation loss so far, which Section 4 uses.
The record log is a dictionary of lists, with one entry appended per epoch. For the gradients and weight changes each entry is a list of 4 numbers (one per Linear layer); at the end np.array turns this list of lists into an array of shape (number of epochs, 4), so that log["grad"][:, k] is the history of layer \(k+1\). The 30 training points form one batch, so every epoch is a single exact gradient step and the loss curves contain no noise from a random choice of mini-batches.
The learning rate lr=1e-2 is a common starting value for Adam on small problems; it was not tuned. With learning rates \(10^{-3}\), \(3\cdot10^{-3}\), \(10^{-2}\) and \(3\cdot10^{-2}\) the smallest validation loss is reached at epochs 753, 419, 293 and 281, and in every case the validation loss rises afterwards. The 3000 epochs are far more than needed to reach the minimum, so that the overfitting after it can be seen.
Three copies in the code protect stored values from later changes. In W0 = [... .detach().clone() ...] the clone() is needed because optimizer.step() changes the weights in place: without it the list would hold the current weight tensors themselves and the relative change would always be zero, while detach() keeps the copy out of the gradient computation. The record best = {"val": np.inf, ...} starts from infinity, so the validation loss of the first epoch is always smaller and becomes the first “best” model. Its parameters are stored with copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict()), because state_dict() returns a dictionary of the parameter tensors themselves, not of copies; without deepcopy the stored “best” state would follow every later optimiser step and end up equal to the final parameters.
model.train() and model.eval() switch layers such as dropout and batch normalisation between their training and evaluation behaviour. This network has no such layers, so here the calls change nothing; they are kept because a general training loop needs them. The training loss of an epoch is computed before optimizer.step(), the validation loss after it; the two curves are shifted by one step, which is irrelevant on a scale of thousands of epochs. Finally, torch.manual_seed(0) before make_mlp gives the same initial weights as in Sections 1–2: the model trained here is exactly the one analysed above.


Code
def train_monitored(model, n_epochs=3000, lr=1e-2):
    linear = [layer for layer in model if isinstance(layer, nn.Linear)]
    W0 = [layer.weight.detach().clone() for layer in linear]          # initial weights, for the relative change
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
    log = {"train": [], "val": [], "grad": [], "change": []}
    best = {"val": np.inf, "epoch": None, "state": None}
    for epoch in range(n_epochs):
        model.train()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X_train), Y_train)
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        log["grad"].append([layer.weight.grad.norm().item() for layer in linear])    # read the gradients before the step
        optimizer.step()

        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val_loss = loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val).item()
            log["change"].append([((layer.weight - w0).norm() / w0.norm()).item() for layer, w0 in zip(linear, W0)])
        log["train"].append(loss.item())
        log["val"].append(val_loss)
        if val_loss < best["val"]:                                     # remember the best model so far
            best = {"val": val_loss, "epoch": epoch, "state": copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())}
    log["grad"], log["change"] = np.array(log["grad"]), np.array(log["change"])
    return log, best

torch.manual_seed(0)
model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
log, best = train_monitored(model)
train_time = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"training took {train_time:.1f} s;  smallest validation loss {best['val']:.3e} at epoch {best['epoch']}")


training took 5.0 s;  smallest validation loss 1.941e-02 at epoch 293



3.1 Learning curves
The losses on the training and validation sets against the epoch are the most important plot of every training run. The dotted line is the noise variance \(\sigma^2\), 0.01, the smallest mean squared error (MSE) that any model can reach on new data; the vertical line marks the epoch with the smallest validation loss.


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.semilogy(log["train"], label="training loss")
ax.semilogy(log["val"], label="validation loss")
ax.axhline(noise**2, color="gray", ls=":", label=r"noise variance $\sigma^2$")
ax.axvline(best["epoch"], color="C3", ls="--", label=f"smallest validation loss (epoch {best['epoch']})")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE"); ax.legend()
plt.show()
print(f"at the end: training loss {log['train'][-1]:.2e}, validation loss {log['val'][-1]:.2e}")





at the end: training loss 3.65e-03, validation loss 8.35e-02


Two phases are visible. At first both losses decrease together: the network learns the function that the training and validation points have in common. Later the training loss keeps decreasing, below the noise variance, while the validation loss increases. Below \(\sigma^2\) the network can only improve on the training set by reproducing its particular noise, which is useless (in fact harmful) for new points. This is overfitting. With 30 points even the true function has a training MSE that fluctuates around \(\sigma^2\) by about \[\sigma^2\sqrt{2/30} \approx 0.25\,\sigma^2 , \tag{19}\] so only a training loss well below \(\sigma^2\), as here at the end of training, is a clear sign of fitting the noise.


3.2 Gradients and weight changes per layer
The same run can be followed inside the network. The gradient norms vary over several orders of magnitude and are plotted on a logarithmic axis; the relative weight changes stay between 0 and about 3 and are readable on a linear axis.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 4))
for k in range(log["grad"].shape[1]):
    axes[0].semilogy(log["grad"][:, k], lw=1, label=f"Linear {k + 1}")
    axes[1].plot(log["change"][:, k], label=f"Linear {k + 1}")
axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$\|\partial L/\partial W\|$"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\|W(e) - W(0)\|\,/\,\|W(0)\|$"); axes[1].legend(fontsize=8)
axes[1].axvline(best["epoch"], color="C3", ls="--")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The gradient norms decay during long stretches, interrupted by sudden spikes: at a spike the Adam step overshoots, the loss jumps up for a few epochs and then decreases again. These episodes are also visible as small jumps in the right panel, which shows how far each weight matrix has moved from its initial values. Relative changes of order one mean that training has substantially rewritten the layer; changes that keep growing after the best epoch (dashed line) are the parameters adapting to the noise of the training set.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
section: 4. Overfitting and the choice of the epoch
text:
4. Overfitting and the choice of the epoch
train_monitored kept a copy of the parameters from the epoch with the smallest validation loss. Loading it gives the model that would have been obtained by stopping the training there (early stopping). Both models are compared with the data.
A state_dict contains only numbers, not the architecture. A network with the same layer sizes is therefore built first, and its random initial parameters are then overwritten by load_state_dict. final_model = model is not a copy, only a second name for the trained network.


Code
final_model = model                                   # parameters after the last epoch
best_model = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
best_model.load_state_dict(best["state"])             # parameters from the epoch with the smallest validation loss

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.5))
ax.plot(t_plot, damped_oscillation(t_plot), "k", lw=1, label="true function")
ax.plot(t_all[:30], y_all[:30], "o", color="C0", label="training data")
with torch.no_grad():
    ax.plot(t_plot, final_model(X_plot), "C3", lw=1.5, label=f"after the last epoch ({len(log['train'])})")
    ax.plot(t_plot, best_model(X_plot), "C2", lw=2, label=f"at the best epoch ({best['epoch']})")
ax.set_xlabel("$t$"); ax.set_ylabel("$y$"); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show()





The model after the last epoch passes close to the training points and makes large excursions in the gaps between them (e.g. around the time 5). The model from the best epoch is smooth and follows the true function over most of the interval, but it misses the small oscillations at times above about 6. The best epoch was chosen with the validation set: the test set has not been used yet.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
5. Evaluation on the test set
Now, and only now, the chosen model is evaluated on the test set. Its test loss is the estimate of the error on new data that would be reported. For illustration only, the test loss of the overfitted final model is printed as well; it was not used to make any choice. The three panels then show the predictions against the measured values, the histogram of the residuals, and the residuals against the input \(t\).


Code
loss_fn = nn.MSELoss()
best_model.eval(); final_model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    test_best = loss_fn(best_model(X_test), Y_test).item()
    test_final = loss_fn(final_model(X_test), Y_test).item()
    pred_test = best_model(X_test).numpy().ravel()
print(f"chosen model (best epoch {best['epoch']}): test MSE = {test_best:.3e}")
print(f"final model (for comparison only)   : test MSE = {test_final:.3e}")
print(f"noise variance                       : {noise**2:.3e}")

residuals = pred_test - Y_test.numpy().ravel()
print(f"residuals: mean {residuals.mean():+.3f}, standard deviation {residuals.std():.3f} (noise level sigma = {noise})")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(16, 4))
axes[0].plot(Y_test.numpy(), pred_test, "o")
lims = [Y_test.min().item() - 0.1, Y_test.max().item() + 0.1]      # the margin 0.1 only extends the diagonal beyond the data
axes[0].plot(lims, lims, "k--", lw=1)
axes[0].set_xlabel("measured $y$ (test set)"); axes[0].set_ylabel("predicted $y$"); axes[0].set_title("prediction vs. measurement")
axes[1].hist(residuals, bins=12)                                  # few bins: only 40 residuals
axes[1].set_xlabel("residual (predicted - measured)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("count"); axes[1].set_title(f"residuals, std {residuals.std():.3f}")
axes[2].plot(t_all[70:], residuals, "o"); axes[2].axhline(0, color="k", lw=1)
axes[2].set_xlabel("$t$"); axes[2].set_ylabel("residual"); axes[2].set_title("residuals vs. input")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


chosen model (best epoch 293): test MSE = 3.197e-02
final model (for comparison only)   : test MSE = 7.065e-02
noise variance                       : 1.000e-02
residuals: mean -0.027, standard deviation 0.177 (noise level sigma = 0.1)





For an ideal model the points of the left panel lie around the diagonal, the residuals have a standard deviation equal to the noise level \(\sigma\), 0.1, and they show no trend with the input \(t\). For \(n\) Gaussian values the sample standard deviation scatters by about \(\sigma/\sqrt{2n}\), so even for an ideal model the standard deviation of the 40 residuals fluctuates around \(0.1\) by about \[\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{2\cdot 40}} \approx 0.011 . \tag{20}\]
residuals.std() subtracts the mean residual, so a constant offset of the model does not enter it, while \(\sqrt{\text{test MSE}}\) includes it. Here the residual standard deviation (in the title of the middle panel) is larger than \(\sigma\) by much more than this fluctuation, and the right panel shows why: at times above about 9 all residuals are negative, i.e. the model is systematically too low in this region (it misses the last oscillation, see Section 4), and between the times 7 and 8.3 all residuals are positive (the minimum of \(y\) near the time 7.9 is too shallow in the model). In the left panel the points at times above 9 form a horizontal row: the model predicts almost the same value, about \(-0.08\), for all of them, whatever the measured value. Residual plots reveal such systematic errors, which a single number such as the test MSE hides.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
6. Model characteristics table
The quantities of this notebook are collected for two models trained on the same data: the network analysed so far and a small network with one hidden layer of 16 nodes. Both are evaluated at their best epoch. The small network, with \[16\cdot 2 + 17 = 49 \tag{21}\] parameters, serves as a contrast: with one narrow hidden layer it can represent only smooth functions, so it overfits much more slowly; its smallest validation loss is reached only at epoch 2880, near the end of the 3000 epochs, and at that epoch its training loss, \(7.8\cdot10^{-3}\), is only slightly below \(\sigma^2\). (With 30 points the training MSE of even the true function fluctuates by about 25% around \(\sigma^2\), equation (19).) Its width 16 is arbitrary.
DataFrame.style.format changes only how the numbers are displayed, not the stored values: "{:.2f}" means two decimal places, "{:.2e}" scientific notation with two decimals. The training time depends on the computer and on other running processes; it is useful only to compare models trained on the same machine.


Code
def characterise(sizes, seed=0):
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    m = make_mlp(sizes)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    lg, bst = train_monitored(m)
    elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
    m.load_state_dict(bst["state"]); m.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        tr = loss_fn(m(X_train), Y_train).item()
        te = loss_fn(m(X_test), Y_test).item()
    return {
        "layer sizes": str(sizes),
        "parameters": sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()),
        "memory (kB)": sum(p.numel() * p.element_size() for p in m.parameters()) / 1024,
        "best epoch": bst["epoch"],
        "train MSE": tr, "val MSE": bst["val"], "test MSE": te,
        "train time (s)": elapsed,
    }

summary_table = pd.DataFrame([characterise([1, 16, 1]), characterise(layer_sizes)])
summary_table.style.format({"memory (kB)": "{:.2f}", "train MSE": "{:.2e}", "val MSE": "{:.2e}", "test MSE": "{:.2e}", "train time (s)": "{:.1f}"})

Such a table is the minimum documentation of a trained model: architecture and size, how it was selected (best epoch by validation loss), and its errors on the three data sets. Only the test column is an unbiased estimate of the error on new data.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
7. Summary
The architecture alone already gives a layer table (shapes and parameters per layer), the total and trainable numbers of parameters (requires_grad), the memory (\(4\) bytes per float32 parameter) and the multiply-adds per sample; the number of parameters grows linearly with depth and quadratically with width. Before training, the weight and activation histograms, the fraction of saturated nodes and the gradient norms per layer show whether the initialisation scale lets signals and gradients shrink, survive or saturate with depth. During training, the training and validation losses against the epoch, together with the gradient norms and relative weight changes per layer, show how the parameters evolve. Overfitting appears as a training loss falling below the noise level while the validation loss rises; the parameters at the epoch with the smallest validation loss are kept (early stopping). The test set is used once, for the chosen model, and residual plots show whether its errors are random or systematic.

title: Lab 008: Analysing a neural network
text:
8. Exercises

Exercise 1 — Analysing an image classifier
The image classifier nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(784, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 64), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(64, 10)) assigns a \(28\times28\) grey-scale image of a handwritten digit (the MNIST data set, Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology database; Y. LeCun, L. Bottou, Y. Bengio and P. Haffner, Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition, Proc. IEEE 86, 2278–2324 (1998), doi:10.1109/5.726791) to one of 10 classes, the digits \(0, \dots, 9\): it has \(784\) inputs, one per pixel, and 10 outputs, one per class. 1. Load the MNIST test images (torchvision.datasets.MNIST, train=False) and show one example of every class with its label. 2. Draw the network and produce its layer table with layer_table for a batch of 16 test images (pixel values divided by 255). 3. Which layer holds most of the parameters, and what fraction? Why is it this layer? 4. Compute the memory of the parameters and the number of multiply-adds per image. 5. Freeze everything except the last layer and report the number of trainable parameters. Check the totals with torchinfo.summary (Section 1.7).

Exercise 2 — Early stopping with patience
In practice training is stopped automatically once the validation loss has not improved for a number of epochs (the patience). Modify the training loop so that it stops after 200 epochs without a new minimum of the validation loss, restore the best parameters, and report the stopping epoch, the best epoch, the time saved compared with 3000 epochs, and the test loss of the restored model.
The patience must be longer than the temporary rises of the validation loss (the spikes of Section 3.2), otherwise training stops at one of them. With the network and data of this notebook a patience of 100 epochs stops at epoch 213 with the best epoch 113 and validation loss 0.036, nearly twice the minimum found in Section 3; patience 200 and 500 both find the minimum at epoch 293.

Solution


Code
def train_early_stopping(model, max_epochs=3000, patience=200, lr=1e-2):
    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    best_val, best_epoch, best_state = np.inf, 0, None
    train_hist, val_hist = [], []
    for epoch in range(max_epochs):
        model.train()
        loss = loss_fn(model(X_train), Y_train)
        optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            val = loss_fn(model(X_val), Y_val).item()
        train_hist.append(loss.item()); val_hist.append(val)
        if val < best_val:
            best_val, best_epoch, best_state = val, epoch, copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        elif epoch - best_epoch >= patience:          # no improvement for `patience` epochs
            break                                     # leave the loop; `epoch` keeps its last value
    model.load_state_dict(best_state)                 # restore the best parameters
    return epoch, best_epoch, train_hist, val_hist

torch.manual_seed(0)
m = make_mlp(layer_sizes)
t0 = time.perf_counter()
stop_epoch, best_epoch, tr_h, va_h = train_early_stopping(m)
elapsed = time.perf_counter() - t0
with torch.no_grad():
    test_mse = loss_fn(m(X_test), Y_test).item()
print(f"stopped at epoch {stop_epoch}, best epoch {best_epoch}, {elapsed:.1f} s instead of about {train_time:.1f} s for 3000 epochs")
print(f"test MSE of the restored model: {test_mse:.3e}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(tr_h, label="training"); ax.semilogy(va_h, label="validation")
ax.axvline(best_epoch, color="C3", ls="--", label="best epoch"); ax.axvline(stop_epoch, color="k", ls=":", label="stop")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("MSE"); ax.legend(); plt.show()

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
1. The original MNIST files

1.1 Download
MNIST is distributed as four compressed files (.gz): images and labels, each for the training part (\(60\,000\) images) and the test part (\(10\,000\) images). Libraries such as torchvision or keras download exactly these files and decode them. Both steps take only a few lines of Python.
urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, path) downloads a file from the internet and saves it on disk. The data set was introduced by Y. LeCun, L. Bottou, Y. Bengio and P. Haffner, Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition, Proc. IEEE 86, 2278–2324 (1998), doi:10.1109/5.726791; its original web page, http://yann.lecun.com/exdb/mnist/, no longer serves the files reliably, so we use two public copies (mirrors) and take the first one that works. A file that is already on disk is not downloaded again.


Code
DATA_DIR = "data/MNIST_raw"
MIRRORS = ["https://ossci-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/mnist/",          # copy used by torchvision
           "https://storage.googleapis.com/cvdf-datasets/mnist/"]     # copy used by tensorflow
FILES = {"train_images": "train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz",
         "train_labels": "train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz",
         "test_images":  "t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz",
         "test_labels":  "t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz"}

def download(filename):
    # Download one MNIST file into DATA_DIR (only if it is not there yet) and return its path.
    path = os.path.join(DATA_DIR, filename)
    if os.path.exists(path):
        return path
    os.makedirs(DATA_DIR, exist_ok=True)
    for mirror in MIRRORS:
        try:
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(mirror + filename, path)
            return path
        except Exception as err:
            print(f"  {mirror} failed: {err}")
            if os.path.exists(path):
                os.remove(path)                 # remove a partially downloaded file
    raise RuntimeError(f"could not download {filename}")

paths = {key: download(name) for key, name in FILES.items()}
for key, path in paths.items():
    print(f"{key:13s} {path:45s} {os.path.getsize(path) / 1e6:5.2f} MB")


train_images  data/MNIST_raw/train-images-idx3-ubyte.gz      9.91 MB
train_labels  data/MNIST_raw/train-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz      0.03 MB
test_images   data/MNIST_raw/t10k-images-idx3-ubyte.gz       1.65 MB
test_labels   data/MNIST_raw/t10k-labels-idx1-ubyte.gz       0.00 MB




1.2 The IDX file format
After decompression each file is a sequence of bytes (ubyte = unsigned byte, an integer \(0\dots255\)) in the very simple IDX format:







bytes
content




0–1
always 0, 0


2
data type; 8 (hex 0x08) means unsigned bytes


3
number of dimensions \(d\): 3 for images (number, rows, columns), 1 for labels


4 … \(4+4d-1\)
the \(d\) sizes, each a 4-byte integer, most significant byte first (big-endian)


then
the data, one byte per pixel or label, row after row



gzip.open decompresses on the fly. We read the first 16 bytes of the training images:


Code
with gzip.open(paths["train_images"], "rb") as f:
    header = f.read(16)                                       # 4 bytes "magic number" + 3 sizes of 4 bytes
print("first 16 bytes:", list(header))

sizes = np.frombuffer(header, dtype=">i4")                     # ">i4" = big-endian 4-byte integer
print("as four big-endian integers:", sizes)
print("data type byte:", header[2], " number of dimensions:", header[3])


first 16 bytes: [0, 0, 8, 3, 0, 0, 234, 96, 0, 0, 0, 28, 0, 0, 0, 28]
as four big-endian integers: [ 2051 60000    28    28]
data type byte: 8  number of dimensions: 3


The four integers are \(2051\) (the “magic number”, 0x00000803: data type 08, \(3\) dimensions), \(60\,000\) images, \(28\) rows and \(28\) columns. For example, the number of images follows from bytes 4–7 above as \[60\,000 = 0\cdot256^3 + 0\cdot256^2 + 234\cdot256 + 96 . \tag{1}\]
A complete reader is a few lines. np.frombuffer interprets raw bytes as an array without copying; offset skips the header.


Code
def read_idx(path):
    # Read an IDX file (gzip-compressed) into a NumPy array of unsigned bytes.
    with gzip.open(path, "rb") as f:
        raw = f.read()
    assert raw[0] == 0 and raw[1] == 0 and raw[2] == 0x08, "not an IDX file of unsigned bytes"
    n_dims = raw[3]
    shape = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=">i4", count=n_dims, offset=4)          # the d sizes
    data = np.frombuffer(raw, dtype=np.uint8, offset=4 + 4 * n_dims)        # all the rest
    return data.reshape(shape)

X_train_full = read_idx(paths["train_images"])
y_train_full = read_idx(paths["train_labels"])

That is the whole data set: an array of \(60\,000\) images \(28\times 28\) with integer pixel values \(0\) (background) to \(255\) (ink), the corresponding labels \(0\dots9\), and the same for the \(10\,000\) test images. Everything that follows works with these NumPy arrays.

imshow draws a 2D array as an image; the colour map "gray_r" shows \(0\) as white and \(255\) as black, as on paper.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 10, figsize=(12, 5))

The classes are nearly balanced (between about \(9\%\) and \(11\%\) each), so a model that always answers the same digit would be right in only about \(10\%\) of the cases, and so would random guessing. Any useful model must do much better than \(10\%\).


2.3 The mean image of every class
Averaging all training images of one digit shows the “typical” shape and how much it varies (blurred regions = places where different writers put the ink differently).


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 10, figsize=(12, 1.6))
for k in range(10):

2.4 Flattening
The networks of this notebook (dense / fully connected) take a vector as input. A \(28\times28\) image becomes a vector of \(m\) numbers, 784 of them, by writing the rows one after another: pixel \((i, j)\) (row \(i\), column \(j\)) goes to position \[p = 28\,i + j . \tag{2}\] This is what reshape does (NumPy and PyTorch store arrays row by row, so no data are moved).


Code
img = X_train_full[0]                         # one image, shape (28, 28)
vec = img.reshape(784)                        # the same numbers, shape (784,)
i, j = 6, 14
print(f"pixel (row {i}, column {j}) = {img[i, j]},   vector element {28 * i + j} = {vec[28 * i + j]}")

axes[1].plot(vec, lw=0.8)
for r in range(1, 28):
    axes[1].axvline(28 * r, color="grey", lw=0.3)              # boundaries between image rows
axes[1].set_xlim(0, 784); axes[1].set_xlabel("position in the vector  (= 28 * row + column)"); axes[1].set_ylabel("pixel value")
axes[1].set_title("the same image as a vector of 784 numbers (grey lines: start of a new image row)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


pixel (row 6, column 14) = 253,   vector element 182 = 253





Each bump in the right panel is one image row crossing the stroke. The network sees only this list of \(784\) numbers: it does not know which pixels are neighbours. (Convolutional networks, discussed later in Chapter 2, use the 2D arrangement.)

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
3. Splitting the data set (Box 2.10)

3.1 Training, validation and test sets
The three sets have different roles. The training set is used to change the parameters (gradient descent). The validation set is used during development: to watch for overfitting and to choose settings (number of epochs, learning rate, architecture). The test set is used once, at the very end, to report the final quality; if it were used to choose settings, it would no longer measure performance on new data. For teaching purposes the analyses and exercises below also look at the test set; in a real project such comparisons would be made on the validation set.
The MNIST test file is our test set. The \(60\,000\) training images are split at random into \(50\,000\) for training and \(10\,000\) for validation. The split must be random: a data file may be ordered (by class, by writer, by date of collection), and the first images of a file need not be representative of the rest. rng.permutation(n) returns the numbers \(0,\dots,n-1\) in a random order; the first \(50\,000\) of them select the training images.


Code
n_full = len(X_train_full)
perm = rng.permutation(n_full)                     # a random order of 0, ..., 59999
idx_train, idx_val = perm[:50_000], perm[50_000:]
print("first 10 entries of the permutation:", perm[:10])
print("training indices:", len(idx_train), "  validation indices:", len(idx_val))
print("common indices:", len(np.intersect1d(idx_train, idx_val)),
      "  together they cover all images:", np.array_equal(np.sort(np.concatenate([idx_train, idx_val])), np.arange(n_full)))

X_tr_img, y_tr_np = X_train_full[idx_train], y_train_full[idx_train]
X_va_img, y_va_np = X_train_full[idx_val],   y_train_full[idx_val]
X_te_img, y_te_np = X_test_raw,              y_test_raw


first 10 entries of the permutation: [ 4013 23840 29603 43011 58703  2290 55984 52800 34316 12976]
training indices: 50000   validation indices: 10000
common indices: 0   together they cover all images: True


Indexing a NumPy array with an array of indices (X_train_full[idx_train]) picks the rows in that order. No image is in both sets, and together they use every image exactly once. The random split gives training and validation sets with the same class proportions, which also match the test file:


Code
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
for shift, (name, y) in zip([-0.27, 0, 0.27], [("training", y_tr_np), ("validation", y_va_np), ("test", y_te_np)]):
    ax.bar(np.arange(10) + shift, np.bincount(y, minlength=10) / len(y), width=0.27, label=f"{name} ({len(y)})")
ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_xlabel("digit"); ax.set_ylabel("fraction"); ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
plt.show()







3.2 Flattening and standardisation
As in the chapter, the input vectors are standardised to mean \(0\) and standard deviation \(1\): \[\mathbf x \;\leftarrow\; \frac{\mathbf x - \mu}{s}, \tag{3}\] with one number \(\mu\) (mean) and one number \(s\) (standard deviation) computed over all pixels of all training images. Inputs of order one keep the pre-activations \(\mathbf W\mathbf x + \mathbf b\) in the range where the sigmoid is not flat, which makes gradient descent work well.
\(\mu\) and \(s\) are computed from the training set only and then applied unchanged to validation and test data. Using statistics of the test set would let information about the test data leak into the model (data leakage); in a real application the test data are not even available when the model is built.
Finally the arrays are converted to PyTorch tensors: inputs as float32 (the default type of PyTorch parameters), labels as int64 (the type PyTorch expects for class indices).


Code
def flatten(images):
    # (N, 28, 28) uint8  ->  (N, 784) float32
    return images.reshape(len(images), -1).astype(np.float32)

X_tr_flat, X_va_flat, X_te_flat = flatten(X_tr_img), flatten(X_va_img), flatten(X_te_img)
mu, s = X_tr_flat.mean(), X_tr_flat.std()          # from the TRAINING set only
print(f"training-set pixel statistics: mean {mu:.2f}, std {s:.2f}  (on the 0..255 scale)")

X_tr = torch.from_numpy((X_tr_flat - mu) / s)
X_va = torch.from_numpy((X_va_flat - mu) / s)
X_te = torch.from_numpy((X_te_flat - mu) / s)
y_tr = torch.from_numpy(y_tr_np.astype(np.int64))
y_va = torch.from_numpy(y_va_np.astype(np.int64))
y_te = torch.from_numpy(y_te_np.astype(np.int64))

for name, X, y in [("train", X_tr, y_tr), ("val", X_va, y_va), ("test", X_te, y_te)]:
    print(f"{name:5s}  X {tuple(X.shape)} {X.dtype}  mean {X.mean():+.3f} std {X.std():.3f}   y {tuple(y.shape)} {y.dtype}")


training-set pixel statistics: mean 33.33, std 78.57  (on the 0..255 scale)
train  X (50000, 784) torch.float32  mean +0.000 std 1.000   y (50000,) torch.int64
val    X (10000, 784) torch.float32  mean -0.001 std 1.000   y (10000,) torch.int64
test   X (10000, 784) torch.float32  mean +0.006 std 1.008   y (10000,) torch.int64


The training inputs have mean \(0\) and standard deviation \(1\) by construction; validation and test inputs are close to that but not exactly, since they were transformed with the training statistics. The background pixels (\(0\)) become about \(-0.42\), full ink (\(255\)) becomes about \(2.8\).

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
text:
4. Mini-batches

4.1 Mini-batches from a random permutation
The gradient of the loss is an average over images. Computing it over all \(50\,000\) images before every parameter update (full-batch gradient descent, as in the chapter’s equations) is expensive. Instead, in every epoch (one pass over the training set):

the training indices are put in a new random order,
the order is cut into consecutive pieces of batch_size indices (mini-batches),
for each mini-batch the loss and its gradient are computed on these images only, and the parameters are updated.

Every image is used exactly once per epoch; one epoch makes \(\lceil 50\,000/B\rceil\) updates (with \(B\) the batch size). The gradient of a mini-batch is a noisy estimate of the full gradient (stochastic gradient descent), but many cheap noisy steps are much faster than a few exact ones.
The function below produces the index arrays of the mini-batches. It is a Python generator: yield hands out one value and pauses the function until the next value is requested by the for loop, so the batches are produced one at a time.


Code
def batch_indices(n, batch_size, shuffle=True, generator=None):
    # Yield index tensors of consecutive mini-batches covering 0, ..., n-1 once.
    order = torch.randperm(n, generator=generator) if shuffle else torch.arange(n)
    for start in range(0, n, batch_size):
        yield order[start:start + batch_size]          # the last batch may be shorter

batch_size = 64
batches = list(batch_indices(len(X_tr), batch_size, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0)))
print("number of mini-batches per epoch:", len(batches), "  ( = ceil(50000 / 64) =", int(np.ceil(50000 / 64)), ")")
print("sizes of the first three and of the last batch:", [len(b) for b in batches[:3]], len(batches[-1]))
print("first batch indices:", batches[0][:10].tolist(), "...")
all_used = torch.sort(torch.cat(batches)).values
print("every training image used exactly once:", torch.equal(all_used, torch.arange(len(X_tr))))


number of mini-batches per epoch: 782   ( = ceil(50000 / 64) = 782 )
sizes of the first three and of the last batch: [64, 64, 64] 16
first batch indices: [36044, 49165, 37807, 11341, 6091, 16904, 36293, 28026, 24681, 17849] ...
every training image used exactly once: True


With batches of 64 images, \[50\,000 = 781\cdot 64 + 16 , \tag{4}\] hence \(782\) batches, the last one with \(16\) images. A batch of data is then X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]: a \(64\times784\) matrix \(X_i\) (one image per row, as in the chapter’s feed-forward pass) and a vector of \(64\) labels.


Code
idx = batches[0]
xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]
print("one mini-batch: inputs", tuple(xb.shape), "  labels", tuple(yb.shape))

fig, axes = plt.subplots(4, 16, figsize=(13, 3.8))
for ax, x, y in zip(axes.flat, xb, yb):
    ax.imshow(x.reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r")        # back to 28 x 28 for display only
    ax.set_title(str(y.item()), fontsize=9); ax.axis("off")
fig.suptitle("the first mini-batch of 64 images (in random order, with their labels)")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


one mini-batch: inputs (64, 784)   labels (64,)







4.2 Dataset and DataLoader
PyTorch packages these two steps into two classes from torch.utils.data. A Dataset knows how many samples there are (__len__) and returns sample number i (__getitem__), here a pair (image vector, label). A DataLoader takes a Dataset, shuffles the indices in every epoch, cuts them into batches, calls __getitem__ for every index of a batch, and stacks the results into batch tensors (collate).
Writing our own Dataset shows that there is nothing more to it. (For tensors already in memory PyTorch also offers the ready-made TensorDataset, which does the same.) For large data sets that do not fit into memory, __getitem__ would read one image from disk; the DataLoader can then load batches in parallel processes (num_workers). This is the main reason the classes exist.


Code
from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

class MNISTDataset(Dataset):
    # Pairs (image vector, label) stored as two tensors in memory.
    def __init__(self, X, y):
        self.X, self.y = X, y

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.X)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        return self.X[i], self.y[i]

ds_tr = MNISTDataset(X_tr, y_tr)
x0, y0 = ds_tr[0]                                       # calls __getitem__(0)
print("len(ds_tr) =", len(ds_tr), "   ds_tr[0]: image", tuple(x0.shape), " label", y0.item())

loader_tr = DataLoader(ds_tr, batch_size=64, shuffle=True, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(0))
print("batches per epoch: len(loader_tr) =", len(loader_tr))
xb_dl, yb_dl = next(iter(loader_tr))                   # the first batch of one epoch
print("one batch from the DataLoader:", tuple(xb_dl.shape), tuple(yb_dl.shape))


len(ds_tr) = 50000    ds_tr[0]: image (784,)  label 1
batches per epoch: len(loader_tr) = 782
one batch from the DataLoader: (64, 784) (64,)


With shuffle=False both methods must give identical batches, and indeed they do. The timing shows the price of the generality: the DataLoader calls __getitem__ \(50\,000\) times per epoch and stacks single images, while X_tr[idx] copies a whole batch in one operation.


Code
loader_fixed = DataLoader(ds_tr, batch_size=64, shuffle=False)
same = all(torch.equal(xd, X_tr[idx]) and torch.equal(yd, y_tr[idx])
           for (xd, yd), idx in zip(loader_fixed, batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64, shuffle=False)))
print("DataLoader(shuffle=False) gives the same batches as our own batching:", same)

t0 = time.perf_counter()
for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), 64):
    xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]
t_hand = time.perf_counter() - t0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for xb, yb in loader_tr:
    pass
t_dl = time.perf_counter() - t0
print(f"one epoch of batches: own function {t_hand:.3f} s,  DataLoader {t_dl:.3f} s")


DataLoader(shuffle=False) gives the same batches as our own batching: True


one epoch of batches: own function 0.020 s,  DataLoader 0.246 s


Both ways are used for training: model A (regression) uses our own batching function, model B (cross-entropy) the DataLoader. Each mini-batch has the same size and is drawn the same way, so the choice does not affect the comparison of the two models.

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
section: 5. Model A: one sigmoid output and the mean squared error
text:
5. Model A: one sigmoid output and the mean squared error

5.1 Regression targets for the digits
The chapter imagines an unknown function \(G\) that maps the 784 pixels of an image to the digit \(0,\dots,9\) it shows, and treats learning \(G\) as non-linear curve fitting (regression), just as in the one-dimensional example of the Universal Approximation Theorem. The network (model A) has one output node with a sigmoid, so \[\bar y = f_{\boldsymbol\theta}(\mathbf x)\in(0,1) . \tag{5}\] The target of an image with digit \(y\) is the rescaled digit \[t = y/10\in\{0, 0.1, \dots, 0.9\}, \tag{6}\] and the loss is the mean squared error over a batch of \(B\) images, \[\mathcal L = \frac1B\sum_{i=1}^B \big(\bar y_i - y_i/10\big)^2 . \tag{7}\] The predicted digit is \(10\,\bar y\) turned into an integer.
How it is turned into an integer matters. int() in Python (and .long() in PyTorch) truncates, e.g. 2.97 becomes 2, although the output is closest to the target \(3\). The correct choice is rounding to the nearest integer, then clipping to \(0\dots9\). (With the sigmoid, \(10\bar y\) lies between 0 and 10, so \(9.6\) would round to \(10\).)


Code
outputs = torch.tensor([0.031, 0.297, 0.304, 0.649, 0.951])         # example values of the sigmoid output
print("10 * y_bar       :", (10 * outputs).tolist())
print("truncated (int)  :", (10 * outputs).long().tolist())
print("rounded + clipped:", (10 * outputs).round().clamp(0, 9).long().tolist())

def predict_digit_regression(y_bar):
    # sigmoid output in (0,1)  ->  digit 0..9
    return (10 * y_bar).round().clamp(0, 9).long()


10 * y_bar       : [0.3100000023841858, 2.9699997901916504, 3.0399999618530273, 6.489999771118164, 9.510000228881836]
truncated (int)  : [0, 2, 3, 6, 9]
rounded + clipped: [0, 3, 3, 6, 9]




5.2 Single-output network
As in the chapter, the input is the flattened standardised image (784 numbers), followed by one hidden layer of \(N^{(1)}\) = 21 nodes and the output node, all with the sigmoid \[\sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z}} , \tag{8}\] \[\bar{\mathbf h} = \sigma\big(\mathbf x W^{(1)T} + \mathbf b^{(1)}\big)\in(0,1)^{21},\qquad \bar y = \sigma\big(\bar{\mathbf h}W^{(2)T} + b^{(2)}\big)\in(0,1). \tag{9}\] The number of hidden nodes is kept in the variable N_HIDDEN, so that it can be changed in one place (Exercise 4 shows what wider and deeper networks do). nn.Linear(n_in, n_out) holds \(W\) of shape (n_out, n_in) and \(\mathbf b\) of length n_out, and computes the affine map inside the sigmoids of equation (9) for a batch of row vectors \(\mathbf x\). (The chapter has no bias in the output layer; with one extra parameter this makes no difference.)


Code
N_HIDDEN = 21                                     # nodes in the hidden layer, as in the chapter

def make_regression_model():
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(784, N_HIDDEN), nn.Sigmoid(),      # hidden layer
        nn.Linear(N_HIDDEN, 1),   nn.Sigmoid(),      # ONE output node, value in (0, 1)
    )

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_reg = make_regression_model()
print(model_reg)
for name, p in model_reg.named_parameters():
    print(f"  {name:9s} {str(tuple(p.shape)):11s} {p.numel():7d} parameters")
print("total:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_reg.parameters()))

with torch.no_grad():
    out = model_reg(X_tr[:5])
print("output for 5 images, shape", tuple(out.shape), ":", out.squeeze(1).tolist())


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=784, out_features=21, bias=True)
  (1): Sigmoid()
  (2): Linear(in_features=21, out_features=1, bias=True)
  (3): Sigmoid()
)
  0.weight  (21, 784)     16464 parameters
  0.bias    (21,)            21 parameters
  2.weight  (1, 21)          21 parameters
  2.bias    (1,)              1 parameters
total: 16507
output for 5 images, shape (5, 1) : [0.49288123846054077, 0.5091497898101807, 0.5078026056289673, 0.48742517828941345, 0.5129513144493103]


The output has shape (B, 1), one column. The targets will have shape (B,), so the output is reshaped with .squeeze(1) before the loss is computed: nn.MSELoss given shapes (B, 1) and (B,) would broadcast them to a (B, B) matrix and compute something else; PyTorch only prints a warning, which is easy to overlook (a classic bug).
The untrained network gives nearly the same output, about 0.5, for every image (small random differences): it has not learned anything yet.


5.3 Loss and evaluation
A function that evaluates a model on a whole data set (all images at once, without gradients) returns the loss and the accuracy, the fraction of images whose predicted digit equals the label. The accuracy is what we care about, but it cannot be minimised by gradient descent: it is piecewise constant in the parameters, so its gradient is zero almost everywhere. The MSE changes smoothly.


Code
mse = nn.MSELoss()

def evaluate_regression(model, X, y):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        y_bar = model(X).squeeze(1)                     # shape (N,)
        loss = mse(y_bar, y.float() / 10).item()
        acc = (predict_digit_regression(y_bar) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss, acc

loss0, acc0 = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_va, y_va)
print(f"untrained network on the validation set: MSE {loss0:.4f}, accuracy {acc0:.3f}")


untrained network on the validation set: MSE 0.0879, accuracy 0.087




5.4 Training loop
The loop is written out in full. The optimiser is Adam with learning rate \(10^{-3}\); the chapter uses plain gradient descent, while Adam is discussed in the section The Zoo of Optimization Algorithms and is much less sensitive to the choice of the learning rate (plain gradient descent is used in Exercise 5). One epoch is one pass over the \(782\) mini-batches of Section 4.1, and for each batch the loop performs the forward pass, computes the loss, clears the old gradients (zero_grad), computes \(\partial\mathcal L/\partial\boldsymbol\theta\) (backward) and updates the parameters (step). The loss of every mini-batch is stored, since it is cheap and shows the noise of stochastic gradient descent, and after every epoch the loss and accuracy on the full training and validation sets are computed with evaluate_regression.
model.train() / model.eval() switch layers (such as dropout, which randomly switches off nodes during training) between training and evaluation behaviour. This network has no such layers, but the calls belong to the standard loop.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_reg = make_regression_model()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model_reg.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
n_epochs, batch_size = 20, 64
shuffle_gen = torch.Generator().manual_seed(1)           # random order of the batches, reproducible
hist_reg = {"batch loss": [], "train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t_start = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    model_reg.train()
    for idx in batch_indices(len(X_tr), batch_size, shuffle=True, generator=shuffle_gen):
        xb, yb = X_tr[idx], y_tr[idx]                    # one mini-batch: (B, 784) and (B,)
        target = yb.float() / 10                         # digit / 10
        y_bar = model_reg(xb).squeeze(1)                 # forward pass, shape (B,)
        loss = mse(y_bar, target)

        optimizer.zero_grad()                            # clear gradients of the previous step
        loss.backward()                                  # backpropagation
        optimizer.step()                                 # theta <- theta - (Adam step)
        hist_reg["batch loss"].append(loss.item())

    tr_loss, tr_acc = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_tr, y_tr)
    va_loss, va_acc = evaluate_regression(model_reg, X_va, y_va)
    for key, v in zip(["train loss", "train acc", "val loss", "val acc"], [tr_loss, tr_acc, va_loss, va_acc]):
        hist_reg[key].append(v)
    if epoch == 1 or epoch % 2 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}:  MSE train {tr_loss:.4f}  val {va_loss:.4f}   accuracy train {tr_acc:.3f}  val {va_acc:.3f}")
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t_start:.0f} s")

The left panel shows the MSE: the thin line is the loss of the individual mini-batches (x-axis converted to epochs: batch \(k\) is at epoch \(k/782\)), and the markers are the losses on the full training and validation sets after every epoch. The right panel shows the accuracies.


Code
def plot_history(hist, loss_name, title):
    n_ep = len(hist["train loss"])
    epochs = np.arange(1, n_ep + 1)
    batch_x = np.arange(1, len(hist["batch loss"]) + 1) / (len(hist["batch loss"]) / n_ep)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
    axes[0].plot(batch_x, hist["batch loss"], color="lightgrey", lw=0.5, label="mini-batches")
    axes[0].plot(epochs, hist["train loss"], "o-", label="training set")
    axes[0].plot(epochs, hist["val loss"], "s-", label="validation set")
    axes[0].set_yscale("log"); axes[0].set_ylabel(loss_name)
    axes[1].plot(epochs, hist["train acc"], "o-", label="training set")
    axes[1].plot(epochs, hist["val acc"], "s-", label="validation set")
    axes[1].set_ylabel("accuracy")
    for ax in axes:
        ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.legend()
    fig.suptitle(title); fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

plot_history(hist_reg, "MSE loss", "Single sigmoid output and MSE")





The network learns, but slowly and not far: the validation accuracy rises from about \(9\%\) before training and \(36\%\) after one epoch to about \(60\%\) after four epochs and then creeps up to about \(64\%\) after twenty. The loss on the validation set flattens after about seven epochs, while the training loss continues to decrease slightly: the small hidden layer cannot do much better with this formulation of the task. The accuracy curve is jagged: a small change of the parameters can push many outputs across a rounding boundary \(k\pm0.5\) at once.


5.6 Confusion matrices (Box 2.11)
The confusion matrix \(C\) counts, for every pair (true digit \(i\), predicted digit \(j\)), how many images of digit \(i\) (in a given set) were predicted as \(j\). We show it for all three sets: training (the data the parameters were fitted to), validation (used during training to monitor the model) and test (used only now). Each row is normalised to sum to one, so \(C_{ij}\) is the fraction of images of digit \(i\) that were classified as \(j\); the diagonal element \(C_{ii}\) is the fraction of digit \(i\) recognised correctly. The mean of the diagonal is the accuracy averaged over classes (Box 2.11); since the MNIST classes are nearly balanced it is almost equal to the plain accuracy.
The matrix is built with one bincount: the pair \((i, j)\) is encoded as the single number \[n = 10\,i + j \in\{0,\dots,99\}, \tag{10}\] the occurrences are counted and arranged as a \(10\times10\) matrix.


Code
def confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, k=10):
    C = torch.bincount(k * y_true + y_pred, minlength=k * k).reshape(k, k).float()
    return C / C.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True)              # each row (true class) sums to 1

def plot_confusion(ax, C, title):
    im = ax.imshow(C, cmap="Blues", vmin=0, vmax=1)
    for i in range(10):
        for j in range(10):
            if C[i, j] >= 0.005:
                ax.text(j, i, f"{C[i, j]:.2f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6.5,
                        color="white" if C[i, j] > 0.5 else "black")
    ax.set_xticks(range(10)); ax.set_yticks(range(10))
    ax.set_xlabel("predicted digit $j$"); ax.set_ylabel("true digit $i$")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}\nmean of diagonal = {C.diagonal().mean():.3f}", fontsize=10)
    return im

      f"   validation {(pred_reg_va == y_va).float().mean():.3f}   test {acc_reg_te:.3f}")

The three matrices look almost the same. Training and test accuracies differ by only about 2–3 points, so overfitting is mild; validation and test agree, so the validation set, which we watched during training, was a reliable estimate of the performance on new data. The model is limited by the task as posed. The confusion matrix shows the characteristic pattern of the regression: the errors form bands next to the diagonal. A \(5\) is predicted as \(4\) or \(6\) in almost half of the cases, an \(8\) as \(7\) or \(9\) and a \(2\) as \(1\) or \(3\) in more than a third. Confusions between digits of similar shape but distant value (such as \(4\) and \(9\)) do not appear as such.
The continuous output shows why. For every true digit we plot the distribution of \(10\,\bar y\) over the test images (a violin plot: the width is the histogram of the values). The dashed horizontal lines are the rounding boundaries \(k\pm 0.5\); an image is classified correctly when its value lies in the band around its own digit.

ax.violinplot([10 * y_bar_te[y_te == k].numpy() for k in range(10)], positions=range(10), widths=0.8, showmedians=True)

The output for each digit is centred near the target, but the distributions are wide, about one unit for most digits, and have long tails (the blue horizontal bars mark the minimum, median and maximum; the black bars the targets). Everything that leaks across a dashed line becomes a wrong digit, and leaking across one line is far more likely than across several: about three quarters of the wrong predictions are off by exactly one. \(0\), \(1\) and \(6\) are narrowest; \(5\) and \(8\), which sit in the middle of many other digits on the number line, are the widest and the worst recognised.

title: Lab 009: MNIST, regression versus cross-entropy
section: 6. Ten outputs, softmax and categorical cross-entropy
text:
6. Ten outputs, softmax and categorical cross-entropy

6.1 One-hot encoding, softmax and the cross-entropy
In model B the network returns, instead of one number, ten numbers \(z_0,\dots,z_9\) (the logits), one per class. The softmax \[q_k = \mathrm{SoftMax}(\mathbf z)_k = \frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{j=0}^{9} e^{z_j}} \tag{11}\] turns them into a probability distribution \(\mathbf q\), \[q_k > 0, \qquad \sum_k q_k = 1 . \tag{12}\] \(q_k\) is read as the probability, according to the network, that the image shows digit \(k\). The predicted digit is the most probable one, \[\hat y = \arg\max_k q_k . \tag{13}\]
The label \(y\) is written as a one-hot vector \(\mathbf p\) (Box 2.7), \[p_k = \delta_{k,y} , \tag{14}\] which is the “true” distribution, with all probability on the correct class. Two distributions are compared with the Kullback–Leibler divergence (Box 2.8), \[\mathrm{KL}(\mathbf p\,\|\,\mathbf q) = \sum_k p_k\log\frac{p_k}{q_k} = \underbrace{\sum_k p_k\log p_k}_{-\,\mathcal H(\mathbf p)\ \text{(no }\boldsymbol\theta\text{)}}\;\underbrace{-\sum_k p_k\log q_k}_{\mathcal L_{\rm ce}} . \tag{15}\] (Here and below \(\log\) denotes the natural logarithm.) Only the second term depends on the network, so the loss is the categorical cross-entropy, averaged over the batch of \(B\) images. For a one-hot \(\mathbf p\) only the term of the true class survives: \[\mathcal L_{\rm ce} = -\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\sum_{k=0}^{9} p_{ik}\log q_{ik} = -\frac1B\sum_{i=1}^{B}\log q_{i,y_i} . \tag{16}\] It is \(0\) if the network gives probability \(1\) to the true class and grows without bound as that probability goes to \(0\).
In PyTorch, nn.CrossEntropyLoss takes the logits of shape (B, 10) and the labels as integers of shape (B,). It applies the softmax itself (in a numerically stable form, via the logarithm of the denominator of equation (11)), so the model must not end with a softmax layer. On random logits equation (16), written out with one-hot vectors, gives the same number.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
z = torch.randn(5, 10)                                  # logits for a batch of 5 images
y5 = y_tr[:5]                                           # their true labels

q = torch.softmax(z, dim=1)                             # probabilities, each row sums to 1
p = nn.functional.one_hot(y5, num_classes=10).float()   # one-hot labels, shape (5, 10)
print("labels:", y5.tolist())
print("one-hot p:\n", p.int())
print("row sums of q:", q.sum(dim=1).tolist())

ce_by_hand = -(p * torch.log(q)).sum(dim=1).mean()
ce_torch = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()(z, y5)
print(f"cross-entropy from the formula: {ce_by_hand:.6f}   nn.CrossEntropyLoss: {ce_torch:.6f}")

6.2 Ten-output network
The hidden layer is exactly that of model A. Only the output layer changes: \(10\) nodes instead of \(1\), and no sigmoid (the softmax is inside the loss).


Code
def make_classification_model():
    return nn.Sequential(
        nn.Linear(784, N_HIDDEN), nn.Sigmoid(),      # hidden layer   (as in model A)
        nn.Linear(N_HIDDEN, 10),                     # TEN output nodes: logits z_0 ... z_9
    )

torch.manual_seed(0)
model_ce = make_classification_model()
print(model_ce)
print("parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_ce.parameters()),
      "  (model A:", sum(p.numel() for p in model_reg.parameters()), ";  difference 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1) =", 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1), ")")


Sequential(
  (0): Linear(in_features=784, out_features=21, bias=True)
  (1): Sigmoid()
  (2): Linear(in_features=21, out_features=10, bias=True)
)
parameters: 16705   (model A: 16507 ;  difference 9 * (N_HIDDEN + 1) = 198 )


An untrained network gives roughly equal probabilities, about 1/10, to all classes, so the cross-entropy should start near \[\mathcal L_{\rm ce} \approx -\log\tfrac{1}{10} = \log 10 \approx 2.30 . \tag{17}\]


Code
ce = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()

def evaluate_classification(model, X, y):
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        logits = model(X)                               # shape (N, 10)
        loss = ce(logits, y).item()
        acc = (logits.argmax(dim=1) == y).float().mean().item()
    return loss, acc

loss0, acc0 = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_va, y_va)
print(f"untrained: cross-entropy {loss0:.3f} (ln 10 = {np.log(10):.3f}),  accuracy {acc0:.3f}")


untrained: cross-entropy 2.356 (ln 10 = 2.303),  accuracy 0.072




6.3 Training loop with the cross-entropy
The loop is the same as for model A with three differences: the batches come from a DataLoader as in Section 4.2, the target is the integer label itself, and the loss is the cross-entropy of the \(10\) logits. Optimiser, learning rate, batch size and number of epochs are the same as for model A.


Code
torch.manual_seed(0)
model_ce = make_classification_model()
optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model_ce.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
n_epochs, batch_size = 20, 64
loader_tr = DataLoader(MNISTDataset(X_tr, y_tr), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=True,
                       generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(1))
hist_ce = {"batch loss": [], "train loss": [], "val loss": [], "train acc": [], "val acc": []}

t_start = time.perf_counter()
for epoch in range(1, n_epochs + 1):
    model_ce.train()
    for xb, yb in loader_tr:                             # the DataLoader shuffles and batches
        logits = model_ce(xb)                            # forward pass, shape (B, 10)
        loss = ce(logits, yb)                            # target: integer labels, shape (B,)

        optimizer.zero_grad()
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()
        hist_ce["batch loss"].append(loss.item())

    tr_loss, tr_acc = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_tr, y_tr)
    va_loss, va_acc = evaluate_classification(model_ce, X_va, y_va)
    for key, v in zip(["train loss", "train acc", "val loss", "val acc"], [tr_loss, tr_acc, va_loss, va_acc]):
        hist_ce[key].append(v)
    if epoch == 1 or epoch % 2 == 0:
        print(f"epoch {epoch:2d}:  CE train {tr_loss:.4f}  val {va_loss:.4f}   accuracy train {tr_acc:.3f}  val {va_acc:.3f}")
print(f"training took {time.perf_counter() - t_start:.0f} s")

7. Output layer and loss

7.1 Comparison of the two models
Both networks have the same hidden layer, the same optimiser, learning rate, batch size and number of epochs. They differ only in the output layer and the loss. The figure shows the training and validation accuracies of both models against the epoch next to their test confusion matrices, and the printed table gives the test accuracy and the number of misclassified test images.

epochs = np.arange(1, n_epochs + 1)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(17, 4.8), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.2, 1, 1]})

axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_reg["train acc"], "o--", color="tab:blue", alpha=0.5, label="A: training")
axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_ce["val acc"], "s-", label="B: 10 outputs + CE (validation)")
axes[0].plot(epochs, hist_ce["train acc"], "o--", color="tab:orange", alpha=0.5, label="B: training")
axes[0].set_xlabel("epoch"); axes[0].set_ylabel("accuracy"); axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
plot_confusion(axes[1], C_reg, "A: regression")
plot_confusion(axes[2], C_ce, "B: cross-entropy")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{'':28s} {'regression (A)':>15s} {'cross-entropy (B)':>18s}")

test accuracy                          0.652              0.948
misclassified test images               3480                516


This is the central result of the notebook. With the same hidden layer, data and training, the single-output regression reaches about \(65\%\) test accuracy and the ten-output cross-entropy network about \(95\%\), with about seven times fewer errors. The difference comes from how the task is posed, that is, from the output layer and the loss together; Exercise 2 shows that the ten outputs account for most of the gain. Model B is better in every epoch: after one epoch it is already far beyond the best value model A ever reaches. The confusion matrices show two different kinds of errors: bands along the diagonal (A: neighbouring values) versus rare, scattered errors (B: similar shapes).


Code
top2 = q_te.topk(2, dim=1)                                # two largest probabilities and their digits
a, b = top2.indices[:, 0], top2.indices[:, 1]
doubtful = torch.nonzero((top2.values[:, 1] > 0.25) & ((a - b).abs() >= 3))[:, 0]

    ax.set_title(f"true {y_te[n].item()}\nB: {a[n].item()} ({q_te[n, a[n]]:.2f}) / {b[n].item()} ({q_te[n, b[n]]:.2f})\n"
                 f"A: 10y = {10 * y_bar_te[n]:.1f} -> {pred_reg_te[n].item()}", fontsize=8.5)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()
