title: Lab 010: Monte Carlo samples of the 2D Ising model
text:
3. Equilibration time
A chain starts from an arbitrary configuration, which is not typical for \(p(\boldsymbol s)\). We therefore discard the first sweeps (burn-in) until the observables stop drifting. Two starting points are natural: a cold start, with all spins up (the ground state, reached at zero temperature), and a hot start, with random spins (the state typical of infinite temperature). They lie at the two extremes, so when chains from both starts arrive at the same values, the chain has (very likely) forgotten where it began.


Code
Lx_demo = 20
masks_demo = checkerboard_masks(Lx_demo, Lx_demo)
T_demo = np.array([1.8, 2.27, 3.0], dtype=np.float32)
n_sweeps = 1500
n_chains_demo = 4

starts = {"cold": np.ones((n_chains_demo, len(T_demo), Lx_demo, Lx_demo), np.float32),
          "hot":  rng.choice(np.array([-1, 1], np.float32), size=(n_chains_demo, len(T_demo), Lx_demo, Lx_demo))}
series = {}
for name, s in starts.items():
    beta = (1.0 / T_demo)[None, :, None, None]
    m_t, e_t = [], []
    for t in range(n_sweeps):
        metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks_demo, rng)
        m_t.append(magnetisation_per_spin(s)); e_t.append(energy_per_spin(s))
    series[name] = (np.array(m_t), np.array(e_t), s.copy())      # arrays of shape (sweep, chain, T)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(13, 5.5), sharex=True)
for k, T in enumerate(T_demo):
    for name, col in (("cold", UJNavy), ("hot", DSOrange)):
        m_t, e_t, _ = series[name]
        for c in range(n_chains_demo):
            axes[0, k].plot(np.abs(m_t[:, c, k]), color=col, lw=0.8, alpha=0.7, label=f"{name} start" if c == 0 else None)
            axes[1, k].plot(e_t[:, c, k], color=col, lw=0.8, alpha=0.7)
    axes[0, k].set_title(f"T = {T:.2f}", loc="left")
    axes[0, k].set_ylabel(r"$|m|$"); axes[1, k].set_ylabel(r"$e$"); axes[1, k].set_xlabel("sweep")
    axes[0, k].set_xscale("log"); axes[1, k].set_xscale("log")
axes[0, 0].legend(frameon=False)
fig.suptitle(f"{Lx_demo}x{Lx_demo} lattice, {n_chains_demo} chains per start", x=0.01, ha="left")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





The three temperatures behave very differently. At the temperature 3.0, in the disordered phase, the curves from both starts merge after a few sweeps. At 1.8, in the ordered phase, a hot start must coarsen: domains of up and down spins grow and merge. Sometimes two domains wrap around the torus as stripes, separated by two flat domain walls. A flat wall costs energy but has no curvature that would make it shrink, so it can survive for a very long time, and such a chain sits at \(|m|\) well below the ordered value with a slightly higher energy. Whether this happens depends on the random seed; a run with another seed (or more chains) shows this in the snapshots below. Close to \(T_c\), at 2.27, the fluctuations are large and slow, an effect called critical slowing down.
For the dataset we use a cold start: below \(T_c\) it is already close to equilibrium, and above \(T_c\) it melts quickly.


Code
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3 * n_chains_demo, figsize=(13, 2.6))
for r, name in enumerate(("cold", "hot")):
    s_final = series[name][2]
    for k in range(len(T_demo)):
        for c in range(n_chains_demo):
            ax = axes[r, k * n_chains_demo + c]
            show_spins(ax, s_final[c, k])
            if c == 0: ax.set_title(f"T={T_demo[k]:.2f}", fontsize=8, loc="left")
    axes[r, 0].set_ylabel(name, fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle(f"configurations after {n_sweeps} sweeps (rows: cold / hot start)", x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=10)
plt.show()

title: Lab 010: Monte Carlo samples of the 2D Ising model
text:
4. Decorrelation of stored samples
Even after equilibration, consecutive configurations of a Markov chain are correlated, because one sweep changes only part of the lattice. For an observable \(O\) (here \(|m|\)) the correlation is measured by the normalised autocorrelation function \[
C_O(t) = \frac{\langle O_{t_0}O_{t_0+t}\rangle - \langle O\rangle^2}{\langle O^2\rangle-\langle O\rangle^2}, \qquad C_O(0)=1, \tag{15}
\] and summarised by the integrated autocorrelation time \[
\tau_{\rm int} = \frac12 + \sum_{t\geq1} C_O(t). \tag{16}
\] Out of \(n\) consecutive measurements only about \[n_{\rm eff}\approx\frac{n}{2\tau_{\rm int}} \tag{17}\] are effectively independent. We sum \(C_O(t)\) up to the first time it drops below zero, because beyond that point the estimate is noise. Two ways of obtaining nearly independent samples follow: store a configuration only after at least about twice \(\tau_{\rm int}\) sweeps, or run many independent chains. We do both.


Code
def autocorrelation(x):
    # x: (time, chains). Normalised autocorrelation averaged over chains, computed with the FFT.
    x = x - x.mean(axis=0)
    n = x.shape[0]
    f = np.fft.rfft(x, n=2 * n, axis=0)
    acf = np.fft.irfft(f * np.conj(f), axis=0)[:n].mean(axis=1)
    return acf / acf[0]

def tau_int(acf):
    cut = np.argmax(acf < 0) if np.any(acf < 0) else len(acf)   # stop at the first negative value
    return 0.5 + acf[1:cut].sum()

T_acf = np.array([1.8, 2.1, 2.27, 2.5, 3.0], dtype=np.float32)
n_chains_acf, n_eq_acf, n_meas_acf = 32, 1000, 3000
s = np.ones((n_chains_acf, len(T_acf), 20, 20), np.float32)
beta = (1.0 / T_acf)[None, :, None, None]
for _ in range(n_eq_acf):
    metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks_demo, rng)
absm = np.empty((n_meas_acf, n_chains_acf, len(T_acf)), np.float32)
for t in range(n_meas_acf):
    metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks_demo, rng)
    absm[t] = np.abs(magnetisation_per_spin(s))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
acf_colours = [UJNavy, UJBlue, DSOrange, "#E3A23B", UJGray]
acf_styles = ["-", "--", "-", "--", ":"]
taus = {}
for k, T in enumerate(T_acf):
    acf = autocorrelation(absm[:, :, k])
    taus[T] = tau_int(acf)
    ax.plot(acf[:300], color=acf_colours[k], ls=acf_styles[k], lw=2, label=fr"$T={T:.2f}$, $\tau_{{\rm int}}={taus[T]:.1f}$")
ax.axhline(0, color=UJGray, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("time lag $t$ (sweeps)"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$C_{|m|}(t)$"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("20x20: autocorrelation of |m|", loc="left"); plt.show()
for T, tau in taus.items():
    print(f"T = {T:.2f}:  tau_int = {tau:6.1f} sweeps")





T = 1.80:  tau_int =    1.3 sweeps
T = 2.10:  tau_int =    7.2 sweeps
T = 2.27:  tau_int =   14.8 sweeps
T = 2.50:  tau_int =    8.2 sweeps
T = 3.00:  tau_int =    1.7 sweeps


The autocorrelation time is largest close to \(T_c\) — critical slowing down: near \(T_c\) the correlated regions are large, and a local single-spin update needs many sweeps to change them. (Cluster algorithms such as Wolff’s avoid this; we stay with Metropolis because it is simple and is the algorithm of the Lecture Notes.)
The dataset uses 20 independent chains per temperature and stores a configuration every n_between sweeps. Compare n_between with the values of \(\tau_{\rm int}\) printed above: far from \(T_c\) the stored samples of one chain are practically independent; close to \(T_c\) they are not fully independent, but the 20 chains are.

title: Lab 010: Monte Carlo samples of the 2D Ising model
text:
5. Generating the dataset
We sample a grid of temperatures from 1.0 to 3.5 in steps of 0.05. All temperatures and all chains are updated together as one array of shape (chains, temperatures, Ny, Nx).
One more detail concerns symmetry. The Ising energy is symmetric under a global spin flip, which reverses every spin, but a cold start puts every low-temperature chain into the state of positive magnetisation, and on our time scales it stays there. We restore the symmetry exactly by flipping each stored configuration with probability one half. Without this step a network could learn the trivial rule “black means ordered”.
One sample of the data set is an \(N_y\times N_x\) array of spins \(\pm1\), stored as 8-bit integers, together with the temperature at which it was drawn; Lab 011 derives its labels (ordered or disordered) from that temperature. For the \(20\times20\) lattice the file holds 51 temperatures with 200 configurations each, 10 200 samples in all. The lattice size is set by Nx and Ny; both must be even.


Code
Nx, Ny = 20, 20                                        # lattice size (even numbers)
temperatures = np.round(np.arange(1.0, 3.5 + 1e-9, 0.05), 2)
n_chains   = 20                                        # independent chains per temperature
n_samples  = 10                                        # stored configurations per chain  -> 200 per temperature
n_equil    = 1000                                      # burn-in sweeps
n_between  = 20                                        # sweeps between stored configurations

def generate_dataset(Nx, Ny, temperatures, n_chains, n_samples, n_equil, n_between, rng):
    masks = checkerboard_masks(Ny, Nx)
    beta = (1.0 / temperatures.astype(np.float32))[None, :, None, None]
    s = np.ones((n_chains, len(temperatures), Ny, Nx), np.float32)       # cold start
    for _ in range(n_equil):
        metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks, rng)
    stored = np.empty((n_samples, n_chains, len(temperatures), Ny, Nx), np.int8)
    for k in range(n_samples):
        for _ in range(n_between):
            metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks, rng)
        stored[k] = s
    configs = stored.transpose(2, 0, 1, 3, 4).reshape(len(temperatures), n_samples * n_chains, Ny, Nx)
    flip = rng.choice(np.array([-1, 1], np.int8), size=configs.shape[:2])  # random global spin flip
    return configs * flip[:, :, None, None]

t0 = time.time()
configs = generate_dataset(Nx, Ny, temperatures, n_chains, n_samples, n_equil, n_between, rng)
print(f"configs: shape {configs.shape} (temperatures, samples, Ny, Nx), dtype {configs.dtype}, "
      f"generated in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
path = f"data/ising_Nx{Nx}_Ny{Ny}.npz"
np.savez_compressed(path, configs=configs, T=temperatures, Nx=Nx, Ny=Ny,
                    n_equil=n_equil, n_between=n_between, n_chains=n_chains)
print(f"saved to {path}  ({os.path.getsize(path) / 1e6:.2f} MB)")

Each column of the figure shows three stored configurations at one temperature, from deep in the ordered phase (temperature 1.2) to the disordered phase (3.2), with the columns between 1.9 and 2.6 bracketing \(T_c\).

show_T = [1.2, 1.9, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 3.2]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, len(show_T), figsize=(13, 5.8))
for k, T in enumerate(show_T):

    for r in range(3):
        ax = axes[r, k]
        show_spins(ax, configs[i, r * 37])
    axes[0, k].set_title(f"T = {temperatures[i]:.2f}" + ("  (< T_c)" if temperatures[i] < TC else "  (> T_c)"),
                         fontsize=9, color=UJNavy if temperatures[i] < TC else DSOrange)
fig.suptitle(f"{Nx}x{Ny} samples (white = +1, black = -1); exact T_c = {TC:.4f}", x=0.01, ha="left")

title: Lab 010: Monte Carlo samples of the 2D Ising model
text:
7. Thermodynamics and Onsager’s exact solution
The samples can now be compared with the exact results for the infinite lattice, with \(J\) set to 1. With the reduced coupling \[K=\beta J \tag{18}\] and \[\kappa = \frac{2\sinh 2K}{\cosh^2 2K}, \tag{19}\] the free energy found by Onsager (1944) reads \[
-\beta f = \frac{\ln Z}{N} = \ln\left(2\cosh 2K\right) + \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi d\phi\, \ln\frac{1+\sqrt{1-\kappa^2\sin^2\phi}}{2}. \tag{20}
\] The energy per spin is its derivative, \[u = -\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\frac{\ln Z}{N}, \tag{21}\] which evaluates to \[
u = -\coth 2K\left[1+\frac{2}{\pi}\left(2\tanh^2 2K-1\right)K_1(\kappa)\right], \tag{22}
\] \[
K_1(\kappa)=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\phi}{\sqrt{1-\kappa^2\sin^2\phi}}. \tag{23}
\] The spontaneous magnetisation was announced by Onsager in 1949 and proved by Yang in 1952: \[
M = \begin{cases}\left[1-\sinh^{-4}2K\right]^{1/8}, & T<T_c,\\[2pt] 0, & T>T_c.\end{cases} \tag{24}
\]
Equation (22) is checked against a numerical derivative of the free-energy integral, equation (20). SciPy’s ellipk(m) takes as its parameter the square of \(\kappa\).


Code
def lnZ_per_spin(T):
    K = 1.0 / T
    kap = 2 * np.sinh(2 * K) / np.cosh(2 * K) ** 2
    integrand = lambda p: np.log(0.5 * (1 + np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1 - kap**2 * np.sin(p) ** 2))))
    I, _ = quad(integrand, 0, np.pi, points=[np.pi / 2], limit=200)
    return np.log(2 * np.cosh(2 * K)) + I / (2 * np.pi)

def u_exact(T):
    K = 1.0 / np.asarray(T, float)
    kap = 2 * np.sinh(2 * K) / np.cosh(2 * K) ** 2
    return -1 / np.tanh(2 * K) * (1 + 2 / np.pi * (2 * np.tanh(2 * K) ** 2 - 1) * ellipk(kap**2))

def M_exact(T):
    T = np.asarray(T, float)
    out = np.zeros_like(T)
    low = T < TC
    out[low] = (1 - np.sinh(2 / T[low]) ** -4) ** 0.125
    return out

for T in (1.5, 2.0, 2.6, 3.5):                        # u from the formula vs -d lnZ / d beta (central difference)
    b, h = 1 / T, 1e-5
    u_num = -(lnZ_per_spin(1 / (b + h)) - lnZ_per_spin(1 / (b - h))) / (2 * h)

Far from \(T_c\) the Monte Carlo points lie on the exact curves: a \(20\times20\) lattice is already “large” there, because the correlation length is short. Near \(T_c\) the finite lattice deviates. \(\langle|m|\rangle\) does not drop to zero at \(T_c\) but has a smooth tail above it, whereas the exact \(M\) of equation (24) has an infinite slope at \(T_c\), which no finite system can have. Likewise \(c\) and \(\chi\) have finite peaks instead of divergences; the peaks (at the temperatures 2.30 and 2.35 in the printed output) lie close to the exact critical temperature \[T_c=\frac{2}{\ln\big(1+\sqrt2\big)}\approx2.2692, \tag{25}\] but not exactly at it.

title: Lab 010: Monte Carlo samples of the 2D Ising model
text:
8. Finite-size effects
A phase transition is a non-analyticity of \(\ln Z\) (Lecture 4). For finite \(N\), \(Z\) is a finite sum of exponentials of \(\beta\), an analytic function, so a finite lattice has no sharp transition. What we see are pseudo-critical features (peaks of \(c\) and \(\chi\), the steepest drop of \(\langle|m|\rangle\)) whose positions \(T^*(L)\) approach \(T_c\) as \(L\) grows without bound, while the peaks grow.
The mechanism is the divergence of the correlation length \(\xi(T)\) at \(T_c\). On a lattice of size \(L\) the critical behaviour is cut off when \[\xi(T)\approx L, \tag{26}\] so the transition is rounded over a window that shrinks as \(L\) grows. Since \[\xi\sim|T-T_c|^{-\nu}, \tag{27}\] the window is \[|T-T_c|\sim L^{-1/\nu}. \tag{28}\]
The prediction is tested by computing \(\chi(T)\) for the lattice sizes 10, 20 and 40 on a fine grid around \(T_c\), measuring after every sweep.


Code
def chi_scan(L, temps, n_chains, n_eq, n_meas, rng):
    # Measure <|m|> and chi on a temperature grid; measurements after every sweep (correlated, but averages are fine).
    masks = checkerboard_masks(L, L)
    beta = (1.0 / temps.astype(np.float32))[None, :, None, None]
    s = np.ones((n_chains, len(temps), L, L), np.float32)
    for _ in range(n_eq):
        metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks, rng)
    m1, m2 = np.zeros(len(temps)), np.zeros(len(temps))
    for _ in range(n_meas):
        metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks, rng)
        m = np.abs(magnetisation_per_spin(s))            # (chains, temps)
        m1 += m.mean(0); m2 += (m**2).mean(0)
    m1, m2 = m1 / n_meas, m2 / n_meas
    return m1, L * L * (m2 - m1**2) / temps

T_fs = np.round(np.arange(1.9, 2.9 + 1e-9, 0.04), 2)
fs = {}
t0 = time.time()
for L, nch in ((10, 32), (20, 16), (40, 8)):
    fs[L] = chi_scan(L, T_fs, n_chains=nch, n_eq=1000, n_meas=2000, rng=rng)
print(f"finite-size scan done in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
for (L, (m1, ch)), col, mk in zip(fs.items(), (UJGray, UJBlue, DSOrange), ("s", "o", "^")):
    axes[0].plot(T_fs, m1, "-" + mk, color=col, ms=4, label=f"L = {L}")
    axes[1].plot(T_fs, ch, "-" + mk, color=col, ms=4, label=f"L = {L}")
Tf2 = np.linspace(1.9, 2.9, 400)
axes[0].plot(Tf2, M_exact(Tf2), color=UJNavy, lw=2, ls="--", label=r"exact $L=\infty$")
for ax, lab in zip(axes, (r"$\langle|m|\rangle$", r"$\chi$")):
    ax.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":", lw=1.2); ax.set_xlabel("$T$"); ax.set_ylabel(lab); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(" L   T*(L) = argmax chi   chi_max    T*(L) - T_c")
for L, (m1, ch) in fs.items():
    i = np.argmax(ch)
    print(f"{L:3d}   {T_fs[i]:.2f}               {ch[i]:7.2f}    {T_fs[i] - TC:+.3f}")

As \(L\) grows, the drop of \(\langle|m|\rangle\) becomes steeper and approaches the exact curve, and the peak of \(\chi\) grows and moves toward \(T_c\): in the table above \(T^*(L)\) goes from 2.46 to 2.38 to 2.30 for the lattice sizes 10, 20 and 40, while \(\chi_{\max}\) rises from 2.64 to 31.62 (the grid spacing 0.04 limits the resolution of \(T^*(L)\)).
Locating \(T_c\) from finite data is therefore a finite-size extrapolation, not a single measurement. The CNN in Lab 011 faces exactly the same limitation: its estimate \(\bar T_c\) is a pseudo-critical temperature of an \(L\times L\) lattice. What the samples do not tell us is why there is a transition, or why it sits at the value of equation (25). That answer came from Onsager’s exact solution (Lecture 4 and Lab 012).

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
1. The data
One sample is a spin configuration \(\boldsymbol s\in\{-1,+1\}^{L\times L}\) of the 2D Ising model with periodic boundaries; each entry is the orientation of one spin. The configurations are drawn from the Boltzmann distribution \[p(\boldsymbol s)\propto e^{-H(\boldsymbol s)/T},\qquad H(\boldsymbol s)=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j, \tag{2}\] by the checkerboard Metropolis algorithm (N. Metropolis, A. W. Rosenbluth, M. N. Rosenbluth, A. H. Teller and E. Teller, J. Chem. Phys. 21, 1087 (1953), doi:10.1063/1.1699114) of Lab 010, where the sampler is derived and tested. A compact copy of it generates the data when the file of Lab 010 is missing, in the same format: configs with shape (temperatures, samples, L, L) and the temperature grid T. For each of the 51 temperatures \(T=1.00, 1.05,\dots,3.50\) there are 200 configurations, each multiplied by a random global sign, since \(H\) is symmetric under \(\boldsymbol s\to-\boldsymbol s\). The data carry no labels of their own: the labels “ordered” and “disordered” are assigned from the temperature in Section 2.


Code
def metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks, rng):
    # One checkerboard Metropolis sweep (in place) of a batch of lattices s: (..., Ny, Nx), periodic boundaries.
    for mask in masks:
        nn_sum = (np.roll(s, 1, -1) + np.roll(s, -1, -1) + np.roll(s, 1, -2) + np.roll(s, -1, -2))
        accept = rng.random(s.shape, dtype=np.float32) < np.exp(-beta * 2.0 * s * nn_sum)
        s[...] = np.where(mask & accept, -s, s)

def generate_dataset(Nx, Ny, temperatures, n_chains, n_samples, n_equil, n_between, rng):
    # Cold start, burn-in, then n_samples stored configurations per chain; random global spin flip at the end.
    y, x = np.indices((Ny, Nx)); black = (x + y) % 2 == 0
    beta = (1.0 / temperatures.astype(np.float32))[None, :, None, None]
    s = np.ones((n_chains, len(temperatures), Ny, Nx), np.float32)
    for _ in range(n_equil):
        metropolis_sweep(s, beta, (black, ~black), rng)
    stored = np.empty((n_samples, n_chains, len(temperatures), Ny, Nx), np.int8)
    for k in range(n_samples):
        for _ in range(n_between):
            metropolis_sweep(s, beta, (black, ~black), rng)
        stored[k] = s
    configs = stored.transpose(2, 0, 1, 3, 4).reshape(len(temperatures), n_samples * n_chains, Ny, Nx)
    flip = rng.choice(np.array([-1, 1], np.int8), size=configs.shape[:2])
    return configs * flip[:, :, None, None]

def load_or_generate(L, rng, samples_per_T=200):
    path = f"data/ising_Nx{L}_Ny{L}.npz"
    if os.path.exists(path):
        d = np.load(path)
        print(f"loaded {path}: configs {d['configs'].shape}")
        return d["configs"], d["T"]
    temperatures = np.round(np.arange(1.0, 3.5 + 1e-9, 0.05), 2)
    n_chains = 20 if L <= 20 else 10                       # fewer, longer chains for large lattices (same 200 samples per T)
    t0 = time.time()
    configs = generate_dataset(L, L, temperatures, n_chains=n_chains, n_samples=samples_per_T // n_chains,
                               n_equil=1000 + 2 * L * L // 4, n_between=20, rng=rng)
    os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
    np.savez_compressed(path, configs=configs, T=temperatures, Nx=L, Ny=L)
    print(f"generated {path}: configs {configs.shape} in {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")
    return configs, temperatures

L = 20
configs, temperatures = load_or_generate(L, rng)

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
2. Labels, loss and confidence
Each configuration gets a label from its temperature: \[
y = \begin{cases} 0 \ (\text{ordered}) & T < T_{\min}=1.5\\ 1 \ (\text{disordered}) & T>T_{\max}=3.0 \\ \text{not used for training} & T_{\min}\le T\le T_{\max}\end{cases} \tag{3}\] The network outputs two numbers (logits) \(z_0, z_1\), turned into probabilities by the softmax \[
p_k(\boldsymbol s) = \frac{e^{z_k}}{e^{z_0}+e^{z_1}}, \qquad p_0+p_1 = 1, \tag{4}\] and is trained by minimising the categorical cross-entropy (Lecture 4) \[\mathcal L = -\frac1n\sum_{a}\ln p_{y_a}(\boldsymbol s_a). \tag{5}\]
For any configuration the prediction is the class with the larger probability, and we call that probability the confidence: \[
\mathrm{conf}(\boldsymbol s) = \max\left(p_0(\boldsymbol s),\,p_1(\boldsymbol s)\right)\in\left[\tfrac12, 1\right]. \tag{6}\] The network is confident on configurations that look like its training data. Close to \(T_c\) the configurations are neither clearly ordered nor clearly disordered, so we expect the confidence to approach \(\frac12\) there. This motivates the estimate \[
\bar T_c = \arg\min_T \ \big\langle \mathrm{conf}\big\rangle_T , \tag{7}\] the temperature of lowest average confidence. A closely related estimate is the temperature where the average \(\langle p_1\rangle_T\) crosses \(\frac12\).


Code
T_MIN, T_MAX = 1.5, 3.0

def make_training_set(configs, temperatures, rng, val_fraction=0.2):
    low, high = temperatures < T_MIN, temperatures > T_MAX
    X = np.concatenate([configs[low].reshape(-1, *configs.shape[2:]), configs[high].reshape(-1, *configs.shape[2:])])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(configs[low].shape[0] * configs.shape[1]), np.ones(configs[high].shape[0] * configs.shape[1])])
    perm = rng.permutation(len(y))
    X, y = X[perm], y[perm]
    n_val = int(val_fraction * len(y))
    to_t = lambda a: torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)   # (n, 1, L, L): one input channel
    return (to_t(X[n_val:]), torch.tensor(y[n_val:], dtype=torch.long),
            to_t(X[:n_val]), torch.tensor(y[:n_val], dtype=torch.long))

X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val = make_training_set(configs, temperatures, rng)
print(f"training: {len(y_tr)} configurations, validation: {len(y_val)};  fraction of label 1 in training = {y_tr.float().mean():.3f}")
print(f"temperatures used for label 0: {temperatures[temperatures < T_MIN]}")
print(f"temperatures used for label 1: {temperatures[temperatures > T_MAX]}")

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
3. The network
As in the Lecture Notes, the network has two convolutional layers with \(32\) kernels of size \(3\times3\), each followed by a rectified linear unit (ReLU) and \(2\times2\) max-pooling, then a dense layer of \(64\) ReLU nodes and an output layer of \(2\) nodes (the softmax is part of the loss).
One detail is motivated by the physics: we use circular padding (padding_mode="circular"). Our lattice is a torus, so the neighbour of the last column is the first column; circular padding makes the convolution see exactly the same neighbourhoods as the Hamiltonian.


Code
class IsingCNN(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, L, channels=32, hidden=64):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, channels, 3, padding=1, padding_mode="circular"), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, padding_mode="circular"), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2))
        side = L // 4                                          # two 2x2 poolings
        self.classifier = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(channels * side * side, hidden), nn.ReLU(),
                                        nn.Linear(hidden, 2))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.classifier(self.features(x))               # logits z_0, z_1

model = IsingCNN(L)
W0 = model.features[0].weight.detach().clone()                 # first-layer filters before training (used in Section 7.3)
print(model)
print("number of parameters:", sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()))


IsingCNN(
  (features): Sequential(
    (0): Conv2d(1, 32, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1), padding_mode=circular)
    (1): ReLU()
    (2): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
    (3): Conv2d(32, 32, kernel_size=(3, 3), stride=(1, 1), padding=(1, 1), padding_mode=circular)
    (4): ReLU()
    (5): MaxPool2d(kernel_size=2, stride=2, padding=0, dilation=1, ceil_mode=False)
  )
  (classifier): Sequential(
    (0): Flatten(start_dim=1, end_dim=-1)
    (1): Linear(in_features=800, out_features=64, bias=True)
    (2): ReLU()
    (3): Linear(in_features=64, out_features=2, bias=True)
  )
)
number of parameters: 60962



Architecture diagrams
The printout lists the layers but not the flow of numbers through them. We show the architecture in two ways: with a drawing function of our own and with two libraries that read it directly from the PyTorch model.
The function draw_network draws a fully connected network as it is usually sketched on a blackboard. Each layer is a column of circles, one per neuron, and thin grey lines join every neuron to every neuron of the next layer, since a dense layer connects all of them. A layer with more than max_nodes neurons is shown by its first and last few neurons with a vertical ellipsis in between, and its true size is written under the column. The height of a column grows with the logarithm of the layer size, so a wide layer is visibly taller than a narrow one. Input and output layers are grey and hidden layers blue; orange is reserved for a latent layer and green for an additional input such as a class label.
For a network of your own, pass the layer sizes from the input to the output, e.g. draw_network([784, 128, 10]); labels, colors and groups (brackets over ranges of columns) are optional, and ax= draws into a panel of an existing figure. An entry of the list may itself be a list of sizes: the column then holds several blocks, which is how two inputs entering the same layer are drawn. Only dense layers can be drawn this way. A convolutional layer is a set of small kernels shared by all positions of the image, not a column of independent neurons, so the convolutional part of a network is left to the library tools further below.


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import Circle

# Colours used for the network drawings: grey for the data (input and output),
# blue for hidden layers, orange for the latent (bottleneck) layer and green
# for an extra conditioning input such as a one-hot class label.
GREY, BLUE, ORANGE, GREEN = "#8C8C8C", "#005CA7", "#EB6709", "#2E8B57"


def draw_network(layer_sizes, labels=None, colors=None, max_nodes=10,
                 groups=None, no_input=None, ax=None, node_radius=0.11,
                 x_gap=1.6, min_height=1.0, height_scale=1.1, fontsize=13):
    """Draw a fully connected network as columns of circles joined by edges.

    Parameters
    ----------
    layer_sizes : list
        One entry per column, from the input to the output. An entry is
        either an int (the number of neurons of one layer) or a list of ints
        (several blocks stacked in the same column, e.g. [16, 16] for the mean
        and the log-variance of a variational autoencoder, or [784, 10] for an
        image together with a one-hot condition).
    labels : list, optional
        Names shown under each column next to the true layer size. An entry
        may be None (size only), a string, or, for a stacked column, a list
        with one string per block.
    colors : list, optional
        Fill colour of the nodes of each column (or a list with one colour per
        block). By default the first and the last column are grey and all
        others blue.
    max_nodes : int
        Largest number of circles drawn for one block. A larger block is shown
        by its first and last few nodes with a vertical ellipsis in between;
        the true size is always shown in the label.
    groups : list of (text, first_column, last_column), optional
        Brackets drawn above a range of columns, e.g. ("encoder", 0, 2).
    no_input : list of (column, block), optional
        Blocks that receive no edges from the previous column, e.g. a condition
        c that enters the decoder from outside.
    ax : matplotlib Axes, optional
        Axes to draw into; a new figure is created when None.
    node_radius, x_gap : float
        Radius of a circle and horizontal distance between columns.
    min_height, height_scale : float
        The height of a block of size s is min_height + height_scale*log10(s),
        so that a narrow layer is visibly shorter than a wide one.
    fontsize : int
        Font size of all labels.

    Returns
    -------
    ax : the matplotlib Axes with the drawing.
    """
    n = len(layer_sizes)
    # Turn every entry into a list of blocks, so that a plain layer is a
    # column with a single block.
    blocks = [s if isinstance(s, (list, tuple)) else [s] for s in layer_sizes]
    if labels is None:
        labels = [None] * n
    if colors is None:
        colors = [GREY] + [BLUE] * (n - 2) + [GREY]
    no_input = set(no_input or [])

    def per_block(value, k):
        # Repeat a single value for all k blocks of a column, or keep a list.
        return list(value) if isinstance(value, (list, tuple)) else [value] * k

    if ax is None:
        _, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(1.9 * n + 1, 5.5))

    # ---- Node positions ---------------------------------------------------
    # Column i sits at x = i * x_gap. Inside a column the blocks are stacked
    # from top to bottom with a small gap, and the whole column is centred
    # on y = 0. Each block gets a height that grows with log10 of its size
    # (but is never too small for its circles to fit without overlapping);
    # the drawn nodes are spread evenly over that height.
    nodes = []            # nodes[i][b] = list of (x, y) of block b in column i
    tops, bottoms = [], []
    gap = 0.9             # vertical space between stacked blocks (holds a label)
    for i, blk in enumerate(blocks):
        cols = per_block(colors[i], len(blk))
        labs = per_block(labels[i], len(blk))
        heights = [max(min_height + height_scale * np.log10(s),
                       (min(s, max_nodes) - 1) * 2.3 * node_radius) for s in blk]
        total = sum(heights) + gap * (len(blk) - 1)
        x, y_top = i * x_gap, total / 2
        column = []
        for s, h, c, lab in zip(blk, heights, cols, labs):
            shown = min(s, max_nodes)
            if s <= max_nodes:
                # Small block: draw every neuron.
                ys = np.linspace(y_top, y_top - h, shown) if shown > 1 else np.array([y_top - h / 2])
            else:
                # ---- Truncation of large layers ----------------------------
                # Draw max_nodes circles: half in the upper 38 % of the block,
                # half in the lower 38 %, and a vertical ellipsis in the
                # middle to show that neurons are omitted.
                k = max_nodes // 2
                ys = np.concatenate([np.linspace(y_top, y_top - 0.38 * h, k),
                                     np.linspace(y_top - 0.62 * h, y_top - h, max_nodes - k)])
                ax.text(x, y_top - 0.5 * h, r"$\vdots$", ha="center", va="center",
                        fontsize=fontsize + 6, color=c, zorder=4)
            for y in ys:
                ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), node_radius, facecolor=c,
                                    edgecolor="black", lw=0.6, zorder=3))
            column.append([(x, y) for y in ys])

            # ---- Labels of stacked blocks ----------------------------------
            # In a column with several blocks each block is labelled just
            # below its last node, in its own colour, on a white box so that
            # the edges behind do not hide the text.
            if len(blk) > 1:
                text = f"{s}" if lab is None else f"{lab} {s}"
                ax.text(x, y_top - h - 0.2, text, ha="center", va="top",
                        fontsize=fontsize - 1, color=c, zorder=5,
                        bbox=dict(facecolor="white", edgecolor="none", pad=0.5))
            y_top -= h + gap

        # ---- Label of a single-block column: name and true size below ----
        if len(blk) == 1:
            lab = labs[0]
            text = f"{blk[0]}" if lab is None else f"{lab}\n{blk[0]}"
            ax.text(x, -total / 2 - 0.3, text, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=fontsize)
        nodes.append(column)
        tops.append(total / 2)
        bottoms.append(-total / 2)

    # ---- Edges ---------------------------------------------------------------
    # A dense layer connects every neuron of one column with every neuron of
    # the next, so we draw a thin grey line for every pair of drawn nodes,
    # skipping the blocks listed in no_input. zorder=1 keeps lines behind
    # the circles.
    for i in range(n - 1):
        sources = [p for block in nodes[i] for p in block]
        for b, block in enumerate(nodes[i + 1]):
            if (i + 1, b) in no_input:
                continue
            for (x0, y0) in sources:
                for (x1, y1) in block:
                    ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color="#B0B0B0", lw=0.35, zorder=1)

    # ---- Group brackets ------------------------------------------------------
    # A bracket above columns first..last with its text, e.g. "encoder".
    y_br = max(tops) + 0.45
    for text, i0, i1 in (groups or []):
        x0, x1 = i0 * x_gap - 0.3, i1 * x_gap + 0.3
        ax.plot([x0, x0, x1, x1], [y_br - 0.12, y_br, y_br, y_br - 0.12],
                color="black", lw=1.2)
        ax.text((x0 + x1) / 2, y_br + 0.1, text, ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=fontsize)

    # ---- Axes limits ----------------------------------------------------------
    # Leave room for the brackets above and the labels below.
    ax.set_xlim(-0.8, (n - 1) * x_gap + 0.8)
    ax.set_ylim(min(bottoms) - 1.3, y_br + (0.7 if groups else 0.2))
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.axis("off")
    return ax


The convolutional part turns an \(L\times L\) configuration into \(32\) feature maps of size \((L/4)\times(L/4)\); for \(L=20\) these are \[32\cdot5\cdot5=800 \tag{8}\] numbers. From there on the network is an ordinary dense network, \(800\to64\to2\). The edges between its first two columns carry \[800\cdot64+64=51\,264 \tag{9}\] of the \(60\,962\) parameters: the bulk of the model is the first dense layer, not the convolutions.


Code

The library way to inspect a PyTorch model is torchinfo.summary. It sends one input through the model and prints one row per layer, with the shape of the layer’s output and its number of parameters, followed by the totals, split into trainable and non-trainable parameters. The input is given by its shape, input_size=(1, 1, L, L), or as a tensor, input_data=.... We pass a tensor of zeros: with input_size the library draws a random input, which would advance PyTorch’s random number generator and change the training runs that follow. col_names selects the columns and depth the level of nested modules that is expanded; the model itself, including its training or evaluation mode, is left unchanged. Both libraries are installed with pip install torchinfo torchview; the first lines of the code install them when they are missing. The output shapes trace the lattice through the two poolings, \(20\times20\to10\times10\to5\times5\), and the total must equal the \(60\,962\) counted above.

torchview.draw_graph traces the same forward pass and draws it as a graph: every layer is a box with the shapes of its input and output tensors, and the arrows follow the data. With expand_nested=True each submodule (an nn.Sequential inside the model, for example) becomes a frame around its own layers. The result is a Graphviz object; graph.visual_graph.render writes it to a PNG file, which needs the Graphviz program dot (preinstalled in Google Colab). The table is the tool for checking shapes and counting parameters, for instance after a layer has been resized; the graph shows the flow of data, which matters once a model has nested blocks, branches or skip connections.

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
4. Training
The network is trained with the Adam optimiser on mini-batches of 64 configurations for 5 epochs. After each epoch the loss and accuracy are printed for the training set and for the validation set, the 20% of labelled configurations held back from training.


Code
def train(model, X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val, epochs=5, batch_size=64, lr=1e-3, verbose=True):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr)
    loss_fn = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()                            # softmax + categorical cross-entropy
    history = []
    for epoch in range(epochs):
        model.train()
        perm = torch.randperm(len(y_tr))
        for i in range(0, len(y_tr), batch_size):
            idx = perm[i:i + batch_size]
            opt.zero_grad()
            loss = loss_fn(model(X_tr[idx]), y_tr[idx])
            loss.backward()
            opt.step()
        model.eval()
        with torch.no_grad():
            out_tr, out_val = model(X_tr), model(X_val)
            rec = (loss_fn(out_tr, y_tr).item(), (out_tr.argmax(1) == y_tr).float().mean().item(),
                   loss_fn(out_val, y_val).item(), (out_val.argmax(1) == y_val).float().mean().item())
        history.append(rec)
        if verbose:
            print(f"epoch {epoch + 1:2d}: train loss {rec[0]:.2e} acc {rec[1]:.4f} | validation loss {rec[2]:.2e} acc {rec[3]:.4f}")
    return np.array(history)

t0 = time.time()
history = train(model, X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val)
print(f"training time: {time.time() - t0:.1f} s")

The two classes are easy to separate (at \(T<1.5\) almost all spins are aligned, at \(T>3\) they are not), so the training and validation accuracies reach \(1\) already after the first epoch. The informative part is what the network says about temperatures it has never seen.

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
5. Predictions at all temperatures
Every configuration at every temperature is passed through the trained network; the averages of \(p_1\) and of the confidence over the samples at each temperature give both estimates of \(T_c\).


Code
def predict(model, configs):
    # Softmax probabilities p_1 (disordered) for all configurations: array (temperatures, samples).
    model.eval()
    X = torch.tensor(configs.reshape(-1, 1, *configs.shape[2:]), dtype=torch.float32)
    with torch.no_grad():
        p = torch.cat([torch.softmax(model(X[i:i + 2048]), dim=1)[:, 1] for i in range(0, len(X), 2048)])
    return p.numpy().reshape(configs.shape[:2])

def estimate_Tc(temperatures, p1):
    conf = np.maximum(p1, 1 - p1)
    conf_mean, p1_mean = conf.mean(1), p1.mean(1)
    T_conf = temperatures[np.argmin(conf_mean)]                       # lowest average confidence
    i = np.argmax(p1_mean >= 0.5)                                     # first temperature where <p_1> >= 1/2
    T_cross = temperatures[i - 1] + (0.5 - p1_mean[i - 1]) * (temperatures[i] - temperatures[i - 1]) / (p1_mean[i] - p1_mean[i - 1])
    return conf_mean, p1_mean, T_conf, T_cross

p1 = predict(model, configs)
conf_mean, p1_mean, T_conf, T_cross = estimate_Tc(temperatures, p1)
print(f"L = {L}:  T_c from minimum of confidence = {T_conf:.2f}   |  T_c from <p_1> = 1/2 crossing = {T_cross:.3f}   |  exact T_c = {TC:.4f}")


L = 20:  T_c from minimum of confidence = 2.20   |  T_c from <p_1> = 1/2 crossing = 2.247   |  exact T_c = 2.2692




Code
def plot_confidence(ax_conf, ax_p, temperatures, p1, label, colour, marker="o", band=True):
    conf = np.maximum(p1, 1 - p1)
    ax_conf.plot(temperatures, conf.mean(1), marker + "-", ms=3.5, lw=1.2, color=colour, label=label)
    if band:                                                   # spread over configurations: 16th to 84th percentile
        ax_conf.fill_between(temperatures, *np.percentile(conf, [16, 84], axis=1), color=colour, alpha=0.15, lw=0)
    ax_p.plot(temperatures, p1.mean(1), marker + "-", ms=3.5, lw=1.2, color=colour, label=label)

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
plot_confidence(ax1, ax2, temperatures, p1, f"L = {L}", UJBlue)
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axvspan(temperatures.min(), T_MIN, color=UJNavy, alpha=0.08, lw=0)
    ax.axvspan(T_MAX, temperatures.max(), color=DSOrange, alpha=0.08, lw=0)
    ax.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":", lw=1.2, label=r"exact $T_c$")
    ax.set_xlabel("$T$")
ax1.axvline(T_conf, color=UJBlue, ls="--", lw=1, label=rf"$\bar T_c = {T_conf:.2f}$")
ax2.axhline(0.5, color=UJGray, lw=0.8)
ax1.set_ylabel(r"confidence $\max(p_0,p_1)$"); ax2.set_ylabel(r"$\langle p_1\rangle_T$ = P(disordered)")
ax1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower left"); ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
ax1.set_title("line: mean; band: 16-84% of configurations; shaded: training T", loc="left", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()





In the shaded regions, where it was trained, the network is nearly certain. Between them it was never told anything, yet its output switches from “ordered” to “disordered” in a narrow window, and the confidence has a sharp minimum there. For \(L=20\) the minimum lies at \(\bar T_c = 2.20\) and the crossing of \(\langle p_1\rangle_T\) with \(\frac12\) at \(2.247\), to be compared with the exact \(T_c = 2.2692\). The band shows the spread over individual configurations: right at the minimum some configurations are classified confidently as ordered and others as disordered. The average confidence is low because the configurations at that temperature are a mixture of both.

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
6. Finite-size effects
The network sees an \(L\times L\) lattice, which has no sharp phase transition (Lab 010, Section 8). We therefore repeat the whole experiment (data, training, prediction) for \(L=10, 20, 40\) with the same network architecture and the same training temperatures. Each training is repeated with \(3\) random seeds, because a single training run is itself a random experiment.


Code
results = {}                                                 # results[L] = list over training seeds of (T, p_1, T_conf, T_cross)
seeds = (0, 1, 2)
t0 = time.time()
for L_fs in (10, 20, 40):
    cfg, Ts = load_or_generate(L_fs, rng)
    results[L_fs] = []
    for seed in seeds:
        torch.manual_seed(seed)                                  # different random initialisation and batches
        Xa, ya, Xb, yb = make_training_set(cfg, Ts, np.random.default_rng(seed))
        m = IsingCNN(L_fs)
        train(m, Xa, ya, Xb, yb, epochs=3, verbose=False)        # the task is easy: 3 epochs are enough (see Section 4)
        pp = predict(m, cfg)
        _, _, Tc1, Tc2 = estimate_Tc(Ts, pp)
        results[L_fs].append((Ts, pp, Tc1, Tc2))
print(f"{len(seeds)} trainings for each of 3 lattice sizes done in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 3.8))
styles = {10: (UJGray, "s"), 20: (UJBlue, "o"), 40: (DSOrange, "^")}
for L_fs in sorted(results):
    Ts = results[L_fs][0][0]
    pp = np.concatenate([r[1] for r in results[L_fs]], axis=1)   # pool the seeds
    plot_confidence(ax1, ax2, Ts, pp, f"L = {L_fs}", *styles[L_fs], band=False)
for ax in (ax1, ax2):
    ax.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":", lw=1.2); ax.set_xlabel("$T$"); ax.set_xlim(1.6, 3.2)
ax2.axhline(0.5, color=UJGray, lw=0.8)
ax1.set_ylabel("mean confidence"); ax2.set_ylabel(r"$\langle p_1\rangle_T$")
ax1.set_title(f"averaged over {len(seeds)} trainings", loc="left", fontsize=9)
ax1.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower left"); ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="upper left")
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print("  L   T_c (min confidence), per seed     T_c (<p_1> = 1/2), per seed       mean +- std of the crossing   exact")
for L_fs in sorted(results):
    t1 = np.array([r[2] for r in results[L_fs]]); t2 = np.array([r[3] for r in results[L_fs]])
    print(f"{L_fs:3d}   {'  '.join(f'{v:.2f}' for v in t1):30s}   {'  '.join(f'{v:.3f}' for v in t2):30s}   "
          f"{t2.mean():.3f} +- {t2.std(ddof=1):.3f}               {TC:.4f}")

The switch from “ordered” to “disordered” becomes sharper as \(L\) grows: the transition region of a finite lattice shrinks, as in Lab 010. The estimates themselves depend on \(L\), on the temperature grid (spacing \(0.05\)) and on the random training run. The per-seed values in the table show that the seed-to-seed spread (a standard deviation of about \(0.04\) for the crossing) is not small compared with the distance to \(T_c\). A single number such as “\(\bar T_c\) for \(L=50\)” is therefore a pseudo-critical temperature; extracting \(T_c\) itself needs several \(L\) and an extrapolation to infinite \(L\).

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
7. Inside the network
The network located the transition, but it did not tell us anything: no order parameter, no mechanism (Lecture 4, The Chinese Room). Three probes look inside it.

7.1 Network output and magnetisation
The first hypothesis is the obvious one from physics: the network may simply measure the magnetisation. For every configuration we compute the absolute magnetisation per spin, \[|m| = \frac1N\Big|\sum_i s_i\Big|, \tag{10}\] and plot it against the network output \(p_1\). If the network had learned “\(p_1\) is a function of \(|m|\)”, all points would collapse onto one curve, whatever their temperature.


Code
L = 20
absm = np.abs(configs.reshape(*configs.shape[:2], -1).mean(-1).astype(np.float64))     # (temperatures, samples)
TT = np.repeat(temperatures[:, None], configs.shape[1], axis=1)

rho, _ = spearmanr(absm.ravel(), p1.ravel())
print(f"Spearman rank correlation between |m| and p_1 over all {absm.size} configurations: {rho:.3f}")

fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
sc = ax1.scatter(absm.ravel(), p1.ravel(), c=TT.ravel(), cmap=cmap_T, norm=TwoSlopeNorm(TC, temperatures.min(), temperatures.max()),
                 s=4, alpha=0.6, lw=0)
plt.colorbar(sc, ax=ax1, label="$T$")
ax1.set_xlabel(r"$|m|$ of the configuration"); ax1.set_ylabel(r"network output $p_1$")

# binned mean of p_1 at fixed |m|, separately for configurations from below and above T_c
bins = np.linspace(0, 1, 21)
centres = 0.5 * (bins[1:] + bins[:-1])
for sel, col, lab in ((TT < TC, UJNavy, r"configurations from $T<T_c$"), (TT > TC, DSOrange, r"configurations from $T>T_c$")):
    idx = np.digitize(absm[sel], bins) - 1
    mean_p = np.array([p1[sel][idx == b].mean() if np.sum(idx == b) >= 20 else np.nan for b in range(len(centres))])
    ax2.plot(centres, mean_p, "o-", color=col, ms=4, label=lab)
ax2.set_xlabel(r"$|m|$ (bins of width 0.05)"); ax2.set_ylabel(r"mean $p_1$ in the bin"); ax2.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax2.set_title("bins with at least 20 configurations", loc="left", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(); plt.show()


Spearman rank correlation between |m| and p_1 over all 10200 configurations: -0.914





The Spearman rank correlation printed above measures how well the ordering of configurations by \(|m|\) agrees with their ordering by \(p_1\) (\(\pm1\) for a perfectly monotonic relation, \(0\) for unrelated quantities). The right panel asks a sharper question: at the same \(|m|\), does the network answer differently for configurations from below and above \(T_c\)? If the two curves lie on top of each other, the output depends (almost) only on \(|m|\). If they separate, the network uses more information than the magnetisation.
In the run stored in this notebook the rank correlation is strongly negative (\(-0.914\): large \(|m|\) goes with “ordered”), so \(|m|\) explains most of the output. But in the overlapping range of \(|m|\) the two curves do not coincide: at equal magnetisation, configurations from \(T>T_c\) get a larger \(p_1\). The network uses more than \(|m|\).


7.2 Shuffled spins
We can test directly whether spatial structure matters. For each configuration we randomly permute the positions of its spins. This keeps \(m\) exactly, but destroys all spatial correlations (domains, clusters, domain walls), so the nearest-neighbour energy changes. A pure “\(|m|\)-detector” would give identical outputs for original and shuffled configurations.


Code
shuffled = configs.reshape(*configs.shape[:2], -1).copy()
for t in range(shuffled.shape[0]):
    for k in range(shuffled.shape[1]):
        rng.shuffle(shuffled[t, k])                                   # random permutation of the sites, same m
shuffled = shuffled.reshape(configs.shape)
p1_shuf = predict(model, shuffled)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.8))
ax.plot(temperatures, p1.mean(1), "o-", color=UJBlue, ms=4, label="original configurations")
ax.plot(temperatures, p1_shuf.mean(1), "s--", color=DSOrange, ms=4, label="same configurations, spins shuffled")
ax.axvline(TC, color=UJGray, ls=":", lw=1.2); ax.axhline(0.5, color=UJGray, lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("$T$"); ax.set_ylabel(r"$\langle p_1\rangle_T$"); ax.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
plt.show()

print("  T     <p_1> original   <p_1> shuffled   <|m|>")
for T in (1.5, 2.0, 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.6, 3.0):
    i = np.argmin(np.abs(temperatures - T))
    print(f"{temperatures[i]:.2f}      {p1[i].mean():.3f}            {p1_shuf[i].mean():.3f}          {absm[i].mean():.3f}")





  T     <p_1> original   <p_1> shuffled   <|m|>
1.50      0.000            0.000          0.987
2.00      0.027            0.091          0.915
2.20      0.356            0.572          0.775
2.30      0.594            0.769          0.658
2.40      0.871            0.940          0.488
2.60      0.999            1.000          0.254
3.00      1.000            1.000          0.133


Where the two curves (and the columns of the printed table) coincide, shuffling did not matter: those configurations are classified by their magnetisation alone. Where they differ, the network’s decision depends on the arrangement of the spins, not only on how many point up, for example on the size of clusters, which is what changes most near \(T_c\).
In the run stored in this notebook, far from \(T_c\) shuffling changes nothing, but around \(T_c\) the shuffled configurations are called “disordered” more often: at \(T=2.20\) the average \(p_1\) rises from \(0.356\) to \(0.572\). Without their large clusters the configurations look more like high-temperature noise to the network, at exactly the same \(m\).


7.3 The learned filters
The last probe looks at the weights themselves. The first layer applies \(32\) different \(3\times3\) filters to the spin image. A filter with all weights of the same sign computes a local (smoothed) magnetisation; a filter with weights of both signs responds to local differences, i.e. to domain walls, which is what the bond energy \(-s_is_j\) measures.


Code
W = model.features[0].weight.detach().numpy()[:, 0]                  # (32, 3, 3)
vmax = np.abs(W).max()

for k, ax in enumerate(axes.ravel()):
    ax.imshow(W[k], cmap=cmap_w, vmin=-vmax, vmax=vmax)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([])
    ax.set_title(f"sum {W[k].sum():+.2f}", fontsize=7)
fig.suptitle("first-layer filters (orange > 0, navy < 0); title: sum of the 9 weights", x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=10)
plt.show()

same_sign = np.mean([np.all(w > 0) or np.all(w < 0) for w in W])

fraction of filters whose 9 weights all have the same sign: 0.00
relative change of the first-layer filters during training, |W - W0| / |W0| = 8.003


The printed relative change shows that training moved the filters far from their random initial values, so they are learned, not leftovers. Yet in the run stored here none of them is a plain local average of the spins: each mixes positive and negative weights, i.e. it responds to local spin patterns. Whatever the network computes is spread over all the layers (the systems reply of Lecture 4). Individual filters are hard to read, and any physical interpretation has to be tested from outside, as in Sections 7.1 and 7.2.
Taken together, the probes give a mixed picture. The network’s output is strongly tied to the magnetisation, the order parameter we know from physics, although nobody told it about \(m\), and the shuffle test shows that it also uses spatial structure. Finding this out, however, required us: we chose \(|m|\) as the hypothesis, designed the shuffle test and interpreted the filters. The network itself gave a number, \(\bar T_c\), not an explanation. This is the point of the Chinese room, and of the effort to open it (interpretability). The exact understanding came from somewhere else: Onsager’s solution (Lecture 4 and Lab 012).

title: Lab 011: Tc of the 2D Ising model from the confidence of a CNN
text:
8. Exercises

Move the training windows: \(T_{\min}=1.8\), \(T_{\max}=2.8\), or asymmetric ones. How does \(\bar T_c\) react? When does it become unreliable?
Replace the CNN by a fully connected network on the flattened image (as for MNIST). Is it as good? Does the shuffle test give a different answer? (Hint: a fully connected network has no notion of neighbours.)
Remove the random global spin flip from the data (Lab 010, Section 5) — i.e. all low-\(T\) configurations have \(m>0\). Train again and test on flipped configurations \(-\boldsymbol s\). What went wrong?
Train with three classes (low, intermediate, high temperature bins) or regress \(T\) directly. What does the network predict near \(T_c\)?

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
section: 1. The free energy and its derivatives
text:
1. The free energy and its derivatives
To “solve” the model means to know the free energy per spin, because everything else follows from it: \[
f(T) = -T\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\ln Z, \tag{3}
\] \[
Z=\sum_{\{s_i\}}e^{-H(\{s_i\})/T}, \tag{4}
\] \[
H = -\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}s_is_j . \tag{5}
\] Observables are derivatives with respect to the inverse temperature \(\beta\): \[
u = \frac{\partial(\beta f)}{\partial\beta} = \frac{\langle H\rangle}{N}, \tag{6}
\] \[
c = \frac{\partial u}{\partial T} = \frac{\langle H^2\rangle-\langle H\rangle^2}{NT^2}. \tag{7}
\]

1.1 Brute force on a tiny lattice
On an \(L\times L\) torus there are \(2^{L^2}\) configurations. For the \(4\times4\) lattice that is 65 536, which is easy. We store every configuration as a row of \(\pm1\): the binary digits of an integer \(n\) from 0 to \(2^N-1\) give the spins, a digit 0 being read as the spin \(+1\) and a digit 1 as \(-1\).
Each configuration has the energy \[E = -2N + 2b, \tag{8}\] where \(b\) is the number of broken bonds (antiparallel neighbours): the torus has two bonds per site, and each contributes \(-1\) if satisfied and \(+1\) if broken. So \(Z\) is determined by the histogram \(n_b\) (the density of states): \[
Z(T) = \sum_{b} n_b\, e^{-(-2N+2b)/T}. \tag{9}
\]


Code
def all_configs(n):
    # all 2^n configurations of n spins, as rows of +-1 (bit k of the row index -> spin k)
    bits = (np.arange(2**n)[:, None] >> np.arange(n)) & 1
    return (1 - 2 * bits).astype(np.int8)

def torus_energies(L):
    # energies of all 2^(L*L) configurations of the L x L periodic square lattice (J = 1)
    S = all_configs(L * L).reshape(-1, L, L).astype(np.int32)
    return -(S * np.roll(S, 1, axis=1)).sum(axis=(1, 2)) - (S * np.roll(S, 1, axis=2)).sum(axis=(1, 2))

dos = {}
for L in (3, 4):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    E = torus_energies(L)
    N = L * L
    b = (E + 2 * N) // 2                         # number of broken bonds
    dos[L] = np.bincount(b, minlength=2 * N + 1)  # n_b
    print(f"L = {L}: {2**N:6d} configurations enumerated in {time.perf_counter()-t0:.2f} s,  sum n_b = {dos[L].sum()}")
print("4x4 torus, number of configurations with b broken bonds:")
print({int(k): int(v) for k, v in enumerate(dos[4]) if v})

L = 4:  65536 configurations enumerated in 0.02 s,  sum n_b = 65536
4x4 torus, number of configurations with b broken bonds:
{0: 2, 4: 32, 6: 64, 8: 424, 10: 1728, 12: 6688, 14: 13568, 16: 20524, 18: 13568, 20: 6688, 22: 1728, 24: 424, 26: 64, 28: 32, 32: 2}




1.2 Thermodynamics of the finite lattice
With \(n_b\) in hand, \(\ln Z\), \(u\) and \(c\) are smooth functions of \(T\): \[
\ln Z = \ln\sum_b n_b e^{(2N-2b)/T}, \tag{10}
\] \[
u = \frac{\sum_b n_b E_b e^{-E_b/T}}{NZ}, \tag{11}
\] \[
c = \frac{\langle E^2\rangle - \langle E\rangle^2}{NT^2}. \tag{12}
\] \(Z\) is a finite sum of exponentials, positive for every real \(T\), so \(\ln Z\) is analytic: a finite lattice has no phase transition. A singularity can only appear in the limit of infinitely many spins.


Code
def thermo_from_dos(nb, N, T):
    # ln Z / N, u and c per spin from the histogram n_b of broken bonds
    T = np.atleast_1d(T)[:, None]
    Eb = -2 * N + 2 * np.arange(len(nb))
    logw = np.log(np.where(nb > 0, nb, 1)) - Eb / T
    logw = np.where(nb > 0, logw, -np.inf)
    shift = logw.max(axis=1, keepdims=True)                  # avoid overflow
    w = np.exp(logw - shift); Zr = w.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True); p = w / Zr
    E1 = (p * Eb).sum(1); E2 = (p * Eb**2).sum(1)
    lnZ = (np.log(Zr) + shift)[:, 0]
    return lnZ / N, E1 / N, (E2 - E1**2) / (N * T[:, 0]**2)

T = np.linspace(0.5, 5.0, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
for L, col in [(3, "#9CC3E6"), (4, UJBlue)]:
    lnz, u, c = thermo_from_dos(dos[L], L * L, T)
    ax[0].plot(T, -T * lnz, color=col, lw=2, label=f"{L}x{L} torus")
    ax[1].plot(T, c, color=col, lw=2, label=f"{L}x{L} torus")
    print(f"L = {L}: specific-heat maximum c = {c.max():.3f} at T = {T[c.argmax()]:.3f}")
for a in ax:
    a.axvline(TC, color=DSOrange, ls=":", lw=1.2); a.set_xlabel("$T$"); a.legend(frameon=False)
ax[0].set_ylabel("free energy per spin $f$"); ax[1].set_ylabel("specific heat per spin $c$")
ax[0].set_title("exact, finite lattice: smooth"); ax[1].set_title("a broad bump, no divergence")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


L = 3: specific-heat maximum c = 0.653 at T = 2.474
L = 4: specific-heat maximum c = 0.816 at T = 2.440





The specific heat has a smooth bump. Brute force cannot go much further: the \(6\times6\) lattice already has \(2^{36}\), about \(7\times10^{10}\), configurations, and the \(20\times20\) images of Lab 010 have \(2^{400}\). We need a smarter way to do the sum — the transfer matrix.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
section: 2. The 1D chain and the transfer matrix
text:
2. The 1D chain and the transfer matrix
The one-dimensional (1D) chain shows the transfer-matrix idea in its simplest form. Take \[H = -\sum_i s_is_{i+1} - h\sum_i s_i \tag{13}\] on a ring of \(N\) spins. With \(J\) set to 1 the coupling \(K\) of equation (2) is \(\beta\) itself, and we write the reduced field as \[\tilde h = \beta h. \tag{14}\] The Boltzmann weight is a product of bond factors \[
e^{-\beta H} = \prod_{i=1}^N \mathsf T_{s_is_{i+1}}, \tag{15}
\] \[
\mathsf T_{ss'} = e^{Kss' + \frac{\tilde h}{2}(s+s')}, \tag{16}
\] \[
\mathsf T = \begin{pmatrix} e^{K+\tilde h} & e^{-K}\\ e^{-K} & e^{K-\tilde h}\end{pmatrix}. \tag{17}
\] The sum over all \(2^N\) configurations is a matrix product, closed into a trace by the periodic boundary: \[
Z = \sum_{s_1,\dots,s_N}\mathsf T_{s_1s_2}\mathsf T_{s_2s_3}\cdots\mathsf T_{s_Ns_1} = \operatorname{Tr}\mathsf T^N = \lambda_+^N + \lambda_-^N . \tag{18}
\] The eigenvalues of a symmetric \(2\times2\) matrix with diagonal entries \(a\), \(d\) and off-diagonal entry \(b\) are \[\lambda=\frac{a+d}{2}\pm\sqrt{\left(\frac{a-d}{2}\right)^2+b^2}, \tag{19}\] which for the matrix (17) gives \[
\lambda_\pm = e^{K}\cosh\tilde h \pm \sqrt{e^{2K}\sinh^2\tilde h + e^{-2K}}, \tag{20}
\] and in zero field \[\lambda_+ = 2\cosh K,\qquad \lambda_- = 2\sinh K . \tag{21}\] The trace in equation (18) is compared with the brute-force sum, and equation (20) with the eigenvalues returned by numpy.


Code
def Z_chain_brute(N, K, ht):
    S = all_configs(N).astype(float)
    E_over_T = -K * (S * np.roll(S, -1, axis=1)).sum(1) - ht * S.sum(1)     # beta*H
    return np.exp(-E_over_T).sum()

def T_chain(K, ht):
    return np.array([[np.exp(K + ht), np.exp(-K)], [np.exp(-K), np.exp(K - ht)]])

N = 14
for K, ht in [(0.3, 0.0), (1.0, 0.0), (0.7, 0.4), (1.5, -0.2)]:
    Zb = Z_chain_brute(N, K, ht)
    Zt = np.trace(np.linalg.matrix_power(T_chain(K, ht), N))
    lam_num = np.sort(np.linalg.eigvalsh(T_chain(K, ht)))[::-1]
    root = np.sqrt(np.exp(2 * K) * np.sinh(ht)**2 + np.exp(-2 * K))
    lam_exact = np.array([np.exp(K) * np.cosh(ht) + root, np.exp(K) * np.cosh(ht) - root])
    print(f"K={K:3.1f}, beta*h={ht:4.1f}:  Z brute = {Zb:.10e}   Tr T^N = {Zt:.10e}   "
          f"max|lambda_numpy - lambda_formula| = {np.abs(lam_num - lam_exact).max():.1e}")

K=1.0, beta*h= 0.0:  Z brute = 7.2668862529e+06   Tr T^N = 7.2668862529e+06   max|lambda_numpy - lambda_formula| = 0.0e+00
K=0.7, beta*h= 0.4:  Z brute = 9.1298799858e+06   Tr T^N = 9.1298799858e+06   max|lambda_numpy - lambda_formula| = 8.9e-16
K=1.5, beta*h=-0.2:  Z brute = 2.3316896955e+10   Tr T^N = 2.3316896955e+10   max|lambda_numpy - lambda_formula| = 4.4e-16



2.1 Free energy and correlations of the infinite chain
For a long chain \[
\ln Z = N\ln\lambda_+ + \ln\Big(1 + \big(\lambda_-/\lambda_+\big)^N\Big)\;\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}\;N\ln\lambda_+ , \tag{22}
\] so \[
f = -T\ln\big(2\cosh(1/T)\big), \tag{23}
\] smooth at every positive temperature: there is no phase transition in 1D (Ising, 1925). The spin–spin correlation is also a matrix product, with the diagonal matrix \(\sigma^z\) whose entries are 1 and \(-1\): \[
\langle s_0s_r\rangle = \frac{\operatorname{Tr}\big(\sigma^z\mathsf T^r\sigma^z\mathsf T^{N-r}\big)}{\operatorname{Tr}\mathsf T^N}
\;\xrightarrow{N\to\infty}\; \Big(\frac{\lambda_-}{\lambda_+}\Big)^r = (\tanh K)^r = e^{-r/\xi}, \tag{24}
\] \[
\xi = -\frac{1}{\ln\tanh K}. \tag{25}
\] \(\xi\) is finite at every positive temperature and diverges only at zero temperature.


Code
sz = np.diag([1.0, -1.0])
N, r = 400, np.arange(0, 25)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
for K, col in [(0.5, "#9CC3E6"), (1.0, UJBlue), (1.5, UJNavy)]:
    Tm = T_chain(K, 0.0) / (2 * np.cosh(K))                 # rescaled, to avoid overflow; ratios are unchanged
    corr = [np.trace(sz @ np.linalg.matrix_power(Tm, k) @ sz @ np.linalg.matrix_power(Tm, N - k)) /
            np.trace(np.linalg.matrix_power(Tm, N)) for k in r]
    ax[0].semilogy(r, corr, "o", color=col, ms=4, label=f"transfer matrix, K={K}")
    ax[0].semilogy(r, np.tanh(K)**r, "-", color=col, lw=1)
    print(f"K = {K}: max |<s0 sr> - tanh(K)^r| over r<25 = {np.max(np.abs(np.array(corr) - np.tanh(K)**r)):.1e},"
          f"  xi = {-1/np.log(np.tanh(K)):.3f}")
ax[0].set_xlabel("distance $r$"); ax[0].set_ylabel(r"$\langle s_0 s_r\rangle$"); ax[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_title(r"dots: $\mathrm{Tr}$ formula, lines: $(\tanh K)^r$")
Tg = np.linspace(0.2, 4, 300)
ax[1].plot(Tg, -1 / np.log(np.tanh(1 / Tg)), color=UJBlue, lw=2)
ax[1].set_yscale("log"); ax[1].set_xlabel("$T$"); ax[1].set_ylabel(r"$\xi$"); ax[1].set_title("1D: finite for every $T>0$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


K = 0.5: max |<s0 sr> - tanh(K)^r| over r<25 = 7.1e-17,  xi = 1.295
K = 1.0: max |<s0 sr> - tanh(K)^r| over r<25 = 1.1e-16,  xi = 3.672
K = 1.5: max |<s0 sr> - tanh(K)^r| over r<25 = 4.4e-16,  xi = 10.034





The 1D chain teaches the lesson we carry into two dimensions: for a long system only the largest eigenvalue matters, \[\ln Z \approx N\ln\lambda_{\max}, \tag{26}\] and the correlation length is set by the ratio of the two largest eigenvalues, \[\xi = \frac{1}{\ln(\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_2)}. \tag{27}\]

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
3. The 2D transfer matrix
Take a strip of width \(L\) (periodic in the vertical direction) and of a length \(L'\) that grows without bound. One column \(\sigma\), the spins \(s_1,\dots,s_L\), has \(2^L\) states. Bonds inside a column and between neighbouring columns give \[
Z = \operatorname{Tr}\mathsf V^{L'}, \tag{28}
\] \[
\mathsf V_{\sigma\sigma'} = \exp\Big[K\sum_{i=1}^L s_is_i' + \frac K2\sum_{i=1}^L\big(s_is_{i+1} + s'_is'_{i+1}\big)\Big], \tag{29}
\] where the vertical bonds are split half–half between the two columns so that \(\mathsf V\) is symmetric. Then \[
f_L(T) = -\frac{T}{L}\ln\lambda_0(L), \tag{30}
\] \[
\xi_L = \frac{1}{\ln(\lambda_0/\lambda_1)}, \tag{31}
\] with \(\lambda_0\) and \(\lambda_1\) the largest and the second-largest eigenvalue. Onsager’s free energy is the limit \[f = \lim_{L\to\infty}f_L . \tag{32}\]
Symmetry halves the work. Reversing all spins of a column does not change \(\mathsf V\), and in our bit encoding it maps the index \(n\) to \[\bar n = 2^L-1-n. \tag{33}\] Pairing each state with its reversed partner splits \(\mathsf V\) into an even and an odd block, \[\mathsf V^{\pm}_{nm}=\mathsf V_{nm}\pm\mathsf V_{n\bar m}, \tag{34}\] each of size \(2^{L-1}\). \(\lambda_0\) is the top of the even block (Perron–Frobenius: all entries are positive), and \(\lambda_1\) the top of the odd block, the eigenvalue that describes how a single spin’s orientation is remembered along the strip.
The construction is first tested on a known case: on an \(L\times L'\) torus equation (28) is exact, so for \(4\times4\) it must agree with the brute-force histogram of Section 1.


Code
def transfer_matrix(L, K, lattice="square"):
    # V[sigma, sigma'] for a periodic column of L spins; 'triangular' adds the diagonal bonds s_i s'_{i+1} (Section 10)
    S = all_configs(L).astype(float)
    intra = (S * np.roll(S, -1, axis=1)).sum(1)                 # sum_i s_i s_{i+1} inside a column
    inter = S @ S.T                                             # sum_i s_i s'_i
    if lattice == "triangular":
        inter = inter + S @ np.roll(S, -1, axis=1).T            # sum_i s_i s'_{i+1}
    return np.exp(K * (inter + 0.5 * (intra[:, None] + intra[None, :])))

def top_eigenvalue(A, symmetric):
    n = A.shape[0]
    if symmetric and n <= 64:
        return eigh(A, eigvals_only=True, subset_by_index=[n - 1, n - 1])[0]
    if symmetric:
        return eigsh(A, k=1, which="LA", tol=0)[0][0]           # Lanczos: only the top eigenvalue
    if n <= 64:
        return np.max(np.linalg.eigvals(A).real)
    return eigs(A, k=1, which="LR", tol=1e-14)[0][0].real

def lambda01(L, K, lattice="square"):
    # (lambda_0, lambda_1): largest eigenvalues in the spin-flip even and odd sectors
    V = transfer_matrix(L, K, lattice)
    n = V.shape[0] // 2
    Vflip = V[:, ::-1]                                          # column m -> its flipped partner 2^L-1-m
    sym = lattice == "square"
    return (top_eigenvalue(V[:n, :n] + Vflip[:n, :n], sym),
            top_eigenvalue(V[:n, :n] - Vflip[:n, :n], sym))

# check: Z of the 4x4 torus from Tr V^4 versus the brute-force histogram
for T in (1.5, TC, 3.5):
    V = transfer_matrix(4, 1 / T)
    Z_tm = np.trace(np.linalg.matrix_power(V, 4))
    lnz_dos, _, _ = thermo_from_dos(dos[4], 16, T)
    print(f"T = {T:.4f}:  ln Z (Tr V^4) = {np.log(Z_tm):.12f}   ln Z (brute force) = {16 * lnz_dos[0]:.12f}")

T = 2.2692:  ln Z (Tr V^4) = 15.521915458755   ln Z (brute force) = 15.521915458755
T = 3.5000:  ln Z (Tr V^4) = 12.600438025330   ln Z (brute force) = 12.600438025330



3.1 Free energy and specific heat of strips
For the widths 4 to 10 we compute \[c_L = -T\,\frac{\partial^2 f_L}{\partial T^2} \tag{35}\] by finite differences on a fine grid; the eigenvalues are accurate to machine precision, so the second difference is reliable. Onsager’s \(f\) (Section 6) is plotted for comparison.


Code
def f_onsager(T):
    # Onsager 1944: -beta f = ln(2 cosh 2K) + (1/2pi) int_0^pi ln[(1 + sqrt(1 - kappa^2 sin^2 phi))/2] dphi
    K = 1.0 / T
    k = 2 * np.sinh(2 * K) / np.cosh(2 * K)**2
    g = lambda p: np.log(0.5 * (1 + np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1 - k**2 * np.sin(p)**2))))
    with warnings.catch_warnings():                 # at T = T_c the integrand has a kink; quad warns but the result is accurate
        warnings.simplefilter("ignore", IntegrationWarning)
        I, _ = quad(g, 0, np.pi, points=[np.pi / 2], limit=200, epsabs=1e-13, epsrel=1e-13)
    return -T * (np.log(2 * np.cosh(2 * K)) + I / (2 * np.pi))

Ls = [4, 6, 8, 10]
Tgrid = np.linspace(1.5, 3.5, 201); dT = Tgrid[1] - Tgrid[0]
strip = {}
t0 = time.perf_counter()
for L in Ls:
    lam = np.array([lambda01(L, 1 / T) for T in Tgrid])
    fL = -Tgrid * np.log(lam[:, 0]) / L
    cL = -Tgrid * np.gradient(np.gradient(fL, dT), dT)
    xiL = 1 / np.log(lam[:, 0] / lam[:, 1])
    strip[L] = dict(f=fL, c=cL, xi=xiL)
print(f"strip transfer matrices: {time.perf_counter() - t0:.1f} s")
f_inf = np.array([f_onsager(T) for T in Tgrid])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 3.6))
for i, L in enumerate(Ls):
    col = blues(i / (len(Ls) - 1))
    ax[0].semilogy(Tgrid, np.abs(strip[L]["f"] - f_inf), color=col, lw=2, label=f"L = {L}")
    s = slice(2, -2)                                                   # drop the one-sided ends of np.gradient
    ax[1].plot(Tgrid[s], strip[L]["c"][s], color=col, lw=2, label=f"L = {L}")
    k = np.argmax(strip[L]["c"][s])
    print(f"L = {L:2d}:  c_max = {strip[L]['c'][s][k]:.4f} at T = {Tgrid[s][k]:.3f};   "
          f"|f_L - f| at T = 1.5, T_c, 3.5:  {abs(strip[L]['f'][0]-f_inf[0]):.1e}, "
          f"{abs(-TC*np.log(lambda01(L, KC)[0])/L - f_onsager(TC)):.1e}, {abs(strip[L]['f'][-1]-f_inf[-1]):.1e}")
    ax[2].plot(Tgrid, strip[L]["xi"] / L, color=col, lw=2, label=f"L = {L}")
for a in ax:
    a.axvline(TC, color=DSOrange, ls=":", lw=1.2); a.set_xlabel("$T$"); a.legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
ax[0].set_ylabel(r"$|f_L - f_{\rm Onsager}|$"); ax[0].set_title("convergence: fast away from $T_c$")
ax[1].set_ylabel("$c_L$"); ax[1].set_title("peak grows and moves towards $T_c$")
ax[2].set_ylabel(r"$\xi_L / L$"); ax[2].set_ylim(0, 3); ax[2].set_title(r"curves cross near $T_c$")

Away from \(T_c\), \(f_L\) converges to Onsager’s \(f\) exponentially fast in \(L\): the correlation length is finite, and a strip wider than \(\xi\) is effectively “infinite”. At \(T_c\) the convergence is only a power law, because the strip is never wider than the infinite correlation length; the peak of \(c_L\) grows (slowly, since the divergence will turn out to be logarithmic, Section 8) and moves towards \(T_c\).
The ratio \(\xi_L/L\) decreases with \(L\) above \(T_c\) (finite \(\xi\)), increases below \(T_c\) (two degenerate ordered states, so that \(\lambda_1\) approaches \(\lambda_0\)), and is \(L\)-independent exactly at \(T_c\), where the only length scale is \(L\) itself. The crossing points of the curves for neighbouring widths therefore locate \(T_c\). This is the same logic as the finite-size analysis of the CNN, but with an exact algorithm.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
4. High- and low-temperature expansions of \(Z\)
At high temperature the natural small parameter is \(\tanh K\). Since the product \(ss'\) of two spins is \(\pm1\), \[e^{Kss'} = \cosh K\,(1 + t\,ss'),\qquad t = \tanh K. \tag{36}\] Expanding the product over all bonds gives a sum over subsets \(G\) of bonds; summing over each spin kills every term in which some site touches an odd number of bonds of \(G\). The survivors are closed graphs: \[
Z = 2^N(\cosh K)^{2N}\sum_{\text{closed } G}t^{|G|} = 2^N(\cosh K)^{2N}\big(1 + N t^4 + 2N t^6 + \dots\big), \tag{37}
\] where the smallest closed graph is an elementary square (4 bonds, \(N\) of them), and the next a \(1\times2\) rectangle (6 bonds, \(2N\) of them: horizontal and vertical).
At low temperature we expand around order instead. Start from all spins up, with energy \(-2N\). Every broken bond costs the energy 2, that is a factor \[x = e^{-2K}, \tag{38}\] and broken bonds form closed walls on the dual lattice: \[
Z = 2e^{2NK}\big(1 + N x^4 + 2N x^6 + \dots\big). \tag{39}
\] One flipped spin breaks 4 bonds (\(N\) ways), a flipped neighbouring pair breaks 6 bonds (\(2N\) ways), and the factor 2 is the all-down copy.
The counting can be checked directly on the \(4\times4\) torus: half the histogram \(n_b\) of Section 1 should be 16, the number of sites, for four broken bonds and 32 for six.

print(f"4x4 torus:  n_4/2 = {dos[4][4]//2} (expected N = {N}),   n_6/2 = {dos[4][6]//2} (expected 2N = {2*N})")
print(f"            n_8/2 = {dos[4][8]//2}  (here also walls that wind around the small torus contribute)")

A second test compares the leading terms with the exact free energy of the infinite lattice. Per spin, \[\frac1N\ln\big(1 + Nt^4 + 2Nt^6+\dots\big) = t^4 + 2t^6 + O(t^8) \tag{40}\] (terms with two separate squares are of order \(N^2t^8\) and are cancelled by the logarithm up to \(O(t^8)\)). So the ratios \[
R_{\rm high}(K) = \frac{\ln Z/N - \ln2 - 2\ln\cosh K}{t^4 + 2t^6}\xrightarrow{K\to0}1, \tag{41}
\] \[
R_{\rm low}(K) = \frac{\ln Z/N - 2K}{x^4 + 2x^6}\xrightarrow{K\to\infty}1 \tag{42}
\] must approach one in their respective limits.

Both series have the same coefficients \(1, N, 2N,\dots\): the closed graphs on the square lattice and on its dual are the same set. This is self-duality.

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
section: 5. Kramers–Wannier duality and the self-dual point
text:
5. Kramers–Wannier duality and the self-dual point
Call \[g(y) = \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\ln\sum_G y^{|G|} . \tag{43}\] The two expansions, equations (37) and (39), say \[
\varphi(K) \equiv \frac{\ln Z(K)}{N} = \ln 2 + 2\ln\cosh K + g(\tanh K) = 2K + g\big(e^{-2K}\big). \tag{44}
\] Define the dual coupling \(K^*\) by \[e^{-2K^*} = \tanh K . \tag{45}\] Using the second form of equation (44) at \(K^*\) and the first at \(K\), both contain \(g(\tanh K)\), so \[
\boxed{\ \varphi(K) - \ln2 - 2\ln\cosh K = \varphi(K^*) - 2K^*\ }. \tag{46}
\] An equivalent form of the duality map (45) is \[\sinh2K\,\sinh2K^* = 1, \tag{47}\] which follows from \[\sinh 2K^* = \frac{1-\tanh^2K}{2\tanh K} = \frac{1}{\sinh2K}. \tag{48}\] Small \(K\) (hot) maps to large \(K^*\) (cold). If there is a single singularity, it must sit at the self-dual point, the coupling \(K_c\) that is its own dual: \[
\sinh 2K_c = 1\ \Rightarrow\ e^{2K_c} = 1+\sqrt2\ \Rightarrow\ T_c = \frac{2}{\ln(1+\sqrt2)}, \tag{49}
\] which is equation (1). We check: (i) equation (47), (ii) Onsager’s modulus \(\kappa\) of equation (51) is the same at \(K\) and \(K^*\), (iii) the identity (46) holds for Onsager’s \(f\), (iv) the fixed point of the duality map, found by root finding, is \(K_c\).


Code

    return -0.5 * np.log(np.tanh(K))

def kappa(K):

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
6. Onsager’s formula
\[
-\beta f = \ln(2\cosh2K) + \frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\pi d\phi\,\ln\Big[\tfrac12\Big(1+\sqrt{1-\kappa^2\sin^2\phi}\Big)\Big], \tag{50}
\] \[
\kappa = \frac{2\sinh2K}{\cosh^22K} = \frac{2s}{1+s^2},\qquad s = \sinh 2K . \tag{51}
\] Since \[2s\le1+s^2, \tag{52}\] \(\kappa\) never exceeds 1, and it reaches 1 only where \(s\) is 1, that is at \(T_c\) by equation (49). There the square root vanishes at the angle \(\pi/2\) and the integrand develops a kink: this is the origin of the non-analyticity.
The energy per spin, equation (6), can be computed in two independent ways, and we use both. The first is numerical: differentiate the integral formula by finite differences in \(\beta\). The second uses the complete elliptic integral of the first kind, \[K_1(\kappa) = \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{d\phi}{\sqrt{1-\kappa^2\sin^2\phi}}, \tag{53}\] in the formula \[
u = -\coth2K\Big[1 + \frac2\pi\big(2\tanh^22K - 1\big)K_1(\kappa)\Big]. \tag{54}
\] scipy.special.ellipkm1(p) returns \(K_1\) as a function of the complementary parameter \[p = 1-\kappa^2 = \Big(\frac{1-s^2}{1+s^2}\Big)^2 . \tag{55}\] Near \(T_c\), \(\kappa^2\) is so close to 1 that \(p\) must be computed from the right-hand form, without cancellation. Yang’s spontaneous magnetisation is \[M = \begin{cases}\big[1-\sinh^{-4}2K\big]^{1/8}, & T<T_c,\\[2pt] 0, & T>T_c.\end{cases} \tag{56}\]


Code
def u_elliptic(T):
    K = 1.0 / np.asarray(T, dtype=float)
    s = np.sinh(2 * K)
    p = ((1 - s**2) / (1 + s**2))**2                 # 1 - kappa^2, without cancellation
    return -1 / np.tanh(2 * K) * (1 + 2 / np.pi * (2 * np.tanh(2 * K)**2 - 1) * ellipkm1(p))

def M_yang(T):
    T = np.asarray(T, dtype=float)
    out = np.zeros_like(T)
    below = T < TC
    out[below] = (1 - np.sinh(2 / T[below])**-4) ** 0.125
    return out

# u from the integral by central differences in beta, versus the elliptic formula

    print(f"  {T:4.2f}       {u_num:.9f}                {u_elliptic(T):.9f}     {u_num - u_elliptic(T):+.1e}")

title: Lab 012: Onsager’s exact solution of the 2D Ising model
text:
7. Energy at the critical point

7.1 The elliptic formula at \(T_c\)
At \(T_c\) the prefactor of \(K_1\) in equation (54) vanishes, because \[
\sinh 2K_c = 1 \;\Rightarrow\; \cosh^2 2K_c = 2 \;\Rightarrow\; \tanh^22K_c = \tfrac12 \;\Rightarrow\; 2\tanh^22K_c - 1 = 0 . \tag{57}
\] It kills the logarithmic divergence of \(K_1\) as \(\kappa\) approaches 1, and \[u(T_c) = -\coth2K_c = -\frac{\cosh 2K_c}{\sinh 2K_c} = -\sqrt2 . \tag{58}\] Numerically, equation (54) is evaluated ever closer to \(T_c\) from both sides and compared with the central difference of the integral formula in \(\beta\) at \(T_c\).

7.2 The value from duality
The same number follows from the duality of Section 5 alone, without Onsager’s formula. Differentiate the duality identity (46) with respect to \(K\). Since \(\varphi\) is \(\ln Z/N\), equation (44), and the derivative of \(\ln Z\) with respect to \(\beta\) is \(-\langle H\rangle\), \[
\varphi'(K) = -u(K) \equiv \varepsilon(K), \tag{59}
\] where, with \(J\) set to 1, \(\varepsilon\) is twice the nearest-neighbour correlation \(\langle s_is_j\rangle_{\rm nn}\) (two bonds per spin). Differentiating equation (46) gives \[
\varepsilon(K) - 2\tanh K = \big(\varepsilon(K^*) - 2\big)\frac{dK^*}{dK}. \tag{60}
\] Differentiating equation (45), \[
-2e^{-2K^*}dK^* = \frac{dK}{\cosh^2K}\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dK^*}{dK} = -\frac{1}{2\tanh K\cosh^2K} = -\frac{1}{\sinh 2K}, \tag{61}
\] which is \(-1\) at \(K_c\) by equation (49). At the self-dual point \(K\) and \(K^*\) both coincide with \(K_c\), and if \(u\) is continuous there (no latent heat), equation (60) becomes \[
\varepsilon - 2\tanh K_c = -(\varepsilon - 2)\ \Rightarrow\ \varepsilon(K_c) = 1 + \tanh K_c . \tag{62}
\] Finally, by self-duality, \[\tanh K_c = e^{-2K_c} = \frac{1}{1+\sqrt2} = \sqrt2 - 1, \tag{63}\] so that \[\varepsilon(K_c) = \sqrt2,\qquad u(T_c) = -\sqrt2 . \tag{64}\] Two exact results, \(T_c\) and \(u(T_c)\), thus come from a symmetry argument; each step of the derivation is evaluated numerically below.
