Use the features of the CNN trained on the labelled cells in Lecture 4 instead of the autoencoder latent space. Do the clusters match the cell types better? Why is that not a fair comparison for unsupervised learning?

title: Unsupervised learning: PCA, t-SNE, clustering, autoencoders and anomalies
text:
8. The 2D Ising model without labels
In Lecture 4 a CNN found the critical temperature \(T_c\), but only because we gave it labels (ordered or disordered) far from the transition. Here the methods receive only the spin configurations.
The configurations are sampled with checkerboard Metropolis updates on a \(32\times32\) lattice with the coupling \(J\) set to 1, no external field and periodic boundaries, at 26 temperatures between 1 and 3.5. At each temperature we run four chains, equilibrate them for 800 sweeps and then store 25 configurations 10 sweeps apart, 2600 configurations in all. Chains below \(T_c\) start from a fully ordered state, chains above it from a random one. One sample is a configuration of \(32\times32\) spins, each \(\pm1\), flattened to a vector of 1024 numbers; its temperature is known but is used only to colour and evaluate the results.


Code
# ---------------- Ising: PCA and autoencoder anomaly detection ----------------
L = 32; Ts = np.round(np.linspace(1.0, 3.5, 26), 2); Tc = 2 / np.log(1 + np.sqrt(2))
mask = (np.add.outer(np.arange(L), np.arange(L)) % 2).astype(bool)
def sweep(s, T):
    for msk in (mask, ~mask):
        nb = np.roll(s, 1, 0) + np.roll(s, -1, 0) + np.roll(s, 1, 1) + np.roll(s, -1, 1)
        dE = 2 * s * nb; acc = (dE <= 0) | (rng.random(s.shape) < np.exp(-dE / T)); s[msk & acc] *= -1
    return s
confs, temps = [], []
for T in Ts:
    for chain in range(4):
        s = rng.choice([-1, 1], (L, L)) if T > Tc else np.ones((L, L), int) * rng.choice([-1, 1])
        for _ in range(800): s = sweep(s, T)
        for k in range(25):
            for _ in range(10): s = sweep(s, T)
            confs.append(s.copy().ravel()); temps.append(T)
C = np.array(confs, float); temps = np.array(temps)
nums["ising_n_configs"] = int(len(C)); nums["ising_L"] = L
log("Ising sampling done")


[3508.0s] Ising sampling done



PCA of spin configurations
PCA receives the spins, never the temperature, which is used only to colour the points. Is its first component the magnetisation \[M=\frac1N\sum_i s_i\ ? \tag{27}\] (Wang, Phys. Rev. B 94, 195105, 2016.) The first component carries 48.4% of the variance, and its correlation with \(M\) over the 2600 configurations is 0.9999999. The figure, saved for the slides, compares \(\langle|\mathrm{PC\,1}|\rangle\), divided by \(\sqrt N\), with \(\langle|M|\rangle\) as functions of temperature.


Code
pi = PCA(2).fit(C); P = pi.transform(C)
nums["ising_pc1_var"] = float(pi.explained_variance_ratio_[0])
M = C.mean(1)
nums["ising_corr_pc1_M"] = float(np.corrcoef(P[:, 0], M)[0, 1])
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.4, 3.7))
sc = axs[0].scatter(P[:, 0], P[:, 1], c=temps, cmap="coolwarm", s=4)
axs[0].set_xlabel("PC 1"); axs[0].set_ylabel("PC 2"); axs[0].set_title("PCA of spin configurations", fontsize=11)
cb = plt.colorbar(sc, ax=axs[0]); cb.set_label("temperature $T$ (only for colour)")
pm = [np.abs(P[temps == T, 0]).mean() / np.sqrt(L * L) for T in Ts]
mm = [np.abs(M[temps == T]).mean() for T in Ts]
axs[1].plot(Ts, pm, "o-", color=orange, label=r"$\langle|\mathrm{PC\,1}|\rangle/\sqrt{N}$")
axs[1].plot(Ts, mm, "s--", color=blue, ms=4, label=r"$\langle|M|\rangle$")
axs[1].axvline(Tc, color="k", ls=":", lw=1); axs[1].text(Tc + 0.03, 0.05, "$T_c$")
axs[1].set_xlabel("$T$"); axs[1].legend(frameon=False); axs[1].set_title("first component = magnetisation", fontsize=11)
for a in axs: clean(a)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/gen_ising_pca.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.close()
log("Ising PCA done")
print({k: nums[k] for k in ['ising_pc1_var', 'ising_corr_pc1_M']})


[3508.6s] Ising PCA done


{'ising_pc1_var': 0.48406358231533997, 'ising_corr_pc1_M': 0.9999998663352911}




The first principal component
Why the first component is the magnetisation can be seen directly. Each configuration is a vector \(\mathbf s\) of \(N\) spins \(\pm1\), here 1024. Below \(T_c\) the configurations are almost all up or almost all down, so the largest variance of the data lies along the uniform direction \[\mathbf v_1\approx\frac{(1,\dots,1)}{\sqrt N}. \tag{28}\] Projecting on it gives \[z_1=\mathbf v_1\cdot(\mathbf s-\bar{\mathbf s})\approx\frac1{\sqrt N}\sum_i s_i=\sqrt N\,M, \tag{29}\] since the mean \(\bar{\mathbf s}\) is close to zero when up and down are equally frequent. So the first component is the magnetisation of equation (27).
We check that \(\mathbf v_1\) is indeed uniform by plotting \(\sqrt N\,v_{1,i}\) on the lattice, which would be 1 everywhere for an exactly uniform vector. The 1024 entries have mean 1.0 and a relative spread of 0.0096.


Code
v1 = pi.components_[0] * np.sign(pi.components_[0].mean())
w = v1 * np.sqrt(L * L)                                       # sqrt(N) * entries: 1 for an exactly uniform vector
nums["ising_v1_rel_spread"] = float(w.std() / w.mean())
nums["ising_v1_mean_times_sqrtN"] = float(w.mean())
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.0), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1, 1.2]))
im = axs[0].imshow(w.reshape(L, L), cmap="viridis", vmin=0.95, vmax=1.05)
plt.colorbar(im, ax=axs[0], fraction=0.046); axs[0].set_xticks([]); axs[0].set_yticks([])
axs[0].set_title(r"$\sqrt{N}\,v_{1,i}$ on the lattice", fontsize=10)
axs[1].hist(w, bins=40, color=blue); axs[1].axvline(1, color="k", ls=":", lw=1)
axs[1].set_xlabel(r"$\sqrt{N}\,v_{1,i}$"); axs[1].set_ylabel("number of entries"); axs[1].set_title("the 1024 entries: all close to 1", fontsize=10); clean(axs[1])
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/gen_ising_v1.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
print("relative spread of the entries:", round(nums["ising_v1_rel_spread"], 4), "| mean of sqrt(N) v_1i:", round(nums["ising_v1_mean_times_sqrtN"], 4))





relative spread of the entries: 0.0096 | mean of sqrt(N) v_1i: 1.0




Autoencoder on ordered configurations
We train an autoencoder only on ordered configurations (temperatures up to 1.6), the “normal” data, and measure its reconstruction error at every temperature. Where does the error grow fastest? (Kottmann et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 125, 170603, 2020, used this idea for quantum phases.) The steepest rise of the error is at the temperature 2.3, the grid temperature closest to the exact critical temperature \[T_c=\frac{2}{\ln\big(1+\sqrt2\big)}\approx2.269 ; \tag{30}\] the figure is saved for the slides.


Code
# autoencoder trained only on ordered configurations (T <= 1.6)
class AE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(s, n=L * L, lat=8):
        super().__init__()
        s.e = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(n, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, lat))
        s.d = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(lat, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, n), nn.Tanh())
    def forward(s, x): return s.d(s.e(x))
ae = AE(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(ae.parameters(), 1e-3)
Ct = torch.tensor(C, dtype=torch.float32); tr = torch.tensor(temps <= 1.6)
Xn = Ct[tr]
for ep in range(300):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(Xn))
    for i in range(0, len(Xn), 64):
        b = Xn[perm[i:i + 64]]; loss = ((ae(b) - b) ** 2).mean(); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
with torch.no_grad(): err = ((ae(Ct) - Ct) ** 2).mean(1).numpy()
em = np.array([err[temps == T].mean() for T in Ts]); es = np.array([err[temps == T].std() for T in Ts])
d = np.gradient(em, Ts); nums["ising_ae_max_slope_T"] = float(Ts[np.argmax(d)])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.4))
ax.axvspan(Ts[0], 1.6, color=blue, alpha=0.15, label="training data (ordered)")
ax.errorbar(Ts, em, yerr=es, fmt="o-", color=orange, ms=4, capsize=2, label="reconstruction error")
ax.axvline(Tc, color="k", ls=":", lw=1); ax.text(Tc + 0.03, em.max() * 0.05, "$T_c$")
ax.set_xlabel("$T$"); ax.set_ylabel("mean squared error"); ax.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper left"); clean(ax)
plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/gen_ising_ae_anomaly.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.close()
log("Ising AE done")
print('steepest rise of the error at T =', nums['ising_ae_max_slope_T'])


[3516.5s] Ising AE done


steepest rise of the error at T = 2.3


For the architecture diagram on the slides we show one ordered training configuration (temperature 1.0) and its reconstruction.


Code
with torch.no_grad():
    s_in = Ct[0]; s_out = ae(Ct[:1])[0]
for arr, name in [(s_in.numpy(), "gen_ising_ae_in.png"), (s_out.numpy(), "gen_ising_ae_out.png")]:
    plt.figure(figsize=(2, 2)); plt.imshow(arr.reshape(L, L), cmap="gray", vmin=-1, vmax=1, interpolation="nearest"); plt.axis("off")
    plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/{name}", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight", pad_inches=0.02); plt.show()
print("temperature of this configuration:", temps[0])








temperature of this configuration: 1.0




Exercise
Train the autoencoder on disordered configurations (temperatures of 3 and above) instead. Does the reconstruction error still point to \(T_c\)?

title: Unsupervised learning: PCA, t-SNE, clustering, autoencoders and anomalies
text:
9. Tabular data

Credit-card fraud
The same tools work on any table of numbers. The data are 284 807 card transactions by European cardholders in two days of September 2013, 492 of them fraudulent (0.17%) (Dal Pozzolo, Caelen, Johnson and Bontempi, IEEE Symposium Series on Computational Intelligence, 159 (2015); from OpenML, data set 1597, 150 MB, downloaded once to data/creditcard). For confidentiality the original features are not given: V1–V28 are already principal components of them, and only Amount (in euros) and Time (seconds since the first transaction) are original. One sample is one transaction with these 30 numbers and the label Class, 1 for fraud and 0 otherwise. We use V1–V28 and the logarithm of the amount shifted by one, 29 columns in all (equation (31) below), and drop Time.
The labels exist, but we use them only to score the methods, as if fraud had never been seen. We first project the data to 2D with PCA to look at them. We then train an autoencoder only on the normal transactions of the training part (80% of the data) and use its reconstruction error as the anomaly score on the test part (20%). As a simple baseline we score each transaction by its distance from the mean of the normal ones.
The table as the autoencoder sees it, as drawn on the slides for the first five transactions, has one row per transaction, \[\mathbf x_i=\big(V_1,\dots,V_{28},\ln(1+A)\big), \tag{31}\] with \(A\) the amount; Class is used only to evaluate.


Code
# the first five rows of the table as the autoencoder sees them: x_i = (V1, ..., V28, log(1 + Amount)); Class only to evaluate
fpath = "data/creditcard/creditcard.arff"
rows_ = []
with open(fpath) as f:
    for line in f:
        if line.startswith("@") or not line.strip(): continue
        rows_.append(line.strip().replace("'", "").split(","))
        if len(rows_) == 5: break
A5 = np.array(rows_, dtype=np.float64)
for r in A5:
    print(f"V1 {r[1]:6.2f}  V2 {r[2]:6.2f}  ...  V28 {r[28]:6.2f}  log(1+Amount) {np.log1p(r[29]):5.2f}  Class {int(r[30])}")


V1  -1.36  V2  -0.07  ...  V28  -0.02  log(1+Amount)  5.01  Class 0
V1   1.19  V2   0.27  ...  V28   0.01  log(1+Amount)  1.31  Class 0
V1  -1.36  V2  -1.34  ...  V28  -0.06  log(1+Amount)  5.94  Class 0
V1  -0.97  V2  -0.19  ...  V28   0.06  log(1+Amount)  4.82  Class 0
V1  -1.16  V2   0.88  ...  V28   0.22  log(1+Amount)  4.26  Class 0




Code
import urllib.request
fpath = "data/creditcard/creditcard.arff"
if not os.path.exists(fpath):
    os.makedirs("data/creditcard", exist_ok=True)
    urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://openml.org/data/v1/download/1673544/creditcard.arff", fpath)
rows_ = []
with open(fpath) as f:
    for line in f:
        if line.startswith("@") or not line.strip(): continue
        rows_.append(line.strip().replace("'", "").split(","))
A = np.array(rows_, dtype=np.float64); del rows_
Xf = A[:, 1:30].copy(); yf = A[:, 30].astype(int); Xf[:, 28] = np.log1p(Xf[:, 28])     # V1..V28, log(1 + Amount)
nums["fraud_n"] = int(len(yf)); nums["fraud_pos"] = int(yf.sum())
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
Xf_tr, Xf_te, yf_tr, yf_te = train_test_split(Xf, yf, test_size=0.2, stratify=yf, random_state=0)
mu_f, sd_f = Xf_tr[yf_tr == 0].mean(0), Xf_tr[yf_tr == 0].std(0)                       # standardise with the normal training data
Zf_tr, Zf_te = (Xf_tr - mu_f) / sd_f, (Xf_te - mu_f) / sd_f
print(f"{len(yf)} transactions, {yf.sum()} frauds; test part: {len(yf_te)} transactions, {yf_te.sum()} frauds")

# PCA to 2D of the test part (all frauds and 5000 normal transactions)
rf_ = np.random.default_rng(11); sub = np.r_[rf_.choice(np.flatnonzero(yf_te == 0), 5000, replace=False), np.flatnonzero(yf_te == 1)]
pf = PCA(2).fit(Zf_tr[yf_tr == 0]); Pf = pf.transform(Zf_te[sub])
nums["fraud_pca2_var"] = float(pf.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())

# autoencoder 29 -> 16 -> 8 -> 16 -> 29, trained on normal transactions only
state = torch.get_rng_state(); torch.manual_seed(0)
encF = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(29, 16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16, 8)); decF = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(8, 16), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(16, 29))
optF = torch.optim.Adam(list(encF.parameters()) + list(decF.parameters()), 1e-3)
Nf = torch.tensor(Zf_tr[yf_tr == 0], dtype=torch.float32)
for ep in range(10):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(Nf))
    for i in range(0, len(Nf), 256):
        b = Nf[perm[i:i + 256]]; loss = ((decF(encF(b)) - b) ** 2).mean(); optF.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optF.step()
torch.set_rng_state(state)
torch.save({"enc": encF.state_dict(), "dec": decF.state_dict()}, f"{RES}/fraud_ae.pt")
with torch.no_grad():
    Tf = torch.tensor(Zf_te, dtype=torch.float32); errF = ((decF(encF(Tf)) - Tf) ** 2).mean(1).numpy()
distF = (Zf_te ** 2).mean(1)                                                             # distance from the normal mean
nums["fraud_ae_auc"] = float(roc_auc_score(yf_te, errF)); nums["fraud_dist_auc"] = float(roc_auc_score(yf_te, distF))
for q in [0.5, 1, 2]:
    fl = errF > np.percentile(errF, 100 - q)
    nums[f"fraud_top{q}_caught"] = float(yf_te[fl].sum() / yf_te.sum()); nums[f"fraud_top{q}_precision"] = float(yf_te[fl].mean())
    print(f"flag the {q}% largest errors: {yf_te[fl].sum()} of {yf_te.sum()} frauds caught ({nums[f'fraud_top{q}_caught']:.0%}); {nums[f'fraud_top{q}_precision']:.1%} of the flagged are fraud")

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(13, 3.7))
s0 = yf_te[sub] == 0
axs[0].scatter(Pf[s0, 0], Pf[s0, 1], s=3, color="lightgrey", label="normal (5000 shown)")
axs[0].scatter(Pf[~s0, 0], Pf[~s0, 1], s=6, color=orange, label="fraud")
axs[0].set_xlim(np.percentile(Pf[:, 0], [0.2, 99.8])); axs[0].set_ylim(np.percentile(Pf[:, 1], [0.2, 99.8]))
axs[0].set_title("PCA of the test transactions", fontsize=10); axs[0].set_xlabel("PC 1"); axs[0].set_ylabel("PC 2"); axs[0].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, markerscale=3)
bins = np.logspace(np.log10(errF.min()), np.log10(errF.max()), 70)
axs[1].hist(errF[yf_te == 0], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, color=blue, label="normal")
axs[1].hist(errF[yf_te == 1], bins=bins, density=True, alpha=0.6, color=orange, label="fraud")
axs[1].axvline(np.percentile(errF, 99), color="k", ls="--", lw=1, label="1% largest errors")
axs[1].set_xscale("log"); axs[1].set_xlabel("reconstruction error"); axs[1].set_ylabel("density"); axs[1].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8)
axs[1].set_title("autoencoder trained on normal transactions", fontsize=10)
for sc, lab, col in [(errF, f"autoencoder, AUC {nums['fraud_ae_auc']:.2f}", orange), (distF, f"distance from the mean, AUC {nums['fraud_dist_auc']:.2f}", navy)]:
    fp_, tp_, _ = roc_curve(yf_te, sc); axs[2].plot(fp_, tp_, color=col, lw=1.8, label=lab)
axs[2].plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k:", lw=1); axs[2].set_xscale("symlog", linthresh=0.01); axs[2].set_xlim(0, 1)
axs[2].set_xlabel("false-positive rate (log scale above 0.01)"); axs[2].set_ylabel("true-positive rate"); axs[2].set_title("ROC curves", fontsize=10); axs[2].legend(frameon=False, fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
for a in axs: clean(a)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/gen_fraud.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
print({k: (round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v) for k, v in nums.items() if k.startswith("fraud")})


284807 transactions, 492 frauds; test part: 56962 transactions, 98 frauds


flag the 0.5% largest errors: 62 of 98 frauds caught (63%); 21.8% of the flagged are fraud
flag the 1% largest errors: 73 of 98 frauds caught (74%); 12.8% of the flagged are fraud
flag the 2% largest errors: 76 of 98 frauds caught (78%); 6.7% of the flagged are fraud





{'fraud_n': 284807, 'fraud_pos': 492, 'fraud_pca2_var': 0.099, 'fraud_ae_auc': 0.941, 'fraud_dist_auc': 0.949, 'fraud_top0.5_caught': 0.633, 'fraud_top0.5_precision': 0.218, 'fraud_top1_caught': 0.745, 'fraud_top1_precision': 0.128, 'fraud_top2_caught': 0.776, 'fraud_top2_precision': 0.067}


Fraud is found well, but not by virtue of the autoencoder. The autoencoder reaches AUC 0.941, the plain distance from the mean 0.949. Flagging the 1% of test transactions with the largest reconstruction errors catches 73 of the 98 frauds (74%), and 12.8% of the flagged transactions are fraud; flagging 0.5% catches 63% with 21.8% precision. In the PCA projection to 2D, which keeps only 9.9% of the variance, part of the frauds lie at the edge of the normal cloud, but many sit inside it. The ROC curves, drawn with a logarithmic false-positive axis, show the autoencoder ahead at small false-positive rates and the distance from the mean ahead at larger ones.


Exercise
The autoencoder is no better than the plain distance from the mean: the 29 columns are already principal components, so a fraud is mostly a transaction with unusually large values. Train the autoencoder with a smaller latent space (four latent numbers), or score with an isolation forest (sklearn.ensemble.IsolationForest). Does anything beat the baseline?


Tumour gene expression
The UCI data set gene expression cancer RNA-Seq (University of California, Irvine, Machine Learning Repository, id 401, CC BY 4.0; S. Fiorini, 2016) is a random extraction from the pan-cancer ribonucleic acid sequencing (RNA-Seq, Illumina HiSeq) data of The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA): 801 tumour samples, each a vector of 20 531 gene-expression values. The gene names are anonymised (gene_0, …). The values range from 0 to about 20.8, which looks like a logarithmic scale; the normalisation is not documented on the UCI page. There are five tumour types: breast invasive carcinoma (BRCA, 300 samples), kidney renal clear cell carcinoma (KIRC, 146), lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD, 141), prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD, 136) and colon adenocarcinoma (COAD, 78). The type is used only to evaluate.
The question is the anomaly question once more: is a tumour type that was never seen in training recognised as unusual?


Code
# TCGA pan-cancer RNA-Seq (UCI data set 401): 801 tumour samples x 20 531 genes, five tumour types
import zipfile, tarfile, io, urllib.request
import pandas as pd
zpath = "data/rnaseq.zip"      # downloaded for Lectures 7-8
if not os.path.exists(zpath):
    zpath = "data/rnaseq.zip"
    if not os.path.exists(zpath):
        os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
        urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/401/gene+expression+cancer+rna+seq.zip", zpath)
with zipfile.ZipFile(zpath) as z:
    tgz = io.BytesIO(z.read("TCGA-PANCAN-HiSeq-801x20531.tar.gz"))
with tarfile.open(fileobj=tgz) as t:
    G = pd.read_csv(t.extractfile("TCGA-PANCAN-HiSeq-801x20531/data.csv"), index_col=0)
    gy = pd.read_csv(t.extractfile("TCGA-PANCAN-HiSeq-801x20531/labels.csv"), index_col=0)["Class"].values
Gx = G.values.astype(np.float32); gtypes = ["BRCA", "KIRC", "LUAD", "PRAD", "COAD"]
print(G.shape, "| genes:", list(G.columns[:3]), "... | values from", Gx.min(), "to", round(float(Gx.max()), 1))
print({c: int((gy == c).sum()) for c in gtypes})
nums["rna_n"], nums["rna_genes"], nums["rna_max"] = int(Gx.shape[0]), int(Gx.shape[1]), float(Gx.max())
print(G.iloc[:5, [1, 2, 3, 20530]].round(2).assign(type=gy[:5]))            # the first rows, as drawn on the slide


(801, 20531) | genes: ['gene_0', 'gene_1', 'gene_2'] ... | values from 0.0 to 20.8
{'BRCA': 300, 'KIRC': 146, 'LUAD': 141, 'PRAD': 136, 'COAD': 78}
          gene_1  gene_2  gene_3  gene_20530  type
sample_0    2.02    3.27    5.48         0.0  PRAD
sample_1    0.59    1.59    7.59         0.0  LUAD
sample_2    3.51    4.33    6.88         0.0  PRAD
sample_3    3.66    4.51    6.66         0.0  PRAD
sample_4    2.66    2.82    6.54         0.0  BRCA


We train on four tumour types and treat the fifth, never seen in training, as the anomaly. The samples of the four known types are split 80/20 into training and test parts. We keep the 2000 genes with the largest variance, computed on the training part only, and standardise them with the training mean and standard deviation; using the test samples here would leak information. An autoencoder \(2000\to256\to32\to256\to2000\) is trained on the training part, and the score \(a(\mathbf x)\) is the mean squared reconstruction error over the 2000 genes. The baseline is the reconstruction error of PCA with the same 32 components. Each of the five types is held out in turn.
Both scores find the unseen type almost perfectly, with AUC between 0.960 and 0.999. PCA is as good as the autoencoder or slightly better for every held-out type, for instance 0.982 against 0.960 for LUAD: with a few hundred samples the linear model is hard to beat.


Code
# anomaly = a tumour type never seen in training; repeated with each of the five types held out
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
def rna_split(held, seed=0):
    r = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    known = np.flatnonzero(gy != held); r.shuffle(known)
    ntr = int(0.8 * len(known)); tr, te_norm = known[:ntr], known[ntr:]
    return tr, te_norm, np.flatnonzero(gy == held)
def rna_scores(held, n_genes=2000, d=32, epochs=300, seed=0):
    tr, te_n, te_a = rna_split(held, seed)
    var = Gx[tr].var(0); genes = np.argsort(var)[::-1][:n_genes]          # most variable genes, TRAINING part only
    mu, sd = Gx[tr][:, genes].mean(0), Gx[tr][:, genes].std(0) + 1e-6       # standardise with training statistics
    Z = lambda idx: (Gx[idx][:, genes] - mu) / sd
    Xtr_, Xn, Xa = map(lambda a: torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32), (Z(tr), Z(te_n), Z(te_a)))
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(n_genes, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, d))
    dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, n_genes))
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(list(enc.parameters()) + list(dec.parameters()), 1e-3, weight_decay=1e-5)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(Xtr_))
        for i in range(0, len(perm), 64):
            b = Xtr_[perm[i:i + 64]]; loss = ((dec(enc(b)) - b) ** 2).mean(); opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    with torch.no_grad():
        a_ae = lambda X: ((dec(enc(X)) - X) ** 2).mean(1).numpy()                 # a(x): mean squared error over the genes
        an, aa, atr = a_ae(Xn), a_ae(Xa), a_ae(Xtr_)
    pc = PCA(d, random_state=0).fit(Z(tr))                                       # baseline: PCA reconstruction, same d
    a_pca = lambda X: ((pc.inverse_transform(pc.transform(X)) - X) ** 2).mean(1)
    yt = np.r_[np.zeros(len(an)), np.ones(len(aa))]
    return dict(an=an, aa=aa, atr=atr, auc_ae=roc_auc_score(yt, np.r_[an, aa]),
                auc_pca=roc_auc_score(yt, np.r_[a_pca(Z(te_n)), a_pca(Z(te_a))]), n_tr=len(tr), n_n=len(te_n), n_a=len(te_a))
t0g = time.time(); rna = {h: rna_scores(h) for h in gtypes}
for h, r in rna.items():
    print(f"held out {h}: train {r['n_tr']}, test normal {r['n_n']}, test anomalies {r['n_a']}; AUC autoencoder {r['auc_ae']:.3f}, PCA {r['auc_pca']:.3f}")
print(f"{time.time() - t0g:.0f} s")

title: Unsupervised learning: PCA, t-SNE, clustering, autoencoders and anomalies
Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
Disentanglement
Suppose the images in a data set are produced by a simulator with a handful of independent inputs \(v_1,\dots,v_K\), the generative factors: the position of an object, its size, its orientation, its shape. A representation \(\mathbf z\) is called disentangled when each coordinate \(z_k\) responds to one factor and is insensitive to the others. Changing \(z_k\) then changes one property of the decoded image and leaves the rest of the image unchanged; conversely, moving the object in the image changes one coordinate only. An entangled representation can carry exactly the same information, mixed by some rotation of the latent space, so that every coordinate depends on several factors at once.
The conditional VAE of the lecture solved a related but easier problem. There the factor of interest, the digit class or the blood-cell type, was supplied as a label \(\mathbf c\) to both networks, \(q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\) and \(p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\), and the latent space kept only the remaining style. Here no labels are given. The factors must be discovered from the images alone, and the only leverage we have is the shape of the objective.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
The β-VAE objective
For one image \(\mathbf x\) the VAE minimises minus the evidence lower bound (ELBO), \[-\mathrm{ELBO}(\mathbf x)=\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)}\big[-\log p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z)\big]+\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big). \tag{2}\] Higgins et al. (2017) start instead from a constrained problem: make the reconstruction as good as possible while keeping the KL divergence of the encoder from the prior below a budget \(\varepsilon\), \[\max_{\phi,\theta}\ \mathbb E_{\mathbf x}\,\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)}\big[\log p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z)\big]\quad\text{subject to}\quad \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big)<\varepsilon . \tag{3}\] The Lagrangian of this problem, with a non-negative Karush–Kuhn–Tucker multiplier \(\beta\), gives after dropping the constant \(\beta\varepsilon\) the β-VAE loss \[\mathcal L_\beta(\mathbf x)=\mathbb E_{q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)}\big[-\log p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z)\big]+\beta\,\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big). \tag{4}\] With β equal to 1, equation (4) is equation (2), the VAE loss of Kingma and Welling (2014). For β larger than 1 it is no longer a bound on the log-likelihood; it is a different trade-off between the two terms.
The encoder outputs a diagonal Gaussian, \[q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x)=\mathcal N\big(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf x),\operatorname{diag}\boldsymbol\sigma^2(\mathbf x)\big), \tag{5}\] and the prior (1) factorises too, into \(d\) independent standard normal coordinates. The KL divergence between two products of independent factors is the sum of the KL divergences of the factors, so the penalty splits into one term per coordinate, \[\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x)\,\|\,p(\mathbf z)\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mathrm{KL}_k, \tag{6}\] \[\mathrm{KL}_k=\tfrac12\big(\mu_k^2+\sigma_k^2-\ln\sigma_k^2-1\big). \tag{7}\] \(\mathrm{KL}_k\) vanishes only for zero mean and unit width, that is, when \(z_k\) is pure prior noise whatever the input: such a coordinate carries no information about \(\mathbf x\). Averaged over the data, \(\mathrm{KL}_k\) is an upper bound on the information, in nats (one nat is about 1.44 bits), that the noisy channel \(z_k\) transmits about the image (Burgess et al., 2018). The loss (4) therefore charges \(\beta\) units per nat sent through each coordinate.
This price explains the pressure towards disentanglement. When information is expensive, the model sends only what reduces the reconstruction error most per nat, and it sends it through as few coordinates as possible; the remaining coordinates collapse onto the prior. Burgess et al. describe the consequence: under a tight bottleneck a β-VAE on dSprites first encodes position, because a sprite misplaced by a few pixels destroys the pixel-wise likelihood, and as the budget grows it adds scale, then other factors, each in a coordinate of its own. Since the prior is isotropic and factorised, independent factors placed on separate axes are also the cheapest arrangement for the KL term. The price is paid in reconstruction: information that does not fit through the bottleneck is lost, and the decoded images become blurrier.


Code
# KL_k from equation (7), checked against torch.distributions for a few (mu, sigma)
from torch.distributions import Normal, kl_divergence
mu_ = torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 0.0]); sd_ = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.5, 1.0, 0.1, 0.05])
kl_formula = 0.5 * (mu_ ** 2 + sd_ ** 2 - torch.log(sd_ ** 2) - 1)
kl_torch = kl_divergence(Normal(mu_, sd_), Normal(0.0, 1.0))
for m, s, a, b in zip(mu_, sd_, kl_formula, kl_torch):
    print(f"mu = {m:4.1f}, sigma = {s:4.2f}:  KL_k = {a:.4f} nats (formula) = {b:.4f} (torch)")


mu =  0.0, sigma = 1.00:  KL_k = 0.0000 nats (formula) = 0.0000 (torch)
mu =  0.0, sigma = 0.50:  KL_k = 0.3181 nats (formula) = 0.3181 (torch)
mu =  1.0, sigma = 1.00:  KL_k = 0.5000 nats (formula) = 0.5000 (torch)
mu =  2.0, sigma = 0.10:  KL_k = 3.8076 nats (formula) = 3.8076 (torch)
mu =  0.0, sigma = 0.05:  KL_k = 2.4970 nats (formula) = 2.4970 (torch)


A coordinate that only shifts its mean by one prior standard deviation costs half a nat. Narrowing the posterior is what becomes expensive: a width of 0.05 costs about 2.5 nats even at zero mean. A sharp, informative coordinate is costly, a vague one is cheap, and the multiplier \(\beta\) decides how many sharp coordinates the model can afford.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
The dSprites data
The data set dSprites, Disentanglement testing Sprites (Matthey et al., 2017), was built at DeepMind as a test bench for disentanglement. Each sample \(\mathbf x_i\) is a binary image of \(64\times64\) pixels; every pixel is either 1, a white pixel of the sprite, or 0, the black background. The images are not photographs: they were rendered by a program from five numbers, the generative factors,

shape: square, ellipse or heart (3 values);
scale: the size of the sprite, 6 values from 0.5 to 1;
orientation: rotation angle, 40 values equally spaced from 0 to \(2\pi\);
position \(x\): horizontal position, 32 values from 0 to 1;
position \(y\): vertical position, 32 values from 0 to 1.

(A sixth factor, colour, has a single value, white.) Every combination of the factors appears exactly once, which gives 737,280 images (\(3\cdot6\cdot40\cdot32\cdot32\)), stored in a fixed order from which the factors of any image can be read off; no noise was added. The factors are therefore independent by construction and known for every image. The data are distributed with a description of the factors at github.com/deepmind/dsprites-dataset under the Apache 2.0 licence.
The archive (about 19 MB, 3 GB once unpacked) is downloaded once into data/dsprites/. To keep training within reach of a CPU we draw 110,000 images at random, 100,000 for training and 10,000 for testing, and reduce them to \(32\times32\) by averaging \(2\times2\) blocks and thresholding at one half, which keeps them binary. The subset, together with a few rows of full-resolution images, is cached, so the 3 GB array is unpacked only on the first run.


Code
DS = os.path.join(DATA, "dsprites"); os.makedirs(DS, exist_ok=True)
NPZ = os.path.join(DS, "dsprites_ndarray_co1sh3sc6or40x32y32_64x64.npz")
SUB = os.path.join(DS, "dsprites_subset_32x32.npz")
URLS = ["https://github.com/google-deepmind/dsprites-dataset/raw/master/dsprites_ndarray_co1sh3sc6or40x32y32_64x64.npz",
        "https://github.com/deepmind/dsprites-dataset/raw/master/dsprites_ndarray_co1sh3sc6or40x32y32_64x64.npz",
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/google-deepmind/dsprites-dataset/master/dsprites_ndarray_co1sh3sc6or40x32y32_64x64.npz"]
FACTORS = ["shape", "scale", "orientation", "position x", "position y"]
SHAPES = ["square", "ellipse", "heart"]
N_TRAIN, N_TEST = 100_000, 10_000
SIZES = np.array([1, 3, 6, 40, 32, 32])                            # colour, shape, scale, orientation, x, y
BASES = np.concatenate([SIZES[::-1].cumprod()[::-1][1:], [1]])    # image index = sum_j class_j * BASES_j
ROWS = {"shape": [0, 1, 2], "scale": list(range(6)), "orientation": [0, 3, 6, 10, 13, 16, 20, 26],
        "position x": [0, 4, 9, 13, 18, 22, 27, 31], "position y": [0, 4, 9, 13, 18, 22, 27, 31]}
BASE = [0, 2, 5, 0, 16, 16]                                       # heart, largest scale, angle 0, centre

if not os.path.exists(SUB):
    if not os.path.exists(NPZ):
        for u in URLS:
            try:
                urllib.request.urlretrieve(u, NPZ); break
            except Exception as e:
                print("download failed:", u, e)
    raw = np.load(NPZ, allow_pickle=True, encoding="latin1")
    imgs, classes, values = raw["imgs"], raw["latents_classes"], raw["latents_values"]
    print("full data set:", imgs.shape, imgs.dtype, " factor sizes:", raw["metadata"][()]["latents_sizes"])
    rng = seed(0)
    idx = rng.choice(len(imgs), N_TRAIN + N_TEST, replace=False)
    small = (imgs[idx].reshape(-1, 32, 2, 32, 2).mean((2, 4)) >= 0.5).astype(np.uint8)   # 2x2 average, threshold
    grid = {}                                                     # full-resolution rows, one factor varied per row
    for j, f in enumerate(FACTORS):
        ids = []
        for v in ROWS[f]:
            cl = list(BASE); cl[j + 1] = v; ids.append(int(np.dot(cl, BASES)))
        grid["g_" + f] = imgs[ids]; grid["gv_" + f] = values[ids, j + 1]
    sq = lambda o: int(np.dot([0, 0, 5, o, 16, 16], BASES))      # a large centred square at orientation index o
    sym = np.array([(imgs[sq(0)] != imgs[sq(o)]).mean() for o in range(40)])
    np.savez_compressed(SUB, x=small, c=classes[idx, 1:], v=values[idx, 1:], idx=idx, sym=sym,
                        angles=raw["metadata"][()]["latents_possible_values"]["orientation"], **grid)
    del raw, imgs, classes, values

sub = np.load(SUB)
X = torch.tensor(sub["x"], dtype=torch.float32).unsqueeze(1)      # (N, 1, 32, 32)
C, V = sub["c"], sub["v"]                                         # factor classes (integers) and values
Xtr, Xte, Cte, Vte = X[:N_TRAIN], X[N_TRAIN:], C[N_TRAIN:], V[N_TRAIN:]
print("training images:", tuple(Xtr.shape), "  test images:", tuple(Xte.shape))
print("values per factor:", {f: len(np.unique(C[:, i])) for i, f in enumerate(FACTORS)})
print(f"mean fraction of white pixels at 32 x 32: {Xtr.mean():.4f}")

In the printed patch of one sample the sprite is a blob of ones in a sea of zeros: on average only 4.5% of the \(32\times32\) pixels are white. A model that places the sprite a few pixels off pays for the missed pixels and for the wrongly painted ones, which is why position is the first thing any of these models learns.
Orientation is the factor the image does not fully reveal. The last printed line compares a large centred square at angle 0 with the same square rotated: at \(92.3^\circ\) not a single pixel differs, while at \(46.2^\circ\) 3% of the canvas changes, and the angles \(0\) and \(2\pi\), both present in the list of 40, give identical images. The ellipse is symmetric under a half turn, so its images near angle \(\pi\) nearly repeat those near 0. Several orientation labels therefore belong to the same image, and no encoder can recover them; any measured mutual information with orientation is limited by this, not only by the model.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
Encoder and decoder
The networks follow the convolutional design of Higgins et al. (2017) and Burgess et al. (2018), which use \(4\times4\) kernels with stride 2, channel numbers 32–32–64–64, a dense layer of 256 units and ten latent coordinates for \(64\times64\) inputs. With \(32\times32\) inputs one strided convolution fewer reaches the same \(4\times4\) feature map, so the encoder has three convolutional layers (32–32–64 channels), each halving the side of the image, from 32 to 16, 8 and 4 pixels. The 1024 numbers of the final \(64\times4\times4\) maps pass through a dense layer of 256 units to 20 outputs, the ten means \(\mu_k\) and the ten log-variances \(\ln\sigma_k^2\) of equation (5).
The decoder mirrors the encoder with transposed convolutions and returns one logit \(G_j(\mathbf z)\) per pixel \(j\). Its sigmoid \(\hat x_j\) is the probability that the pixel is white, which makes the decoder a product of Bernoulli distributions, \[p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z)=\prod_{j=1}^{1024}\hat x_j^{\,x_j}\,(1-\hat x_j)^{1-x_j},\qquad \hat x_j=\operatorname{sigmoid}\big(G_j(\mathbf z)\big), \tag{8}\] and its negative logarithm the binary cross-entropy summed over the pixels, \[-\log p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z)=-\sum_{j=1}^{1024}\big[x_j\ln\hat x_j+(1-x_j)\ln(1-\hat x_j)\big]. \tag{9}\]


Code
d = 10                                                            # latent coordinates

class ConvVAE(nn.Module):
    # convolutional VAE for 1 x 32 x 32 binary images; d latent coordinates; Bernoulli decoder
    def __init__(self, d=10):
        super().__init__()
        self.d = d
        self.encoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 4, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(),                 # 1 x 32 x 32  -> 32 x 16 x 16
            nn.Conv2d(32, 32, 4, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(),                # 32 x 16 x 16 -> 32 x 8 x 8
            nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 4, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(),                # 32 x 8 x 8   -> 64 x 4 x 4
            nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(1024, 256), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Linear(256, 2 * d))                                # mu and log sigma^2
        self.decoder = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Linear(d, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 1024), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Unflatten(1, (64, 4, 4)),
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, 4, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(),       # -> 32 x 8 x 8
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 32, 4, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(),       # -> 32 x 16 x 16
            nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 1, 4, 2, 1))                   # -> 1 x 32 x 32 logits
    def encode(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encoder(x).chunk(2, dim=1); return mu, logvar
    def decode(self, z):
        return self.decoder(z)
    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x)
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)   # reparametrisation trick
        return self.decode(z), mu, logvar

print(f"parameters: {sum(p.numel() for p in ConvVAE(d).parameters()):,}")

The same information as a block diagram, one block per stage, read off the model itself: a forward pass with hooks on every layer records the output shape and the number of parameters of each stage, and the height of a block grows with the logarithm of the number of values it holds, so that the narrowing towards the ten latent coordinates and the widening back to the image are visible. Encoder and decoder are drawn in two rows; the sampling step of the reparametrisation trick closes the first row.


Code
def layer_stages(model, x):
    """
    Record one stage per layer of model.encode and model.decode.

    model : a VAE with methods encode(x) -> (mu, logvar) and decode(z)
    x     : one input batch, e.g. torch.zeros(1, 1, 32, 32)
    Returns two lists (encoder, decoder) of dicts with keys
      name   short description of the layer (type, kernel, stride)
      shape  output shape without the batch dimension
      params number of trainable parameters of the layer
    """
    names = {nn.Conv2d: "conv", nn.ConvTranspose2d: "t. conv", nn.Linear: "dense",
             nn.Flatten: "flatten", nn.Unflatten: "reshape"}
    record = []
    def hook(m, inp, out):
        n = names[type(m)]
        if isinstance(m, (nn.Conv2d, nn.ConvTranspose2d)):
            n += f" {m.kernel_size[0]}×{m.kernel_size[1]}\nstride {m.stride[0]}"
        record.append(dict(name=n, shape=tuple(out.shape[1:]), params=sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())))
    hs = [m.register_forward_hook(hook) for m in model.modules() if type(m) in names]
    with torch.no_grad():
        mu, _ = model.encode(x); enc_stages = list(record); record.clear()
        model.decode(torch.zeros_like(mu)); dec_stages = list(record)
    for h in hs: h.remove()
    first = dict(name="input", shape=tuple(x.shape[1:]), params=0)
    enc_stages[-1]["name"] = "dense\nμ, ln σ²"                    # the last encoder layer gives the 2d numbers
    latent = dict(name="z = μ + σ⊙ε", shape=(mu.shape[1],), params=0, latent=True)
    return [first] + enc_stages + [latent], [dict(latent, name="z")] + dec_stages

def draw_blocks(ax, stages, title="", width=1.0, gap=0.55, colors=None):
    """
    Draw a list of stages as a row of blocks joined by arrows.

    ax     : matplotlib axes to draw on
    stages : list of dicts from layer_stages (keys name, shape, params, optional latent)
    title  : title written above the row
    width  : width of one block in axis units
    gap    : horizontal space between neighbouring blocks (holds the arrow)
    colors : dict mapping the first word of a stage name to a face colour
    """
    colors = colors or {"input": "#DDDDDD", "conv": "#8FB8E0", "t.": "#8FB8E0", "flatten": "#E3ECF6",
                        "reshape": "#E3ECF6", "dense": "#C9DCF0", "z": orange}
    hmax = max(np.log2(np.prod(s["shape"])) for s in stages)
    for i, s in enumerate(stages):
        x0 = i * (width + gap)
        h = 0.6 + 2.4 * np.log2(np.prod(s["shape"])) / hmax   # height grows with log2 of the number of values
        key = "z" if s.get("latent") else s["name"].split()[0]
        ax.add_patch(Rectangle((x0, -h / 2), width, h, fc=colors.get(key, "#C9DCF0"), ec="k", lw=1))
        # output shape inside the block, layer description above, parameter count below
        shp = "×".join(str(v) for v in s["shape"])
        ax.text(x0 + width / 2, 0, shp, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=12, rotation=90 if len(shp) > 6 else 0)
        ax.text(x0 + width / 2, h / 2 + 0.12, s["name"], ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=12, color=navy)
        if s["params"]:
            ax.text(x0 + width / 2, -h / 2 - 0.12, f"{s['params']:,}", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11, color="0.3")
        if i > 0:
            ax.annotate("", xy=(x0, 0), xytext=(x0 - gap, 0), arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.3, color="0.3"))
    ax.set_xlim(-0.2, len(stages) * (width + gap)); ax.set_ylim(-2.4, 2.9)
    ax.axis("off")
    if title: ax.text(-0.2, 2.75, title, fontsize=15, ha="left", va="top")

enc_st, dec_st = layer_stages(conv_vae, torch.zeros(1, 1, 32, 32))
assert sum(s["params"] for s in enc_st + dec_st) == n_conv        # every parameter belongs to one drawn stage
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 6.6))

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
Training
The loss (4) is averaged over a mini-batch of 128 images, with one sample \(\mathbf z\) per image for the reconstruction term (9) and the KL term computed from equations (6) and (7). Every model sees the same 8,000 mini-batches (1,024,000 images, about ten passes over the 100,000 training images), with the Adam optimiser at learning rate \(10^{-3}\) and the same seed, so that \(\beta\) is the only difference between the runs. Three values are trained: β of 1 (the VAE), 4 (the value used for dSprites by Higgins et al.) and 8. During training the per-coordinate \(\mathrm{KL}_k\) of each batch is recorded every 20 steps. The weights and the training history are saved in results/ and reloaded if present.
Eight thousand steps is short by the standards of the literature, where dSprites models are trained for hundreds of thousands of steps; it is what a CPU allows in a few minutes per model, and all measurements refer to these short runs.


Code
BETAS = [1, 4, 8]
STEPS, BS, LR = 8000, 128, 1e-3

def beta_vae_loss(logits, x, mu, logvar, beta):
    # per image: Bernoulli reconstruction term + beta * sum_k KL_k
    rec = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, x, reduction="sum") / len(x)
    kl_k = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - logvar - 1).mean(0)    # KL per coordinate, averaged over the batch
    return rec + beta * kl_k.sum(), rec, kl_k

def train_beta_vae(beta, steps=STEPS, bs=BS, lr=LR, seed_=0):
    seed(seed_); model = ConvVAE(d); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr)
    g = torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed_)                      # same mini-batches for every beta
    hist = {"step": [], "rec": [], "kl": []}
    for s in range(steps):
        x = Xtr[torch.randint(0, len(Xtr), (bs,), generator=g)]
        logits, mu, logvar = model(x)
        loss, rec, kl_k = beta_vae_loss(logits, x, mu, logvar, beta)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        if s % 20 == 0 or s == steps - 1:
            hist["step"].append(s); hist["rec"].append(rec.item()); hist["kl"].append(kl_k.detach().numpy())
        if s % 2000 == 0 or s == steps - 1:
            print(f"  beta = {beta}, step {s:4d}: reconstruction {rec.item():6.1f}, KL {kl_k.sum().item():5.2f} nats")
    return model.eval(), {k: np.array(v) for k, v in hist.items()}

models, hists = {}, {}
for beta in BETAS:
    w, h = f"{RES}/beta_vae_dsprites_beta{beta}.pt", f"{RES}/beta_vae_dsprites_beta{beta}_history.npz"
    if os.path.exists(w) and os.path.exists(h):
        m = ConvVAE(d); m.load_state_dict(torch.load(w)); models[beta] = m.eval()
        hists[beta] = dict(np.load(h)); print(f"beta = {beta}: weights loaded from {w}")
    else:
        t0 = time.time()
        models[beta], hists[beta] = train_beta_vae(beta)
        torch.save(models[beta].state_dict(), w); np.savez(h, **hists[beta])
        print(f"beta = {beta}: trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

For the first 400 steps or so every coordinate has KL close to zero: the decoder learns the average image, a faint blob near the centre, and the encoder transmits nothing. Between steps 400 and 600 several coordinates switch on at once, and most of them collapse again within a few hundred steps. What survives depends on β. For β of 1 three coordinates settle near 3 nats and a fourth rises to 2 nats, decays almost to zero by step 2,000 and returns to about 1 nat after step 2,500, a late addition of a further factor. For β of 4 and 8 only three coordinates survive, two of them with equal KL (2.4 nats for β of 4, 1.9 for β of 8) and a third with less (1.2 and 0.75 nats). Two equal channels are what two factors of equal entropy would require; the alignment section identifies them as the two positions.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
KL per latent coordinate
The 10,000 test images are encoded and \(\mathrm{KL}_k\) of equation (7) is averaged over them. A coordinate whose average KL is close to zero has zero mean and unit width for every input: it has collapsed onto the prior and the decoder ignores it. We call a coordinate active when its average KL exceeds 0.1 nats.


Code
ACTIVE = 0.1                                                      # nats
enc = {}
with torch.no_grad():
    for beta in BETAS:
        mu, logvar = models[beta].encode(Xte)
        kl = (0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - logvar - 1)).mean(0).numpy()
        rec = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(models[beta].decode(mu), Xte, reduction="sum").item() / len(Xte)
        enc[beta] = dict(mu=mu.numpy(), sd=torch.exp(0.5 * logvar).numpy(), kl=kl, order=np.argsort(-kl), rec=rec)
        nums[f"beta{beta}_kl_per_dim_sorted"] = [round(float(v), 3) for v in np.sort(kl)[::-1]]
        nums[f"beta{beta}_kl_total"] = round(float(kl.sum()), 2)
        nums[f"beta{beta}_n_active"] = int((kl > ACTIVE).sum())
        print(f"beta = {beta}: KL per coordinate (sorted) {np.round(np.sort(kl)[::-1], 2)}, total {kl.sum():.2f} nats, "
              f"active {int((kl > ACTIVE).sum())}")

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, len(BETAS), figsize=(10, 4.2), sharey=True)
for ax, beta in zip(axs, BETAS):
    kl = enc[beta]["kl"]; o = enc[beta]["order"]
    ax.bar(range(d), kl[o], color=[blue if v > ACTIVE else grey for v in kl[o]])
    ax.set_xticks(range(d)); ax.set_xticklabels([str(k + 1) for k in o], fontsize=12); ax.set_xlabel("coordinate $k$")
    ax.set_title(f"β = {beta}: {int((kl > ACTIVE).sum())} active\ntotal {kl.sum():.1f} nats"); clean(ax)
axs[0].set_ylabel(r"average KL$_k$ (nats)")
for ax in axs: ax.axhline(ACTIVE, color=orange, lw=1, ls="--")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/beta_vae_kl_per_dim.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()


beta = 1: KL per coordinate (sorted) [3.3  3.23 2.52 1.09 0.   0.   0.   0.   0.   0.  ], total 10.15 nats, active 4


beta = 4: KL per coordinate (sorted) [2.4  2.37 1.2  0.   0.   0.   0.   0.   0.   0.  ], total 5.98 nats, active 3


beta = 8: KL per coordinate (sorted) [1.87 1.83 0.75 0.   0.   0.   0.   0.   0.   0.  ], total 4.46 nats, active 3





Of the ten available coordinates the VAE uses four, carrying 3.30, 3.23, 2.52 and 1.09 nats, 10.15 nats in total. With β of 4 three coordinates remain (2.40, 2.37 and 1.20 nats, total 5.98), and with β of 8 the same three shrink further (1.87, 1.83 and 0.75 nats, total 4.46). The extra coordinates are not needed to describe five factors at this resolution, and the price per nat in equation (4) decides how much information the remaining ones carry: going from β of 1 to β of 8 removes more than half of the transmitted information. All other coordinates have an average KL below 0.01 nats; they have collapsed onto the prior.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
Latent traversals
A traversal makes a coordinate visible. One test image is encoded to its mean \(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf x)\); then a single coordinate \(z_k\) is moved from \(-3\) to \(3\) while the other nine stay at their encoded values, and each point is decoded. Rows are coordinates sorted by their average KL, and each row is labelled with the factor it aligns with according to the alignment matrix (a normalised mutual information (11) of at least 0.2 and at least twice the second largest in the row), “mixed” otherwise, and “off” below 0.1 nats.


Code
ZS = np.linspace(-3, 3, 7)
# seed image: a heart of medium scale near the centre of the canvas, so that traversals stay inside it
cand = np.where((Cte[:, 0] == 2) & (Cte[:, 1] == 3) & (np.abs(Cte[:, 3] - 16) <= 3) & (np.abs(Cte[:, 4] - 16) <= 3))[0]
i_seed = int(cand[0]); nums["traversal_seed_factors"] = dict(zip(FACTORS, [int(v) for v in Cte[i_seed]]))
print("seed image factors:", nums["traversal_seed_factors"])

def traversal(model, x, order, zs=ZS):
    with torch.no_grad():
        mu, _ = model.encode(x[None])
        rows = []
        for k in order:
            z = mu.repeat(len(zs), 1); z[:, k] = torch.tensor(zs, dtype=torch.float32)
            rows.append(torch.sigmoid(model.decode(z))[:, 0].numpy())
    return np.array(rows)                                          # (rows, len(zs), 32, 32)

    fig.text((l + rr_) / 2, 0.955, title, fontsize=17, ha="center")

For β of 4 the three active rows do what the matrix says: one coordinate moves the sprite vertically, one horizontally, and one changes its size from large to a dot, each leaving the other properties of the image in place. The seven collapsed rows do not change the image at all. The VAE rows are different. Its first coordinate moves the sprite upwards while also enlarging it, the second moves it along a diagonal while enlarging it, the third changes the size but empties the canvas for negative values, and the fourth stretches the blob into an ellipse and turns it, shape and orientation together. Each VAE coordinate changes several properties at once, which is what an entangled representation looks like. For β of 8 the picture is that of β of 4, with three clean rows (vertical position, horizontal position, scale) and slightly blurrier images. None of the models draws a recognisable square or heart: the decoded sprites are blobs, in line with the low shape scores.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
Sampling
A trained VAE can be used in four ways, and they differ in which network is involved and what is random.
Generation uses the decoder alone. A code is drawn from the prior (1), the decoder turns it into the pixel probabilities \(\hat{\mathbf x}(\mathbf z)\) of equation (8), and a pixel image is drawn from the Bernoulli distribution (8): \[\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\qquad \mathbf x\sim p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z). \tag{13}\] These two steps are ancestral sampling of the model distribution \[p_\theta(\mathbf x)=\int p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z)\,p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z . \tag{14}\] The encoder plays no part. What is usually displayed, in the papers as in the figures that follow, is not the pixel sample but its mean, the array of probabilities \(\hat{\mathbf x}(\mathbf z)\); one row of pixel samples makes the difference visible.
Reconstruction is a statement about a given image rather than about the distribution: \(\mathbf x\) is encoded, a code is taken from \(q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x)\) (its mean \(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf x)\)), and decoded. Traversals start from such a code and move one coordinate. Interpolation encodes two images \(\mathbf x_a\) and \(\mathbf x_b\) to their means \(\boldsymbol\mu_a\) and \(\boldsymbol\mu_b\) and decodes the straight path between them, \[\mathbf z(t)=\boldsymbol\mu_a+t\,(\boldsymbol\mu_b-\boldsymbol\mu_a),\qquad 0\le t\le1; \tag{15}\] whether the intermediate images are plausible depends on whether the path stays where the decoder was trained.
As a number for the blur of a decoded image we use the mean per-pixel Bernoulli entropy, \[h=-\frac1{N_{\mathrm{pix}}}\sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{pix}}}\big[\hat x_j\ln\hat x_j+(1-\hat x_j)\ln(1-\hat x_j)\big], \tag{16}\] which is 0 when every pixel is decided and \(\ln2\) (about 0.69 nats) when every pixel is a coin toss.


Code
def pixel_entropy(p):
    p = p.clamp(1e-6, 1 - 1e-6)
    return float((-(p * p.log() + (1 - p) * (1 - p).log())).mean())

The pixel sample in the second row is what the model of equation (13) actually generates: a binary image whose border pixels are coin tosses with the probabilities shown in the first row, hence the ragged edges. The mean images of the first row are smoother because they are averages. The same eight codes produce different images in different models, since each model has its own latent axes.
Generation shows the other side of the trade-off. The VAE’s means are sharper, with a mean pixel entropy (16) of 0.0171 nats against 0.0310 for β of 4 and 0.0366 for β of 8 (for reconstructions 0.0220, 0.0308 and 0.0392), but one of its eight samples is an empty canvas and another a dot of a few pixels: its codes do not fill the prior, and some prior draws land where no training image was encoded. All samples of the β-VAEs are plausible blobs. The interpolation makes the same point. Between a large sprite in the upper left and a smaller one in the lower right, the VAE’s path shrinks the sprite to a dot at \(t\) of 0.57 and to an empty canvas at 0.71 before it reappears, while the β-VAEs move and shrink it continuously: along their axes position and size change independently, and the straight line between two codes stays inside the region the decoder knows.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
Handwritten digits
On dSprites the factors are known. Handwritten digits have no such list, but they have obvious candidates, and the same experiment can be repeated on them to connect with the VAE of the lecture.
The MNIST data set (Modified National Institute of Standards and Technology; LeCun et al., 1998) contains 70,000 images of handwritten digits, 60,000 for training and 10,000 for testing, derived from handwriting collected by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Each sample \(\mathbf x_i\) is a grey-level image of \(28\times28\) pixels, stored as integers from 0 (background) to 255 (full ink) and scaled to the interval from 0 to 1, so that \(\mathbf x_i\) is a vector of 784 numbers. Each image carries a label, the digit from 0 to 9, which the VAE does not use. Unlike dSprites, the images were not generated from a known list of factors: the variation between two 4s comes from the writers. The files are read from data/MNIST_raw and downloaded once if missing.

RAW = os.path.join(DATA, "MNIST_raw"); os.makedirs(RAW, exist_ok=True)
LOCAL = os.path.expanduser("~/.pytorch/MNIST_data/MNIST/raw")
MIRRORS = ["https://ossci-datasets.s3.amazonaws.com/mnist/", "https://storage.googleapis.com/cvdf-datasets/mnist/"]
def mnist_file(name):
    for dd in (RAW, LOCAL):
        p = os.path.join(dd, name)
        if os.path.exists(p): return open(p, "rb").read()
        if os.path.exists(p + ".gz"): return gzip.open(p + ".gz").read()
    for m in MIRRORS:
        try:
            urllib.request.urlretrieve(m + name + ".gz", os.path.join(RAW, name + ".gz"))
            return gzip.open(os.path.join(RAW, name + ".gz")).read()
        except Exception: pass
    raise RuntimeError("MNIST could not be found or downloaded")
def idx_file(name):
    b = mnist_file(name)
    if b[3] == 3:
        n, r, c = np.frombuffer(b[4:16], ">i4"); return np.frombuffer(b[16:], np.uint8).reshape(n, r * c)
    return np.frombuffer(b[8:], np.uint8)

The model is the dense VAE of the lecture (784–512–256 units, ten latent coordinates), trained for 10 epochs with β of 1 and of 4. Candidate factors can be measured directly on each image from its ink distribution: pixel \(j\) at column \(u_j\) and row \(w_j\) carries ink \(x_j\). The total ink is a proxy for stroke thickness, \[m=\sum_j x_j , \tag{17}\] the width is the standard deviation of the column under the ink distribution, \[\mathrm{width}=\Big(\frac1m\sum_j x_j\,(u_j-\bar u)^2\Big)^{1/2},\qquad \bar u=\frac1m\sum_j x_j\,u_j , \tag{18}\] and the slant is the regression coefficient of column on row, the horizontal shift of the stroke per row, \[\mathrm{slant}=\frac{\mathrm{cov}(u,w)}{\mathrm{var}(w)} , \tag{19}\] with covariance and variance taken under the same ink distribution. Rows are counted downwards, so an upright digit has zero slant and a digit leaning to the right a negative one.


Code
class DenseVAE(nn.Module):
    # dense VAE of the lecture: 784 -> 512 -> 256 -> (mu, log sigma^2) in d dimensions, and back
    def __init__(self, D=784, d=10, hidden=(512, 256)):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(D, hidden[0]), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden[0], hidden[1]), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden[1], 2 * d))
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(d, hidden[1]), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden[1], hidden[0]), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden[0], D))
    def encode(self, x): return self.enc(x).chunk(2, dim=1)
    def decode(self, z): return self.dec(z)
    def forward(self, x):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x); z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)
        return self.decode(z), mu, logvar

dense_info = summary(DenseVAE(), input_size=(1, 784), col_names=("output_size", "num_params"), depth=2, verbose=0)
print(dense_info)
assert dense_info.total_params == sum(p.numel() for p in DenseVAE().parameters()) == 1_074_980
nums["dense_vae_parameters"] = int(dense_info.total_params)

def train_mnist(beta, epochs=10, bs=128, lr=1e-3, seed_=1):
    seed(seed_); model = DenseVAE(); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(Mtr)); tot = np.zeros(2)
        for i in range(0, len(perm), bs):
            x = Mtr[perm[i:i + bs]]
            logits, mu, logvar = model(x)
            loss, rec, kl_k = beta_vae_loss(logits, x, mu, logvar, beta)
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            tot += np.array([rec.item(), kl_k.sum().item()]) * len(x)
        if ep % 5 == 4: print(f"  beta = {beta}, epoch {ep + 1}: reconstruction {tot[0] / len(Mtr):.1f}, KL {tot[1] / len(Mtr):.1f} nats")
    return model.eval()

mnist = {}
for beta in [1, 4]:
    w = f"{RES}/beta_vae_mnist_beta{beta}.pt"
    if os.path.exists(w):

    else:
        t0 = time.time(); mnist[beta] = train_mnist(beta); torch.save(mnist[beta].state_dict(), w)
        print(f"beta = {beta}: trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

# measured properties of every test digit: total ink, width, slant
u, w = np.meshgrid(np.arange(28), np.arange(28))                 # column and row of each pixel
u, w = u.ravel().astype(np.float32), w.ravel().astype(np.float32)
P = Mte.numpy(); m0 = P.sum(1)
mu_u, mu_w = P @ u / m0, P @ w / m0
var_u = P @ u ** 2 / m0 - mu_u ** 2; var_w = P @ w ** 2 / m0 - mu_w ** 2; cov_uw = P @ (u * w) / m0 - mu_u * mu_w
props = {"ink": m0, "width": np.sqrt(var_u), "slant": cov_uw / var_w}
PROPS = list(props)

    for beta in [1, 4]:
        mu, logvar = mnist[beta].encode(Mte)
        kl = (0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - logvar - 1)).mean(0).numpy()
        rec = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(mnist[beta].decode(mu), Mte, reduction="sum").item() / len(Mte)
        mu = mu.numpy()
        corr = np.array([[np.corrcoef(mu[:, k], props[p])[0, 1] for p in PROPS] for k in range(10)])

On digits the VAE keeps nine active coordinates (KL between 1.41 and 2.54 nats) with a reconstruction term of 83.4 nats per test image; the β-VAE with β of 4 keeps six (between 0.91 and 1.79 nats) and reconstructs at 102.7 nats. Each measured property has a single best coordinate in both models: width correlates with one coordinate at \(r\) of −0.82 for β of 1 and −0.76 for β of 4, slant at 0.69 and 0.75, total ink at −0.70 and −0.68. The second-best coordinates are not small, however (0.51 and 0.52 for slant), and the traversals show why. The leading coordinate of both models turns a wide 0 into a narrow 1 or 7, width and digit class together, and the slant coordinate of the β-VAE turns a strongly right-leaning 9 into an upright one but ends in a different digit. On MNIST the largest factor of variation is the class, which is discrete and not independent of style, and ten Gaussian coordinates cannot separate it cleanly from slant and width; β of 4 makes the slant coordinate somewhat purer but does not produce one coordinate per property.
Generation shows the same trade-off as on dSprites: the digits generated by the β-VAE are blurrier, with a mean pixel entropy of 0.155 nats against 0.123 for the VAE over 1,000 prior draws, and several of them are ambiguous between two classes.

title: Disentangled latent features with the beta-VAE
text:
Summary
Raising β from 1 to 4 on dSprites cut the transmitted information from 10.2 to 6.0 nats, reduced the number of active coordinates from four to three, and doubled the mutual information gap from 0.15 to 0.30: position \(x\), position \(y\) and scale each moved into a coordinate of its own, visible directly in the traversals. The cost was 6.2 nats of reconstruction per image, blurrier images and the loss of the only coordinate that carried shape. The linear probes show that the VAE contains the positions almost as completely as the β-VAE; what β changes is the orientation of the axes. Samples and interpolations of the β-VAE stay plausible across the whole prior, while those of the VAE occasionally fall into empty regions of its latent space.
These are results of short runs: 8,000 steps of training at \(32\times32\), one seed per model, and mutual information estimated from binned means. Orientation, which Higgins et al. found in two coordinates of a β-VAE with β of 4 at \(64\times64\), and shape, which appears as a separate coordinate in the longer training of Burgess et al., did not emerge in these runs, and the numbers should be read as an illustration of the mechanism rather than as benchmark values. On handwritten digits, where the factors are not independent and the class dominates, a higher β made the slant coordinate somewhat purer but did not separate style from class.

title: Conditional generation of digits and blood cells
Conditional generation of digits and blood cells
section: Variational autoencoder in a two-dimensional latent space
text:
Variational autoencoder in a two-dimensional latent space
An encoder compresses an image \(\mathbf x\), a vector of 784 pixel values, into a few numbers \(\mathbf z\), its latent representation: coordinates in which similar images are close. A decoder \(G\) maps \(\mathbf z\) back to an image. With two latent numbers the latent space can be drawn.
A plain autoencoder sends \(\mathbf x\) to a single point. A VAE instead sends it to a Gaussian cloud, \[q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x)=\mathcal N\big(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf x),\operatorname{diag}\boldsymbol\sigma^2(\mathbf x)\big): \tag{1}\] the encoder outputs the centre \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and the widths \(\boldsymbol\sigma\), the latter as \(\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2\), which can take any sign. In training, a random point of the cloud is decoded, so every point near \(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf x)\) must decode to something like \(\mathbf x\).
The loss has two terms per image, \[\mathcal L(\mathbf x)=\underbrace{-\sum_{j=1}^{784}\big[x_j\log\hat x_j+(1-x_j)\log(1-\hat x_j)\big]}_{\text{reconstruction: } -\log p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z)}+\underbrace{\tfrac12\sum_{k=1}^{d}\big(\mu_k^2+\sigma_k^2-\ln\sigma_k^2-1\big)}_{\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(\mathbf z|\mathbf x)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,I))},\qquad \hat{\mathbf x}=\operatorname{sigmoid}\big(G(\mathbf z)\big), \tag{2}\] with \(d\) the number of latent coordinates. The first term is the binary cross-entropy between the image and its reconstruction. The second, the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence, pulls every cloud towards the standard Gaussian \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), so that the clouds of all training images together fill it without gaps. A latent vector drawn at random from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) then lands where the decoder was trained, and this is what makes generation possible.
One obstacle remains: drawing \(\mathbf z\) from the cloud has no derivative with respect to \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\boldsymbol\sigma\). The reparametrisation trick removes it by writing \[\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\qquad\boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I). \tag{3}\] The randomness is now an input \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) that does not depend on the weights, with the derivatives \[\frac{\partial z_k}{\partial\mu_k}=1,\qquad \frac{\partial z_k}{\partial\sigma_k}=\varepsilon_k, \tag{4}\] and backpropagation runs through \(\mathbf z\) into the encoder.
The class VAE serves both for the plain VAE (cond=0) and for the conditional VAE (cond=10, with the condition concatenated to the inputs of both networks). The first model is a plain VAE with two latent numbers, trained for 20 epochs.


Code
def mlp(sizes):
    layers = []
    for a, b in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]): layers += [nn.Linear(a, b), nn.ReLU()]
    return nn.Sequential(*layers[:-1])

class CVAE(nn.Module):
    # VAE with dense layers; cond > 0 makes it conditional: c is concatenated to the inputs of encoder and decoder
    def __init__(self, D=784, d=8, cond=10, hidden=(512, 256)):
        super().__init__()
        self.d, self.cond = d, cond
        self.enc = mlp([D + cond, *hidden]); self.enc.append(nn.ReLU())
        self.mu, self.logvar = nn.Linear(hidden[-1], d), nn.Linear(hidden[-1], d)
        self.dec = mlp([d + cond, *hidden[::-1], D])                  # logits of the pixels
    def encode(self, x, c=None):
        h = self.enc(x if c is None else torch.cat([x, c], 1)); return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)
    def decode(self, z, c=None):
        return self.dec(z if c is None else torch.cat([z, c], 1))
    def forward(self, x, c=None):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x, c)
        eps = torch.randn_like(mu)                                    # the randomness, outside the network
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * eps                        # reparametrisation trick
        return self.decode(z, c), mu, logvar

def vae_loss(logits, x, mu, logvar):
    rec = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, x, reduction="sum") / len(x)
    kl = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - logvar - 1).sum() / len(x)
    return rec + kl, rec, kl

def train_vae(model, X, C=None, epochs=20, lr=1e-3, bs=128):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(X)); tot = np.zeros(3)
        for i in range(0, len(perm), bs):
            j = perm[i:i + bs]; c = None if C is None else C[j]
            logits, mu, logvar = model(X[j], c)
            loss, rec, kl = vae_loss(logits, X[j], mu, logvar)
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            tot += np.array([loss.item(), rec.item(), kl.item()]) * len(j)
        if ep % 5 == 4: print(f"epoch {ep + 1}: loss per image {tot[0] / len(X):.1f} = reconstruction {tot[1] / len(X):.1f} + KL {tot[2] / len(X):.1f}")
    return model.eval()

The clouds are narrow, with a mean width of 0.041, and their centres are concentrated around the origin, where \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) puts its probability: 48.8%, 79.7% and 96.5% of them lie within radius 1, 2 and 3, against 39.3%, 86.5% and 98.9% for \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) in two dimensions. The KL term pulls the clouds towards the origin, the reconstruction term pushes the classes apart, and some classes (0, 1, 7) sit at the edge.


Reparametrisation trick
To see what the decoder must learn for a single input, we take one test image and let the encoder give its cloud \((\boldsymbol\mu,\boldsymbol\sigma)\). Eight noise vectors \(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) are drawn from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), turned into latent vectors by equation (3), and decoded: these are the images the decoder must produce during training for this one input. Automatic differentiation computes the derivatives of \(z_1\) with respect to \(\mu_1\) and \(\sigma_1\), to be compared with equation (4).


Code
# a test digit 0 that the 2D VAE rebuilds well: the smallest reconstruction error among the 0s
with torch.no_grad():
    zeros = (yte == 0).nonzero()[:, 0]
    rec0 = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(vae2.decode(vae2.encode(Xte[zeros])[0]), Xte[zeros], reduction="none").sum(1)

with torch.no_grad():
    mu0, lv0 = vae2.encode(Xte[i0:i0 + 1]); sd0 = torch.exp(0.5 * lv0)
    torch.manual_seed(40); eps = torch.randn(8, 2)
    z8 = mu0 + sd0 * eps                                          # reparametrisation: z = mu + sigma * eps
    dec8 = torch.sigmoid(vae2.decode(z8)).reshape(-1, 28, 28).numpy()

All eight decoded images are versions of the input digit: nearby points of the latent space decode to similar images. With only two latent numbers the VAE cannot rebuild every digit well, so we picked the 0 it rebuilds best; a badly rebuilt input, such as an unusual 5, can land in the region of another digit and decode to it. Automatic differentiation confirms equation (4): the derivative with respect to \(\mu_1\) is 1, and the derivative with respect to \(\sigma_1\) is the noise value \(\varepsilon_1\), here −0.2367. The noise enters as a constant, and the gradient of the loss reaches \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\boldsymbol\sigma\), and hence the encoder.


Conditioning
A conditional VAE receives the label as a one-hot vector \(\mathbf c\) in both networks, the encoder \(q_\phi(\mathbf z\,|\,\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\) and the decoder \(p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\), and models the class-conditional distribution \[p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf c)=\int p_\theta(\mathbf x\,|\,\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\,p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z . \tag{5}\] Since the decoder already knows from \(\mathbf c\) which digit to draw, the latent space no longer needs to encode the class and keeps only what \(\mathbf c\) does not say, the style. A conditional VAE with two latent numbers is trained, and its latent space drawn with the same colours.


Code

The conditional VAE reaches a lower loss per image than the plain one, 127.3 against 138.7, because the label supplies part of the information. In the left panel the colours are mixed: with the label given separately, the position in the latent space no longer says which digit it is. In the right panel each row uses one fixed \(\mathbf z\) with all ten conditions, and the digit changes along the row while the slant and thickness stay the same.
