New digits
After training, the encoder plays no part in generation. A new image is an ancestral sample of the model distribution, the integral of the decoder over the prior: first a latent vector is drawn from the prior, then an image from the decoder, \[\mathbf z\sim\mathcal N(0,I),\qquad \mathbf x\sim p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z). \tag{31}\] The decoder gives, for each pixel \(j\), the probability \[\hat x_j=\operatorname{sigmoid}\big(G(\mathbf z)\big)_j \tag{32}\] of a Bernoulli distribution, the distribution behind the BCE loss, and the second step of equation (31) would set pixel \(j\) to 1 with probability \(\hat x_j\). The images shown are the means \(\hat{\mathbf x}\), not such draws; the difference is shown at the end of this section.
The left panel shows the decoder of the two-dimensional VAE on a regular \(15\times15\) grid of \(\mathbf z\) over \([-2.5,2.5]^2\), the region where \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) puts its probability. It is read like the grid of the autoencoder: each small image is \(G(z_1,z_2)\), with \(z_1\) increasing from left to right and \(z_2\) from bottom to top. The right panel shows 32 new digits from the VAE with 16 latent dimensions, each decoded from a random \(\mathbf z\) drawn from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\). To see whether the model only copies its training data, we also measure the distance of each generated digit to the nearest training image and compare it with the same distance for real test digits.

Latent densities of the autoencoder and the VAE
The left panel shows the codes of 2000 test digits in the plane of the two-dimensional autoencoder, four latent points far from every training code, marked by crosses, and the images the decoder produces there. The middle panel shows the aggregate posterior of the two-dimensional VAE, \[q(\mathbf z)=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\mathcal N\big(\mathbf z;\boldsymbol\mu_i,\operatorname{diag}\boldsymbol\sigma_i^2\big), \tag{33}\] the continuous counterpart of equation (26), on a logarithmic colour scale, with the circles of radius 1 and 2 of \(\mathcal N(0,I)\). The right panel shows 25 images decoded from random \(\mathbf z\) drawn from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\). Three numbers quantify the difference. The first is the median distance from random latent points to the nearest training code, in units of the median spacing between neighbouring codes, for the autoencoder, with points drawn from a Gaussian fitted to its codes, and for the VAE, with points drawn from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\). The second is the median cloud width \(\sigma\) of the VAE in the same units. The third is the fraction of draws from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) at which \(q(\mathbf z)\) is below a tenth of the prior density.

# the autoencoder fills the latent plane at N points, the VAE with a continuous density
from scipy.spatial import cKDTree
from scipy.interpolate import RegularGridInterpolator
from matplotlib.offsetbox import OffsetImage, AnnotationBbox
from matplotlib.colors import LogNorm

with torch.no_grad():
    Z_tr = enc_ae(Xtr_t).numpy()                                 # the N training codes of the autoencoder
    Z_te = enc_ae(Xte_t[:2000]).numpy()
    mu_tr, lv_tr = [t.numpy() for t in vae2.encode(Xtr_t)]       # the N clouds of the VAE
N = len(Z_tr); sd_tr = np.exp(0.5 * lv_tr)
rng_l = np.random.default_rng(5)

# four latent points far from every training code of the autoencoder, and what the decoder makes of them
tree_ae = cKDTree(Z_tr)
lo_, hi_ = np.percentile(Z_tr, 3, 0), np.percentile(Z_tr, 97, 0)
cand = rng_l.uniform(lo_, hi_, size=(4000, 2)); dist = tree_ae.query(cand)[0]
empty = []
for j in np.argsort(-dist):
    if all(np.linalg.norm(cand[j] - cand[k]) > 0.25 * np.linalg.norm(hi_ - lo_) for k in empty): empty.append(j)
    if len(empty) == 4: break
z_empty = cand[empty]
with torch.no_grad(): img_empty = dec_ae(torch.tensor(z_empty, dtype=torch.float32)).numpy()

# aggregate posterior of the VAE, q(z) = (1/N) sum_i N(z; mu_i, diag sigma_i^2), on a grid
gq = np.linspace(-3.5, 3.5, 141); GX, GY = np.meshgrid(gq, gq)
P = torch.tensor(np.stack([GX.ravel(), GY.ravel()], 1), dtype=torch.float32)
mu_t, sd_t = torch.tensor(mu_tr), torch.tensor(sd_tr); q = torch.zeros(len(P))
for i in range(0, N, 1000):
    m, s = mu_t[i:i + 1000], sd_t[i:i + 1000]
    e = (((P[:, None, :] - m[None]) / s[None]) ** 2).sum(2)
    q += (torch.exp(-0.5 * e) / (2 * np.pi * s.prod(1))[None]).sum(1)
q = (q / N).reshape(GX.shape).numpy()

# the numbers: distance to the nearest code in units of the code spacing, cloud width, empty prior mass
def gap_ratio(codes, z):
    t = cKDTree(codes); spacing = np.median(t.query(codes, k=2)[0][:, 1])
    return np.median(t.query(z)[0]) / spacing, spacing
z_ae = rng_l.multivariate_normal(Z_tr.mean(0), np.cov(Z_tr.T), 2000)    # a Gaussian fitted to the autoencoder codes
z_vae = rng_l.standard_normal((2000, 2))
r_ae, _ = gap_ratio(Z_tr, z_ae); r_vae, sp_vae = gap_ratio(mu_tr, z_vae)
zz = z_vae[np.all(np.abs(z_vae) < 3.5, 1)]
q_at = RegularGridInterpolator((gq, gq), q.T)(zz)
frac_low = float(np.mean(q_at < 0.1 * np.exp(-0.5 * (zz ** 2).sum(1)) / (2 * np.pi)))
print(f"N = {N} training codes")
print(f"median distance to the nearest code / median code spacing: autoencoder {r_ae:.1f}, VAE {r_vae:.2f}")
print(f"median cloud width sigma of the VAE / median code spacing: {np.median(sd_tr) / sp_vae:.1f}")
print(f"fraction of N(0, I) draws where q(z) < 0.1 N(z; 0, I): {frac_low:.3f}")

with plt.rc_context({"font.size": 13}):
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=(12, 4.5))
    a0 = fig.add_axes([0.04, 0.11, 0.29, 0.76]); a1 = fig.add_axes([0.385, 0.11, 0.29, 0.76]); a2 = fig.add_axes([0.72, 0.11, 0.27, 0.76])
    cm = plt.get_cmap("tab10")
    for k in range(10): a0.scatter(*Z_te[yte[:2000] == k].T, s=3, color=cm(k), rasterized=True)
    a0.scatter(*z_empty.T, s=110, marker="x", color="k", lw=2.5, zorder=4)
    c0 = Z_tr.mean(0)
    for zp, im in zip(z_empty, img_empty):
        off = (-40 * (np.sign(zp[0] - c0[0]) or 1), -40 * (np.sign(zp[1] - c0[1]) or 1))     # inset towards the centre
        a0.add_artist(AnnotationBbox(OffsetImage(im.reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r", zoom=1.0), zp, xybox=off, boxcoords="offset points",
                                     arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="k", lw=1), pad=0.15))
    a0.set_xlabel("$z_1$"); a0.set_ylabel("$z_2$")
    a0.set_title(f"autoencoder: $\\mathbb{{R}}^2$ filled only at {N:,} points".replace(",", " "), fontsize=12)
    a1.pcolormesh(GX, GY, np.maximum(q, q.max() * 1e-4), norm=LogNorm(vmin=q.max() * 1e-4, vmax=q.max()), cmap="magma", shading="auto", rasterized=True)
    for r_ in (1, 2): a1.add_patch(plt.Circle((0, 0), r_, fill=False, ls="--", color="white", lw=1.5))
    a1.set_aspect("equal"); a1.set_xlabel("$z_1$"); a1.set_ylabel("$z_2$")
    a1.set_title("VAE: $\\mathbb{R}^2$ filled by a continuous density", fontsize=12)
    with torch.no_grad():
        zs = torch.randn(25, 2, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(7))
        ims = torch.sigmoid(vae2.decode(zs)).reshape(5, 5, 28, 28).numpy()
    a2.imshow(ims.transpose(0, 2, 1, 3).reshape(140, 140), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1); a2.axis("off")
    a2.set_title("VAE: decoded $\\mathbf{z}\\sim\\mathcal{N}(0,I)$", fontsize=12)
    fig.savefig(f"{RES}/gen_discrete_vs_continuous_latent.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
    plt.show()


N = 60000 training codes
median distance to the nearest code / median code spacing: autoencoder 1.6, VAE 1.32
median cloud width sigma of the VAE / median code spacing: 5.6
fraction of N(0, I) draws where q(z) < 0.1 N(z; 0, I): 0.036





Random points from a Gaussian fitted to the autoencoder codes lie a median 1.6 code spacings from the nearest training code; draws from the prior of the VAE lie 1.32 spacings away. The decisive number is the width of the VAE clouds, a median of 5.6 code spacings: each cloud covers many neighbouring codes, and the clouds overlap into the continuous density of the middle panel. Only 3.6% of draws from the prior fall where this density is below a tenth of the prior, in the dark wedges, and the 25 decoded draws of the right panel are digits, some of them blurred.


Reconstruction and generation
Reconstruction and generation use the same decoder on different inputs. Reconstruction encodes a given image and decodes the centre of its cloud, \(\operatorname{sigmoid}(G(\boldsymbol\mu(\mathbf x)))\); it measures how much of \(\mathbf x\) survives the compression to 16 numbers, and it needs the encoder. Generation decodes a \(\mathbf z\) drawn from the prior, with no input image. The figure shows, from top to bottom, eight test digits, their reconstructions, the means decoded from eight random \(\mathbf z\), and one Bernoulli draw of every pixel for the same \(\mathbf z\).


Code
# reconstruction (encode, decode the centre mu) against generation (decode z ~ N(0, I)); mean against Bernoulli draw
gen_ = torch.Generator().manual_seed(20)
with torch.no_grad():
    x8 = Xte_t[:8]
    rec = torch.sigmoid(vae16.decode(vae16.encode(x8)[0]))
    gen_mean = torch.sigmoid(vae16.decode(torch.randn(8, 16, generator=gen_)))
    gen_draw = torch.bernoulli(gen_mean, generator=gen_)
rows = [("test digit", x8), ("reconstruction", rec), ("generated: mean", gen_mean), ("generated: draw", gen_draw)]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(4, 8, figsize=(8, 4.4))
for r, (name, imgs) in enumerate(rows):
    for j in range(8):
        axs[r, j].imshow(imgs[j].reshape(28, 28).numpy(), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1); axs[r, j].set_xticks([]); axs[r, j].set_yticks([])
    axs[r, 0].set_ylabel(name, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=10)
plt.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.04, hspace=0.06); plt.show()
print(f"reconstruction error (BCE) per image of these 8 digits: {F.binary_cross_entropy(rec, x8, reduction='sum').item() / 8:.1f}")
print(f"fraction of pixels with a mean between 0.1 and 0.9: {((gen_mean > 0.1) & (gen_mean < 0.9)).float().mean():.3f}")





reconstruction error (BCE) per image of these 8 digits: 66.4
fraction of pixels with a mean between 0.1 and 0.9: 0.197


The reconstructions keep the identity and most of the shape of the eight test digits, with soft edges; their binary cross-entropy is 66.4 per image. The decoded means of random latent vectors look like digits but are less clean, and some lie between two classes. The decoder output is a probability for every pixel, and 19.7% of the pixels of the generated means lie between 0.1 and 0.9, so a Bernoulli draw of every pixel gives the speckled images of the last row. Showing the mean is the usual convention for VAEs on images; the draw is what the model, read literally as the distribution of equation (31), generates.


Interpolation
In a latent space without gaps, the straight line between the codes of two images decodes to a continuous sequence of plausible images. We encode a test 2 and a test 7 to the centres \(\boldsymbol\mu_a,\boldsymbol\mu_b\) of their clouds and decode \[\mathbf z(t)=(1-t)\,\boldsymbol\mu_a+t\,\boldsymbol\mu_b,\qquad 0\le t\le 1. \tag{34}\] The bottom row interpolates the pixels instead, \[\mathbf x(t)=(1-t)\,\mathbf x_a+t\,\mathbf x_b. \tag{35}\]


Code
# interpolation between a test 2 and a test 7: in latent space (top) and in pixel space (bottom)
ia, ib = int(np.flatnonzero(yte == 2)[0]), int(np.flatnonzero(yte == 7)[0])
ts = np.linspace(0, 1, 9)
with torch.no_grad():
    ma, mb = vae16.encode(Xte_t[[ia, ib]])[0]
    lat = torch.sigmoid(vae16.decode(torch.stack([(1 - t) * ma + t * mb for t in ts]))).numpy()
pix = np.stack([(1 - t) * Xte[ia] + t * Xte[ib] for t in ts])
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 9, figsize=(9, 2.5))
for j, t in enumerate(ts):
    for r, imgs in enumerate((lat, pix)):
        axs[r, j].imshow(imgs[j].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1); axs[r, j].set_xticks([]); axs[r, j].set_yticks([])
    axs[0, j].set_title(f"t = {t:.2f}", fontsize=9)
for r, name in enumerate(("latent", "pixels")): axs[r, 0].set_ylabel(name, rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=10)
plt.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.04, hspace=0.06); plt.show()





In latent space the 2 turns into a 7 through images that each look like handwriting, passing through a shape resembling a 3 near the middle of the path. In pixel space the two images are blended: every intermediate image shows both digits superimposed, which no writer produces. The latent path stays on the set of digit-like images, the pixel path leaves it.


Latent coordinates
Each latent coordinate \(z_k\) is a direction in latent space, and moving along it changes the decoded image. The grid of the two-dimensional VAE is such a scan in both directions at once: along \(z_1\) and along \(z_2\) the digit changes its identity, slant and width together. For the VAE with 16 latent dimensions we move one coordinate at a time from \(-3\) to \(3\), with the others at 0. The rows are sorted by the KL divergence of the coordinate, averaged over the test digits, which measures how much information about the image the coordinate carries.


Code
# one latent coordinate at a time: z_k from -3 to 3, all other coordinates 0; rows sorted by the KL of z_k
with torch.no_grad():
    mu_t, lv_t = vae16.encode(Xte_t)
kl_k = (0.5 * (mu_t ** 2 + lv_t.exp() - lv_t - 1)).mean(0).numpy()      # KL divergence per coordinate, mean over test digits
order = np.argsort(-kl_k)
vals = np.linspace(-3, 3, 9)
z = torch.zeros(16 * len(vals), 16)
for r, k in enumerate(order): z[r * len(vals):(r + 1) * len(vals), k] = torch.tensor(vals, dtype=torch.float32)
with torch.no_grad(): imgs = torch.sigmoid(vae16.decode(z)).numpy()
fig, axs = plt.subplots(16, len(vals), figsize=(5.4, 10.4))
for r, k in enumerate(order):
    for j in range(len(vals)):
        a = axs[r, j]; a.imshow(imgs[r * len(vals) + j].reshape(28, 28), cmap="gray_r", vmin=0, vmax=1); a.set_xticks([]); a.set_yticks([])
    axs[r, 0].set_ylabel(f"$z_{{{k + 1}}}$, KL {kl_k[k]:.2f}", rotation=0, ha="right", va="center", fontsize=9)
for j, v in enumerate(vals): axs[0, j].set_title(f"{v:+.1f}", fontsize=8)
plt.subplots_adjust(wspace=0.04, hspace=0.04); plt.show()
print("KL per coordinate, largest first:", kl_k[order].round(2), " sum:", round(float(kl_k.sum()), 1))





KL per coordinate, largest first: [2.58 2.46 2.24 2.   1.89 1.82 1.76 1.73 1.34 1.3  0.99 0.   0.   0.
 0.   0.  ]  sum: 20.1


Eleven of the sixteen coordinates carry information, with an average KL divergence between 0.99 and 2.58 nats, and five are unused, with KL 0.00: moving them does not change the decoded image. The sum, 20.1 nats on the test digits, is close to the KL term of 19.6 nats measured at the end of training. The informative coordinates move between digit identities rather than changing one property: the first row turns a 1 into a 0 through an 8, the second a slanted 8 into a 9, the third a 9 into a 3.
Nothing in the VAE loss asks a coordinate to correspond to one property of the digit. The prior \(\mathcal N(0,I)\) looks the same in every rotated coordinate system and does not single out the axes; in general one coordinate changes several properties at once, and one property, such as the slant, is spread over several coordinates. A representation with one coordinate per property is called disentangled. The β-VAE (Higgins et al. 2017) pursues it by weighting the KL term with a factor \(\beta\) larger than 1; it is the subject of the notebook notebook_2026-10-27-beta_vae.ipynb.

title: Generative models: probability, autoencoder and VAE
text:
Conditional VAE
Often we want to say what to generate. A conditional VAE receives a known label \(\mathbf c\) as an extra input of both networks, \(E(\mathbf x,\mathbf c)\) and \(G(\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\), while the loss stays unchanged. Since \(\mathbf c\) already tells the decoder which digit to draw, the latent vector \(\mathbf z\) only needs to carry what \(\mathbf c\) does not say: the style, such as slant, thickness and size.
Here \(\mathbf c\) is the one-hot vector of the digit. Generation samples \[p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf c)=\int p_\theta(\mathbf x|\mathbf z,\mathbf c)\,p(\mathbf z)\,d\mathbf z : \tag{36}\] the condition is fixed, \(\mathbf z\) is drawn from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), and the decoder is applied to \([\mathbf z,\mathbf c]\). Fixing \(\mathbf c\) chooses what is drawn, drawing \(\mathbf z\) chooses how. In the figure each row is one digit and each column one random \(\mathbf z\), the same in every row. Read down a column, one \(\mathbf z\) with ten different \(\mathbf c\) should keep the style; read along a row, eight \(\mathbf z\) for one \(\mathbf c\) give the variety within the class.


Code
rng = seed(2)
Ctr = F.one_hot(torch.tensor(ytr.astype(np.int64)), 10).float()
cvae = VAE(d=8, cond=10); hc = train_vae(cvae, Xtr_t, Ctr, epochs=20); cvae.eval()
print(f"loss per image {hc[-1, 0]:.1f} = reconstruction {hc[-1, 1]:.1f} + KL {hc[-1, 2]:.1f}")
torch.manual_seed(11); zc = torch.randn(8, 8)
rows = []
with torch.no_grad():
    for dgt in range(10):
        c = F.one_hot(torch.full((8,), dgt), 10).float()
        rows.append(torch.sigmoid(cvae.decode(zc, c)).numpy())
show_grid(np.concatenate(rows), 10, 8, f"{OUT}/gen_cvae_mnist.png", size=0.6)


loss per image 97.6 = reconstruction 83.4 + KL 14.2






Conditional VAE architecture
The conditional VAE has the layers of the VAE above, and the 10 numbers of the one-hot label \(\mathbf c\) (green) are appended to the input of the encoder and to the input of the decoder. The first encoder layer therefore receives \(784+10\) numbers, and the first decoder layer \(8+10\) for the eight latent dimensions used here. The label enters the decoder from outside; it is not computed from \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2\), so the drawing shows no edges into it. The figure is also saved as arch_cvae.png for the slides. The torchinfo table needs both inputs of the model, the image and the label, which we pass as a list. Compared with the VAE, only the first layer of the encoder and the first layer of the decoder gain parameters, \(10\times512\) and \(10\times256\) weights for the label.


Code
# conditional VAE: the one-hot digit c is concatenated to the inputs of encoder and decoder
with torch.random.fork_rng():
    cvae_d8 = VAE(d=8, cond=10)                                  # the architecture trained above
    table = summary(cvae_d8, input_data=[torch.zeros(1, 784), torch.zeros(1, 10)], col_names=("output_size", "num_params"), verbose=0)
cols = vae_columns(cvae_d8)
print("columns read from the model:", cols)
assert dense_params(cols, sampled={len(cols) - 4}) == table.total_params

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 5.2))                      # slide size: labels of 12 pt at full slide width
draw_network(cols, **vae_style(cols), x_gap=1.9, fontsize=12, ax=ax)
fig.savefig(f"{OUT}/arch_cvae.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight", facecolor="white")
plt.show()
print(table)


columns read from the model: [[784, 10], 512, 256, [8, 8], [8, 10], 256, 512, 784]

VAE                                      [1, 784]                  --
├─Sequential: 1-1                        [1, 256]                  --
│    └─Linear: 2-1                       [1, 512]                  407,040
│    └─ReLU: 2-2                         [1, 512]                  --
│    └─Linear: 2-3                       [1, 256]                  131,328

├─Linear: 1-2                            [1, 8]                    2,056
├─Linear: 1-3                            [1, 8]                    2,056

Classifier test of the generated digits
Looking at the pictures is not enough to decide whether the generated digits really show the digit we asked for. We therefore train a small classifier on the real MNIST training images (a dense network \(784\to256\to10\), cross-entropy loss, 3 epochs), check its accuracy on the real test images, and then let it label 200 generated images for each requested digit. The fraction labelled as the requested digit measures how well the conditional VAE respects its condition.


Code
rng = seed(4)
clf = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(784, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 10))
optc = torch.optim.Adam(clf.parameters(), 1e-3)
for ep in range(3):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(Xtr_t))
    for i in range(0, len(perm), 128):
        j = perm[i:i + 128]; loss = F.cross_entropy(clf(Xtr_t[j]), torch.tensor(ytr[j.numpy()].astype(np.int64)))
        optc.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optc.step()
clf.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    acc = (clf(Xte_t).argmax(1).numpy() == yte).mean()
    agree_cvae = []
    for dgt in range(10):
        cc = F.one_hot(torch.full((200,), dgt), 10).float()
        agree_cvae.append(float((clf(torch.sigmoid(cvae.decode(torch.randn(200, 8), cc))).argmax(1).numpy() == dgt).mean()))
nums["clf_acc"] = float(acc); nums["cvae_agreement"] = [round(a, 3) for a in agree_cvae]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 2.8))
ax.bar(range(10), agree_cvae, color=blue); ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05); ax.set_xticks(range(10))
ax.set_xlabel("requested digit"); ax.set_ylabel("recognised as requested"); clean(ax)
plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/gen_cvae_mnist_check.png", dpi=170, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()
print(f"classifier accuracy on real test digits: {acc:.3f}")
print("fraction of generated digits recognised as the requested digit:", np.round(agree_cvae, 2), " mean", round(float(np.mean(agree_cvae)), 3))





classifier accuracy on real test digits: 0.971
fraction of generated digits recognised as the requested digit: [0.98 0.94 0.98 0.98 0.96 0.94 0.96 0.96 0.96 0.96]  mean 0.963


The classifier reaches an accuracy of 0.971 on real test digits, and it recognises on average 96.3% of the generated digits as the digit that was requested, between 94% and 98% for each digit. The conditional VAE therefore respects its condition about as well as the classifier can judge.
As an exercise, keep \(\mathbf c\) fixed and move along one latent coordinate, \(z_1\) from \(-3\) to \(3\), with the others at 0. Which property of the digit changes?

title: Generative models: probability, autoencoder and VAE
section: Blood-cell images of a chosen type
text:
Blood-cell images of a chosen type
The conditional VAE applies equally to the blood-cell images of BloodMNIST (Lecture 4).

BloodMNIST data
BloodMNIST belongs to the MedMNIST collection (Yang et al. 2023). It is built from 17 092 microscope images of individual normal blood cells of healthy donors, taken at the Hospital Clinic of Barcelona (Acevedo et al. 2020) and reduced to \(28\times28\) pixels. One sample is the RGB (red, green, blue) image of one cell, three values from 0 to 255 per pixel, divided by 255 here. Its label is one of eight cell types: basophil, eosinophil, erythroblast, immature granulocyte, lymphocyte, monocyte, neutrophil and platelet. The images are split into 11 959 for training, 1712 for validation (not used here) and 3421 for testing, and the classes are unbalanced, from 849 lymphocytes to 2330 neutrophils in the training set. The file is taken from the Lecture 4 folder, or downloaded from Zenodo.


Convolutional conditional VAE
The condition \(\mathbf c\) is the one-hot cell type. The images have three colour channels, so encoder and decoder are convolutional, like the convolutional neural networks (CNNs) of Lecture 4. To check whether the generated cells look like their type, we train a small CNN classifier on the real images, generate 100 cells of each type, and count how many the classifier assigns to the requested type. Both networks are trained on the BloodMNIST training images, and generated cells are shown next to real cells of each type.


Code
import urllib.request
bpath = "data/bloodmnist.npz"
if not os.path.exists(bpath):
    bpath = "data/bloodmnist.npz"
    if not os.path.exists(bpath):
        os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True)
        urllib.request.urlretrieve("https://zenodo.org/records/10519652/files/bloodmnist.npz?download=1", bpath)
bd = np.load(bpath)
names = ["basophil", "eosinophil", "erythroblast", "immature granulocyte", "lymphocyte", "monocyte", "neutrophil", "platelet"]
to_t = lambda a: torch.tensor(a.astype(np.float32) / 255).permute(0, 3, 1, 2)      # (n, 3, 28, 28)
Btr, Bte = to_t(bd["train_images"]), to_t(bd["test_images"])
bytr, byte = bd["train_labels"].ravel(), bd["test_labels"].ravel()
Cb = F.one_hot(torch.tensor(bytr.astype(np.int64)), 8).float()
print("training images:", tuple(Btr.shape), " test images:", tuple(Bte.shape))

class ConvCVAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d=16, cond=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3 + cond, 32, 3, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, 2, 1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Flatten())
        self.mu, self.logvar = nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, d), nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, d)
        self.fc = nn.Linear(d + cond, 64 * 7 * 7)
        self.dec = nn.Sequential(nn.ReLU(), nn.Unflatten(1, (64, 7, 7)), nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, 3, 2, 1, output_padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
                                 nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 3, 3, 2, 1, output_padding=1))
        self.cond = cond
    def encode(self, x, c):
        cmap_ = c[:, :, None, None].expand(-1, -1, x.shape[2], x.shape[3])        # the condition as extra input channels
        h = self.enc(torch.cat([x, cmap_], 1)); return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)
    def decode(self, z, c): return self.dec(self.fc(torch.cat([z, c], 1)))       # logits of the pixels
    def forward(self, x, c):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x, c); z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)
        return self.decode(z, c), mu, logvar

rng = seed(7); t0 = time.time()
bcvae = ConvCVAE(); optb = torch.optim.Adam(bcvae.parameters(), 1e-3)
for ep in range(30):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(Btr))
    for i in range(0, len(perm), 128):
        j = perm[i:i + 128]; logits, mu, logvar = bcvae(Btr[j], Cb[j])
        loss, rec, kl = vae_loss(logits.flatten(1), Btr[j].flatten(1), mu, logvar)
        optb.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optb.step()
bcvae.eval(); print(f"trained in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s; last batch: reconstruction {rec.item():.1f} + KL {kl.item():.1f}")

# a classifier of the real cells, for the check
rng = seed(8)
clfb = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3, 32, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2), nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
                     nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(64 * 7 * 7, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, 8))
optk = torch.optim.Adam(clfb.parameters(), 1e-3); ybt = torch.tensor(bytr.astype(np.int64))
for ep in range(8):
    perm = torch.randperm(len(Btr))
    for i in range(0, len(perm), 128):
        j = perm[i:i + 128]; loss = F.cross_entropy(clfb(Btr[j]), ybt[j]); optk.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optk.step()
clfb.eval()
with torch.no_grad(): accb = (clfb(Bte).argmax(1).numpy() == byte).mean()
nums["blood_clf_test_acc"] = float(accb)

torch.manual_seed(13)
with torch.no_grad():
    zb = torch.randn(8, 16); rows = []
    for c in range(8):
        rows.append(torch.sigmoid(bcvae.decode(zb, F.one_hot(torch.full((8,), c), 8).float())).permute(0, 2, 3, 1).numpy())
    agree = []
    for c in range(8):
        g = torch.sigmoid(bcvae.decode(torch.randn(100, 16), F.one_hot(torch.full((100,), c), 8).float()))
        agree.append(float((clfb(g).argmax(1).numpy() == c).mean()))
nums["blood_cvae_class_agreement"] = [round(a, 2) for a in agree]
fig, axs = plt.subplots(8, 9, figsize=(8.2, 7.6), gridspec_kw=dict(width_ratios=[1] * 8 + [1.6]))
for c in range(8):
    for j in range(8):
        axs[c, j].imshow(rows[c][j]); axs[c, j].axis("off")

title: Generative models: probability, autoencoder and VAE
section: Boltzmann distribution of the 2D Ising model
text:
Boltzmann distribution of the 2D Ising model
For spins we know the true distribution (Lecture 4), \[p(\mathbf s\,|\,T)=\frac{e^{-H(\mathbf s)/T}}{Z}, \tag{37}\] and Metropolis Monte Carlo samples it exactly. This makes the Ising model a good test of whether a network can learn a distribution from samples alone.

Ising data
The data are spin configurations of the Ising model (Ising 1925) on a \(20\times20\) square lattice with periodic boundaries, \[H(\mathbf s)=-J\sum_{\langle ij\rangle}s_is_j, \tag{38}\] with coupling \(J\) of 1 and the sum over nearest neighbours, sampled with the Metropolis algorithm (Metropolis et al. 1953). This is the data set of Lecture 4, regenerated here if missing. One sample is a configuration of 400 spins, each \(+1\) or \(-1\), and its label is the temperature \(T\) at which it was drawn: 51 temperatures from 1.0 to 3.5 in steps of 0.05, with 200 configurations each, 10 200 in total. On the infinite lattice the order is lost at the critical temperature \[T_c=\frac{2}{\ln\big(1+\sqrt2\big)}\approx2.269 \tag{39}\] (Onsager 1944): below it most spins point the same way, above it the magnetisation vanishes. Example configurations at several temperatures illustrate the data.


Conditional VAE on spin configurations
We train a conditional VAE with the temperature as condition \(\mathbf c\), rescaled to about \([-1.7,1.7]\), on all 10 200 configurations. Spins are mapped to pixels \((s_i+1)/2\), which are 0 or 1, so the same BCE loss applies. To generate at a chosen \(T\) we draw \(\mathbf z\) from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), decode, and draw each spin up with the decoded probability. The generated configurations are compared with Monte Carlo through two observables at each temperature: the magnetisation \(\langle|M|\rangle\) and the energy per spin.


Code
path = "data/ising_Nx20_Ny20.npz"
if not os.path.exists(path):
    path = "data/ising_Nx20_Ny20.npz"
    if not os.path.exists(path):                              # regenerate (checkerboard Metropolis, about a minute)
        r = np.random.default_rng(0); L = 20; Ts = np.round(np.arange(1.0, 3.5 + 1e-9, 0.05), 2)
        y_, x_ = np.indices((L, L)); masks = ((x_ + y_) % 2 == 0, (x_ + y_) % 2 == 1)
        beta = (1 / Ts.astype(np.float32))[None, :, None, None]; s = np.ones((20, len(Ts), L, L), np.float32)
        def sweep(s):
            for m in masks:
                nb = np.roll(s, 1, -1) + np.roll(s, -1, -1) + np.roll(s, 1, -2) + np.roll(s, -1, -2)
                s[...] = np.where(m & (r.random(s.shape, dtype=np.float32) < np.exp(-beta * 2 * s * nb)), -s, s)
        for _ in range(1200): sweep(s)
        st = []
        for k in range(10):
            for _ in range(20): sweep(s)
            st.append(s.copy())
        cf = np.stack(st).transpose(2, 0, 1, 3, 4).reshape(len(Ts), 200, L, L).astype(np.int8)
        os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True); np.savez_compressed(path, configs=cf, T=Ts)
d = np.load(path); cfg, Ts = d["configs"].astype(np.float32), d["T"]
L = cfg.shape[-1]; N = L * L
print("Monte Carlo data:", cfg.shape, "temperatures", Ts[0], "...", Ts[-1])
Xs = torch.tensor(((cfg + 1) / 2).reshape(-1, N))
Tn = lambda T: (np.asarray(T, np.float32) - 2.25) / 0.75          # the condition: T, rescaled to about [-1.7, 1.7]
Cs = torch.tensor(np.repeat(Tn(Ts), cfg.shape[1]))[:, None]

rng = seed(6)
ivae = VAE(D=N, d=8, cond=1, hidden=(256, 128)); hi_ = train_vae(ivae, Xs, Cs, epochs=60); ivae.eval()
print(f"loss per configuration {hi_[-1, 0]:.1f} = reconstruction {hi_[-1, 1]:.1f} + KL {hi_[-1, 2]:.1f}")

def energy(s):        # energy per spin, J = 1, periodic boundaries; s: (..., L, L) with values +-1
    return -(s * (np.roll(s, 1, -1) + np.roll(s, 1, -2))).mean((-1, -2))
gen_rng = torch.Generator().manual_seed(12)
with torch.no_grad():
    z = torch.randn(len(Ts) * 200, 8, generator=gen_rng)
    prob = torch.sigmoid(ivae.decode(z, Cs))
    gen = (torch.bernoulli(prob, generator=gen_rng) * 2 - 1).numpy().reshape(len(Ts), 200, L, L)
M_mc, M_gen = np.abs(cfg.mean((-1, -2))).mean(1), np.abs(gen.mean((-1, -2))).mean(1)
E_mc, E_gen = energy(cfg).mean(1), energy(gen).mean(1)
nums["ising_cvae_M_maxdiff"] = float(np.abs(M_mc - M_gen).max())
nums["ising_cvae_E_maxdiff"] = float(np.abs(E_mc - E_gen).max())
nums["ising_cvae_E_maxdiff_T"] = float(Ts[np.argmax(np.abs(E_mc - E_gen))])

axs[1].plot(Ts, E_mc, "o-", ms=3, color=blue, label="Monte Carlo"); axs[1].plot(Ts, E_gen, "s--", ms=3, color=orange, label="generated by the CVAE")

The last figure shows Monte Carlo configurations of the training data. At temperature 1 almost all spins are aligned, all up or all down, since \(H\) does not change when all spins are flipped; near \(T_c\) domains of all sizes appear; at 3.5 neighbouring spins are only weakly correlated.
The comparison rests on the curves, not only on the pictures. The magnetisation tells whether the model learned the global order at each temperature; the energy counts aligned neighbours, i.e. the local correlations. The largest deviation from Monte Carlo is 0.234 in the magnetisation and 0.634 in the energy per spin, the latter at temperature 2.3, close to the critical temperature. The spins are drawn independently once the decoder has given their probabilities, so any correlation between neighbours must come through the latent vector \(\mathbf z\); where the energy of the generated configurations deviates from Monte Carlo, the model has not captured those correlations.
As an exercise, generate at temperature 2.27, a value between two of the training temperatures. Do the generated configurations interpolate sensibly? Increase the latent dimension \(d\): does the energy improve?

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
Monte Carlo data
One sample is a configuration of the \(20\times20\) lattice: an array of 400 numbers \(s_i\), one per site, with \(+1\) for a spin pointing up and \(-1\) for a spin pointing down. The lattice has periodic boundaries, so it is a torus: the right neighbour of a site in the last column is the site in the first column of the same row, and likewise for rows. Each configuration carries one label, the temperature \(T\) of the MC run that produced it.
The configurations are those of Lecture 4, sampled by the Metropolis algorithm [2]. A proposed flip of spin \(i\) changes the energy of equation (2) by \[
\Delta E_i=2\,s_i\sum_{j\in\mathrm{nn}(i)}s_j , \tag{4}
\] where \(\mathrm{nn}(i)\) are the four nearest neighbours of site \(i\), and the flip is accepted with probability \[
A_i=\min\left(1,\,e^{-\Delta E_i/T}\right). \tag{5}
\] This rule obeys detailed balance with respect to equation (1), so after many updates the chain visits configurations with the Boltzmann probability. In the checkerboard version all sites of one colour of a chessboard pattern are updated at once, since their neighbours all have the other colour; one sweep, one attempted flip per spin, consists of two such half-updates.
For each of the 51 temperatures 1.00, 1.05, …, 3.50, 20 independent chains start from the fully ordered state and run 1000 sweeps of equilibration, long enough to forget the starting point. Each chain then stores one configuration every 20 sweeps, ten times. The gap reduces the correlation between consecutive stored configurations, although near \(T_c\), where the Metropolis dynamics slows down, consecutive configurations of a chain remain partly correlated. This gives 200 configurations per temperature and 10 200 in total. Each stored configuration is finally multiplied by a random global sign: the energy of equation (2) does not change when all spins are flipped, but a cold start would otherwise leave every low-temperature configuration with positive magnetisation.
Where the file of Lecture 4 is not available, as in Google Colab, a local copy in data/ is used, or else the data set is regenerated with the same sampler in about a minute.


Code
def metropolis_sweep(s, beta, masks, rng):
    # one checkerboard Metropolis sweep (in place) of a batch of lattices s: (..., L, L), periodic boundaries
    for mask in masks:
        nn_sum = np.roll(s, 1, -1) + np.roll(s, -1, -1) + np.roll(s, 1, -2) + np.roll(s, -1, -2)
        accept = rng.random(s.shape, dtype=np.float32) < np.exp(-beta * 2.0 * s * nn_sum)
        s[...] = np.where(mask & accept, -s, s)

def generate_dataset(L, temperatures, n_chains=20, n_samples=10, n_equil=1000, n_between=20, rng=None):
    y, x = np.indices((L, L)); black = (x + y) % 2 == 0
    beta = (1.0 / temperatures.astype(np.float32))[None, :, None, None]
    s = np.ones((n_chains, len(temperatures), L, L), np.float32)            # cold start
    for _ in range(n_equil): metropolis_sweep(s, beta, (black, ~black), rng)
    stored = np.empty((n_samples, n_chains, len(temperatures), L, L), np.int8)
    for k in range(n_samples):
        for _ in range(n_between): metropolis_sweep(s, beta, (black, ~black), rng)
        stored[k] = s
    configs = stored.transpose(2, 0, 1, 3, 4).reshape(len(temperatures), n_samples * n_chains, L, L)
    flip = rng.choice(np.array([-1, 1], np.int8), size=configs.shape[:2])   # random global spin flip
    return configs * flip[:, :, None, None]

candidates = ["data/ising_Nx20_Ny20.npz", "data/ising_Nx20_Ny20.npz"]
path = next((p for p in candidates if os.path.exists(p)), None)
if path is None:
    t0 = time.time(); Ts_new = np.round(np.arange(1.0, 3.5 + 1e-9, 0.05), 2)
    configs_new = generate_dataset(20, Ts_new, rng=np.random.default_rng(0))
    os.makedirs("data", exist_ok=True); path = candidates[1]
    np.savez_compressed(path, configs=configs_new, T=Ts_new, Nx=20, Ny=20)
    print(f"regenerated the data set in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

m=\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N s_i . \tag{6}
\] At temperature 1.5 nearly all spins are aligned, apart from a few isolated flipped spins, and both signs of the ordered state occur. Around \(T_c\) domains of many sizes appear, and at 3.5 the spins are correlated only over a few lattice spacings. On a finite lattice \(\langle|m|\rangle_T\) drops smoothly rather than sharply, and it stays above zero at high temperature because the magnetisation of \(N\) nearly independent spins is of the order of one over the square root of \(N\).

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
The conditional VAE
The model is the cVAE of the Lecture 6 notebook, unchanged. Each spin becomes a pixel \[
x_i=\frac{s_i+1}{2}\in\{0,1\}, \tag{7}
\] so a configuration is a vector \(\mathbf x\) of \(D\) zeros and ones, with \(D\) equal to 400. The condition is the rescaled temperature \[
c=\frac{T-2.25}{0.75}, \tag{8}
\] which runs from \(-1.67\) to \(1.67\) and is of the same order as the other inputs of the network.
The encoder receives \(\mathbf x\) together with \(c\) and passes them through fully connected layers of 256 and 128 rectified linear units (ReLU). Two linear output layers give the mean \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and the logarithm of the variance \(\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2\) of a Gaussian distribution over the 8 latent variables. During training a latent vector is drawn with the reparametrisation trick, \[
\mathbf z=\boldsymbol\mu+\boldsymbol\sigma\odot\boldsymbol\varepsilon,\qquad \boldsymbol\varepsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I), \tag{9}
\] where \(\odot\) is the element-wise product. The decoder receives \(\mathbf z\) together with \(c\) and passes them through layers of 128 and 256 units to 400 outputs \(y_j\) between 0 and 1, the probability that spin \(j\) points up. Given \(\mathbf z\) and \(c\), the decoder therefore describes a configuration by a product of independent Bernoulli distributions, \[
p_\theta(\mathbf s\,|\,\mathbf z,c)=\prod_{j=1}^{400}y_j^{(1+s_j)/2}\,(1-y_j)^{(1-s_j)/2}, \tag{10}
\] where \(\theta\) denotes the weights of the decoder. The loss for one configuration is the binary cross-entropy (BCE) between \(\mathbf x\) and \(\mathbf y\) plus the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence between the encoder’s Gaussian and the prior \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), \[
\mathcal L=-\sum_{j=1}^{400}\left[x_j\ln y_j+(1-x_j)\ln(1-y_j)\right]+\frac12\sum_{k=1}^{8}\left(\mu_k^2+\sigma_k^2-\ln\sigma_k^2-1\right), \tag{11}
\] averaged over the configurations of a mini-batch.


Code
def mlp(sizes):
    # fully connected layers with ReLU in between (no activation after the last layer)
    layers = []
    for a, b in zip(sizes[:-1], sizes[1:]):
        layers += [nn.Linear(a, b), nn.ReLU()]
    return nn.Sequential(*layers[:-1])

class VAE(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, D=784, d=2, cond=0, hidden=(512, 256)):
        super().__init__()
        self.d, self.cond = d, cond
        self.enc = mlp([D + cond, *hidden]); self.enc.append(nn.ReLU())
        self.mu, self.logvar = nn.Linear(hidden[-1], d), nn.Linear(hidden[-1], d)
        self.dec = mlp([d + cond, *hidden[::-1], D])                  # outputs logits; sigmoid gives probabilities
    def encode(self, x, c=None):
        h = self.enc(x if c is None else torch.cat([x, c], 1))
        return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)
    def decode(self, z, c=None):
        return self.dec(z if c is None else torch.cat([z, c], 1))
    def forward(self, x, c=None):
        mu, logvar = self.encode(x, c)
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5 * logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)      # reparametrisation trick
        return self.decode(z, c), mu, logvar

def vae_loss(logits, x, mu, logvar):
    rec = F.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits(logits, x, reduction="sum") / len(x)
    kl = 0.5 * (mu ** 2 + logvar.exp() - logvar - 1).sum() / len(x)
    return rec + kl, rec, kl

def train_vae(model, X, C=None, epochs=20, lr=1e-3, bs=128):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr)
    hist = []
    for ep in range(epochs):
        perm = torch.randperm(len(X)); tot = np.zeros(3)
        for i in range(0, len(perm), bs):
            j = perm[i:i + bs]; x = X[j]; c = None if C is None else C[j]
            logits, mu, logvar = model(x, c)
            loss, rec, kl = vae_loss(logits, x, mu, logvar)
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
            tot += np.array([loss.item(), rec.item(), kl.item()]) * len(j)
        hist.append(tot / len(X))
    return np.array(hist)



Network architecture
torchinfo lists the layers of the encoder and of the decoder with the tensor shapes for one configuration and the numbers of trainable parameters. The layer sizes of the drawing are read from the same model. Every layer is a column of nodes; a layer with more than six units is drawn with its first and last three nodes around an ellipsis, and its true number of units is written under it. The lines are the trainable connections between consecutive layers, drawn between the visible nodes. The condition \(T\) enters twice, as an extra input of the encoder and of the decoder. The dashed lines from \(\boldsymbol\mu\) and \(\log\boldsymbol\sigma^2\) to \(\mathbf z\) are not weights but the sampling step of equation (9).


Code
class Encoder(nn.Module):                       # view of the encoder part of a VAE
    def __init__(self, vae):
        super().__init__(); self.enc, self.mu, self.logvar = vae.enc, vae.mu, vae.logvar
    def forward(self, x, c):
        h = self.enc(torch.cat([x, c], 1)); return self.mu(h), self.logvar(h)
class Decoder(nn.Module):                       # view of the decoder part of a VAE
    def __init__(self, vae):
        super().__init__(); self.dec = vae.dec
    def forward(self, z, c):
        return torch.sigmoid(self.dec(torch.cat([z, c], 1)))

ivae = VAE(D=N, d=8, cond=1, hidden=(256, 128))
cols = ("input_size", "output_size", "num_params")

s_dec = summary(Decoder(ivae), input_data=[torch.zeros(1, 8), torch.zeros(1, 1)], col_names=cols, verbose=0)

Code
def draw_network(ax, columns, gaps, max_full=6, n_edge=3, dx=3.0, dy=0.45, r=0.16, fs=20,
                 edge_colour="#A9B0B8", groups=None):
    '''Draw a layered network as columns of nodes connected by edges.

    ax         : matplotlib axes to draw on
    columns    : list of columns from left to right; each column is a list of blocks, each block a dict with
                 size (number of units), colour (node fill colour), label (text written under the block) and
                 incoming (False for an input injected at this column, such as the condition, which gets no edges)
    gaps       : one entry per pair of consecutive columns: "dense" (every unit connected to every unit of the
                 next column, a fully connected layer) or "sample" (unit k of each block connected to unit k of
                 the next column, dashed: the sampling step z = mu + sigma * eps)
    max_full   : blocks with at most this many units are drawn completely
    n_edge     : larger blocks show their first n_edge and last n_edge units around an ellipsis
    dx, dy     : horizontal distance between columns and vertical distance between nodes (data units)
    r          : radius of a node (data units)
    fs         : font size of all labels, in points
    edge_colour: colour of the dense connections
    groups     : optional list of (first column, last column, text) brackets drawn above the network
    '''
    # node positions: each block is a vertical run of slots (a node or the ellipsis);
    # consecutive blocks of a column are separated by two empty slots, which leave room for the label
    pos, label_y = [], []                        # pos[c][b] = list of (x, y, unit index) of the visible nodes
    top = 0.0
    for c, col in enumerate(columns):
        slots = []                               # entries: (block, unit index), (block, "dots") or None
        for b, blk in enumerate(col):
            if b > 0: slots += [None, None]
            if blk["size"] <= max_full:
                slots += [(b, k) for k in range(blk["size"])]
            else:                                # truncation of a large layer
                slots += [(b, k) for k in range(n_edge)] + [(b, "dots")] + \
                         [(b, blk["size"] - n_edge + k) for k in range(n_edge)]
        ys = (np.arange(len(slots))[::-1] - (len(slots) - 1) / 2) * dy
        top = max(top, ys.max())
        x = c * dx
        pos.append([[] for _ in col])
        for sl, y in zip(slots, ys):
            if sl is None: continue
            b, k = sl
            if k == "dots":
                ax.text(x, y, r"$\vdots$", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=gray)
            else:
                pos[c][b].append((x, y, k))
        # label under each block: the true number of units (and the layer type)
        for b, blk in enumerate(col):
            y_low = min(p[1] for p in pos[c][b]) - r - 0.05
            ax.text(x, y_low, blk["label"], ha="center", va="top", fontsize=fs, linespacing=1.0)
    # edges between consecutive columns
    for c, kind in enumerate(gaps):
        for b2, blk2 in enumerate(columns[c + 1]):
            if not blk2.get("incoming", True): continue
            for b1 in range(len(columns[c])):
                for (x1, y1, k1) in pos[c][b1]:
                    for (x2, y2, k2) in pos[c + 1][b2]:
                        if kind == "dense":
                            ax.plot([x1 + r, x2 - r], [y1, y2], color=edge_colour, lw=0.6, alpha=0.6, zorder=1)
                        elif kind == "sample" and k1 == k2:
                            ax.plot([x1 + r, x2 - r], [y1, y2], color=orange, lw=1.4, ls="--", zorder=1)
    # nodes, drawn last so that they cover the ends of the edges
    for c, col in enumerate(columns):
        for b, blk in enumerate(col):
            for (x, y, k) in pos[c][b]:
                ax.add_patch(plt.Circle((x, y), r, facecolor=blk["colour"], edgecolor=navy, lw=1.0, zorder=3))
    # encoder / decoder brackets above the network
    for (c1, c2, text) in (groups or []):
        yb = top + 0.6
        ax.plot([c1 * dx - 0.4, c1 * dx - 0.4, c2 * dx + 0.4, c2 * dx + 0.4], [yb - 0.25, yb, yb, yb - 0.25], color=navy, lw=1.5)
        ax.text((c1 + c2) * dx / 2, yb + 0.1, text, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=fs + 2, color=navy, weight="bold")
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_xlim(-1.3, (len(columns) - 1) * dx + 1.3)

# layer sizes read from the model
lin_enc = [m for m in ivae.enc if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]
lin_dec = [m for m in ivae.dec if isinstance(m, nn.Linear)]
D_in, n_cond, d_lat = lin_enc[0].in_features - ivae.cond, ivae.cond, ivae.mu.out_features
h_enc, h_dec, D_out = [m.out_features for m in lin_enc], [m.out_features for m in lin_dec[:-1]], lin_dec[-1].out_features
print("encoder:", D_in, "+", n_cond, "->", h_enc, "-> mu, log sigma^2:", d_lat, "| decoder:", d_lat, "+", n_cond, "->", h_dec, "->", D_out)

# colours of the node types
c_in, c_T, c_h, c_mu, c_lv, c_z = "#9CC3E6", orange, blue, "#2E8B57", "#8E44AD", "#F6C08F"
columns = ([[dict(size=D_in, colour=c_in, label=f"{D_in} spins"), dict(size=n_cond, colour=c_T, label="$T$")]]
           + [[dict(size=h, colour=c_h, label=f"{h}\nReLU")] for h in h_enc]
           + [[dict(size=d_lat, colour=c_mu, label=rf"$\mu$ ({d_lat})"), dict(size=d_lat, colour=c_lv, label=rf"$\log\sigma^2$ ({d_lat})")]]
           + [[dict(size=d_lat, colour=c_z, label=rf"$\mathbf{{z}}$ ({d_lat})"), dict(size=n_cond, colour=c_T, label="$T$", incoming=False)]]
           + [[dict(size=h, colour=c_h, label=f"{h}\nReLU")] for h in h_dec]
           + [[dict(size=D_out, colour=c_in, label=f"{D_out}\n$P(s_j=+1)$")]])
gaps = ["dense"] * (len(h_enc) + 1) + ["sample"] + ["dense"] * (len(h_dec) + 1)
n_enc = len(h_enc) + 1                                              # index of the (mu, log sigma^2) column
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(9, 6.5)); ax = fig.add_axes([0, 0, 1, 1])        # axes fill the figure: 9 in of drawing
draw_network(ax, columns, gaps, groups=[(0, n_enc, "encoder"), (n_enc + 1, len(columns) - 1, "decoder")])
ax.text(16.3, -3.35, r"$z_k=\mu_k+\sigma_k\,\varepsilon_k,\ \varepsilon_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$",
        ha="center", va="top", fontsize=17, color=orange)
plt.savefig(f"{OUT}/ising_cvae_arch.png", dpi=200, bbox_inches="tight"); plt.show()

Training
The model is trained for 60 epochs with the Adam optimiser (learning rate \(10^{-3}\), mini-batches of 128 configurations) on all 10 200 MC configurations, with the same seed as in the Lecture 6 notebook.


Code
Xs = torch.tensor(((cfg + 1) / 2).reshape(-1, N))                      # spins -> pixels 0/1
Tn = lambda T: (np.asarray(T, np.float32) - 2.25) / 0.75              # the condition c
Cs = torch.tensor(np.repeat(Tn(Ts), nS))[:, None]

rng = seed(6)
ivae = VAE(D=N, d=8, cond=1, hidden=(256, 128))
t0 = time.time(); hist = train_vae(ivae, Xs, Cs, epochs=60); ivae.eval()
t_vae = time.time() - t0

print(f"loss per configuration after 60 epochs: {hist[-1, 0]:.1f} = reconstruction {hist[-1, 1]:.1f} + KL {hist[-1, 2]:.1f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.6))
ax.plot(np.arange(1, 61), hist[:, 1], color=blue, label="reconstruction (BCE)")
ax.plot(np.arange(1, 61), hist[:, 2], color=orange, label="KL divergence")
ax.set_xlabel("epoch"); ax.set_ylabel("per configuration"); ax.legend(frameon=False); clean(ax)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()


training time 31 s
loss per configuration after 60 epochs: 139.2 = reconstruction 132.8 + KL 6.3





After 60 epochs the loss is 139.2 per configuration, of which 132.8 comes from the reconstruction and 6.3 from the KL divergence. Spread over 400 spins, the reconstruction cost is 0.33 nats per spin, about half of the cost of a fair coin for every spin, 0.69 nats (the natural logarithm of 2). The KL term measures how much information the encoder stores in the latent vector: 6.3 nats, about 9 bits, per configuration. This is enough for a coarse description of a configuration, such as the sign of its magnetisation and a rough outline of its largest domains; everything finer is left to the independent draws of equation (10).

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
Generation at a chosen temperature
Generation does not use the encoder. For a chosen temperature \(T\) we fix the condition of equation (8), draw a latent vector \(\mathbf z\) from \(\mathcal N(0,I)\), let the decoder compute the 400 probabilities \(y_j\), and draw each spin independently from equation (10): up with probability \(y_j\), down otherwise. Repeating this 200 times at each of the 51 training temperatures gives a generated data set of the same size and shape as the MC one. The figure shows two MC and two generated configurations at each of four temperatures.


Code
gen_rng = torch.Generator().manual_seed(12)
t0 = time.time()
with torch.no_grad():
    z = torch.randn(nT * nS, 8, generator=gen_rng)
    prob = torch.sigmoid(ivae.decode(z, Cs))                           # y_j = P(s_j = +1 | z, T)
    gen = (torch.bernoulli(prob, generator=gen_rng) * 2 - 1).numpy().reshape(nT, nS, L, L)
prob = prob.numpy().reshape(nT, nS, L, L)
print(f"generated {gen.shape} in {time.time() - t0:.2f} s")

generated (51, 200, 20, 20) in 0.11 s





At temperature 1.5 the generated configurations are ordered, as in MC, but carry more scattered single flipped spins. At 2.25, where MC shows large compact domains, the generated configurations are nearly uniform with isolated flipped spins. At 2.5 and 3.0 they resemble salt-and-pepper noise on a weak large-scale pattern, without the compact clusters of MC. An isolated flipped spin breaks four bonds, so many of them raise the energy, and the observables quantify this.

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
Observables
Besides the magnetisation of equation (6), we compute for every configuration the energy per spin, \[
e=\frac{H(\mathbf s)}{N}=-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N s_i\left(s_{i+\hat x}+s_{i+\hat y}\right), \tag{12}
\] where \(i+\hat x\) and \(i+\hat y\) are the right and the lower neighbour of site \(i\) (periodic boundaries), so that every bond is counted once. Averages \(\langle\cdot\rangle_T\) run over the 200 configurations at temperature \(T\). Fluctuations are a sharper test than averages, since a model can place the mean correctly and still produce too narrow or too broad distributions. We therefore also compare the fluctuation of \(|m|\), a finite-lattice analogue of the magnetic susceptibility, \[
\chi'=\frac{N\,\mathrm{Var}_T(|m|)}{T}, \tag{13}
\] and the energy fluctuation, which equals the heat capacity per spin, \[
C'=\frac{N\,\mathrm{Var}_T(e)}{T^2}, \tag{14}
\] where \(\mathrm{Var}_T\) is the variance over the configurations at temperature \(T\). On a finite lattice \(\chi'\) and \(C'\) have a maximum near, but not exactly at, \(T_c\); the temperature of the maximum is a pseudo-critical temperature of the lattice. The fluctuations are plotted on a logarithmic scale.


Code
def energy(s):       # energy per spin, J = 1, periodic boundaries; s: (..., L, L) with values +-1
    return -(s * (np.roll(s, 1, -1) + np.roll(s, 1, -2))).mean((-1, -2))

def observables(s):
    m, e = np.abs(s.mean((-1, -2))), energy(s)                        # (temperatures, configurations)
    return dict(M=m.mean(1), E=e.mean(1), chi=N * m.var(1) / Ts, C=N * e.var(1) / Ts ** 2)
obs_mc, obs_gen = observables(cfg), observables(gen)

names = dict(M=r"$\langle |m| \rangle$", E=r"$\langle e \rangle$", chi=r"$\chi' = N\,\mathrm{Var}(|m|)/T$", C=r"$C' = N\,\mathrm{Var}(e)/T^2$")
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7.5))
for a, k in zip(axs.ravel(), names):
    if k in ("chi", "C"): a.set_yscale("log")                       # fluctuations span several decades
    a.plot(Ts, obs_mc[k], "o-", ms=4, color=blue, label="Monte Carlo")
    a.plot(Ts, obs_gen[k], "s--", ms=4, color=orange, label="generated (cVAE)")
    a.axvline(TC, color="k", ls=":", lw=1); a.set_xlabel("$T$"); a.set_ylabel(names[k]); clean(a)
axs[0, 0].legend(frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

The magnetisation of the generated configurations follows the MC curve in shape and drops around \(T_c\), but it is too low in the ordered phase and too high in the disordered one: the largest deviation is 0.234, at temperature 2.10, and the mean deviation over the 51 temperatures is 0.109. The energy per spin is too high at every temperature, by 0.434 on average and by up to 0.634 at temperature 2.30, close to \(T_c\). These are the numbers quoted on the Lecture 6 slides (0.23 and 0.63 at 2.3), reproduced by the retrained model.
The fluctuations fail most clearly. In the MC data \(\chi'\) and \(C'\) have their maxima at temperatures 2.35 and 2.30, the pseudo-critical temperatures of the \(20\times20\) lattice, with maximal values 10.2 and 1.89. For the generated configurations both quantities grow towards low temperature instead, up to 22.9 at temperature 1.15 and 89.5 at 1.10, where the MC fluctuations are two to three orders of magnitude smaller. The cause is a minority of wrong configurations. At temperatures up to 1.5, 8.5% of the generated configurations have \(|m|\) below 0.5, against none of the MC configurations, while the median of \(|m|\) is 0.99 for both. A variance is dominated by such rare outliers, whereas the average hides them. A plausible origin, not tested here, is the latent space: the two signs of the ordered state occupy two separate regions of \(\mathbf z\), and latent vectors drawn from the Gaussian prior between these regions decode to mixed probability maps.

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
Spin–spin correlation function
The energy of equation (12) measures correlations between nearest neighbours only. The correlation function extends this to larger distances. For a configuration \(\mathbf s\) and a distance \(r\) (in lattice units) we average the product of spins \(r\) sites apart along \(x\) and along \(y\), \[
g_{\mathbf s}(r)=\frac1{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N s_i\left(s_{i+r\hat x}+s_{i+r\hat y}\right), \tag{15}
\] with periodic boundaries, and average over the configurations at temperature \(T\), \[
G(r)=\left\langle g_{\mathbf s}(r)\right\rangle_T . \tag{16}
\] At distance 1, equations (12) and (16) are related by \[
G(1)=-\tfrac12\,\langle e\rangle_T . \tag{17}
\] Equation (16) is the full, not the connected, correlation function. Because of the random global sign the average of a single spin vanishes, and below \(T_c\) the function \(G(r)\) does not decay to zero but levels off near \(\langle m^2\rangle_T\), the squared spontaneous magnetisation of the finite lattice. The part that decays with distance is the connected correlation function \[
G_c(r)=G(r)-\langle m^2\rangle_T . \tag{18}
\] The plots show \(G(r)\) for distances 1 to 10 (half the lattice size) at four temperatures, with dotted lines at \(\langle m^2\rangle_T\).
For the generated configurations equation (10) adds a constraint. Given \(\mathbf z\), spin \(j\) has the mean \[
\bar s_j=2y_j-1, \tag{19}
\] and, because the spins are drawn independently, the expected product of two different spins is \[
\mathbb E\left[s_is_j\,|\,\mathbf z,c\right]=\bar s_i\,\bar s_j . \tag{20}
\] For every distance of at least 1, \(G(r)\) of the generated configurations therefore equals, up to sampling noise, the same function computed from the decoder means \(\bar{\mathbf s}\). All correlations between different spins must come from the shape of the probability map \(\mathbf y(\mathbf z,c)\), that is, through \(\mathbf z\).


Code
def corr(s, r_max=10):
    # G(r) = < (1/2N) sum_i s_i (s_{i + r x} + s_{i + r y}) >, r = 1..r_max; s: (configurations, L, L)
    return np.array([0.5 * (s * np.roll(s, -r, -1) + s * np.roll(s, -r, -2)).mean() for r in range(1, r_max + 1)])

The generated correlation functions are too flat. At short distances they are far too small: at temperature 3.2 the connected correlation of nearest neighbours, equation (18) at distance 1, is 0.352 for MC and 0.080 for the generated configurations, and at 2.6 it is 0.422 against 0.080. At large distances they are too large: at 3.2 and distance 10, \(G\) is 0.003 for MC and 0.035 for the generated configurations, and at 2.6 and 3.2 the generated \(\langle m^2\rangle_T\) (0.178 and 0.059) exceeds the MC value (0.093 and 0.022). The largest difference between the MC and the generated \(G(r)\) over the ten distances is 0.217, 0.279, 0.257 and 0.234 at temperatures 1.8, 2.25, 2.6 and 3.2.
The correlation function computed from the decoder means agrees with that of the generated configurations to within 0.008 at all four temperatures, as equation (19) requires: every correlation between spins passes through \(\mathbf z\). A probability map that varies smoothly over the lattice can place large domains, which produces the long-range part, but the short-range order of the Ising model, which neighbour is aligned with which, differs from configuration to configuration. Encoding it would need a different probability map for each microscopic arrangement, far more than 8 latent numbers carry (about 9 bits, from the KL term). The missing short-range correlation is the same defect that raised the energy.

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
Phase classifier and critical temperature
Lab 011 found the critical temperature with a classifier that never sees the transition region, following Carrasquilla and Melko [3]. A related approach, in which networks are trained with labels split at a trial critical temperature and the true one is recognised by the accuracy of the training, is “learning by confusion” [4]. Configurations from temperatures below \(T_{\min}\) are labelled ordered, those above \(T_{\max}\) disordered, and the rest are not used for training: \[
y=\begin{cases}0\ (\text{ordered}), & T<T_{\min}=1.8,\\ 1\ (\text{disordered}), & T>T_{\max}=2.8 .\end{cases} \tag{21}
\] This selects 16 temperatures for the ordered and 14 for the disordered class, 6000 labelled configurations, of which 20% are kept aside for validation. The network outputs two numbers \(o_0,o_1\), turned into probabilities by the softmax function, \[
p_k(\mathbf s)=\frac{e^{o_k}}{e^{o_0}+e^{o_1}},\qquad k\in\{0,1\}, \tag{22}
\] and is trained with the cross-entropy loss. Its confidence on a configuration is \[
\mathrm{conf}(\mathbf s)=\max\left(p_0(\mathbf s),\,p_1(\mathbf s)\right). \tag{23}
\] After training the classifier is applied at every temperature. Near \(T_c\) the configurations look like neither class, the confidence drops towards \(\frac12\), and the average \(\langle p_1\rangle_T\) passes through \(\frac12\). The estimate \(\bar T_c\) is the temperature of this crossing, \[
\left\langle p_1\right\rangle_{\bar T_c}=\tfrac12 , \tag{24}
\] found by linear interpolation between the two neighbouring temperatures of the grid.
The network is that of Lab 011 and fits the \(20\times20\) lattice without change: two convolutional layers with 32 kernels of size \(3\times3\) and circular padding (the lattice is a torus), each followed by ReLU and \(2\times2\) max-pooling (20 → 10 → 5 sites per side), then a dense layer of 64 ReLU units and 2 outputs; it is trained with Adam for 5 epochs.
Three experiments test the generated configurations from three sides:


the classifier trained on MC configurations and applied to MC configurations at all temperatures, the reference;


the same classifiers applied to the generated configurations, which shows whether a network that learned the phases from MC data sees the transition of the generated data at the same temperature;


a classifier trained on generated configurations (same temperature windows) and applied to MC configurations, which shows whether the generated data can teach a network the transition of the real system.


A single training run is itself a random experiment (Lab 011 found a spread of a few hundredths in \(\bar T_c\)), so each classifier is trained with three seeds.


Code
class IsingCNN(nn.Module):                         # the network of Lab 011
    def __init__(self, L, channels=32, hidden=64, out=2):
        super().__init__()
        self.features = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(1, channels, 3, padding=1, padding_mode="circular"), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2),
            nn.Conv2d(channels, channels, 3, padding=1, padding_mode="circular"), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2))
        side = L // 4                                                  # two 2x2 poolings
        self.head = nn.Sequential(nn.Flatten(), nn.Linear(channels * side * side, hidden), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(hidden, out))
    def forward(self, x):
        return self.head(self.features(x))

T_MIN, T_MAX = 1.8, 2.8
torch.set_num_threads(8)                           # the convolutional networks use all 8 allowed cores
to_t = lambda a: torch.tensor(a, dtype=torch.float32).reshape(-1, 1, L, L)

def labelled_set(configs, rng, val_fraction=0.2):
    low, high = Ts < T_MIN, Ts > T_MAX
    X = np.concatenate([configs[low].reshape(-1, L, L), configs[high].reshape(-1, L, L)])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(low.sum() * nS), np.ones(high.sum() * nS)])
    perm = rng.permutation(len(y)); X, y = X[perm], y[perm]; n_val = int(val_fraction * len(y))
    return to_t(X[n_val:]), torch.tensor(y[n_val:]).long(), to_t(X[:n_val]), torch.tensor(y[:n_val]).long()

def train_classifier(model, X, y, epochs=5, bs=64, lr=1e-3):
    opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model.train(); perm = torch.randperm(len(y))
        for i in range(0, len(y), bs):
            j = perm[i:i + bs]; loss = F.cross_entropy(model(X[j]), y[j])
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return model.eval()

def predict_p1(model, configs):                # softmax probability of "disordered": (temperatures, configurations)
    X = to_t(configs)
    with torch.no_grad():
        p = torch.cat([torch.softmax(model(X[i:i + 2048]), 1)[:, 1] for i in range(0, len(X), 2048)])
    return p.numpy().reshape(configs.shape[:2])

def T_cross(p1):                                # temperature where <p_1>_T crosses 1/2 (linear interpolation)
    pm = p1.mean(1); i = int(np.argmax(pm >= 0.5))
    return float(Ts[i - 1] + (0.5 - pm[i - 1]) * (Ts[i] - Ts[i - 1]) / (pm[i] - pm[i - 1]))

print("labelled temperatures, ordered:   ", Ts[Ts < T_MIN])
print("labelled temperatures, disordered:", Ts[Ts > T_MAX])

On MC data the classifier locates the transition at 2.292 ± 0.012 (mean and standard deviation over three seeds), 0.023 above Onsager’s value. This is not an error of the method but a property of the finite lattice: on an \(L\times L\) lattice the transition is smeared out, and a pseudo-critical temperature \(T_c(L)\), defined by any feature of the transition region, approaches \(T_c\) as \[
T_c(L)-T_c\propto L^{-1/\nu}, \tag{25}
\] with the correlation-length exponent \(\nu\), which equals 1 for the 2D Ising model, and a prefactor that depends on the chosen feature. For \(L\) equal to 20 shifts of a few hundredths are therefore expected; the maxima of \(\chi'\) and \(C'\) of the same MC data lie at 2.35 and 2.30.

The classifier trained on MC data places the transition of the generated configurations at 2.056 ± 0.012, about 0.24 lower than for MC data. Generated configurations look disordered too early, consistent with their excess of isolated flipped spins and too-high energy, and even deep in the ordered phase the average probability of “disordered” stays between about 0.1 and 0.2 instead of 0, partly because of the minority of generated configurations with small \(|m|\).
The classifier trained on generated configurations reaches 95% validation accuracy on its own data, and on the labelled MC configurations it calls 90 of the 572 disordered ones ordered (confusion matrix). Applied to MC data at all temperatures, it places the transition at 2.501 ± 0.057, 0.21 above the MC reference, with three times the seed-to-seed spread, and even at temperature 3.5 the average probability of “disordered” for MC configurations stays below 0.9. Having learned “disordered” from the speckled generated configurations, the network finds the MC configurations, with their compact clusters, too ordered. Both transfer experiments shift the transition by about 0.2 in opposite directions, roughly ten times the finite-size shift of the reference estimate.

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
Temperature regression
The phase classifier only distinguishes two phases. A stricter test asks for the temperature itself. A CNN with the same architecture but a single output \(\hat c\) is trained to predict the condition of equation (8) from a configuration, with the mean squared error as loss, and the prediction is converted back to a temperature, \[
\hat T=2.25+0.75\,\hat c . \tag{26}
\] To have unseen test data, the 200 configurations at each temperature are split at random into 150 for training and 50 for testing, for the MC and the generated data alike. Applied to generated configurations at requested temperature \(T\), the regressor trained on MC data tells at which temperature these configurations look as if they had been sampled. A second regressor, trained on generated data, completes a \(2\times2\) table of the mean absolute error over a test set, \[
\mathrm{MAE}=\left\langle\,\left|\hat T-T\right|\,\right\rangle . \tag{27}
\] The cVAE was trained on all 200 MC configurations per temperature, so the MC test configurations are new for the regressors but not for the generator.


Code
split_rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
perm = np.array([split_rng.permutation(nS) for _ in range(nT)])                  # random split, per temperature
tr_idx, te_idx = perm[:, :150], perm[:, 150:]
take = lambda data, idx: np.take_along_axis(data, idx[:, :, None, None], 1)   # (temperatures, k, L, L)
sets = {"mc": (take(cfg, tr_idx), take(cfg, te_idx)), "gen": (take(gen, tr_idx), take(gen, te_idx))}

def train_regressor(data, epochs=12, bs=64, lr=1e-3, sd=0):
    torch.manual_seed(sd)
    X = to_t(data); y = torch.tensor(np.repeat(Tn(Ts), data.shape[1]))[:, None]
    model = IsingCNN(L, out=1); opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        model.train(); p = torch.randperm(len(y))
        for i in range(0, len(y), bs):
            j = p[i:i + bs]; loss = F.mse_loss(model(X[j]), y[j])
            opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
    return model.eval()

def predict_T(model, data):
    with torch.no_grad(): c = model(to_t(data)).numpy().reshape(data.shape[:2])
    return 2.25 + 0.75 * c

title: Ising configurations from a conditional VAE
text:
Conclusion
The conditional VAE learns the coarse temperature dependence of the Ising model: the magnetisation drops around \(T_c\), the energy rises with temperature, and the generated configurations change from ordered to disordered as the condition is varied. Every finer test exposes the same defect. The energy per spin is too high at every temperature (by up to 0.634), the fluctuations in the ordered phase are wrong by orders of magnitude because 8.5% of the generated low-temperature configurations have small magnetisation, and the correlation function is too small at short distances and too large at long ones. Networks confirm this from the outside: a classifier trained on MC data places the transition of the generated data at 2.056 instead of 2.292, a classifier trained on generated data places that of MC data at 2.501, and a regressor reads the generated configurations as hotter than requested by up to 0.78. The cause lies in the model itself: given \(\mathbf z\) the decoder draws spins independently, so all correlations must pass through a latent vector of 8 numbers, and the short-range order of the Ising model does not fit through it. Generative models that keep the dependence between spins, such as autoregressive models, which draw one spin at a time conditioned on the previous ones, or diffusion models, address exactly this defect.
